title: Acute AP-1 degradation after a priming pulse
description: Apply a transient stimulus, then rapidly degrade FOS or JUN with an inducible degron (e.g., dTAG or auxin-inducible) at defined times after washout. Track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), enhancer marks (H3K27ac), and expression of putative memory genes over days. Persistence after AP-1 loss would support a self-sustaining memory, while rapid decay would indicate AP-1 is only a transient readout.

title: Chromatin persistence time course at AP-1 sites with motif-mutant controls
description: After a single pulse with washout, profile AP-1 CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq/H3K4me1/H3K27ac at multiple timepoints out to weeks. Compare enhancers with intact AP-1 motifs against CRISPR-edited motif-mutant versions of the same elements to test whether AP-1 binding is required for the persistent chromatin state.

title: Priming and re-induction assay for transcriptional memory
description: Prime cells with a sub-threshold stimulus, wait variable intervals, then re-stimulate and measure the speed and magnitude of FOS/JUN induction and downstream target expression relative to naive cells. Repeat in cells carrying AP-1 binding-site mutations or lacking a chromatin-remodeling cofactor to test whether faster or stronger re-induction depends on AP-1 itself.

title: Live reporter lineage tracing of AP-1 activity across divisions
description: Use a destabilized-fluorescent AP-1 target reporter combined with a stable lineage barcode or histone label to follow individual cells through several divisions after stimulation. Sort subpopulations by heritable reporter state and compare their chromatin landscapes and responses to a second stimulus, testing whether AP-1 activity states are inherited through cell division.

title: Stabilized AP-1 variant sufficiency and ensemble reactivation test
description: Express a degradation-resistant or long-lived AP-1 isoform (e.g., a ΔFosB-like stabilized FOS) and test whether it extends the duration of induced chromatin and behavioral or functional changes beyond wild-type lifetimes. Pair this with activity-dependent ensemble tagging and optogenetic or chemogenetic reactivation to determine whether reactivating the tagged, AP-1-positive population is necessary and sufficient to recall the stored state.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after a stimulus pulse
description: Use a degron-tagged FOS or JUN allele (e.g., dTAG or auxin-inducible) to degrade AP-1 at defined times after a single stimulus. If AP-1 is the memory mechanism, the later response to restimulation should be lost or reduced when AP-1 is removed during the rest period, but not when it is removed before the first stimulus.

title: Time course of chromatin persistence after AP-1 occupancy is lost
description: After a stimulus pulse, run ATAC-seq, H3K27ac/H3K4me1 CUT&RUN, and FOS/JUN CUT&RUN at several time points during washout. A memory mechanism predicts that enhancers keep open or primed chromatin after AP-1 leaves them, and that this persistence depends on the AP-1 motifs and on the stimulus having occurred.

title: Motif-mutation test of recall at endogenous memory loci
description: Use CRISPR base editing or prime editing to mutate AP-1 motifs at enhancers of genes that show a primed, faster response on restimulation. Compare the stimulus-recall response (fold induction and kinetics) of mutant and wild-type cells in a rested-then-restimulated paradigm to test whether the motifs are required for memory.

title: Single-cell tracking of AP-1 history through divisions
description: Combine a live AP-1 activity reporter (e.g., a destabilized fluorescent protein under an AP-1-responsive or Fos promoter) with lineage barcodes and single-cell multiome readout. Compare cells with different prior AP-1 histories to test whether the prior state is inherited by daughter cells and predicts their later response, which separates heritable memory from stochastic cell-to-cell variation.

title: In vivo necessity test with activity-tagged cells
description: In a mouse model such as hippocampal engrams or tissue-resident immune memory, label cells active during a learning or priming event with an activity-dependent tag (e.g., a Fos-based TRAP system). Then apply time-restricted dominant-negative or conditional Fos/Jun inhibition during consolidation or recall. Measure whether memory-dependent reactivation and the chromatin state of the tagged cells are disrupted.

title: Post-stimulus washout time course of AP-1 occupancy, chromatin and transcription
description: After a defined AP-1-inducing stimulus, track c-Jun/c-Fos/ATF3 occupancy (CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and transcription (RNA-seq) at many time points after withdrawal. Memory is supported if AP-1 binding and enhancer opening persist after transcripts return to baseline, and the persistence window is quantified per locus.

title: Inducible AP-1 degradation in distinct phases of the memory window
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron or dTAG system on Fos or Jun to deplete AP-1 at different times: during priming, during the quiescent interval, and at re-stimulation. If memory is AP-1-dependent, depletion during the maintenance phase should abolish the enhanced or faster re-induction of memory genes, while depletion only during priming should have a different effect.

title: Motif and enhancer perturbation with sufficiency tests
description: Use base editing or CRISPR deletion to mutate AP-1 motifs within enhancers that carry the memory signature, and measure whether priming-dependent faster or stronger re-induction is lost while the first response is preserved. Complement this with dCas9-tethered c-Jun, Fos, or p300 at silent sites to test whether AP-1 recruitment alone is sufficient to install a memory-like state.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1 memory heritability
description: Combine a live AP-1 transcriptional reporter with lineage barcoding, then pulse stimulate and follow cells over several divisions without further stimulus. Measure whether daughter cells inherit the primed state and its re-inducibility, and whether the memory is a stable cell-intrinsic state or a population-level drift that dissipates.

title: In vivo tagging and recall challenge of stimulus-experienced cells
description: Label cells that experienced an AP-1-inducing stimulus in vivo using a Fos-based activity tag such as Fos-CreER or TRAP, then challenge the animal or transplant the tagged cells and measure the recall response. Test necessity by ablating or AP-1-depleting the tagged population and checking whether the enhanced recall response disappears.

title: Lineage-resolved, time-stamped AP-1 reporter tracing
description: Build an inducible lineage-tracing system (e.g., a Cre- or Dre-recombinase reporter driven by AP-1-responsive enhancers) that permanently marks cells that experienced a transient AP-1 pulse. Then wash out the stimulus and track whether marked cells retain altered chromatin or transcription after days to weeks; persistence without ongoing AP-1 activity would be direct evidence of memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation or inhibition at defined times
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron (or a dominant-negative c-Jun/Fos or a photo-controllable AP-1 inhibitor) to remove AP-1 during the stimulus, after the stimulus, and during re-stimulation. If AP-1 is a memory mechanism, the altered chromatin state or primed gene response should persist when AP-1 is removed after induction, but be lost when AP-1 is removed during the initial pulse or the reactivation step.

title: Chromatin persistence profiling across a stimulus-washout time course
description: Profile AP-1 occupancy (c-Fos/c-Jun CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and histone marks (H3K27ac) at multiple timepoints after a transient stimulus and after a second stimulus. Test whether enhancers bound by AP-1 during the pulse remain open or marked after AP-1 leaves the chromatin, which would distinguish epigenetic memory from ongoing transcription.

title: Re-stimulation kinetics and priming assays
description: Compare the transcriptional and AP-1 binding response to a second identical stimulus in naive versus previously stimulated cells, measuring the speed, amplitude, and gene set of the response (e.g., by time-resolved RNA-seq or live single-cell reporters). Faster or stronger re-induction of the same target genes in primed cells, and dependence of that priming on the original AP-1 pulse, would support a memory function rather than a simple dose response.

title: Mechanistic dissection of memory determinants with targeted perturbations
description: Combine targeted epigenome editing (dCas9-based writers/erasers such as p300 or LSD1 fused to AP-1-bound loci) with mutations in the AP-1 binding motifs and in putative self-reinforcing partners (e.g., BAF complex, bromodomain proteins) to test which features are necessary and sufficient for persistence. If a chromatin mark at a single AP-1-bound enhancer can by itself reproduce or abolish the memory effect, this would establish a causal mechanism rather than correlation.

title: Washout and re-challenge assay with AP-1 mutants
description: Pulse cells with a stimulus, withdraw it, and track AP-1 target gene expression over time. Memory would appear as persistent expression after withdrawal and faster or stronger re-induction on re-challenge, which should be lost in AP-1 mutants lacking DNA binding or dimerization.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the rest phase
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron on FOS or JUN to remove AP-1 after priming but before re-challenge. If AP-1 is the memory substrate, degradation should erase the primed state, while degradation before priming should prevent it from forming.

title: Chromatin persistence time course after stimulus withdrawal
description: Profile AP-1 occupancy and enhancer accessibility and acetylation (ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN, H3K27ac) at primed and naive sites across a stimulus-withdrawal time course. This tests whether chromatin opening outlasts AP-1 binding and whether it is maintained by AP-1 itself or by a separate epigenetic mechanism.

title: Live single-cell reporter with lineage tracking
description: Express a fluorescent AP-1 target reporter, prime cells, and follow individual lineages through several divisions by time-lapse imaging. Quantify how long the primed state persists and whether daughter cells inherit it, and test whether perturbing mitotic bookmarking or chromatin remodeling shortens that inheritance.

title: Feedback-loop perturbation and bistability testing
description: Disrupt candidate positive feedback loops (FOS autoregulation, ATF3 or JUN loops) and inhibit co-activators (p300/CBP or BRD4) in single-cell reporter lines. Memory should scale with loop strength and show bimodal, cell-autonomous persistence rather than population-average decay, and this should be validated in vivo with a repeated-stimulus model.

title: Stimulus washout with chromatin profiling and re-stimulation time course
description: After a defined AP-1-inducing stimulus, wash it out and track FOS/JUN occupancy (CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and enhancer marks (H3K27ac) over days. Then re-stimulate and compare the speed and magnitude of target gene induction against naive cells; faster or stronger re-induction without new AP-1 binding would indicate memory.

title: Inducible AP-1 degradation during and after a priming window
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-degradable FOS or JUN allele to remove AP-1 at different times relative to a priming stimulus. Measure whether the memory-like transcriptional and chromatin state persists after AP-1 is gone, to separate a requirement for AP-1 in establishing memory from a requirement in maintaining it.

title: Synthetic tethered AP-1 at a reporter locus
description: Tether engineered AP-1 components (or a dimerized bZIP fusion) to a single-copy reporter with a dox-controlled recruiter, then turn the recruiter off and measure reporter expression, chromatin state, and H3K27ac/H3K4me1 over weeks. Persistence without the tether would show that AP-1 is sufficient to establish a self-maintaining state, while mutating its DNA-binding domain would test necessity.

title: Live single-cell AP-1 reporter tracking across repeated pulses
description: Track AP-1 activity in individual cells with a live fluorescent reporter during repeated stimulus pulses of varying spacing and strength. Test whether prior pulse history predicts later response magnitude or timing (e.g., with mutual information or Markov models), and whether this history-dependence is lost when cells are imaged in heterogeneous or lineage-tracked populations.

title: AP-1 protein turnover versus persistence of memory
description: Use SNAP- or HaloTag-labelled FOS/JUN with pulse-chase labelling to measure AP-1 protein and DNA-bound half-lives in the same cells where memory persists. Also mutate AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers (base editing) and measure 3D contacts by Micro-C or Hi-C. If memory lasts well beyond AP-1 turnover, this would point toward an epigenetic or 3D-architecture-based mechanism rather than a self-sustaining AP-1 feedback loop.

title: Stimulus washout with persistence tracking
description: Induce AP-1 activity with a controlled stimulus or an inducible Fos/Jun system, then withdraw it and track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac, and target-gene expression over days. Memory is supported if these marks and transcripts stay elevated after AP-1 activity returns to baseline; decay kinetics can be compared with control sites.

title: Rechallenge test of primed responses
description: Compare first and second exposures to the same stimulus after a rest period, measuring the speed, amplitude, and AP-1 target-gene induction in each. Repeat in Fos or Jun knockout and dominant-negative cells to test whether AP-1 is required for the faster, stronger secondary response.

title: Mutation of AP-1 motifs at persistently open enhancers
description: Identify enhancers that stay open after washout, then disrupt their AP-1 motifs with CRISPR base editing or saturation mutagenesis. Check whether persistent accessibility and faster re-induction are lost, and use dCas9-based epigenetic editing to test whether AP-1 binding alone is sufficient to restore the memory signal.

title: AP-1 occupancy versus histone mark retention over time
description: Run CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for c-Fos and c-Jun together with histone marks across a stimulation and washout time course. This shows whether memory is carried by histone marks retained after AP-1 has left the chromatin (bookmarking), or whether AP-1 must rebind at each re-exposure.

title: Single-cell live reporting of activation history across divisions
description: Use a destabilized fluorescent reporter driven by the Fos promoter, with live imaging and lineage tracking, to record each cell's prior activation history. Test whether past AP-1 activity predicts future response in the same cell and whether that history is inherited by daughter cells, to distinguish cell-intrinsic memory from population-level effects.

title: Inducible, time-resolved AP-1 perturbation with chromatin readout
description: Use an acute, reversible degron (e.g., dTAG or AID) or optogenetic control to deplete or activate FOS/JUN for defined windows. Then track whether chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac, and AP-1 motif occupancy at enhancers persist after the stimulus is withdrawn. Persistence without AP-1 present would be direct evidence of memory, while rapid collapse would argue against it.

title: Stimulus re-exposure (recall) assay
description: Apply a priming stimulus (e.g., a short TNF or growth-factor pulse), allow a rest period, then re-stimulate and compare the magnitude and kinetics of AP-1 target gene induction (RNA-seq, nascent transcription via PRO-seq) with naive cells. Faster or stronger responses on re-challenge, lost when AP-1 binding sites are mutated or AP-1 is degraded during the rest period, would demonstrate functional memory.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1 activity history
description: Combine a live AP-1 reporter (e.g., FOS-promoter-driven fluorescent timer or destabilized reporter) with barcoded lineage tracing or CRISPR-based recorders to link each cell's past AP-1 activity to its later transcriptional state after a delay. Correlating prior pulse history with future responses across single-cell clones tests whether history is stored and inherited rather than just reflecting current state.

title: Site-specific mutagenesis of AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing or prime editing to mutate individual TRE/AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers. In the same cells, measure the effect on persistence of chromatin opening and on re-induction kinetics after washout. Mutations that abolish memory while leaving the initial response intact would separate a storage function from the acute transcriptional function.

title: Self-propagation of AP-1 chromatin states versus dilution through cell division
description: Track histone marks and AP-1/co-factor occupancy through cell division using pulse-chase labeling (e.g., SNAP-tag or histone turnover reporters) and CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq, with and without DNA replication. Re-establishment of AP-1 binding and associated marks through sister chromatids or inheritance of modified histones would support a self-propagating mechanism, whereas dilution after division would indicate that memory requires continuous AP-1 presence.

title: Transient AP-1 pulse and withdrawal with inducible system
description: Use an optogenetic or degron-based system to pulse AP-1 (e.g., Fos/Jun) activity briefly, then withdraw it and track ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for AP-1 and H3K27ac, and target-gene transcription over days. Memory is supported only if the chromatin and transcriptional state persist without ongoing AP-1 input, and the persistence should disappear when AP-1 binding sites are mutated.

title: Faster re-induction after rest compared with naive cells
description: Stimulate cells with a first exposure, rest them, then re-stimulate and compare the speed, amplitude, and magnitude of AP-1 target induction (time-resolved RNA-seq or live Fos/Jun reporters) against naive cells. An enhanced re-induction that is lost in cells lacking AP-1 or with binding-site mutations would support a memory role specifically for AP-1.

title: Stable genetic or fluorescent recorder of past AP-1 activity
description: Use a stable recorder, such as inducible CreER or a slow-maturing fluorescent timer under an AP-1-responsive promoter, to permanently mark cells that had AP-1 activity at a defined time. Then measure by flow cytometry or imaging whether marked cells respond differently to a later stimulus and whether the mark is retained across divisions and after AP-1 withdrawal.

title: Serial-passage test of AP-1-induced state propagation
description: Stimulate a culture, then passage cells through many divisions without stimulus, sampling at intervals for chromatin accessibility and transcription at AP-1 targets. Persistence across passages, compared with lineage-matched controls and AP-1 knockouts, would indicate heritable memory rather than a transient response.

title: Mitotic bookmarking dissection with degron-based AP-1 removal
description: Synchronize cells, remove AP-1 specifically in mitosis or G1 using a degron, and measure whether AP-1-bound enhancers keep accessibility and H3K27ac through mitosis and into daughter cells. Comparing retention with versus without AP-1 binding, and with dCas9 site-specific mutants, would separate active memory maintenance from passive chromatin persistence.

title: Hysteresis test of path dependence
description: Sweep stimulus strength up and then back down, measuring phospho-Jun/Fos levels and AP-1 target accessibility (ATAC or CUT&RUN) at each step. Memory is supported if the descending branch stays elevated relative to the ascending one, the loop area scales with prior exposure, and the loop is abolished by an AP-1 dominant-negative.

title: Priming, variable rest periods, and timed AP-1 removal
description: Prime cells, then rest them for different durations before re-stimulation. Use a degron-tagged or inducible Fos/Jun to remove AP-1 either during the rest period or only at recall. If memory is AP-1-dependent, faster reactivation should require AP-1 to persist through rest, and its loss during rest should erase the advantage.

title: Pulse-chase labelling of endogenous FOS/JUN to age-date bound sites
description: Tag endogenous Fos or Jun with a HaloTag or SNAP tag, label it with a dye during a priming pulse, and chase for increasing times. Measuring which AP-1-occupied enhancers still carry the old label reveals whether a long-lived, distinct subset of sites constitutes the memory, versus transient occupancy that turns over.

title: Retroactive interference test with a competing stimulus
description: Prime cells with an AP-1-driving stimulus, then expose them to an unrelated or competing stimulus set before testing the primed response. An AP-1-based memory should show decay that depends on interference strength, and its retention should be predicted by the magnitude of AP-1 target occupancy measured right after priming.

title: Heritable recorder of AP-1 activity across divisions
description: Build an AP-1-responsive recorder (e.g., a Cre or CRISPR-scar reporter, or a timer fluorophore) to log past activity, then sort daughter cells after several divisions and challenge them. Memory is cell-intrinsic and inherited if the recorded history predicts the progeny's recall response independent of population-level selection, which can be checked with clonal barcoding.

title: Hysteresis of AP-1 occupancy across stimulus dose
description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., phorbol ester or growth factor dose) up and then back down, and measure AP-1 genomic occupancy (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN) and target-gene output at matched doses on each branch. A memory mechanism predicts a hysteresis loop, where ascending and descending curves diverge at the same stimulus level, while a purely reactive system retraces the same path.

title: Secondary-response test with degron-mediated AP-1 depletion during the rest interval
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, let them rest, then restimulate, comparing primary and secondary AP-1 target-gene induction kinetics and chromatin opening. Apply a dTAG or auxin degron to JUN or FOS only during the rest interval. If memory depends on persistent AP-1, the secondary response should revert to the primary response, which separates the role of persistent AP-1 from its acute activity.

title: Pulse-chase half-life of AP-1 binding
description: Pulse-label endogenous JUN/FOS with a HaloTag or SNAP-tag and track the fraction of tagged protein and of chromatin-bound AP-1 after the stimulus is withdrawn, fitting decay curves at individual enhancers. Compare the half-life of bound complexes with the half-life of the transcript and protein to determine whether AP-1 occupancy outlasts its trigger for long enough to count as memory.

title: Synthetic bistable circuit with AP-1 positive feedback
description: Build a synthetic circuit in which an inducible FOS/JUN cassette drives its own expression through AP-1 sites and drives a fluorescent reporter, then test whether a brief inducer pulse produces a persistent ON state after the inducer is removed. Vary the positive feedback strength and the number of AP-1 sites to map the conditions required for bistability, which is a necessary property of a memory element.

title: Recording past AP-1 activity with a CRISPR-based lineage recorder
description: Use an AP-1-responsive promoter to drive a CRISPR-based or base-editing recorder that writes irreversible barcode mutations into a target locus whenever AP-1 is active. Then track recorded cells by single-cell lineage and transcriptomics, comparing responses to a later, unrelated stimulus between cells with a prior AP-1 record and unrecorded sister cells, to test whether past AP-1 activity causally shapes future behavior.

title: History dependence of response to repeated AP-1 stimulation
description: Apply pulsed AP-1 stimuli (e.g., TPA or growth factor) with varied pulse number, spacing, and amplitude, then apply a second identical stimulus. Quantify hysteresis in target gene expression and chromatin accessibility at AP-1 enhancers. Memory is supported if the response to the second pulse depends on the first pulse's history beyond what the current AP-1 level predicts.

title: Acute AP-1 depletion after stimulus with tracking of enhancer priming and sub-threshold reactivation
description: Use an acute, degron-based FOS or JUN depletion to end AP-1 signaling after a stimulus, then track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN), enhancer accessibility (ATAC-seq), and target transcription over days. Memory predicts that enhancers stay primed after AP-1 protein is gone and that a later sub-threshold stimulus reactivates them faster than in naive cells.

title: Synthetic AP-1 positive-feedback circuit
description: Build an engineered AP-1 positive-feedback loop, with an AP-1-responsive promoter driving a FOS or JUN transgene, and test bistability using transient inducer pulses and a flow-cytometry readout. Breaking the loop (mutating the AP-1 sites in the feedback element or using a non-feedback control) should abolish the stored state, which would show that the self-reinforcing loop, not the pulse itself, is the memory element.

title: Lineage-barcoded tracking of inheritance of AP-1-primed states
description: Combine lineage barcoding with a live AP-1 activity reporter, sort cells by prior exposure history, and use single-cell multiome to track whether AP-1-primed chromatin states are inherited through mitosis and show faster re-induction in daughter clones. Memory requires that the primed state is heritable across divisions, not just re-established by each new stimulus.

title: Sequential pulse-chase labeling of AP-1 components at enhancers
description: Use sequential pulse-chase labeling of AP-1 components with orthogonal tags (e.g., HaloTag or SNAP-tag pulses at successive time points) and map which enhancers retain each labeled AP-1 cohort using CUT&Tag and ATAC-seq. Retention at enhancers after the tag signal has cleared, not explained by dilution through cell division, would indicate durable, time-stamped AP-1 memory at specific loci.

title: Dose-dependent persistence after degron-controlled AP-1 removal
description: Apply graded AP-1 stimulation doses, then rapidly deplete c-Fos or JunB with an auxin-inducible degron and track enhancer accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac, and target-gene transcription over days. Memory is supported if the chromatin and expression state persists after AP-1 is gone and the persistence scales with prior dose, unlike a transient response that returns to baseline.

title: Repeated stimulation cycles at varying intervals
description: Expose cells to repeated AP-1-inducing pulses at varying inter-pulse intervals and compare second-round kinetics with naive cells. Live single-cell AP-1 reporters (e.g., FosB-driven or ATF3 reporters) would show whether priming produces faster, stronger, or more sustained re-activation, and whether the effect depends on interval length.

title: Time-stamping AP-1 binding events across successive stimulations
description: Pair a time-resolved tag (e.g., a tamoxifen-inducible or photoconvertible reporter, or pulse-labeled histone marks) with AP-1 ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN at successive time points to identify which enhancers were occupied during each stimulation. Sites that retain an early-stimulation tag after AP-1 has left would constitute a durable molecular record of past activity.

title: Irreversible labeling of stimulated cells and re-stimulation
description: Irreversibly label cells that experienced an AP-1 pulse (e.g., with a Cre/Tamoxifen-based or CaMPARI-type photoconversion marker), then later re-stimulate and measure what fraction of the marked population responds more strongly than unlabeled cells. Quantifying retention and re-response of the marked population over time estimates how long and how reliably the memory persists per cell.

title: Rescue of AP-1 after loss to test self-sustaining memory
description: Delete AP-1 at varying times after induction, then re-express it at defined windows, or use dCas9-based recruitment of Fos/Jun to a single memory-associated locus. If the memory state is self-sustaining, re-expression will not be required to maintain it, and locus-specific reinstatement will test whether the memory is autonomous at that enhancer.

title: Path dependence from pulse dose and duration sweeps
description: Vary the dose and duration of an inducible FOS/JUN pulse, then wash out and measure chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target transcription at multiple later times. Memory is supported if the post-washout state depends on the path taken (a loop rather than a single dose-response curve) and persists past the point where AP-1 binding has returned to baseline.

title: Primary versus secondary response with AP-1 depletion during rest
description: Compare primary and secondary responses to identical AP-1 stimuli, measuring the speed, amplitude, and target-gene breadth of the second response in cells with and without a rest interval. Memory requires the secondary response to be faster or stronger, and this advantage should disappear when AP-1 is depleted with a degron (e.g., dTAG-FOS) during the rest period.

title: Dependence of the primed state on continued AP-1 presence
description: Degrade AP-1 (dTAG or auxin system) during the quiescent interval and check whether the primed state is retained. If the state persists without AP-1, the memory is stored in a self-sustaining chromatin or feedback state; if it is lost, the memory depends on continuous AP-1 activity.

title: Lineage-tracked heritability of a pulse-labeled AP-1 reporter state
description: Use a barcoded, live AP-1 reporter to pulse-label a cell population, then follow single-cell lineages through several divisions without stimulus, sorting cells at each generation for re-challenge. Heritable memory is shown if the primed fraction persists across divisions and the re-challenge response is enriched in descendants.

title: Pulse-chase timestamping of AP-1 binding events
description: Use HaloTag or SNAP-tag pulse-chase on endogenous FOS/JUN to label when each AP-1 binding event occurred, then perform ChIP-seq at several chase times to record occupancy by binding age. Marks that persist at sites after the tagged protein is gone would indicate epigenetic memory, while sites that clear along with the protein would indicate transient binding.

title: Hysteresis test with graded AP-1 levels
description: Ramp FOS/JUN levels up and down using an inducible degron (AID or dTAG) or a titratable Dox system, and measure chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target transcription at each level. A memory mechanism should show different on and off thresholds, with loop area reflecting stored state, while AP-1 motif-mutant enhancers should show no loop.

title: Time-stamped AP-1 activity recording with sequential lineage tags
description: Use sequential, orthogonally inducible lineage tags such as Fos-CreERT2 pulses at different times to mark cells by when AP-1 was active. After stimulus withdrawal, test whether cells marked earlier keep elevated target expression or open chromatin, and whether that persistence scales with the duration and recency of AP-1 activity.

title: Re-challenge after rest, with AP-1 site disruption
description: Prime cells with a brief AP-1 stimulus, rest them for several days, then re-challenge and compare the speed and magnitude of target induction with naive cells. Repeat in cells with mutated AP-1 sites in the primed enhancers or lacking AP-1 binding; a memory mechanism should specifically lose the faster secondary response when its binding sites are disrupted.

title: History-dependence in pulse-train system identification
description: Deliver randomized optogenetic AP-1 pulse trains with varying inter-pulse intervals and fit models of target output with and without a persistent state variable. If a memory term is needed, the response to later pulses should depend on earlier pulse timing with a decay constant that matches chromatin persistence rather than mRNA or protein half-life.

title: Time-resolved AP-1 occupancy versus histone marks with timed degradation
description: After a stimulus, use SNAP/Halo-tagged FOS pulse-chase and sequential ChIP-seq at multiple time points to build a time-resolved record of AP-1 occupancy alongside histone marks such as H3K27ac and H3K4me1 at each enhancer. If memory exists, enhancers that keep their marks after AP-1 dissociates should be the ones that stay accessible, and acutely degrading AP-1 at a chosen time point should then test whether the marks are necessary to hold that state.

title: Hysteresis test with graded stimulus pulses
description: Apply TPA or EGF pulses of varying dose and duration, then withdraw the stimulus. Measure AP-1 target accessibility and transcription at multiple times after withdrawal, and test whether the response shows a threshold and a state that persists after the input is removed (hysteresis) rather than simply tracking the input.

title: Pulse-chase occupancy of labelled AP-1
description: Tag endogenous Fos or Jun with a photoconvertible or HaloTag system and label AP-1 proteins at a defined time. Follow the labelled cohort of bound sites with CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq, and compare how long AP-1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility persist relative to mRNA and protein half-lives.

title: Inducible AP-1 degradation to test memory without the factor
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron to remove Fos and Jun after a stimulus window, then measure the enhancers they opened. Quantify whether accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac, and the induced transcriptional state persist without AP-1 for days. Persistence would indicate that AP-1 acts as a memory mechanism rather than a continuous driver.

title: Synthetic AP-1 positive-feedback circuit with write, read, and erase steps
description: Build a synthetic reporter in which AP-1 binding sites drive an AP-1 or Fos expression cassette, forming a positive-feedback loop. Set the state with a transient input, read it out with a reporter, and erase it by CRISPRi or dCas9 silencing of the loop. A stable, switchable state that follows the set and erase steps would support AP-1 feedback as a memory mechanism.

title: Lineage-barcoded single-cell multiome tracking of heritable AP-1 memory
description: After a transient AP-1-inducing stimulus, combine lentiviral lineage barcodes with single-cell multiome (RNA plus ATAC). Measure whether the primed chromatin state and faster or stronger AP-1 target re-induction are inherited by daughter clones across several divisions, and whether memory is heterogeneous across lineages.

title: Hold-and-wait re-stimulation test
description: Apply a sustained AP-1 stimulus (e.g., inducible c-Fos/c-Jun or a defined growth factor pulse), hold it at an intermediate level for varying wait times, then withdraw and re-apply the stimulus while measuring the AP-1 target response (luciferase reporter, qPCR of targets). If AP-1 stores a memory, the re-stimulated response should show a wait-time-dependent signature that reappears when the hold is repeated.

title: Continuous versus interrupted exposure with no-stimulus controls to separate memory from aging
description: Run matched-duration protocols in which the same total AP-1 exposure is delivered either continuously or interrupted by rests, and include control conditions with equal elapsed time but no stimulus. Any history-dependent difference that persists beyond what time alone (aging) produces is the candidate memory signal.

title: Long-timescale persistence of AP-1 occupancy, accessibility and enhancer marks
description: After removing the AP-1 stimulus, measure the retained state at many later times (hours to weeks) using AP-1 occupancy (ChIP-qPCR or CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and enhancer marks at AP-1 target loci, and fit the decay of the residual signal. Persistence well beyond transcript and protein half-lives would indicate a stored state rather than simple carryover.

title: Frequency-dependent probing of the AP-1 response
description: Drive AP-1 with small periodic pulses across a range of frequencies in naive versus previously stimulated cells, and measure the amplitude and phase lag of a live-cell reporter (e.g., a FRET or luciferase AP-1 sensor). A history-dependent change in the slow relaxation component, absent in naive cells, would indicate an internal memory state that the fast pulses cannot erase.

title: Genetic dissection with AP-1 component perturbation
description: Repeat the stop-and-wait and thermoremanent-style protocols in cells with inducible dominant-negative c-Jun (TAM67), c-Fos or JunB knockdown, and in cells lacking specific AP-1 partners, rescuing with wild-type constructs. If the memory signature disappears specifically when AP-1 function is lost and returns on rescue, AP-1 is necessary for the memory rather than just correlated with it.

title: Repeated stimulation, rest, and re-exposure with response-threshold readout
description: Apply repeated AP-1-inducing pulses (e.g., TPA or EGF) with defined rest periods, then measure the dose-response or activation threshold of an AP-1 reporter on re-exposure. A lasting threshold shift or faster re-induction after rest, compared with naive cells, would indicate a stored state rather than residual signal.

title: Continuous tracking of AP-1 output after stimulus withdrawal
description: Track AP-1 reporter activity and target mRNA/protein continuously through stimulus withdrawal. Fit the decay of the output and check whether a fraction persists beyond the expected half-lives of the Fos/Jun transcripts and proteins, which would point to a self-sustaining state.

title: Mapping AP-1 dimer occupancy and chromatin accessibility at memory timepoints
description: Map which AP-1 dimer compositions (Fos, Fra1, Jun, JunB, ATF) occupy which enhancers, using ChIP or CUT&RUN, and measure chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq, H3K27ac) at multiple times after stimulation. Persistence of a specific occupancy and accessibility pattern at stimulated loci after AP-1 protein levels return to baseline would identify the stored state.

title: Degron-mediated AP-1 clearance after training
description: Use degron-tagged or auxin-inducible Fos/Jun to clear AP-1 protein after training while leaving the epigenetic and transcript landscape intact. If the trained response is retained without AP-1 protein, the memory lies in a downstream state; if it is lost, AP-1 itself is required to hold it.

title: Separating AP-1-dependent memory from stress damage using dominant-negative and damage-matched controls
description: Train cells with a stimulus that causes damage without engaging AP-1, or block AP-1 during training with TAM-67 or a dominant-negative Jun, then test retention. Memory that requires AP-1 engagement during training and is absent when AP-1 is blocked, while damage-matched controls show no retention, would support a specific AP-1-encoded state over nonspecific cellular injury.

title: Up-and-down stimulus ramps to test hysteresis
description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., growth factor or TPA dose) up and then back down over the same range, and measure AP-1 target output (reporter, RT-qPCR, or CUT&RUN occupancy at canonical sites) on both branches. Different ascending and descending curves at matched stimulus levels would show that the response depends on stimulus history rather than only on the present input.

title: Lag of chromatin state behind AP-1 occupancy after washout
description: Track AP-1 (Fos/Jun, via HaloTag or CUT&RUN) and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) through a time course after stimulus withdrawal. If accessibility and H3K27ac persist after AP-1 has left its sites, the chromatin state is retaining a record of prior AP-1 activity.

title: Priming and rest-interval re-stimulation
description: Pre-condition cells with a priming pulse, then vary the rest interval before a standard re-challenge, and compare induction kinetics and magnitude with naive cells at each interval. Faster or stronger responses that decay with rest time and are absent in naive cells indicate a stored memory of past exposure.

title: Degron-based removal of AP-1 during the memory window
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on Jun or Fos to remove the factor at defined times after priming. If the memory phenotype persists after AP-1 degradation but is lost when chromatin marks are erased (e.g., with a histone acetyltransferase or chromatin remodeler inhibitor), the memory is carried by chromatin state rather than by AP-1.

title: Lineage-tracked test of heritable persistence
description: Prime cells, then track single-cell lineages with live reporters of AP-1 activity and chromatin state through several divisions, comparing with mock-treated lineages. Persistence of the primed state across divisions without ongoing stimulation, measured against a null model of stochastic heterogeneity, would indicate a self-sustaining, heritable memory rather than transient signaling.

title: Washout and re-stimulation with protein versus chromatin separation
description: Pulse cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus (e.g., TPA or EGF), wash out, and wait variable rest intervals before re-stimulating. Measure re-induction kinetics of AP-1 target genes against a naive control. To separate memory stored in AP-1 protein from memory stored in chromatin, repeat the rest period with a degron-tagged c-Fos or c-Jun so the protein is depleted while the chromatin state is retained.

title: Knockout or degradation of candidate memory components
description: Knock out or acutely degrade candidate components, such as FOSL1, JUNB, p300/CBP, BRD4 and histone writers, individually and in combination. Test which perturbations abolish the faster or stronger second response, to identify the component that carries the memory.

title: Residual-state profiling with a history classifier
description: After stimulus washout, profile AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and H3K27ac at enhancers over time. Train a classifier on this residual state to predict whether a cell or population had prior stimulation; accuracy that stays above chance after the protein has cleared would show that the residual state retains the history.

title: Cross-stimulus test of memory specificity
description: Prime cells with one AP-1-inducing stimulus, then challenge them with an unrelated stimulus that activates a non-AP-1 program, or with an AP-1 stimulus that activates a different gene set. Measure whether priming shifts the response to the new stimulus, to test whether the memory carries across contexts and whether it is specific to AP-1 target loci or global.

title: Live single-cell reporter with decay-curve fitting and binding-site mutants
description: Use a live AP-1-responsive reporter (for example, a destabilized fluorescent protein knocked into a memory-gene locus) to track single cells through stimulus, rest, and re-stimulation. Fit the decay of the memory effect against rest interval to estimate a half-life, and compare wild-type loci with AP-1 motif-mutant alleles and with a non-AP-1 stimulus matched for transcriptional output, to test whether memory depends on AP-1 binding rather than on overall activation level.

title: Pulse-withdrawal time-course profiling of response and chromatin
description: Apply a brief, calibrated AP-1 pulse (e.g., TPA, EGF, or an optogenetic c-Jun/Fos driver), then measure AP-1 target expression and chromatin accessibility at dense timepoints for days after AP-1 activity returns to baseline. Memory is supported if a later identical stimulus gives a larger or faster response than the first, and if the residual change persists after the reporter and nuclear AP-1 signal have fully decayed.

title: Pulse amplitude and duration grid to test scaling of the imprint
description: Cross a range of pulse amplitudes with pulse durations and quantify the residual enhancer activation or gene priming after washout for each combination. A genuine memory mechanism predicts a dose- and duration-dependent imprint with threshold or bistable behavior, whereas a simple decaying-transient model predicts the imprint vanishes in proportion to the signal.

title: Unit-root and persistence testing of single-cell AP-1 reporter time series
description: Track live single-cell AP-1 reporter levels (e.g., FRET or fluorescent Fos/Jun reporters) over long periods. Apply unit-root and autocorrelation tests to determine whether the post-stimulus state returns to a fixed baseline or shifts to a new stable level. A unit-root-like or multi-stable result would indicate a stored cell state rather than simple relaxation to baseline.

title: Delayed acute AP-1 degradation after priming to separate imprint from ongoing signaling
description: After priming with a pulse, rapidly degrade c-Jun or Fos with an inducible degron (e.g., dTAG) at varying delays, then re-stimulate the cells. If memory depends on AP-1 itself, degradation at early delays should erase the imprint, and chromatin-level marks should protect it only when the factor is removed late. This separates the AP-1-dependent component from persistence driven by ongoing signaling dynamics or by chromatin.

title: Comparison of injury severity and exposure history in vivo
description: Use inducible lineage-traced reporters with ATAC-seq or ChIP-seq in tissues subjected to injuries of different severity and duration (e.g., skin wounding, fibrosis, inflammatory challenge). Compare AP-1 site accessibility weeks later across matched cell populations with different prior exposure, to separate AP-1-dependent memory from persistence caused by tissue repair dynamics or systemic inflammation.

title: Antecedent-state model with residual diagnostics
description: Fit models that predict target-gene induction or enhancer activity from the current stimulus plus an exponentially weighted index of prior AP-1 activity. If the prior-activity term improves prediction and the residuals lose autocorrelation, that supports AP-1 carrying state forward beyond what the present stimulus explains.

title: Hysteresis of AP-1 activity versus stimulus dose
description: Ramp stimulus intensity up and then back down in single-cell time series (e.g., Fos or c-Jun reporter intensity against stimulus level) and compare the rising and falling limbs. A loop that persists, with nonzero enclosed area, means AP-1 output depends on stimulation history rather than on the current dose alone.

title: Paired-lineage AP-1 perturbation with long-term rechallenge
description: Split genetically matched cell populations into an AP-1-perturbed arm (for example, a degron-tagged or CRISPR-disrupted Jun/Fos) and an untreated control, then give repeated stimulation cycles over weeks and compare the second-response and later-response magnitudes. The difference in memory-like priming between arms, measured against the control over many cycles, isolates AP-1's contribution.

title: Decay-curve analysis of AP-1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility after washout
description: After removing the stimulus, track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN or ChIP at multiple time points) and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) across hours to days, and fit exponential decay curves to obtain decay constants. Long decay constants at specific enhancers indicate persistence of AP-1-dependent state, and comparing these timescales with those of non-AP-1 transcription factors tests whether AP-1 specifically provides the storage.

title: Pulse-interval and storage-disruption experiments
description: Deliver the same total AP-1 stimulation as pulses separated by different intervals, then measure re-induction after a standard challenge, and disrupt the putative storage (for example, by blocking AP-1 protein stability or chromatin retention) to see whether the memory effect disappears. Memory that depends on the interval and vanishes when storage is disrupted is direct evidence of an AP-1-based mechanism rather than a correlation with the current stimulus.

title: Stimulus withdrawal with difference-in-differences analysis of chromatin
description: Pulse cells with an AP-1 inducer (e.g., TPA or EGF), then withdraw it. Compare the decay of ATAC-seq accessibility and H3K27ac at AP-1-bound enhancers in treated cells against matched unbound control enhancers in untreated cells, using a difference-in-differences estimate of persistence after the trigger is gone. Persistence at treated loci but not controls would indicate memory rather than simple following of the signal.

title: Survival analysis of enhancer closure after trigger removal
description: Collect dense time-course ATAC-seq or CUT&RUN after washout and model time-to-closure of each AP-1 site with a Cox or discrete-time hazard model. Covariates include motif strength, co-bound factors such as BRD4 or p300, and pulse dose. A memory mechanism predicts that sites with self-reinforcing features (e.g., AP-1 binding near Fos/Jun or other AP-1 target genes) have lower closure hazards.

title: Early-pulse timing and trajectory comparison
description: Deliver the same AP-1 pulse at different early windows or doses, and let each cohort evolve for days under identical conditions. Use sequence analysis on chromatin and transcriptional state trajectories, then test whether early-pulse differences produce divergent late states that a later identical challenge cannot erase. This separates history dependence from a simple read-out of current conditions.

title: Re-challenge test for primed responses
description: After washout, re-stimulate with a different or the same signal and measure the speed and magnitude of AP-1 target induction (e.g., time to mRNA and chromatin opening) relative to naive cells, including a control of cells that never received the pulse. Faster or stronger responses in primed cells indicate a stored state. Repeat in knock-in lines with mutated AP-1 sites to test whether AP-1 binding itself is required for the primed response.

title: Interrupting AP-1 autoregulation and tracking heritability
description: Use an inducible degron on Fos or Jun, or dCas9-based recruitment to a specific enhancer, to interrupt AP-1 autoregulation after the stimulus pulse. Combine this with single-cell lineage tracing or live reporters to measure whether memory persists across cell divisions and is lost when the feedback is broken.

title: Lag-dependent re-stimulation decay curves
description: Prime cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus, then re-challenge after variable rest intervals filled with neutral or non-AP-1 stimuli. Measure the secondary induction of AP-1 target genes (RNA-seq or qPCR) and fit decay models: pure activation decay predicts exponential loss of the boost, while true memory predicts a persistent plateau that outlasts the transcription factor's own occupancy.

title: Dissociating AP-1 occupancy from the memory trace via inducible depletion
description: After priming, use an auxin- or degron-inducible system to deplete c-Jun/c-Fos during the rest window, then test the secondary response. If memory depends on ongoing AP-1 binding, depletion should abolish the boost, whereas a chromatin-based trace should survive depletion; check this with ATAC-seq and H3K27ac at the same time points.

title: Site-specific versus generalized transfer of priming across enhancers
description: Test whether priming transfers to other AP-1 sites that share a motif family but not sequence context, and to sites with identical motifs in different chromatin contexts. Quantify transfer with Jun/Fos ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq, so that site-specific (site-bound) memory can be separated from motif-level memory.

title: Interference from intervening non-AP-1 stimuli
description: Insert stimuli that activate unrelated transcription factors (e.g., NF-kB, glucocorticoid, or cAMP/CREB pathways) between priming and challenge, varying their number and strength. If the AP-1 memory is specific, its decay should depend mainly on AP-1-relevant intervening events, which helps separate general activation decay from specific memory.

title: Single-cell lineage tracking of memory inheritance
description: Use a live AP-1 reporter (or fluorescent Jun/Fos knock-in) with time-lapse imaging to track primed cells through division. Measure whether the primed state is inherited by daughter cells or reset stochastically. Fitting the distribution of responses across cells and generations can distinguish graded decay from a bistable, heritable memory state.

title: Epigenetic-editor sufficiency test after AP-1 removal
description: After acutely degrading JUN/FOS (for example with a dTAG system) following priming, target dCas9-p300 or dCas9-KRAB to a single primed AP-1 enhancer. Test whether re-establishing its acetylation or silencing state alone reproduces or erases the memory response, which tests whether the epigenetic mark, rather than the transcription factor, is sufficient to carry the memory.

title: MPRA with AP-1 motif saturation mutagenesis across prime, washout and rechallenge
description: Build a massively parallel reporter library of memory-bearing enhancers with saturation mutagenesis of AP-1 and cofactor motifs, and run each library through a prime, washout, and rechallenge design. Comparing rechallenge responses across variants identifies which sequence features are required to encode memory, separating them from features needed for the initial response.

title: Live imaging of AP-1 binding through mitosis
description: Use endogenous HaloTag-tagged FOS or JUN and live single-molecule or time-lapse imaging to determine which AP-1 sites remain bound on mitotic chromosomes. Then test whether daughter cells that inherit bound sites reactivate target genes faster than those that do not.

title: Single-cell activity-history reporter with lineage barcodes
description: Combine a fluorescent timer or destabilized reporter under an AP-1 target promoter with CRISPR lineage barcodes to record each cell's past AP-1 activity. Test whether prior activity history predicts future response within clonal lineages, after conditioning on current cell state.

title: Pol II pause-release kinetics at memory genes after washout
description: Use PRO-seq or NET-seq after priming and washout to measure paused RNA polymerase II and pause-release rates at memory genes, comparing primed and naive cells with and without AP-1 degradation. This tests whether the memory is held as a poised transcriptional state that is independent of persistent chromatin marks.

title: Single-molecule residence-time tracking of JUN/FOS after pulsed versus sustained stimulation
description: Use single-molecule tracking (HaloTag or SNAP-tagged JUN/FOS) to measure chromatin dwell times of AP-1 after a brief pulse versus continuous stimulation. If memory is encoded kinetically, cells with prolonged AP-1 dwell after a pulse should show persistent enhancer activity, and this dwell-time difference should predict the strength of later responses.

title: Parental-histone pulse-chase at AP-1 enhancers
description: Label pre-existing histones (e.g., SNAP-tagged H3.1/H3.3 quenched before stimulation, then pulse-label new histones) and track old versus new nucleosomes at AP-1 sites through stimulation, washout, and cell division. Retention of parental, modified nucleosomes at AP-1 enhancers would indicate that memory is carried by histone inheritance rather than by ongoing AP-1 occupancy.

title: Binding-only AP-1 tethering without transactivation domains
description: Fuse DNA-binding-competent but transactivation-deficient JUN or FOS (or a bZIP domain alone) to a synthetic recruitment system at a single reporter enhancer, then test whether occupancy alone sustains chromatin opening after the stimulus is gone. Showing that binding is sufficient, or that activation is required, would separate AP-1 as a structural marker from AP-1 as an active driver of memory.

title: Synthetic AP-1 site arrays at a safe-harbor locus
description: Knock in arrays of AP-1 motifs with graded affinities and spacings at a silent safe-harbor locus, then measure which configurations generate persistent accessibility after a single stimulus. This would reveal the minimal site architecture (number, affinity, and cooperativity) required for a locus to retain an AP-1 exposure.

title: Phospho-degron stabilized versus wild-type FOS and JUN
description: Generate matched FOS or JUN variants with altered phospho-degron or ubiquitin-site mutations that change protein half-life while keeping transcriptional output comparable, using pulse-chase protein measurements. If longer-lived AP-1 protein extends chromatin memory independently of transcript levels, protein persistence itself would be the memory substrate, as with stabilized ΔFosB.

title: Hysteresis test with inducible AP-1 dosing
description: Ramp an inducible AP-1 (e.g., dox- or auxin-tunable Fos/Jun) up and down in a dose series, then measure the same downstream readout at a fixed final dose reached from different histories. A history-dependent (hysteretic or bistable) response that differs between up-ramp and down-ramp cells would be a direct signature of a memory state, distinct from testing whether AP-1 is required.

title: Acute degradation after priming to separate AP-1 protein presence from memory
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron on endogenous c-Fos or JunB to remove AP-1 protein within minutes after a priming pulse, then track a re-stimulation readout over days. If priming persists after near-complete protein loss, the memory is carried by a self-sustaining chromatin or cofactor state rather than continued AP-1 occupancy, and proteomic or CUT&Tag profiling of the surviving state can identify the carrier.

title: Domain-swap test of AP-1 identity versus generic occupancy
description: Fuse the AP-1 bZIP DNA-binding domain to non-AP-1 activation domains, and fuse unrelated DNA-binding domains to AP-1 activation domains, matching occupancy at the same enhancers by ChIP and dosing. If memory tracks AP-1 identity and not just occupancy or transactivation strength, systematic swapping should identify the domains that matter for persistence.

title: Mitotic retention and sublineage re-induction timing
description: Use live imaging of HaloTag-tagged JunB or Fos and mitotic ChIP-seq to measure whether AP-1 remains bound to mitotic chromosomes. Sort daughter-cell sublineages from a barcoded or photoconvertible lineage and measure whether re-induction latency is inherited through division, testing heritability of the memory state rather than its maintenance in interphase.

title: Time-resolved proximity labeling of AP-1 partners
description: Use TurboID fused to Fos or JunB and sample labeled interactomes at multiple times after a stimulus and during the quiet period. Shifts in the partner set (e.g., swaps among Fos, ATF3, JDP2, or cofactors) that precede or track the persistence phase would indicate a compositional switch that establishes and then maintains memory, which can be tested by perturbing the partner that changes.

title: Timed degron removal of AP-1 during the rest period
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on JUN or FOS to remove AP-1 protein only during the quiescent interval after a priming pulse, then re-stimulate. If the re-response is retained, memory is carried by chromatin state rather than persisting AP-1 protein; if it is lost, the protein itself is required during the rest period.

title: Synthetic tethering of AP-1 to a neutral locus
description: Fuse an AP-1 activation domain or the bZIP domain to dCas9 or a zinc-finger array and tether it transiently to a silent reporter locus, with no endogenous signal. Measure whether chromatin opening, reporter expression, and faster re-induction persist after tether removal, to test whether AP-1 binding alone is sufficient to write memory.

title: Division-coupled inheritance of memory in sorted daughter cells
description: Track HaloTag-labeled JUN or FOS with live imaging through one or more cell divisions after a priming stimulus, then sort daughter cells by nuclear AP-1 level and challenge them with re-stimulation. This tests whether memory is inherited through mitosis via bookmarking or re-established de novo by each daughter.

title: Single-cell information encoding of priming dose and duration
description: Vary the intensity and duration of a priming stimulus across a grid, then measure both nuclear AP-1 dynamics during priming and the re-response in the same single cells, using barcoded or live reporters. Compute mutual information between priming history and re-response to quantify whether AP-1 encodes memory in pulse features such as amplitude, duration, or frequency.

title: Targeted epigenome editing at memory-associated AP-1 enhancers
description: Use dCas9 fused to KRAB, DNMT3A, or TET1 catalytic domains to erase or write chromatin marks at a few individual AP-1-bound enhancers identified as memory-associated, while leaving AP-1 binding itself intact. If editing these specific enhancers abolishes or creates memory without changing AP-1 occupancy, the chromatin mark rather than the factor is the causal memory element.

title: Temporal necessity mapping with inducible degradation
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron knock-in on endogenous FOS or JUN to remove the protein at defined times after a priming pulse. If memory depends on AP-1 only during induction, degradation after washout should leave the primed state intact; if it depends on ongoing AP-1, the primed state should be lost at the time of degradation, which defines the length of the necessity window.

title: Pulse-chase turnover of endogenous AP-1 protein and its phosphorylation state
description: Tag endogenous JUN or FOS with a HaloTag or SNAP tag and perform pulse-chase labeling after stimulation, measuring protein half-life and parallel phospho-site (e.g., c-Jun S63/S73) and ubiquitination status by quantitative mass spectrometry. Comparing the decay of the protein pool with the decay of memory-gene priming tests whether a stable post-translationally modified AP-1 pool, rather than chromatin marks, carries the memory.

title: Saturation mutagenesis of AP-1 sites in a barcoded synthetic reporter locus
description: Integrate a library of barcoded reporter constructs carrying a minimal enhancer with variable AP-1 site number, spacing, and flanking sequence into a single landing-pad locus, then pulse, wash out, and measure barcode-resolved reactivation after days. This tests which sequence features are sufficient to encode persistent priming, separate from the native genomic context.

title: Mitotic inheritance assay for AP-1-dependent memory
description: Combine a stable (long-lived) fluorescent reporter of prior AP-1 activity with lineage tracking through several cell divisions, sorting and re-challenging daughter cells by their inherited reporter state. If primed responsiveness is inherited by daughters at rates above chance and tracks reporter dilution, memory is transmitted through mitosis; if it is lost, the memory must be re-established after each division.

title: Pulse-frequency dependence of AP-1 memory
description: Deliver the same total stimulus dose in microfluidic chambers as a single pulse, several spaced pulses, or continuous exposure, then measure the strength and persistence of the priming signature at a fixed later time. Whether memory scales with integrated dose, the number of pulses, or the timing of the last pulse distinguishes cumulative memory from a reporter of only the most recent event.

title: Mitotic retention and clonal inheritance of AP-1 occupancy
description: Tag endogenous c-Jun with HaloTag, pulse-stimulate, then follow single cells through mitosis by live imaging and sort mitotic cells for ChIP to determine whether AP-1 remains on chromosomes at memory loci. Daughter cells that inherit the mark should respond faster on re-stimulation than sister lineages without it.

title: Tethered AP-1 at a silent non-enhancer locus
description: Use a dCas9 or zinc-finger tether to recruit c-Jun/Fos to a transcriptionally silent, non-AP-1 locus for a single transient pulse, then track H3K27ac and transcription for weeks. Persistence there, independent of native enhancer context, would show that AP-1 itself establishes a durable state rather than only reading a pre-existing one.

title: Optogenetic pulse-pattern encoding of memory
description: Use light-inducible AP-1 (optoFos/optoJun) to deliver trains that vary pulse number and inter-pulse interval, then measure the magnitude of the second response. Dependence on interval rather than total dose would show that AP-1 encodes temporal history, not just its last state.

title: TurboID proximity labeling of cofactors that persist after AP-1 leaves
description: Fuse TurboID to AP-1 and perform time-resolved biotin labeling across a washout series. Use proteomics to identify cofactors that remain near memory loci after AP-1 has left. Cofactors that persist without AP-1 would be candidate memory carriers, and degrading them should erase the memory while leaving AP-1 intact.

title: Single-molecule residence time as a kinetic readout
description: Track single HaloTag-c-Jun molecules by live-cell single-molecule imaging before, during, and after stimulation, comparing dwell times on target enhancers. A stable change in residence time after washout, with no change in occupancy, would indicate kinetic memory and distinguish it from bulk ChIP signal.

title: Inducible tethering of AP-1 at a silent reporter locus
description: Tether a dimerized FOS-JUN (or bZIP fusion) to a transgenic silent reporter locus using dCas9 or a synthetic zinc-finger system under a doxycycline switch. After the tether is removed, measure whether accessibility and transcription persist, which tests whether AP-1 occupancy alone is sufficient to carry a self-sustaining memory state.

title: Chromatin residence-time shift of endogenous FOS/JUN by single-molecule tracking
description: Knock in HaloTag at the endogenous FOS and JUN loci and use single-molecule tracking with pulse-chase labeling to measure chromatin dwell-time distributions before, during, and after stimulation. A persistent lengthening of dwell time without changes in total occupancy would indicate that memory is encoded in binding kinetics rather than in presence or absence of the factor.

title: Optogenetic pulse-train encoding of AP-1 history
description: Drive a light-inducible AP-1 (e.g., optogenetic JUN or FOS) with trains that vary in pulse number, spacing, and total dose, then measure a standardized later response to a fixed challenge. If the response scales with pulse count or spacing rather than with the last pulse, AP-1 is acting as an integrator of activation history, which is a defining property of memory.

title: Mitotic inheritance of AP-1 priming across cell divisions
description: Track endogenously tagged AP-1 occupancy and reactivation kinetics through mitosis in live imaging, sorting or following daughter cells that inherited different amounts of bound factor. Faster or stronger reactivation in daughters that inherited high AP-1 occupancy would show that the memory is passed through cell division, distinguishing it from a cell-autonomous, reversible state.

title: Lineage-barcoded clonal tracing of primed AP-1 states
description: Combine an AP-1 activity reporter with a heritable CRISPR-based lineage barcode so each clone's history of activation is recorded. Then challenge sorted clones with a secondary stimulus and test whether clonal response biases are stable across many generations and across tissue transplantation, which would show heritable memory at the clone level.

title: Mitotic retention of AP-1 at primed enhancers
description: Tag endogenous c-Jun or Fos (e.g., with HaloTag) and image it through mitosis after a priming stimulus, then sort daughter cells and run ATAC-seq or CUT&Tag. If AP-1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility persist through mitotic chromosome condensation without re-stimulation, the memory is mitotically inherited; if not, it must be re-established each cell cycle.

title: Site-specific writing and erasing of AP-1 memory with dCas9
description: Tether a dCas9-fused AP-1 subunit or a CBP/p300 activator to one defined AP-1 enhancer and, separately, dCas9-KRAB to the same site, then test whether the response to a later stimulus is potentiated or lost at that locus alone. This tests per-locus necessity and sufficiency without disturbing the global AP-1 pool.

title: Protein turnover measurement and degradation-resistant AP-1 variants
description: Measure Fos and Jun protein half-lives and phosphorylation states across the post-stimulus interval with pulse-chase labeling, to identify whether a long-lived AP-1 pool exists. Then express ubiquitin-resistant or phospho-mimetic Fos mutants that extend protein lifetime and test whether memory duration scales with protein stability rather than with transcription.

title: Swapping heterodimer identity to test which bZIP pairing carries memory
description: Replace Fos with ATF3, or knock in leucine-zipper chimeras that alter dimer stability and partner preference, while keeping DNA binding fixed. Compare persistence of accessibility and the re-stimulation response to determine whether memory depends on the specific Fos-Jun dimer composition or on any bZIP protein occupying the site.

title: Motif-swap specificity control at memory-bearing enhancers
description: At enhancers that show AP-1-dependent memory, replace the AP-1 motif with motifs for other stimulus-responsive factors (CREB, NFAT, ISRE, or a scrambled sequence) using CRISPR editing or MPRA-scale libraries, then measure whether the primed state persists. Memory that persists only with AP-1 motifs would support AP-1 specificity, while memory that persists with any motif would indicate a generic chromatin-level mechanism.

title: Timed degron removal of Fos or Jun after a stimulus pulse
description: Use an inducible degron (auxin or dTAG) to remove Fos or Jun at different times after a stimulus pulse, then re-stimulate. If memory requires AP-1 only during establishment, late removal leaves re-induction intact. If it requires ongoing AP-1, late removal erases it.

title: AP-1 occupancy versus chromatin persistence time course
description: Run CUT&Tag for Fos/Jun alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac at memory-gene enhancers across a time course after pulse withdrawal. If accessibility and H3K27ac outlast AP-1 occupancy, the chromatin state rather than the transcription factor carries the memory.

title: Mitotic bookmarking and heritable memory
description: Image whether AP-1 remains on mitotic chromosomes, and combine barcoded lineage tracing with a stimulus pulse to test whether the primed state is inherited by daughter cells. Persistence through division would support a heritable, cell-intrinsic memory rather than a signal supplied anew each time.

title: Heterodimer partner swap knock-ins
description: Replace c-Jun with JunB, or Fos with Fra1 or ATF3, at the endogenous locus and compare the strength and duration of memory after a pulse. If memory depends on partner identity rather than total AP-1 activity, then specific dimer composition, not just AP-1 presence, encodes the memory.

title: Locus-specific synthetic AP-1 recruitment and hysteresis
description: Briefly recruit a tethered AP-1 fragment, or a dimerizer-recruited Jun, to a silent reporter and then release it, and monitor whether the reporter stays active. Combine this with stepwise dose increases and decreases to test whether AP-1 alone can produce a stable, hysteretic switch at a locus.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the post-stimulus window
description: Use dTAG or auxin-inducible degradation of Fos or Jun after an initial stimulus, then re-stimulate. If the second response and chromatin priming fail when AP-1 is removed during washout, AP-1 is necessary for memory maintenance and not only for initial induction.

title: Pulse-interval series to measure memory decay kinetics
description: Deliver two stimulus pulses separated by systematically varied intervals, using optogenetic or precisely timed ligand pulses, and measure the second response (transcription, AP-1 binding, accessibility). The interval-dependence curve gives a quantitative memory timescale that can be compared against models of simple signal carryover.

title: Motif-level editing of AP-1 sites at memory enhancers
description: Use base editing or CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at enhancers that gain accessibility or activity after stimulation, leaving neighboring sequence intact. Measure whether motif loss abolishes priming and faster re-induction, to test whether the AP-1 site itself, rather than the bound factor or general chromatin state, encodes memory.

title: Mitotic inheritance of AP-1-primed chromatin
description: Synchronize cells, stimulate them, and track AP-1 occupancy and accessibility through mitosis into daughter cells, combining mitotic ChIP or CUT&Tag with clonal readouts. Retention of the primed state across division would indicate heritable memory, whereas loss would indicate that memory depends on continuous AP-1 presence.

title: Barcoded lineage tracing of memory heterogeneity
description: Introduce lineage barcodes and a fluorescent AP-1 target reporter, then stimulate cells and follow clonal lineages over several divisions. Comparing memory between sister and unrelated clones shows whether memory is cell-autonomous, inherited, and bistable, or a graded, population-level effect.

title: Washout and re-challenge chromatin persistence
description: After a defined AP-1-inducing stimulus is removed, track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) and accessibility (ATAC-seq) at target enhancers over days, then re-stimulate. Memory is supported if persistent AP-1 binding predicts faster or stronger secondary transcription, and not supported if binding decays first.

title: Degron-timed necessity test
description: Use AID or dTAG to deplete c-Fos or JunB in defined windows: during the initial stimulus, and only during the post-stimulus washout period. Comparing re-challenge responses shows whether AP-1 is required to write the memory or only to execute the first response.

title: Tether-and-release sufficiency test
description: Use inducible dCas9 fused to Fos-Jun or ATF3 at a minimal enhancer, then remove the tether. If accessibility and transcription persist without the original stimulus, AP-1 binding itself is sufficient to hold a chromatin state, which is the core claim of a memory mechanism.

title: AP-1 occupancy on mitotic chromosomes and memory across division
description: Track AP-1 occupancy on mitotic chromosomes (live imaging or mitotic ChIP) and measure whether the secondary response in daughter cells depends on the parent's prior stimulation. This tests whether AP-1 acts as a mitotic bookmark that carries memory through proliferation.

title: Stimulus-history dependence with a live reporter
description: Vary the timing, duration, and frequency of stimuli while imaging a live AP-1-responsive reporter in single cells. Hysteresis or history-dependent thresholds that match a fitted bistable model would show that AP-1 encodes past input rather than just reporting the current signal.

title: Washout time course with paired ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN
description: After a defined AP-1-inducing stimulus, withdraw it and profile AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for Fos/JunB) and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) at multiple time points. Memory is supported if accessibility and faster re-induction persist at sites where AP-1 has left, and the persistence rate distinguishes it from simple binding.

title: Degron-based necessity test after priming
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on Fos or Jun, degrading the protein only after the priming window closes and before re-stimulation. If the primed response is lost, AP-1 is required to maintain memory; if it persists, AP-1 only establishes the state.

title: dCas9-AP-1 tethering for sufficiency, followed by tether removal
description: Tether Jun or Fos to a normally silent locus with dCas9 to test whether AP-1 alone can establish a primed state. Then remove the tether and track whether the locus stays accessible and responsive on re-stimulation, which would indicate self-sustaining memory.

title: Mitotic bookmarking and inheritance by daughter cells
description: Profile AP-1 binding and chromatin accessibility in mitotically arrested cells, and combine live imaging of fluorescent AP-1 reporters with division tracking. This tests whether AP-1 binding or the primed state is inherited through mitosis, a key criterion for a cellular memory mechanism.

title: Recording of past AP-1 activity linked to single-cell state
description: Use a Fos-driven recorder (such as FosTRAP) to label cells by their prior AP-1 activity, then run single-cell multiome on the labeled and unlabeled populations after re-stimulation. This links the history of AP-1 activity to later chromatin and transcriptional variability within the same tissue.

title: Degron timing to separate maintenance from establishment
description: Add an auxin-inducible degron to endogenous Fos and JunB, then deplete AP-1 at varying times after a priming pulse. If the primed response or chromatin state is lost only when AP-1 is removed during the memory window, AP-1 is required to maintain the memory rather than only to establish it.

title: Protein turnover versus chromatin residence
description: Use Halo or SNAP tags on Fos or Jun to measure protein half-life and chromatin dwell time by pulse-chase. If the chromatin mark outlasts the protein, memory must be carried by something other than the AP-1 protein, such as a self-sustaining chromatin state.

title: AP-1 motif necessity at endogenous enhancers
description: Use base or prime editing to mutate AP-1 motifs in endogenous enhancers, then track accessibility and H3K27ac through a stimulus-washout time course. Retained chromatin opening that depends on the intact motif would directly test AP-1 as the memory element.

title: Heritability of the primed state through cell division
description: Use live single-cell reporters with barcoded lineage tracking to determine whether the primed state passes to daughter cells. Combine this with AP-1 perturbation to test whether heritability depends on AP-1 itself.

title: Pulse-history and re-stimulation kinetics
description: Vary the number, spacing and interval of AP-1-inducing pulses, then measure how fast and how strongly cells respond on re-stimulation. This shows whether AP-1 encodes input history in a way consistent with training-dependent memory, and the data can be fitted to a model.

title: Acute AP-1 depletion after stimulus washout
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron (e.g., AID2) to remove FOS or JUN after the stimulus is withdrawn, and measure whether target gene expression and chromatin states persist. If memory collapses on depletion, AP-1 is required to maintain it rather than only to establish it.

title: Enhancer motif mutants tested for chromatin memory
