description: CRISPR-mutate AP-1 motifs in candidate memory enhancers, then run ATAC-seq and H3K27ac time courses after washout in wild-type and mutant cells. Loss of persistence at mutant enhancers would show that AP-1 binding is required for chromatin-level memory.

title: Pulsed optogenetic AP-1 training with hysteresis readout
description: Drive AP-1 with light pulses that vary in frequency, number, and spacing, then measure gene expression and the speed and magnitude of re-induction after a rest period. This tests whether the system encodes stimulus history and how the encoding depends on pulse pattern.

title: Barcoded lineage tracing of memory across divisions
description: Pair AP-1-responsive reporters with heritable barcodes and track single-cell memory states across many generations. Determining whether the primed state is passed to daughter cells, and with what fidelity, distinguishes heritable memory from memory re-established each cell cycle.

title: Synthetic AP-1 feedback circuit for bistability
description: Build an AP-1 autoregulatory loop in a controlled cell line and test whether it sustains expression after the inducer is removed and whether it shows bistable switching. This tests whether AP-1 self-reinforcement is sufficient for memory, independent of native chromatin context.

title: Degron-mediated AP-1 depletion during quiescence after priming
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus, then acutely degrade Fos or Jun (dTAG or auxin system) during the quiescent window. If AP-1 is required to maintain memory, accessibility and re-induction should collapse; if not, memory is self-sustaining after AP-1 leaves the chromatin.

title: Single-molecule footprinting of AP-1 occupancy after washout
description: Use single-molecule footprinting on memory enhancers after stimulus washout to measure what fraction of alleles still carry AP-1 and how long footprints persist. Distinguishing continuous occupancy from re-binding by a fresh AP-1 pool directly tests whether the memory is held by persistent AP-1 binding.

title: Motif deletion or base editing at memory enhancers
description: Use CRISPR deletion or base editing to disrupt AP-1 motifs at enhancers that retain accessibility after priming, then measure retained accessibility, H3K27ac, and the speed and magnitude of re-induction. This tests necessity at the sequence level rather than relying on correlation.

title: Mitotic inheritance of AP-1 memory
description: Tag endogenous Fos or Jun and image it through mitosis, while tracking accessibility or reporter output in daughter cells. Persistence of AP-1 on mitotic chromatin together with matched inherited memory would support a heritable, bookmarking-based mechanism.

title: dCas9-tethered AP-1 sufficiency test at silent loci
description: Tether c-Jun or a p300-recruiting AP-1 fragment to silent loci with dCas9, then wash out and measure whether the locus keeps an open, primed state and responds faster on re-stimulation. This tests whether AP-1 recruitment alone can install memory, independent of upstream signaling.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, then rapidly degrade c-Fos or c-Jun using a dTAG or AID system and test whether the primed transcriptional response to a second stimulus is lost. If memory survives degradation, AP-1 is not required to store it; if it disappears, AP-1 itself carries the memory.

title: Chromatin persistence time course after washout
description: Run ATAC-seq and H3K27ac CUT&Tag at many time points after stimulus removal to measure how long AP-1-bound enhancers stay open and active. Pair this with CRISPR mutation of AP-1 motifs at those enhancers to test whether persistence depends on AP-1 binding.

title: Mitotic inheritance of AP-1 memory
description: Use live imaging of Fos/Jun reporters through mitosis, and sort daughter cells after division to measure whether AP-1 occupancy and enhancer accessibility are passed to them. Retention across division would support mitotic bookmarking as a mechanism for memory.

title: Pulse-pattern encoding with optogenetic AP-1
description: Drive AP-1 activity with optogenetic pulses that vary in frequency, duration, and number, then measure how each pattern changes the response to a later test stimulus. This tests whether memory depends on the history of AP-1 dynamics rather than on a single active state.

title: Barcoded lineage tracing of past AP-1 activity
description: Label cells according to their AP-1 activity history with a heritable reporter and barcode them, then profile the population later to determine whether past AP-1 activity predicts present transcriptional state. This tests memory in individual cells across time and division.

title: Washout and rechallenge time course to test persistence
description: Pulse cells with the stimulus at defined durations and doses, wash out, then rechallenge after multiple rest intervals (hours to weeks). Measure AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for JUN/FOS), chromatin accessibility, and the speed and amplitude of target-gene re-induction. Memory is supported only if rechallenge responses persist beyond the decay of the acute signal and scale with pulse dose and duration.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the rest interval
description: Tag endogenous JUN and/or FOS with an auxin-inducible degron (or use another rapid optogenetic or chemical degradation system) and degrade AP-1 during the quiescent interval between stimulus and rechallenge. If the rechallenge response is lost while chromatin accessibility is preserved, AP-1 protein is required for maintenance; if the response is retained, AP-1 is only required for re-initiation.

title: Paralog-resolved dissection and dimer-swap rescue
description: Perform CUT&RUN and rechallenge assays for each AP-1 family member separately (JUN, JUNB, FOS, FOSL1, ATF3) and knock out individual members to find which carry the memory. Then perform dimer-swap rescue, for example replacing JUN with ATF3 or JUNB, to test whether memory depends on the stability or DNA-binding properties of a specific heterodimer.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing with live AP-1 reporters
description: Use a live FOS or ATF3 transcriptional reporter together with a lineage barcode or nuclear label, and image cells over several divisions after a pulse. Measure whether memory is heterogeneous across the population, whether sister cells are correlated, and whether memory passes through mitosis. Pair this with HaloTag-JUN imaging on mitotic chromosomes to test mitotic bookmarking directly.

title: Enhancer AP-1 site knock-in to separate chromatin from feedback
description: Use CRISPR knock-in to mutate the AP-1 motifs in an endogenous autoregulatory enhancer (for example, the FOS or ATF3 enhancer) while leaving the chromatin context intact, then compare acute induction and rechallenge memory. If memory is lost while baseline chromatin accessibility persists, memory depends on AP-1 binding and positive feedback. If memory persists, the chromatin landscape is the store and AP-1 only reads it out.

title: Dimer-resolved AP-1 occupancy after a priming pulse
description: Use CUT&Tag or CUT&RUN with knock-in tags for FOS, JUN, and ATF3 at several times after stimulus washout to see whether the sites that stay bound are occupied by a distinct dimer composition, which would identify the memory-bearing complex. This tests whether AP-1 acts as a single uniform complex.

title: Savings-based memory assay across rest intervals
description: Define memory operationally as 'savings': prime cells with a fixed pulse, rest them for hours to days, then re-stimulate and measure the speed and amplitude of re-induction of AP-1 targets. Plot savings against rest time and compare it with the decay of AP-1 occupancy to determine whether memory outlasts binding.

title: Acute FOS/JUN degradation after priming
description: Use dTAG or auxin-degron knock-ins to deplete FOS and JUN at defined times after a priming pulse, then re-stimulate to test whether memory requires persistent AP-1 protein. Retained enhanced response implies storage in chromatin or other marks, while loss implies the protein itself is required; pair with ATAC-seq and H3K27ac to identify what persists.

title: Single-cell lineage-tracked reporter for an AP-1 enhancer
description: Build a knock-in destabilized fluorescent reporter at an AP-1-responsive enhancer, pulse cells, sort by reporter state after rest, and track daughter cells by live imaging over several generations. This tests whether memory is bimodal rather than a population average and whether it is inherited across divisions.

title: Locus-specific necessity and sufficiency of AP-1 binding
description: Use base editing to mutate only the TRE motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and separately tether a dimerizable or dCas9-fused AP-1 activator to one enhancer without upstream signal. If synthetic activity recreates the primed (faster re-induction) phenotype and motif mutation abolishes it, AP-1 is causal at that locus.

title: Time-windowed AP-1 degradation (dTAG/AID) to test whether AP-1 or chromatin stores memory
description: Acutely degrade c-Fos or JunB with a degron during priming only, during the washout interval, or only at re-stimulation, then measure re-induction kinetics and enhancer accessibility (ATAC-seq, H3K27ac) at each window. If memory survives loss of AP-1 during washout while chromatin marks persist, the memory is stored in chromatin rather than in AP-1 itself. This tests whether AP-1 must persist to hold memory.

title: Live single-cell reporter tracking through divisions
description: Knock a fluorescent reporter into an AP-1 target locus (e.g., FOSL1 or an enhancer-driven reporter) and track primed and naive cells by time-lapse microscopy across several generations after washout. Quantify whether the faster re-induction state is bimodal and whether it is inherited by daughter cells (sibling and lineage correlations), testing population averaging and mitotic heritability.

title: Subunit-resolved occupancy and combinatorial knockouts
description: Use CUT&Tag or ChIP for each Fos, Jun, and ATF family member at memory-associated enhancers during priming and after washout. Then test single and double knockouts or knockdowns of the dominant heterodimer partners. This shows which dimer composition persists and whether compensation masks the phenotype, testing whether AP-1 composition is uniform and whether single knockouts are clean.

title: Cell-autonomy test by co-culture, transwell, and conditioned medium
description: Prime one population, then co-culture it with naive, differently labeled cells, separate them with a transwell, or transfer conditioned medium, and measure whether the naive cells acquire faster re-induction. Repeat the experiment in an in vivo or transplant setting to check generalization. If the naive cells acquire the memory, it is not cell-intrinsic.

title: Priming-history matrix with mutual information
description: Systematically vary priming dose, pulse duration, pulse frequency, and interval, and measure re-stimulation response at multiple decay timepoints. Compute the mutual information between priming history and the response to determine how much information the AP-1 system stores and for how long. This tests the single-stimulus, single-timescale, and fixed-definition assumptions.

title: Degron-based maintenance test after stimulus washout
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron on endogenous c-Fos or JUNB, stimulate, wash out, and degrade AP-1 at different times after the pulse. Track enhancer accessibility (ATAC-seq) and target transcription to determine whether persistence requires continued AP-1 presence, and compare with histone-mark readouts (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) to separate AP-1-dependent maintenance from chromatin-encoded memory.

title: Paralog- and dimer-specific dissection of memory
description: Apply paralog-specific degrons or CRISPR knockouts (e.g., FOS vs FOSB, FOSL1 vs FOSL2, JUNB vs c-JUN, ATF3) and run CUT&Tag for each member after a pulse. Determine which dimer combinations occupy memory-associated enhancers after the stimulus is removed and whether losing one member abolishes persistence.

title: Single-cell live reporter and lineage tracing of persistence
description: Build a destabilized fluorescent reporter driven by an AP-1-responsive enhancer and track individual cells through repeated pulses with time-lapse imaging. Quantify bimodality, the fraction of cells that retain a primed state, and whether the state is inherited by daughter cells, to test whether memory is a subpopulation phenomenon hidden in bulk data.

title: Inducible AP-1 sufficiency without the upstream stimulus
description: Use an optogenetic or chemically inducible AP-1 construct (for example, a light-controlled Fos/Jun heterodimer) to drive AP-1 activity in the absence of the native signal, with matched total-activity controls. Test whether defined pulses of AP-1 activity alone generate a primed state that enhances later responses, separating AP-1 memory from memory held in upstream MAPK/ERK signaling.

title: Mitotic persistence and inheritance timing of the primed state
description: Synchronize cells after a pulse, then track AP-1 occupancy (live-cell imaging of tagged AP-1 or CUT&RUN at defined mitotic stages) and enhancer accessibility through mitosis and into G1 over several cell cycles. Measure whether the primed state is retained through mitotic chromatin disruption and how long it lasts, distinguishing heritable memory from a state that must be rebuilt after each division.

title: Degron-timed necessity test during the rest window
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUNB with an auxin-inducible degron and degrade the protein only during the quiescent interval after priming, then measure re-stimulation kinetics and AP-1 occupancy by CUT&RUN. If the memory is lost, the protein itself carries it; if it survives, the carrier is chromatin or another factor.

title: Subunit-by-subunit knockout and rescue
description: Knock out individual AP-1 members (FOS, FOSB, FOSL1, FOSL2, JUN, JUNB, JUND, ATF3) in a priming paradigm, then rescue with wild-type or DNA-binding and dimerization-mutant variants. This shows which subunits and dimer combinations are required for the memory-dependent faster re-induction of target genes.

title: Live single-cell reporter tracking across divisions
description: Express a destabilized fluorescent reporter driven by an AP-1-responsive promoter and track individual cells by time-lapse microscopy through priming, rest, and re-stimulation. Compare the fraction of cells that retain the primed state and whether daughter cells inherit it, to determine whether memory is confined to a subpopulation and whether it is heritable.

title: Cross-stimulus priming with orthogonal pathway controls
description: Prime cells with two or more stimuli that converge on AP-1 through different upstream routes (e.g., phorbol ester, EGF, or a stress stimulus), then cross-challenge each. Include MEK inhibitor and NF-kB or STAT inhibitor arms and profile their target genes, to test whether the memory encodes stimulus identity specifically and is AP-1-dependent rather than a generic activation signature.

title: Sufficiency test with a controlled ectopic AP-1 pulse
description: Induce a defined dose and duration of c-Jun or c-Fos with a dox-inducible or optogenetic clustering system, bypassing upstream signaling, and measure whether the same persistent priming signature appears at endogenous targets upon later challenge. If an artificial pulse is sufficient, AP-1 is the rate-limiting node for memory; if not, memory requires upstream signaling.

title: Subunit-resolved, time-gated degradation of AP-1 members
description: Tag endogenous c-Fos, FosB, JunB, c-Jun, and ATF3 with dTAG or AID degrons and degrade each one individually and in combination, only during the quiescent interval after priming, then measure recall. This identifies which dimers are necessary for memory, reveals compensation, and avoids confounds from constitutive loss.

title: AP-1 degradation during the rest period to separate trigger from substrate
description: After priming, degrade AP-1 during the rest period, not during re-stimulation, and track chromatin accessibility, H3K27ac, CUT&RUN occupancy, and recall over time. If primed chromatin persists without AP-1 and recall is intact, the memory lies in chromatin; if recall fails, AP-1 itself is the persistent substrate.

title: Single-cell tracking of AP-1 activity across divisions
description: Use a destabilized fluorescent AP-1 activity reporter with live imaging and tracking across cell divisions, paired with single-cell multiome readouts. Test whether the primed state is bimodal, whether mother and daughter cells share it, and whether it predicts later recall at single-cell resolution.

title: Synthetic AP-1 tethering with washout and factor-specificity controls
description: Recruit the c-Jun activation domain or full-length c-Jun to a silent enhancer or promoter with dCas9 or optogenetic CRY2/CIB, then wash out the tether and test for a persistent primed state. Run the same design with NF-kB, C/EBP, or STAT tethers as controls, and complement with motif mutations at endogenous enhancers.

title: In vivo Fos-based tagging with repeated, patterned stimulation
description: Use Fos-TRAP2 or an AP-1-responsive reporter mouse to permanently label cells activated by a defined stimulus, then re-expose the animal weeks later and measure reactivation of the tagged cells, transcriptional priming, and chromatin state. Vary dose, duration, and frequency of the initial stimulus to test whether the memory encodes input patterns.

title: Paralog-specific acute degradation of AP-1 family members
description: Knock in auxin-inducible degron tags to endogenous Fra1, c-Fos, JunB and Jun, then degrade each member separately after priming. Measure which paralog is required for retention of accessibility and re-induction at memory loci, and test whether swapping in another family member rescues the memory.

title: AP-1 removal during the post-stimulus washout window
description: After priming, use a degron to acutely remove AP-1 during the post-stimulus interval, then measure chromatin accessibility, H3K27ac and H3K4me1 by CUT&Tag, and re-induction on re-stimulation. Persistence of marks without AP-1 would indicate chromatin-encoded memory, while loss of marks would indicate that AP-1 maintains the state.

title: Kinetic washout and re-stimulation series
description: Vary pulse number and duration, then re-stimulate at a graded series of intervals. Score memory as a stimulus-specific change in re-induction speed or amplitude that decays with a measurable time constant, using a non-AP-1 stimulus and an unrelated transcription factor as controls. This distinguishes persistence from altered responsiveness.

title: Single-cell lineage-traced AP-1 reporter to test bimodality and heritability
description: Knock in a destabilized fluorescent reporter at an AP-1-responsive locus and pair time-lapse imaging with single-cell multiome. Sort daughter pairs and sibling versus unrelated cells to test whether the memory state is bimodal and heritable across divisions, rather than a uniform bulk-average state.

title: In vivo repeated exposure with ex vivo recall
description: In a tissue model with repeated natural stimulation (e.g., repeated injury or mechanical load), lineage-trace AP-1-responsive cells, then isolate them for ex vivo re-stimulation and CUT&Tag. Compare with naive cells and with conditional AP-1 deletion in a mosaic subset to test whether memory is cell-intrinsic and independent of the tissue niche.

title: Paralog degron matrix to identify which AP-1 members carry memory
description: Knock in dTAG or AID degrons to JUN, JUNB, JUND, FOS, FOSL1/2, and ATF3, then degrade individual and combinatorial subsets at defined windows after a priming stimulus and washout. Measure ATAC, H3K27ac, and re-induction of primed genes to identify which paralog set is required for memory, without assuming AP-1 acts as a single unit.

title: Separating AP-1 occupancy from chromatin state by single-molecule tracking and CUT&RUN during washout
description: Use HaloTag-JUN or FOS single-molecule tracking to measure residence time, and CUT&RUN to track occupancy at primed enhancers over a washout time course. If accessibility or H3K27ac at these loci persists after AP-1 unbinds, the carrier is a chromatin state rather than AP-1 occupancy; this can be tested further with pioneer- or acetylation-deficient AP-1 mutants.

title: Two-pulse re-stimulation assay with single-cell quantification
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, vary the rest interval, then re-stimulate and quantify lag, amplitude, and magnitude of re-induction of AP-1 targets by smFISH or single-cell RT-qPCR. Repeat with AP-1 degraded during the rest period; memory is defined as a faster or stronger secondary response that depends on AP-1 presence, not as a persistent marker.

title: Lineage-resolved memory tracing across divisions
description: Combine CRISPR lineage barcodes with a recorder of prior AP-1 activity, such as a Fos-promoter-driven recombinase or stable reporter, and follow clonal lineages through several divisions. Use single-cell multiome readouts to test whether the primed state is inherited within clones, and whether it is uniform or confined to a subpopulation.

title: In vivo activity-dependent tagging and necessity test
description: Use Fos-CreERT2 or TRAP labeling to mark cells with AP-1 activity during a repeated physiological stimulus in mouse tissue, such as neurons or trained macrophages. Sort tagged cells at several post-stimulus intervals for ATAC or CUT&Tag. Test necessity by inducing a dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS or TAM67) during the consolidation window and checking whether the memory signature and later reactivation response disappear.

title: Persistence of AP-1 chromatin opening after stimulus withdrawal
description: Analyze public stimulus-washout ATAC-seq or H3K27ac time courses (e.g., ENCODE, GEO, ImmGen) to determine whether AP-1 motif sites stay open after the signal is removed, and whether this persistence exceeds that of matched non-AP-1 enhancers. Compare decay half-lives of AP-1 and non-AP-1 sites to test whether AP-1 specifically confers memory.

title: Re-stimulation kinetics in public sequential-challenge datasets
description: Use public datasets with primary and secondary challenges (for example, memory versus naive T cells, trained-immunity macrophages, or repeated-stimulation fibroblasts) to test whether AP-1 activity at the first exposure predicts faster or stronger gene induction on re-exposure. Control for baseline chromatin state and for the effector or differentiation state of each cell population.

title: Single-cell test of AP-1 accessibility as a predictor of memory state
description: Analyze public single-cell multiome (scRNA plus scATAC) datasets from infection, tumor, or inflammation models to ask whether the AP-1 motif accessibility score in a cell predicts its membership in a memory-like versus terminally differentiated state. Check whether the association holds after conditioning on lineage markers and on the cell's stimulation history.

title: Hysteresis analysis of AP-1 target genes in time-resolved expression data
description: Fit bistable or hysteresis models to public time-course RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data with stimulus up-ramps and down-ramps, to test whether AP-1 target genes show different on and off thresholds, which would indicate path-dependent memory. Compare the fit with that for targets of other immediate-early factors such as NF-kB or STAT.

title: Loss-of-function evidence from public AP-1 perturbation screens
description: Mine public CRISPR knockout and Perturb-seq resources (such as DepMap, Perturb-seq atlases, and knockout data for JUN, FOS, BATF, and ATF3) to test whether loss of AP-1 components abolishes the transcriptional carry-over that follows a prior stimulus. Include controls for proliferation and cell death, and check whether the effect is specific to AP-1 targets.

title: Washout time-course of AP-1 occupancy and chromatin state
description: After a defined AP-1-inducing stimulus (e.g., TPA or serum), wash out and profile c-Fos/JunB/ATF3 occupancy (CUT&Tag) alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac at days 0 to 7. Memory is supported if enhancers stay open and retain AP-1 binding or priming marks after the TF signal has returned to baseline. Estimated cost is about $8k to $12k for a single cell line with 6 timepoints in duplicate.

title: Acute degron-mediated necessity test during the memory window
description: Tag endogenous FOS or JUN with an auxin-inducible degron, prime cells, then degrade the factor only during the stimulus-free interval before re-stimulation. If AP-1 is the memory store, degradation should abolish faster or amplified re-induction of primed target genes (measured by RT-qPCR/RNA-seq) without affecting the naive response. Estimated cost: about $10k to $15k for knock-in, validation, and RNA-seq.

title: Base-editing of AP-1 motifs at endogenous primed enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editors or prime editors to mutate the TRE/AP-1 motifs in 3 to 5 enhancers that show memory-like priming, then compare primed-state accessibility and re-stimulation kinetics in edited versus control clones. This tests whether the specific motif sites, rather than general AP-1 presence, carry the memory. Estimated cost is about $9k to $14k for guide design, clone isolation, and ATAC/RNA readouts.

title: Single-cell reporter lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Build a destabilized-fluorescent-protein reporter driven by an AP-1-responsive enhancer and track individual cells by time-lapse microscopy through several divisions after a pulse of stimulus. Memory is supported if the re-induction response is heritable in daughter cells and decays on a timescale matching the measured chromatin persistence. Estimated cost is about $5k to $9k for the lentiviral reporter, imaging, and analysis.

title: Protein-synthesis block and mitotic bookmarking assay
description: Pulse the stimulus, then add cycloheximide or another translation inhibitor to remove newly made AP-1 protein, and use CUT&Tag or ChIP in mitotic cells to test whether AP-1 stays bound to condensed chromatin through mitosis. Retention of AP-1 at memory enhancers without new protein synthesis would indicate self-sustaining, bookmarking-like memory, while loss would indicate that protein turnover is the main driver. Estimated cost is about $4k to $7k for the inhibitor experiments, sorted mitotic cells, and sequencing.

title: Reporter persistence after washout as a function of pulse duration
description: Expose cells carrying a live AP-1 transcriptional reporter (for example, a destabilized fluorescent protein under AP-1 response elements) to stimulus pulses of varying length, then wash out and track reporter decay for days. Memory is supported if persistence time scales with pulse duration and outlasts both reporter protein turnover and stimulus clearance.

title: Two-pulse test with varied inter-pulse intervals
description: Give two stimulus pulses separated by different rest intervals and compare the second response's latency, amplitude, and duration with the first, using endogenous AP-1 subunit tags (e.g., JUNB or FOSL1 knock-in fluorescent fusions). A faster or stronger second response that decays with longer intervals is a quantifiable signature of memory.

title: Heritability of AP-1 state across cell divisions
description: Stimulate cells, remove the stimulus, and track lineages with a nuclear marker while recording an AP-1 reporter in each cell and its daughters. Quantify how well the pre-division state predicts daughter states (lineage autocorrelation); carrying AP-1 activity through divisions would indicate a heritable memory rather than a signal-dependent state.

title: Degron-based causal test during the memory window
description: Once persistent AP-1 activity is established, use an inducible degradation tag (e.g., auxin or dTAG) on a JUN or FOS subunit to remove the protein while following the reporter in real time. If the persistent state collapses on degradation, AP-1 is necessary to maintain it; persistence after degradation would argue against AP-1 being the memory store.

title: Chromatin residence time of AP-1 after stimulus removal
description: Use HaloTag-labeled JUN or FOS with live-cell FRAP or single-molecule tracking to measure how long AP-1 remains bound to chromatin after stimulus withdrawal and how that residence time changes over days. A residence time that stays elevated after the signal ends would provide a binding-level readout of memory.

title: Pulse-washout chromatin time course
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., TPA, EGF, or serum) for varying pulse lengths, wash out, and profile endogenous c-Fos/JunB occupancy (CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq) alongside chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and H3K27ac over days. If AP-1 acts as memory, enhancer accessibility and activity should persist after AP-1 occupancy decays, and a second stimulus should trigger a faster or stronger response at those same sites.

title: Time-gated small-molecule inhibition
description: Apply AP-1 pathway inhibitors (e.g., the c-Jun/AP-1 DNA-binding inhibitor T-5224) or upstream JNK/ERK inhibitors only before, during, or after a priming stimulus, then measure chromatin state and re-stimulated transcription. Inhibition during priming versus after it separates whether AP-1 is needed to establish or to maintain a memory; inhibitor specificity must be validated with dose-response and orthogonal readouts.

title: Single-cell history dependence with multiplexed imaging
description: Prime cells with varying stimulus histories, then use cyclic immunofluorescence or multiplexed smFISH on endogenous FOS, JUN, and downstream targets to measure per-cell AP-1 levels and response to a challenge stimulus. Testing whether a cell's prior AP-1 history predicts its challenge response, beyond population averages, directly tests cell-intrinsic memory.

title: Mitotic persistence of AP-1-bound sites
description: Sort or synchronize cells in mitosis after priming and compare AP-1 occupancy and accessibility on mitotic chromatin to interphase, asking whether AP-1 remains bound at the same enhancers through mitosis (bookmarking). Then track whether post-mitotic daughters retain the primed state across several divisions after stimulus removal, which tests whether AP-1 memory is heritable through cell division.

title: Natural genetic variation and trained-immunity cohort
description: Use primary monocytes or iPSC-derived macrophages from genetically diverse donors, stimulated with a trained-immunity inducer (e.g., β-glucan) and then re-challenged after a rest period. Correlate AP-1 binding strength and allele-specific AP-1 occupancy at heterozygous sites with the magnitude and duration of the trained response, using natural genetic variation rather than engineered perturbation to test whether AP-1 binding causally predicts memory.

title: Pulse-washout with reactivation kinetics in Drosophila S2 cells
description: Induce a defined AP-1 (Jun/Fos or Kayak/Jra) pulse with an inducible system, wash it out, and track target-gene expression, AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN), and H3K27ac/H3K4me1 at enhancers over days. Re-stimulate after washout and test whether faster or stronger re-induction persists, then repeat with TRE-mutated enhancers to test whether the memory depends on AP-1 binding rather than on the stimulus alone.

title: Tethered AP-1 sufficiency test with dCas9 or zinc-finger tethers in Drosophila cells
description: Use a dCas9-based or synthetic zinc-finger tether to recruit Jun or Fos to a silent reporter locus for a short period, then release it and measure whether the locus remains primed (chromatin opening, Pol II poising, reporter expression on re-challenge). Compare with tethers of an unrelated transcription factor to test whether AP-1 specifically establishes a persistent state rather than only transient activation.

title: Repeated stress pulses in yeast with single-cell tracking
description: In S. cerevisiae carrying an AP-1-like bZIP (Yap1) or a heterologous Jun/Fos, use microfluidic time-lapse imaging of a fluorescent reporter across repeated stress pulses with varying intervals. Quantify whether cells with a prior pulse respond faster on the next exposure, whether memory decays with interval, and whether it is lost with auxin- or anchor-away-mediated depletion of the factor or with binding-site mutations.

title: Learning-dependent AP-1 requirement in C. elegans behavior
description: Train worms in a pathogen-avoidance or aversive olfactory paradigm while knocking down jun-1 or fos-1 with a temporally controlled degron or heat-shock promoter, separating the training window from the retention interval and recall test. Pair this with calcium imaging of the relevant interneurons and neuron-specific rescue to determine whether AP-1 is needed for acquisition, consolidation, or retention.

title: Injury priming of AP-1 enhancers during zebrafish regeneration
description: Perform a first fin amputation, allow recovery, then re-amputate and compare regeneration speed and fos/jun enhancer reporter activity with naive fish. Use scATAC-seq or single-cell RNA-seq at the second injury to identify primed cell states, and CRISPR knockout of jun or fos paralogs to test whether the faster second response, and the enhancer's persistent accessibility between injuries, depends on AP-1.

title: Degron-based AP-1 depletion during rest and rechallenge
description: Use a dTAG or auxin-inducible degron on endogenous c-Jun or c-Fos in primary cells or a cell line. Give a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, EGF, or LPS), wash out, and rest cells for 1-2 weeks, with or without AP-1 depletion during the rest period. Then restimulate and measure the speed and magnitude of target-gene induction by RT-qPCR or RNA-seq. If memory requires AP-1 persistence, the faster response should be lost when AP-1 is degraded during rest.

title: Time-resolved CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq across a stimulus-rest cycle
description: Profile AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for c-Fos, JunB, ATF3), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and H3K27ac at multiple timepoints through stimulation, washout, and the quiescent interval. Test whether enhancers that stay accessible or acetylated after AP-1 leaves the chromatin predict the rechallenge response, and pair this with a degron approach to separate AP-1-dependent retention from chromatin-intrinsic retention.

title: Live single-cell AP-1 reporter across repeated pulses
description: Build a destabilized fluorescent reporter driven by an AP-1-responsive promoter, or knock a reporter into an endogenous AP-1 target such as FOS or ATF3, and track individual cells by live imaging or microfluidics. Apply pulses at varied intervals and quantify, per cell, whether the second response is faster or larger than the first. Correlate memory with nuclear c-Jun or c-Fos levels and their persistence to test whether memory is a graded, cell-autonomous property.

title: Mutagenesis of AP-1 motifs in enhancers to test necessity for memory
description: Using CRISPR knock-in or base editing, mutate the AP-1 (TGAnTCA) sites in one or several memory-associated enhancers identified from CUT&RUN data, or block binding at those sites with dCas9-KRAB. Compare the primed response to rechallenge in wild-type and mutant clones, including a non-AP-1 control enhancer, to test whether the AP-1 sites are necessary for memory and not just correlated with it.

title: Fos-CreERT2 lineage tagging of AP-1-active cells in vivo
description: Use Fos-CreERT2 reporter mice to permanently label cells that were AP-1-active during a defined stimulus such as a skin irritant, tissue injury, or inflammatory challenge. After a rest period, rechallenge the animals and compare reactivation of AP-1 targets in tagged versus untagged neighboring cells by flow cytometry or spatial transcriptomics, to test whether AP-1 history alters later responses in a physiological setting.

title: Chromatin persistence at AP-1 enhancers after signal washout
description: Give a transient stimulus, then harvest separate animal or cell cohorts at different washout intervals, each sampled once, for ATAC-seq or CUT&Tag of H3K27ac and AP-1 (Fos/Jun) occupancy. If AP-1-bound enhancers stay open or acetylated after c-Fos/JunB protein returns to baseline, this supports chromatin-based memory rather than a transient signaling response.

title: Single-cell multiome linking prior exposure to later response
description: Split a population into groups with different prior AP-1-activating histories, then challenge each group with a standard stimulus and collect one multiome snapshot per sample at the response peak. Test whether residual AP-1 motif accessibility before the challenge predicts the magnitude and speed of secondary target-gene induction, and whether that predictive signal is absent in cells lacking the pre-exposure.

title: AP-1 loss-of-function necessity test of persistent state
description: Compare the persistent chromatin and transcriptional state at a single late timepoint in wild-type cells versus cells with Fos or Jun knockdown, dominant-negative A-FOS/TAM67 expression, or conditional deletion, each sampled once after the same stimulus history. If the persistent enhancer marks or memory-associated gene expression disappear without AP-1, AP-1 is required for memory rather than merely correlated with it.

title: Comparing AP-1 protein decay with chromatin memory decay
description: Use mass cytometry or intracellular/phospho flow cytometry to measure c-Fos, JunB and other AP-1 protein levels in single cells across a series of washout durations, with each cell measured once. If AP-1 protein returns to baseline while chromatin marks or target-gene poised states remain elevated, this indicates a durable state separate from ongoing AP-1 signaling.

title: Ex vivo re-stimulation of explants after in vivo experience
description: Expose animals to a single in vivo stimulus, then at a fixed later time harvest tissue explants and stimulate each ex vivo with the same challenge, fixing each explant once for AP-1 target-gene and AP-1 motif-enhancer readouts. Explants from experienced animals showing faster or stronger AP-1 target induction than naive controls would indicate a latent, cell-intrinsic memory that survives removal of the tissue from its original context.

title: Longitudinal chromatin profiling of patient biopsies across a stimulus cycle
description: Collect paired biopsies or blood samples from the same patients at baseline, peak activation, and after resolution, then run ATAC-seq and FOS/JUN CUT&RUN. If memory exists, AP-1 motif accessibility and JUN/FOS occupancy should stay elevated at loci induced during the flare even after clinical and transcriptional markers return to baseline, and this persistence should be specific to AP-1 motifs compared with matched control motifs such as CEBP or RUNX.

title: Ex vivo stimulus washout and re-challenge in patient-derived primary cells
description: Stimulate patient-derived monocytes, T cells, or fibroblasts with a defined AP-1-inducing signal, wash out for several days, then re-challenge and measure the speed and magnitude of AP-1 target gene induction (for example by RNA-seq time courses and nascent transcription). Memory is supported if re-challenged cells respond faster or more strongly than naive cells from the same donor, and the effect is abolished by a pharmacological AP-1 inhibitor or by a degron-based JUN knockdown.

title: Pulse-chase single-cell multiome in patient-derived organoids
description: Treat patient-derived organoids with a transient pulse of a stimulus or drug, then profile them with single-cell multiome (scRNA plus scATAC) at multiple times after washout. Track whether AP-1-linked open chromatin persists in specific cell states and whether those states show a faster transcriptional response to a second pulse, using per-cell barcoding to link memory state to later response.

title: Tracking persister cells across therapy and drug holiday in patient tumors
description: Obtain matched tumor samples before treatment, during treatment, and at relapse after a drug holiday, and use scATAC-seq and lineage barcodes to follow the same clones over time. Test whether AP-1-accessible persister states that survive therapy are re-enriched at relapse and show faster re-induction of AP-1 targets than treatment-naive clones, which would support AP-1 as a memory of prior drug exposure.

title: Locus-specific dCas9 epigenome editing in patient-derived cells
description: In patient-derived cells, use dCas9 fused to a p300 activator or KRAB repressor to open or close AP-1 sites at selected memory loci, then remove the effector and track chromatin state and transcription over time. If AP-1 is the memory mechanism, the edited state should persist after effector removal only when the AP-1 motif is intact, which is tested by pairing each site with a motif-mutant control.

title: Single-molecule residence-time tracking of JUN/FOS after a pulse
description: Use HaloTag-labeled JUN or FOS in live cells with single-molecule tracking to measure chromatin dwell-time distributions before, during, and for days after a stimulus. A long-dwell bound fraction that persists beyond the pulse without a change in total protein level would suggest that memory is stored as altered factor kinetics rather than as a new steady-state binding pattern.

title: Phosphosite knock-in alleles to test whether post-translational state carries memory
description: Knock in phosphomimetic and phospho-dead alleles at key JUN and FOS regulatory sites (for example JUN Ser63/Ser73), then use phospho-specific mass spectrometry and washout time courses to track how long each modification persists. If the memory-related transcriptional response tracks the phospho-state rather than AP-1 protein abundance or occupancy, the modification itself is the stored variable.

title: Pulse-chase separation of carryover from chromatin-based memory
description: Combine SLAM-seq or 4sU pulse-chase labeling with transcription inhibition (e.g., flavopiridol or triptolide) applied at defined washout times, then re-stimulate. Persistence of memory despite transcriptional shutdown would indicate carryover of mRNA or protein, while loss of memory under shutdown would indicate that new transcription is needed to maintain the state.

title: Kinase-route test with orthogonal upstream stimuli
description: Prime cells with equivalent AP-1 induction achieved through different upstream routes (ERK, JNK, or p38, using pathway-selective stimuli or inhibitors) and then cross-challenge with each route. If reinduction is pathway-specific despite similar AP-1 levels, the memory encodes the signaling route rather than the AP-1 level, which would make AP-1 a readout rather than the storage element.

title: Coactivator-recruitment rescue in a JUN-null background
description: Replace endogenous JUN with variants that have matched DNA binding but differ in their ability to recruit BRD4 or p300/CBP, and measure how long induced enhancer acetylation and target expression persist after washout. If memory duration tracks coactivator recruitment rather than AP-1 occupancy, persistence depends on a coactivator feedback loop rather than on the AP-1 complex itself.

title: Parental histone inheritance at AP-1 enhancers through replication
description: Pulse-label pre-existing H3.3 with SNAP or Halo tags before and after a stimulus, then follow the old-versus-new histone ratio at AP-1 enhancers through one or two cell divisions. If AP-1 memory depends on nucleosome inheritance, old stimulus-era histones should stay enriched at these enhancers in daughter cells, and blocking histone recycling (e.g., MCM2 or FACT perturbation) should erase the primed state.

title: Paused Pol II persistence after AP-1 loss
description: Use PRO-seq or GRO-seq during washout to measure promoter-proximal Pol II pausing at AP-1 target genes, and ask whether paused polymerase persists after AP-1 has left the enhancer. A memory mechanism predicts faster pause release on restimulation, and this effect should be blocked by a transient CDK9 or P-TEFb inhibitor applied only during the rest period.

title: Partner switching within the AP-1 dimer
description: Use TurboID or APEX proximity labeling on FOS and JUN at several washout times to test whether repressive partners such as ATF3, JDP2, or JUNB replace the original dimer partner after the stimulus. Then knock out the substitute partner and test whether recall is altered, which would show that memory depends on dimer composition rather than on AP-1 presence.

title: Nuclear-periphery relocalization of primed loci
description: Label an AP-1 target locus with an ANCHOR or ParB array and track its distance to the nuclear lamina and nuclear pore complexes by live imaging across stimulus and rest periods. Persistent pore association after the stimulus, which disappears in cells with nuclear pore anchoring mutations, would indicate that spatial repositioning stores the memory.

title: Cross-stimulus priming matrix to define memory specificity
description: Prime cells with stimuli that act through AP-1 alone, through NF-kB, or through cAMP-CREB, then measure the response to every restimulation pairing with an AP-1-dependent reporter. An AP-1 memory should show a pattern of cross-priming that tracks the AP-1 binding sites of each stimulus and disappears when those sites are mutated, which discriminates better than asking whether any memory exists.

title: Heterokaryon fusion of primed and naive cells
description: Fuse primed cells with naive cells, or use chemically induced nuclear transfer, to create a shared cytoplasm containing one primed and one naive nucleus. If the naive nucleus becomes re-inducible while the primed nucleus keeps its advantage, memory is nuclear-intrinsic; if the state spreads through the shared cytoplasm, it is a diffusible signaling or protein-pool property.

title: Parental histone inheritance at AP-1 enhancers
description: Label pre-existing H3 or H3.3 with a SNAP/Halo tag, pulse with AP-1 stimulus, then chase through one or two divisions and use quantitative CUT&Tag to measure whether old versus newly synthesized histones are retained at primed enhancers. Preferential retention of old histones at AP-1-bound sites would suggest that memory is carried by histone recycling rather than by the transcription factor itself.

title: Transcription-dependent versus binding-dependent memory
description: Use CRISPRi with dCas9-KRAB or a promoter-directed transcriptional-interference strategy to silence eRNA or nascent transcription at primed enhancers while c-Jun or Fos occupancy remains intact, and separately block transcription of the memory gene itself. Dissociating occupancy from ongoing transcription would show whether memory requires active transcription in the quiescent phase or only a stable bound configuration.

title: Pulse-pattern decoding with microfluidic stimulation
description: Expose cells to AP-1-inducing stimuli in microfluidic devices with systematically varied pulse number, duty cycle, and inter-pulse interval, then measure re-induction after a fixed rest. Fitting the resulting response surface would show whether memory encodes integrated dose, pulse count, or timing, and would give a quantitative rule that a mechanistic model must reproduce.

title: Pulse-chase proteomics of AP-1 dimer stoichiometry
description: Use SILAC or a tagged pulse-chase to measure half-lives and heterodimer composition of Fos, Jun, JunB, and ATF3 after stimulation, quantified by immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry at several time points. A stimulus-induced shift toward long-lived, stable dimer partners during quiescence would identify a protein-level memory that can be tested directly for necessity.

title: Mitotic bookmarking and sister-cell inheritance of the primed state
description: Use HaloTag-tagged c-Jun or c-Fos with single-molecule tracking through mitosis to test whether AP-1 remains on mitotic chromosomes after a pulse, then compare re-induction kinetics between sister cells that inherit the same pulse history. If both sisters inherit the primed state without ongoing AP-1, this supports bookmarking-based memory rather than a per-cell state that resets at division.

title: Nucleosome turnover pulse-chase at AP-1-bound enhancers
description: Express SNAP-tagged H3.3 (or H2A.Z) and measure nucleosome exchange rates at AP-1-bound versus unbound enhancers during and after a transient stimulus using pulse-chase labeling and ChIP-seq. A memory mechanism would predict that enhancers retaining a primed state show slower nucleosome exchange that persists after AP-1 leaves, which is distinct from simply measuring whether the chromatin mark is present.

title: Protein lifetime readout with fluorescent timers
description: Knock in tandem fluorescent timers (or FAST-tagged versions) to JunB, ATF3, and c-Jun to measure the age and half-life of the chromatin-bound AP-1 pool after a stimulus, and pair this with cycloheximide chase and phospho-proteomics. If a long-lived chromatin-bound AP-1 pool or stable post-translational modification predicts response duration, memory may be stored in protein turnover rather than in a chromatin mark.

title: Enhancer-promoter loop persistence after pulse by Micro-C
description: Perform Micro-C or HiChIP on AP-1 target loci at multiple time points after a transient pulse. Test whether loops that formed during stimulation persist after AP-1 is gone and after the promoter is transiently silenced with CRISPRi. Loop persistence independent of transcription would point to 3D genome architecture as the memory substrate, which ATAC or histone-mark profiling cannot detect.

title: Information-theoretic quantification of memory capacity from AP-1 pulses
description: Deliver AP-1 pulses varying in duration, amplitude, and spacing, then use single-cell reporter readouts at several later times to estimate the mutual information between pulse history and the subsequent response. A genuine memory mechanism should carry more information about the past than a simple decaying dose-response model predicts. Test this by comparing against a fitted null model that uses only the current AP-1 level.

title: Ectopic landing-pad test of locus-autonomous memory
description: Integrate a primed AP-1 enhancer and a naive copy into the same site-specific landing pad at a neutral genomic locus, then compare retention of the primed state. If memory follows the transplanted enhancer sequence regardless of native chromatin context, the substrate is local DNA/chromatin; if it depends on the native locus, it is a genome-wide or trans-acting state.

title: Single-molecule residence-time tracking of JUN and FOS
description: Tag endogenous JUN and FOS with HaloTag and use single-molecule tracking in naive versus primed cells to measure chromatin-bound dwell times and bound fraction. This tests whether memory is encoded as a change in factor residence kinetics rather than in occupancy, which bulk ChIP cannot distinguish.

title: Phosphosite knock-ins and pulse-chase of phosphorylation
description: Knock in non-phosphorylatable or phosphomimetic alleles at JUN and FOS regulatory sites (for example JUN Ser63/Ser73) and track phosphoprotein half-lives by pulse-chase phosphoproteomics after priming. Persistent phosphorylation or altered protein turnover after mRNA returns to baseline would show that memory resides in the protein modification state rather than in transcription.

title: SLAM-seq separation of AP-1 target mRNA synthesis and decay
description: Use metabolic RNA labeling (SLAM-seq or 4sU) to separately estimate synthesis and degradation rates of AP-1 targets during and after priming. A post-stimulus increase in mRNA half-life, especially if it depends on 3′UTR AU-rich elements, would indicate that memory is encoded as altered mRNA stability rather than as a persistent transcriptional program.

title: Metabolic gating of memory via acetyl-CoA supply
description: During the rest phase, vary acetyl-CoA availability with ACLY inhibition, acetate supplementation, or glucose withdrawal, and trace 13C-glucose or 13C-acetate into histone acetylation at primed enhancers. If re-induction tracks acetyl-CoA-dependent acetylation rather than AP-1 levels, memory is metabolically gated and AP-1 may be a reader rather than a writer of the primed state.

title: Pulse-chase labelling of parental histones at memory enhancers
description: Use inducible SNAP- or Halo-tagged H3.3 to label nucleosomes present during priming, then quench and chase through one to several cell divisions and pulse-label new histones. Compare retention of parental versus newly deposited marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) at AP-1-bound memory enhancers, with sorted daughter cells, to test whether memory is inherited through recycled nucleosomes rather than through AP-1 itself.

title: Reversible cell-cycle block during the priming window
description: Prime cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus while holding them in G1 with a reversible CDK4/6 or CDC7 inhibitor, or in G2/M with a comparable block, then release and test re-induction. If memory is lost or diluted without DNA replication, it depends on replication-coupled chromatin dilution rather than on a stable, non-replicative state.

title: Signaling-layer memory via feedback-regulator levels rather than transcription factor state
description: Measure ERK-responsive negative feedback regulators (DUSP6, SPRY2/4) and their protein half-lives across the priming and recovery window, then clamp their levels with inducible knock-in or degron alleles during priming. If AP-1 target memory tracks feedback-regulator dosage rather than AP-1 occupancy, the memory resides in the upstream kinase circuit and not in the transcription factor.

title: Mapping bZIP heterodimer partners at memory loci
description: Use proximity labelling (TurboID or APEX) fused to JUN, FOS, ATF3 and JUNB, plus split-HaloTag complementation, to quantify which heterodimer partners occupy memory enhancers before, during and after priming. A persistent shift in partner composition, such as JUN-ATF3 replacing JUN-FOS, would indicate memory is encoded in a stable heterodimer switch rather than in AP-1 binding alone.

title: Acetyl-CoA supply during priming and memory strength
description: Manipulate acetyl-CoA availability during the priming window with ACLY inhibition, acetate supplementation, or a citrate-transporter block, then measure H3K27ac at memory enhancers and re-induction kinetics after washout. A dose-dependent effect on memory strength without changes in AP-1 binding would show that metabolic substrate supply, not AP-1 occupancy, sets how much memory is established.

title: Change in AP-1 heterodimer composition as a stored state
description: Use endogenous HaloTag or degron knock-ins with proximity ligation to track which Fos-family and Jun-family partners (e.g., c-Fos vs. Fra1, JunB vs. c-Jun, ATF3) form dimers at target sites across stimulation and washout. Test whether a persistent shift in partner ratio, rather than AP-1 presence, predicts faster re-induction, then fix a specific dimer using a fusion construct to see if memory changes.

title: Phosphorylation-site knock-ins as a durable mark
description: Generate Fos and Jun phosphosite knock-ins (phospho-null and phospho-mimetic at ERK/JNK-dependent sites) and run phosphoproteomics across a pulse-washout-rechallenge series. If a long-lived phospho-state carries information after total protein has returned to baseline, the phospho-mimetic and phospho-null lines should differ in second-exposure responses even when first-exposure responses match.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse patterns with varied number and spacing
description: Use a light-inducible AP-1 or upstream ERK control to deliver the same total dose as different numbers of pulses and different inter-pulse intervals. Measure how long memory persists as a function of spacing, to distinguish dose-encoded from timing-encoded memory and to identify the interval beyond which prior pulses no longer influence the response.

title: Paused Pol II and nascent transcription after washout
description: Apply PRO-seq or NET-seq at AP-1 target genes during washout to measure paused RNA polymerase II density and elongation competence, independent of chromatin marks. Paused polymerase persisting after AP-1 has left would indicate transcriptional-level memory, and its loss after inhibition of promoter-proximal pause release would test causality.

title: Enhancer-promoter contacts and lamina positioning after stimulus washout
description: Combine DNA FISH or Micro-C at AP-1 target loci with lamina-association mapping (DamID or Lamin-GFP tracking) to test whether looping and nuclear-periphery positioning persist after stimulus removal independently of accessibility. Disrupting cohesin or lamina tethers and then measuring re-induction speed would show whether 3D architecture, rather than chromatin opening, is the memory substrate.

title: Heterologous cross-priming test
description: Prime cells with a pulse that activates AP-1 and then challenge them with an unrelated pathway (e.g., NF-κB, STAT3, or hypoxia) using a dual-reporter panel. If the AP-1 pulse changes responses to the unrelated stimulus, the history is stored at a shared chromatin or cofactor level rather than being specific to AP-1 target genes.

title: Pooled saturation mutagenesis of JUN with separable readouts
description: Build a barcoded c-JUN (or FOS) variant library and sort cells by acute induction versus retained chromatin or transcriptional state after washout, using sort-seq to score each variant on both readouts. Variants that selectively lose retained state while preserving acute activity would map the domains specific to maintaining the state.

title: TurboID mapping of cofactors that persist after AP-1 leaves
description: Fuse TurboID to JUN and label proximal proteins during stimulation and again after washout, when JUN has left chromatin. Proteins still labeled or still chromatin-bound after JUN removal would be candidate memory carriers, such as chromatin remodelers or histone-modifying enzymes, rather than AP-1 itself.

title: Transcriptional burst frequency at the endogenous FOS locus
description: Use MS2 or PP7 stem-loop knock-ins at the endogenous FOS or another immediate early gene locus to measure transcriptional burst frequency and amplitude in single live cells before and after priming. A change in burst frequency that persists through rest, even when mean mRNA has returned to baseline, would show that memory is encoded in promoter firing dynamics rather than bulk expression.

title: Persistence of phosphorylation states of AP-1 factors
description: Quantify c-JUN and FOS phosphosites (e.g., S63/S73) and their turnover by phosphoproteomics across a pulse and rest window. Then test whether non-phosphorylatable or phosphomimetic knock-ins alter re-induction kinetics. Persistent modified states of the factor itself, independent of chromatin, would indicate a post-translational memory layer.

title: Degron removal of AP-1 after priming
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron to remove Fos or Jun after a priming stimulus, then measure chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and the transcriptional response to re-stimulation at days to weeks. If the primed state survives AP-1 loss, AP-1 is needed to establish but not maintain memory; if it collapses, AP-1 is the maintenance mechanism.

title: Tracking AP-1 through mitosis
description: Tag endogenous Jun or Fos with HaloTag or a similar label for live imaging across cell divisions, and run CUT&Tag on sorted mitotic cells to see whether AP-1 stays bound to memory enhancers during mitosis. Then test whether daughter cells inherit accessibility and the primed response. Mitotic retention would support mitotic bookmarking as a memory mechanism.

title: Optogenetic pulse-pattern encoding of AP-1
description: Build light-controlled Fos/Jun constructs and deliver the same total AP-1 dose as pulses of different frequency, duration, or spacing. Compare the resulting memory after a long rest, measured by response strength on re-stimulation, to test whether memory depends on dose, timing, or pattern.

title: Activity-dependent tagging and manipulation of AP-1-active cells in vivo
description: Use an activity-dependent system (such as a TRAP-style tamoxifen-inducible Fos reporter) to permanently label AP-1-active cells during a learning or immune-challenge event in vivo. Later reactivate or ablate the labeled cells to test whether they are necessary and sufficient for the memory-driven response, which tests causation in a living animal.

title: Lineage-barcoded multiomics of trained immunity
description: Introduce a DNA barcode into hematopoietic progenitors, prime them in vivo with a single AP-1-driving stimulus, and run single-cell multiome (RNA plus ATAC) on barcoded clonal descendants months later. Compare primed and unprimed clones to determine whether AP-1-dependent memory is carried by specific progenitor lineages and whether it is heritable across the clone.

title: Chromatin persistence after AP-1 withdrawal
description: Use a degron-tagged JUN or FOS that can be switched on for a short pulse and then removed within minutes, and track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac, and AP-1 occupancy (CUT&Tag) at primed enhancers over days to weeks. If the enhancer state outlasts AP-1 binding, that supports a self-sustaining memory rather than one dependent on ongoing transcription factor activity.

title: Base or prime editing of AP-1 motifs at endogenous enhancers
description: Use base or prime editing to mutate AP-1 motifs (TGAnTCA) at individual memory-associated enhancers, leaving neighboring sequence intact, and test whether priming and recall are lost. This separates motif-dependent occupancy from downstream feedback loops and identifies which sites are necessary for memory.

title: Lineage-barcoded memory tracing across divisions
description: Combine a live AP-1 activity reporter with heritable DNA barcodes and single-cell multiome readout to ask whether a cell's past AP-1 activation predicts its response to a later stimulus, including after mitosis. This tests whether memory is inherited through cell division, a core requirement for a cellular memory mechanism.

title: Re-stimulation kinetics after factor depletion
description: Prime cells with a brief AP-1 pulse, fully deplete JUN or FOS with an auxin-inducible degron, then re-stimulate with a fixed dose. Measure the speed and magnitude of target gene induction compared with naive cells. Faster, stronger induction without the factor present would indicate that memory is stored in chromatin or cofactor states rather than in factor levels.

title: Multi-week in vivo cofactor dependence screen
description: After a defined inflammatory or stress challenge in mice, use conditional knockouts or inhibitors of cofactors such as p300, BRD4, or SWI/SNF components at different times to see which ones must stay active for AP-1-driven chromatin changes to persist. Tissue-level CUT&Tag and ATAC-seq over weeks would show whether the memory is maintained by a cofactor-dependent chromatin state.

title: Time-resolved AP-1 degradation after a learning-like stimulus
description: Use auxin-inducible degrons on endogenous c-Fos and JunB to remove AP-1 at defined windows after a learning-like stimulus, then score later recall. This tests whether memory requires AP-1 during induction, during a consolidation window, or only at retrieval.

title: Persistence of AP-1 motif accessibility after stimulus washout
description: Track AP-1 motif accessibility and occupancy in single cells with paired ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag over days after stimulus removal, separating chromatin states that persist from transcription that has returned to baseline. This could be done in primary neurons or T cells, with the key readout being whether accessibility outlasts AP-1 binding.

title: Enhancer-level memory tested by re-induction kinetics
description: Measure how quickly previously stimulated enhancers respond to a second stimulus, using CRISPRi or dCas9 blocking of AP-1 sites and CUT&RUN for H3K27ac and 3D contacts. The test is whether faster or stronger re-induction depends on enhancer marks that outlast AP-1 occupancy.

title: Optogenetic reactivation of AP-1-tagged cells to test sufficiency
description: Label cells that were active during an AP-1 pulse with a light- or drug-inducible tag, using activity-dependent tagging systems adapted to AP-1 target promoters. Then reactivate only the tagged cells optogenetically and test whether a behavior or downstream program is restored, i.e. whether reactivating the tagged population is sufficient to recall the state.

title: In vitro reconstitution of AP-1 on nucleosomal templates with signal withdrawal
description: Reconstitute AP-1 with nucleosome-containing templates in vitro using purified Fos/Jun and defined chromatin. Measure dimer dwell time, nucleosome remodeling, and residual accessibility after the activating signal is removed. Use phosphosite or bZIP domain mutants to separate binding-dependent from remodeling-dependent memory.

title: Degron-based AP-1 removal after priming
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, then use an auxin or dTAG degron to acutely deplete endogenous c-Jun or c-Fos and re-stimulate at timed intervals. Measure whether primed enhancers still re-induce faster and stronger than naive ones, to test whether AP-1 is needed to maintain the memory or only to establish it.

title: Lineage-barcoded single-cell memory tracing
description: Combine CRISPR lineage barcodes with single-cell multiome (scATAC plus RNA) to follow cells through days of divisions after a transient AP-1-inducing stimulus. Track whether AP-1 motif accessibility and primed gene responses persist in clonal descendants and how they vary between clones, to distinguish heritable chromatin memory from stochastic re-induction.

title: Synthetic AP-1 write-and-read recorder
description: Build a genetic circuit in which a synthetic AP-1-responsive promoter drives an irreversible recombinase or base-editor 'write' event, with a separate reporter to read it out. Vary stimulus dose and duration, then measure how long the recorded state persists without input, to test whether AP-1 activity alone is sufficient to create durable memory.

title: Live-cell imaging of AP-1 mitotic bookmarking
description: Tag endogenous Fos and Jun with a live-cell reporter and image their chromatin occupancy through mitosis in synchronized cells, complemented by CUT&RUN on sorted mitotic cells. Whether AP-1 stays bound to memory-associated enhancers during division would indicate whether bookmarking transmits memory to daughter cells.

title: In vivo Fos-TRAP tagging and AP-1 blockade on reactivation
description: Use an activity-dependent Fos-TRAP tag to label cells engaged by a defined in vivo experience, then profile their chromatin accessibility at AP-1 sites weeks later. Reactivate the tagged cells after selectively blocking AP-1 in them, to test whether AP-1-dependent chromatin states are required for the later response.

title: Washout chromatin persistence test
description: After a defined AP-1 stimulus (e.g., PMA or EGF) is washed out, track CUT&RUN for Fos/Jun, ATAC-seq, and H3K27ac over days. Memory is supported if enhancer accessibility and transcription persist after AP-1 occupancy has already left.

title: Degron-based necessity test for AP-1 memory
description: Use auxin-inducible degron knock-ins of Fos or JunB to remove AP-1 at set times after a priming stimulus, followed by re-challenge. If the faster or stronger re-induction depends on AP-1 being present during priming, AP-1 is necessary for the memory, not just correlated with it.

title: Optogenetic pulse-pattern encoding
description: Use light-inducible Jun/Fos variants to deliver pulses that differ in frequency, duration, and spacing at equal total dose. Measure enhancer state and re-response afterward to test whether memory encodes pulse history rather than cumulative exposure.

title: Epigenome-editing dissociation experiment
description: Target dCas9-KRAB or dCas9-p300 to AP-1 motifs to erase or write chromatin marks without changing AP-1 binding. If the memory follows the edited chromatin state rather than the presence of the transcription factor, the chromatin state, not the factor, carries the memory.

title: In vivo barcoded lineage recording of AP-1 history
description: Use an AP-1-responsive enhancer to drive a heritable barcode recorder, and track it through divisions in vivo (e.g., during infection or stress) with scRNA-seq and ATAC readouts. Determine whether AP-1-experienced cells pass their primed state to daughters and for how many generations, as a direct test of memory across cell divisions.

title: Enhancer occupancy persistence after stimulus washout
description: Knock in endogenous HaloTag or degron-tagged FOS and JUN, and track single-cell AP-1 occupancy and enhancer accessibility by live imaging and CUT&Tag for days after a transient stimulus is removed. Memory requires that occupancy or chromatin state outlast both the signal and the transcriptional output, so a decoupling of these timescales would be the key result.

title: Acute AP-1 depletion after an optogenetic AP-1 pulse
description: Drive FOS:JUN activity with a light-inducible dimerization system for a short pulse, then acutely degrade AP-1 with an auxin-inducible degron at a later time point. If the downstream gene program and enhancer state are maintained without AP-1, the response is self-sustaining, which is a defining property of a memory mechanism.

title: Mitotic inheritance of AP-1-induced states via lineage barcoding
description: Barcode cells with lentiviral lineage tags, apply a single AP-1 pulse, and use paired single-cell ATAC and RNA profiling to follow the response through multiple divisions. Quantify how many generations the enhancer state and transcriptional response persist, with and without Polycomb or H3K27ac perturbation, to test whether memory is transmitted through cell division.

title: Mitotic bookmarking and faster re-activation
description: Use live imaging of tagged FOS and JUN through mitosis to measure whether AP-1 stays bound to chromosomes, then compare how quickly target enhancers reopen in daughter cells with and without retained AP-1. Depleting candidate bookmarking factors would show whether retention is required for the faster reactivation.

title: Sequential-stimulation test of re-induction in mouse tissue
description: In mice, deliver a first AP-1-driving stimulus, wait weeks to months, then deliver an identical second stimulus. Measure the speed and magnitude of re-induction of target genes and chromatin opening using a time-stamped reporter. A faster or stronger second response, independent of the direct effects of the first stimulus, would indicate memory in vivo.

title: Degron washout time-course for memory necessity
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on c-Jun or Fos to remove AP-1 after a defined priming stimulus. Then re-challenge at intervals and track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and reporter re-induction. If memory persists after degradation, AP-1 is needed for establishment but not maintenance; if it disappears, AP-1 itself is the maintenance mechanism.

title: Optogenetic pulse-train coding of AP-1 history
description: Drive a light-inducible AP-1 dimerizer or nuclear-shuttling construct with pulse trains that vary in number, spacing, and frequency while holding total dose constant. Then measure a downstream enhancer reporter days later in single cells to test whether memory encodes timing and not just cumulative exposure.

title: Mitotic inheritance of AP-1 occupancy
description: Combine live-cell imaging of endogenously tagged Fos/Jun through mitosis with CUT&RUN or CUT&Tag on FACS-sorted daughter cells at G1 entry. Test whether AP-1 remains bound to memory enhancers during mitosis, and whether its loss at specific sites predicts failure to re-activate in daughters, which would establish mitotic bookmarking as the heritable step.

title: In vivo rechallenge with cell-type-specific AP-1 knockout
description: Delete Jun or Fosb conditionally in a defined population (for example, monocytes or tissue-resident macrophages) after a primary inflammatory or stimulatory insult, then rechallenge weeks later and measure the secondary response with scRNA-seq and chromatin profiling. Comparing the memory response in knockout and wild-type animals tests whether AP-1 is required for memory in vivo, not just in culture.

title: Single-molecule residence time of c-Jun at memory enhancers
description: Use single-molecule tracking (e.g., HaloTag-based) to measure c-Jun residence time on chromatin in cells with and without a prior stimulus. Then test whether sites with prolonged residence are the ones that retain accessibility, and whether mutating the bZIP dimer partner or the binding motif shortens residence and erases the memory.

title: Degron-timed AP-1 removal after a stimulus pulse
description: Use auxin-inducible degrons on endogenous Fos and Jun, remove the proteins at defined times after a stimulus pulse, and measure whether the primed transcriptional response to a second stimulus persists. If the memory survives AP-1 loss, AP-1 is required for induction but not for maintenance of the memory.

title: Locus-specific necessity via epigenetic editing of AP-1 sites
description: Use dCas9-based epigenetic silencers or site-specific mutations to block AP-1 occupancy at individual enhancers, then run time-course ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN after a pulse. Persistent chromatin accessibility that disappears only when AP-1 binding is blocked at a given site would show that the memory is written locally at that enhancer.

title: Single-cell recorder of AP-1 activity history
description: Engineer a barcoded or fluorescent-timer AP-1 reporter that records the cumulative history of AP-1 activity in each cell, then sort cells by recorded history and challenge them with a second stimulus. If differences in second-stimulus responses track the recorded history, AP-1 activity is stored at the single-cell level rather than being an average population effect.

title: Optogenetic pulse-pattern test at constant total dose
description: Drive AP-1 activity with optogenetic or chemogenetic inputs using different frequencies, durations, and interval patterns while holding total dose constant, then measure the response to a later challenge. If memory depends on temporal pattern rather than total dose, AP-1 acts as a temporal integrator and memory store rather than just a dose-responsive switch.

title: Cell-intrinsic memory after removal from the in vivo environment
description: Tag cells that experienced AP-1 activity in vivo using a Fos-CreERT2 or TRAP-style system, isolate them, and transplant or culture them without the original signal before challenging them. If tagged cells keep a primed response after removal from the in vivo environment, the memory is cell-intrinsic and not carried by the surrounding tissue niche.

title: Washout time-course with inducible AP-1 degradation
description: Test whether an AP-1-dependent transcriptional state outlasts the stimulus. Pulse cells with a defined stimulus, wash it out, and use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron to remove c-Fos or c-Jun at different times. Track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac, and target-gene expression over days. If the state persists after AP-1 protein is gone, AP-1 triggers a self-sustaining state rather than being the memory itself.

title: Priming test under interference
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, then expose them to unrelated stressors or competing signals before re-stimulation. Compare the speed and magnitude of the second response (CUT&RUN for AP-1 occupancy plus nascent transcription, e.g., NET-seq or 4sU labeling) with unprimed controls. A memory should still produce a faster or stronger response despite the intervening conditions.

title: Lineage-resolved memory with a live AP-1 reporter
description: Test whether the memory is heritable using a fluorescent AP-1-responsive reporter or a FosTRAP-style lineage recorder, following single cells through several divisions by time-lapse microscopy. Measure whether daughter cells inherit the primed state and whether the fraction that retains it decays on a predictable schedule, as expected for a memory rather than a transient response.

title: Necessity and sufficiency of AP-1 binding sites for memory maintenance
description: After priming, use CRISPRi/dCas9-KRAB or base editing to disrupt AP-1 motifs at specific enhancers, or use optogenetic AP-1 pulses to re-engage them at defined times. If memory depends on continued binding, site disruption should erase it; if it persists, the site was needed only to establish the state. Compare with knockouts of chromatin modifiers (e.g., p300/CBP or BRD4) to separate initiation from maintenance.

title: Cross-context generalization of AP-1 memory
description: Prime cells or an in vivo tissue (e.g., a Fos-based engram labeling system in neurons or a stimulated epithelium) with one stimulus, then challenge with a different stimulus, cell type, or dose. Use single-cell multiome to determine whether the same enhancers and gene modules are reused in the new context; reuse of the same primed loci across contexts would argue for a genuine memory mechanism rather than a context-specific response.

title: Stimulus-withdrawal time course with AP-1 and chromatin readouts
description: Pulse cells with a stimulus (e.g., TPA or growth factor), withdraw it, and track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for Fos/Jun), ATAC-seq, and H3K27ac at target enhancers over days. Memory requires these marks to persist after AP-1 protein and mRNA return to baseline.

title: Inducible AP-1 degradation during the memory window
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron tag on endogenous c-Fos or c-Jun to remove AP-1 protein at defined times after a priming stimulus, then re-challenge. If AP-1 is the memory mechanism, degrading it after priming should abolish the faster, stronger secondary response, while degradation before priming should not.

title: Re-stimulation kinetics as a memory readout
description: Define memory as a primed-versus-naive difference in the second response: compare the latency, amplitude, and duration of AP-1 target gene induction (single-cell RNA-seq or smFISH) after a rest period. Repeat with AP-1 binding-site mutants at primed enhancers to test whether faster reactivation depends specifically on AP-1 motifs.

title: Single-cell lineage tracking of heritable AP-1 states
description: Combine a live AP-1 reporter (e.g., a Fos-promoter destabilized fluorophore or a Fos-TetOff-to-Cre lineage recorder) with time-lapse imaging to follow cell fate across several divisions. Heritable, bimodal persistence of the reporter after the stimulus is gone would show a self-maintaining state rather than a transient response.

title: AP-1 motif mutation at persistent enhancers with feedback-loop modeling
