description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at enhancers that stay open after stimulation, then measure persistence of chromatin marks and gene expression. Fit a bistable feedback model (AP-1 inducing its own enhancers and chromatin remodelers) to the data, to test whether memory requires the positive feedback loop or only an epigenetic mark that AP-1 deposits.

title: Washout-and-recall time course with inducible AP-1 degradation
description: Pulse a stimulus to activate AP-1, then acutely degrade c-Jun/c-Fos with an auxin- or dTAG-inducible system either during the pulse or only after washout. Track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN), and transcription at AP-1-bound enhancers over days to weeks, then re-challenge with the same stimulus. If AP-1 is required for memory, degrading it after washout should erase the faster or stronger second response, while degradation during the initial pulse should not.

title: Enhancer motif mutation to test whether AP-1 sites are necessary for retention
description: Use CRISPR base editing or homology-directed repair to mutate the TGAC/TCA AP-1 motifs in the enhancers of memory-associated genes, leaving neighbouring sequence intact. Compare accessibility, H3K27ac, and priming of these loci after a stimulus and during a rest period, against wild-type and against sites that bind other factors. Persistence that depends on the intact motif would support AP-1 as the carrier of memory rather than a bystander.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1-experienced cells
description: Combine a Fos-driven recombinase or TRAP reporter with a heritable lineage barcode and single-cell multiome (scRNA + scATAC) to tag cells that activated AP-1 during a stimulus. Follow them after washout and during re-stimulation to test whether the tagged subset is a stable, heterogeneous population that responds faster, and whether memory is carried by a minority of cells rather than uniformly across the population.

title: Dilution-independent persistence across divisions and quiescence
description: Label a stimulus-experienced population with a live AP-1 reporter and a division-tracking dye, then separate cells into quiescent and proliferating fractions over a long rest period. Measure whether AP-1-dependent accessibility and priming decay with division, dilution, or time alone, and compare the decay curve with that of stable marks such as DNA methylation or H3K4me1. This separates epigenetic memory from a transient signaling state that persists only while the cell stays alive.

title: Chromatin conformation persistence after AP-1 activity ends
description: Perform Micro-C or Hi-C at AP-1-responsive loci at several timepoints after stimulus removal, together with live-cell imaging of locus distance in reporter lines. Test whether AP-1-formed enhancer-promoter loops remain after AP-1 is no longer bound and whether they are required for faster re-induction; loops outlasting AP-1 occupancy would indicate structural memory, and CTCF or cohesin depletion would test whether the loops are necessary.

title: Chromatin persistence after stimulus washout
description: Pulse cells with a transient AP-1 stimulus (e.g., TPA or EGF), then measure AP-1 occupancy (Fos/Jun CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and H3K27ac at each time point after withdrawal. Memory requires that accessibility or enhancer marks persist longer than AP-1 binding.

title: Degron-mediated AP-1 removal during the quiescent interval
description: Prime cells with a first stimulus, then use an auxin-inducible or dTAG degron to deplete Fos or Jun during the rest period before a second stimulus. If the faster or stronger re-induction of target genes disappears only when AP-1 is removed in the gap, AP-1 is necessary to carry the memory, not just to read it out.

title: Primary versus secondary response with enhancer motif mutants
description: Use CRISPR base editing or prime editing to disrupt individual TRE/AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers, then compare primary and secondary responses of nearby genes in wild-type and mutant clones. A memory mechanism predicts that losing a specific motif selectively abolishes the faster secondary response while leaving the first response intact.

title: Heritability of AP-1 state through mitosis
description: Use a knock-in Fos or Jun live reporter with lineage tracking to sort cells by prior AP-1 history and follow them through several divisions, then test whether daughter cells retain the primed response. Live imaging of chromatin binding during mitosis (mitotic bookmarking) will show whether AP-1 stays bound across division, which would make the memory cell-heritable.

title: Single-molecule residence time versus memory duration
description: Measure the chromatin residence time of AP-1 subunits by single-molecule tracking or FRAP in live cells, and pair it with pulse-chase protein half-life measurements (SNAP/HaloTag). Test whether a longer-lived or more stably bound AP-1 population predicts how long the memory lasts across perturbations such as cycloheximide or stabilizing mutants.

title: Washout time course of AP-1 occupancy versus chromatin state
description: After a defined stimulus pulse, remove the stimulus and sample at multiple time points with AP-1 (JUN/FOS) CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq. A memory mechanism predicts that accessibility and H3K27ac at AP-1-bound enhancers outlast AP-1 occupancy, whereas a simple transcriptional response predicts that all decay together. The difference in decay kinetics is the test.

title: Re-stimulation priming assay with time-gated AP-1 depletion
description: Give cells a priming stimulus, wait a rest interval, then re-stimulate and measure the speed and magnitude of target gene induction. Use an auxin-inducible degron on JUN or FOS to deplete AP-1 either during the rest interval or only during re-stimulation; if memory relies on AP-1, depleting it during rest should abolish faster re-induction, while depleting it only during re-stimulation should not.

title: Sequential ChIP for histone marks at sites lacking AP-1
description: Perform sequential ChIP-seq for AP-1 followed by H3K4me1, H3K27ac, or H3K4me3 at memory-associated enhancers, comparing primed cells after a rest period with naive cells. If the marks remain at sites where AP-1 is no longer bound, memory is likely carried by chromatin state rather than continued AP-1 occupancy.

title: Single-cell heritability test with an AP-1-responsive lineage barcode
description: Pair an AP-1-responsive reporter (for example an Fos-promoter-driven recombinase or tTA system) with a heritable lineage barcode, then pulse the stimulus and track whether reporter-positive or memory-positive states persist through several cell divisions. Heritable retention across generations without continued stimulation supports a self-maintaining memory, while rapid dilution through divisions supports a transient response.

title: Perturbing AP-1 dimer composition during the rest interval
description: Use dominant-negative or ectopic c-Jun/ATF3/JDP2 variants to alter AP-1 dimer composition during the quiescent window and measure both chromatin accessibility at memory loci and re-induction kinetics. Because different dimers differ in stability and chromatin-opening capacity, a memory mechanism predicts that specific composition shifts change persistence of primed states, while a purely reactive, non-memory role predicts no effect on the difference between rest-period and reactivation states.

title: Chromatin persistence after AP-1 washout
description: Pulse cells with a stimulus, wash it out, and track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for c-Jun/c-Fos) alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac over days. If accessibility and enhancer marks outlast AP-1 binding, the state is carried by chromatin rather than by the transcription factor, which is the core prediction of a memory mechanism.

title: Acute AP-1 depletion during the inter-stimulus interval
description: Prime cells with one stimulus, then use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on Fos or Jun to remove AP-1 during the rest period before a second stimulus. Memory is defined as faster or stronger re-induction; if the primed advantage disappears only when AP-1 is degraded during the gap, AP-1 is required to store the memory and not just to read it out.

title: Mutating AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing to mutate AP-1 motifs on individual primed enhancers, with each mutation mirrored on a matched control enhancer. Then measure whether persistence of accessibility, H3K27ac, and re-induction kinetics are lost, to test whether motif occupancy at specific loci is necessary for the memory.

title: Lineage-resolved tracking of primed states through division
description: Combine an AP-1-responsive fluorescent reporter with lineage barcoding and time-lapse imaging to follow single cells after priming. Test whether daughter cells inherit the primed state and whether it fades without reactivation, which distinguishes self-sustaining epigenetic memory from a transient signaling state that is reset.

title: Protein turnover and bistability modeling
description: Measure the half-lives of Fos, Jun and Fra1 with SNAP/HaloTag pulse-chase and FRAP, then build a kinetic model with and without an AP-1-dependent feedback loop. Test whether the model with feedback predicts a long-lived, bistable primed state that persists longer than protein turnover alone allows, and whether that prediction holds in the unstimulated state.

title: Persistence after signal withdrawal
description: Pulse cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus (e.g., TPA, EGF, or LPS), wash it out, and track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for c-Jun/c-Fos), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and nascent transcription (PRO-seq) at target enhancers over days. Memory requires that the altered state outlasts the stimulus, so loci that stay open or bound after the signal is gone are the strongest candidates.

title: Inducible degron depletion during the quiescent gap
description: Tag endogenous JUN or FOS with an auxin-inducible degron (e.g., AID2), prime cells, then degrade the factor during the quiescent interval before re-challenge. If AP-1 stores the memory, degradation should erase the primed chromatin state and the faster reinduction; if the primed state survives, AP-1 is only a readout of an independent store.

title: Re-stimulation kinetics at primed versus naive loci
description: Compare first and second responses to the same stimulus, measuring time-to-peak, fold induction, and the number of activated AP-1 target genes, alongside locus-specific CRISPR deletion or mutation of individual AP-1 motifs. A memory mechanism predicts faster, stronger reinduction that depends on the specific motifs at primed enhancers, not on global AP-1 levels.

title: Single-cell AP-1 reporter with lineage tracing
description: Build a fast-degrading AP-1 reporter (destabilized fluorescent protein under AP-1 response elements) and track single cells through several divisions after stimulus pulses of different duration and frequency. Heritable, history-dependent reporter states that persist across mitosis and correlate between sister cells would indicate stable cellular memory rather than a transient response.

title: Mitotic inheritance of AP-1-marked chromatin and in vivo conditional knockout
description: Prime cells, arrest them in mitosis, and use mitotic ChIP or ATAC on sorted mitotic cells to test whether AP-1 and its primed accessibility persist on chromosomes through division. Repeat in vivo with a tissue-specific Fos or Jun conditional knockout, priming with a repeated inflammatory or injury stimulus and challenging weeks later, to test whether the memory requires AP-1 at the organismal level.

title: Degron-based AP-1 removal after priming
description: Give a transient priming stimulus, then use an acute degron system (dTAG or AID) to deplete c-Fos or c-Jun at set times afterward. Measure whether the primed response (faster or stronger reinduction of target genes on a second stimulus) survives AP-1 protein loss. Persistence without AP-1 indicates a chromatin-based memory, while loss of the primed state shows AP-1 is required to maintain memory.

title: Time-resolved chromatin persistence at AP-1 sites
description: After one brief stimulus, profile AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for Fos/Jun), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and histone marks such as H3K27ac at multiple time points until AP-1 returns to baseline. Sites that stay open or marked after AP-1 is gone, and that predict faster transcription on re-exposure, are the strongest candidate memory marks. Adding an AP-1 perturbation at this stage separates the marks from the transient binding that caused them.

title: Pattern-dependent optogenetic AP-1 pulsing
description: Use a light-inducible AP-1 construct (e.g., a LOV-domain-controlled Fos/Jun) to deliver pulses that vary in number, frequency, and spacing. Test which temporal patterns produce a lasting primed state and whether memory depends on pulse history rather than total AP-1 dose, i.e., whether AP-1 encodes information in its dynamics.

title: Activity-tagged ensemble reactivation test
description: Label cells that were AP-1-active during a learning-like stimulus using an activity-dependent reporter (for example, a TRAP-style Fos-CreER system), then re-expose the animal or culture to a partial cue and check whether the tagged cells reactivate preferentially. Compare with animals or cultures carrying a Fos loss-of-function or dominant-negative allele. Selective reactivation of tagged cells that depends on AP-1 function would show that AP-1 marks memory-encoding cells.

title: Single-cell AP-1 history predicts future response
description: Use a live knock-in fluorescent reporter of AP-1 activity to track individual cells through repeated stimuli, recording each cell's prior AP-1 pulse history. Test whether that history predicts the magnitude and speed of the cell's response to a later stimulus, and whether AP-1 inhibitors such as T-5224 erase this predictive relationship. A history-dependent response that disappears with AP-1 inhibition directly links AP-1 activity to cellular memory.

title: Acute AP-1 depletion during the interval between stimuli
description: Use an inducible degron (e.g., auxin-inducible) on endogenous FOS or JUN to remove AP-1 during a washout window after a priming stimulus. Then re-stimulate and compare second-response gene induction with that in unperturbed cells. If AP-1 stores the memory, depletion during the interval should abolish the faster or stronger re-induction at its target genes.

title: Time-resolved persistence of AP-1 occupancy and chromatin marks
description: Run CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for FOS/JUN, together with ATAC-seq and H3K27ac, at multiple time points during stimulus, washout, and days-long rest. A memory mechanism predicts AP-1 binding or accessibility that outlasts the transcriptional response at a subset of enhancers, with persistence that tracks the length of the original stimulus.

title: Motif-specific mutation of AP-1 sites in a defined enhancer
description: Use CRISPR to mutate only the AP-1 motifs in a defined enhancer, or to replace them with a non-AP-1 binding site, while keeping the surrounding sequence and nearby transcription factor sites intact. Then measure whether priming and re-induction behavior is lost, which would show that the memory depends on AP-1 binding itself rather than on the locus or general enhancer activity.

title: Lineage-stable reporter of cell-state memory across divisions
description: Combine an activity-dependent Fos reporter or FosTRAP-style recorder with single-cell lineage barcoding, and follow the marked cells through several divisions and days after stimulus. If AP-1 maintains a memory, reporter-positive lineages should keep a primed transcriptional state and faster response even when AP-1 protein has returned to baseline.

title: Separating AP-1 protein persistence from mitotic chromatin bookmarking
description: Combine cycloheximide or other protein-synthesis blockers, and a light-inducible AP-1 nuclear export switch, with the re-stimulation assay to test whether memory needs ongoing AP-1 protein or only the chromatin state it left behind. Mitotic chromatin retention assays, such as live imaging of AP-1 on mitotic chromosomes, test whether AP-1 stays bound to its sites through division.

title: Washout and re-stimulation priming test
description: Pulse cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus (e.g., TPA or EGF), wash out, and wait through a quiescent interval. Then re-stimulate and compare naive and primed cells by time-resolved RNA-seq and ATAC-seq. Memory is supported if primed cells show faster or stronger induction of AP-1 target genes, and the advantage disappears when the interval is extended. Persistence after stimulus removal serves as the control.

title: Acute degradation of c-Jun or c-Fos during the quiescent interval
description: Tag endogenous c-Jun or c-Fos with a degron (e.g., dTAG or AID) and degrade it after priming but before re-stimulation. If the primed response survives loss of AP-1 protein, memory is stored in chromatin or other marks rather than in the transcription factor; if the advantage is lost, AP-1 must be continuously present to maintain memory.

title: Heritable lineage recording of AP-1 activity history
description: Drive a stable reporter (Cre-loxP switch, or a CRISPR-based cumulative recorder) from AP-1-responsive enhancers so that each past AP-1 activation leaves a permanent, heritable mark. Sort or image cells by mark and track their clonal descendants, to test whether prior AP-1 activity is inherited through divisions and predicts later responses.

title: Motif-level mutagenesis of memory-associated enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing or prime editing to mutate AP-1 motifs in candidate enhancers one at a time, leaving other elements and baseline transcription intact. Then test whether each mutation removes the priming-dependent gain in re-induction without affecting the first response, separating the role of AP-1 binding in memory from its role in initial activation.

title: Enhancer mark persistence by CUT&RUN with p300/CBP or BRD4 inhibition
description: Map AP-1 (Fos/Jun family) occupancy, H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and Pol II pausing by CUT&RUN and ChIP-seq at multiple time points after priming, including the quiescent phase. Then inhibit p300/CBP or BRD4 during the interval to test whether retained enhancer marks are required for faster re-induction. If memory depends on these marks, blocking their maintenance should erase the primed response while leaving the first response intact.

title: Stimulus washout and chromatin persistence time course
description: Stimulate cells with a defined AP-1 inducer (e.g., TPA or EGF), then withdraw it and profile AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for c-Jun/c-Fos) and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) at multiple time points over days. Memory predicts that AP-1 sites stay open or bound after the signal is gone; compare these sites with sites that return to baseline. Washout separates true memory from ongoing signaling.

title: Re-stimulation test for faster or stronger secondary response
description: Compare naive cells with cells that had a prior stimulus and washout, then re-stimulate both and measure AP-1 target gene induction (RNA-seq or smFISH) and the speed and amplitude of the response. A memory mechanism predicts a faster or larger response in primed cells, and this effect should disappear when AP-1 is acutely depleted with an auxin or dTAG degron during the interval. Use single-allele knock-in reporters so the readout is not confounded by copy number.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Use an inducible degron tag on c-Jun or c-Fos to remove AP-1 at different stages: during the initial stimulus, during the washout interval, or just before re-stimulation. Then determine which stage is needed for the memory signature (chromatin marks, transcriptional priming, and altered response). This shows whether AP-1 is required to maintain the memory or only to establish it, i.e., whether the factor must stay bound to keep the state.

title: Inducible AP-1 reporter and lineage tracking in single cells
description: Build an inducible AP-1 activity reporter (e.g., a tamoxifen-dependent FosTRAP-style recorder or a destabilized fluorescent Fos-responsive reporter) and follow single cells by live imaging or lineage tracing across divisions. Memory predicts that cells that once had high AP-1 activity keep a heritable, altered response state in their progeny after the signal is gone. Also test whether pulse frequency, not just total exposure, sets the state.

title: Mathematical model with a falsifiable memory signature
description: Build an ODE or stochastic model of AP-1 feedback (for example, AP-1 inducing its own Fos/Jun expression and chromatin opening) and fit it to the time-course and re-stimulation data. Compare a model with a bistable or hysteretic chromatin switch to one with purely transient signaling, and design a perturbation that the two models predict differently, such as a timed pulse or a partial degradation. This tests whether the data require a memory mechanism, ruling out a transient response that only resembles memory.

title: Washout time course testing persistence and bimodality of chromatin marks
description: Pulse cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus, wash it out, and track AP-1 site accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac, and AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) at memory loci over days. A memory mechanism predicts that marks persist after stimulus removal and that the population splits into bimodal states rather than decaying smoothly, as expected for a bistable switch.

title: Degron-based necessity test during the quiescent interval
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron to deplete FOS or JUN only during the quiescent window after stimulation, then re-challenge and measure whether primed (faster or stronger) transcription of memory genes is lost. This separates AP-1 needed to maintain the memory from AP-1 needed only for the initial response.

title: Mitotic inheritance across cell divisions
description: Induce AP-1 transiently, sort cells by FACS at several generations after washout, and measure chromatin state and re-stimulation responses in daughter cells. Persistence through divisions, especially when AP-1 protein is absent, would indicate heritable, self-maintained memory rather than a direct readout of ongoing AP-1 activity.

title: Dose-timing and delay-dependent recall assay
description: Pre-stimulate with varying doses and durations, then re-challenge after increasing delays and fit the decay of the primed response to estimate memory half-life and recall strength. Repeat with DNA-binding-deficient or site-mutant AP-1 at the memory enhancers; a memory mediated by AP-1 should be abolished or shortened in these mutants.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of heterogeneous memory states
description: Combine a live AP-1 reporter with lineage barcoding and single-cell multiome sequencing to follow individual cells after stimulation, asking whether memory is retained in a subset of cells with a stable chromatin state. This state should predict later responses, and its persistence should correlate with AP-1 occupancy at specific enhancers rather than with reporter signal alone.

title: Persistence of AP-1-driven chromatin opening after stimulus washout
description: Pulse cells with a defined stimulus, then wash it out and track FOS/JUN occupancy (CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq) alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac at AP-1 enhancers over days. If AP-1 is a memory mechanism, enhancer accessibility and marks should outlast the decline in AP-1 binding, and the duration should scale with the length of the priming pulse.

title: Primed versus naive re-stimulation kinetics
description: Compare first and second exposures to the same stimulus after a rest period, measuring the timing, amplitude, and recruitment speed of AP-1 binding and target gene transcription (nascent RNA-seq, qPCR time courses). A memory mechanism predicts faster and stronger responses on re-exposure, and this advantage should disappear when AP-1 binding sites are mutated.

title: Time-resolved AP-1 depletion during priming, rest, and recall
description: Use a dTAG or auxin degron on endogenous JUN or FOS (or an optogenetic AP-1 switch) to remove AP-1 separately during the priming pulse, the rest interval, and the re-stimulation. Memory is expected to be lost only when AP-1 is depleted during the interval or at recall, not when depleted only during priming, giving a causal test of necessity at each phase.

title: Single-cell lineage tracking of AP-1 history across divisions
description: Combine a live AP-1 reporter (for example a destabilized FOS-GFP or an AP-1-responsive fluorescent sensor) with time-lapse imaging and lineage barcoding to test whether a cell's prior AP-1 activity predicts its response to a later stimulus and whether this predictive value is inherited by daughter cells. Quantify heritability (for example with variance decomposition) to separate true memory from transient, stimulus-driven variation.

title: Mitotic bookmarking test of AP-1-marked enhancers
description: After priming, sort or image cells in mitosis and measure whether AP-1 and its associated enhancer marks remain on DNA through mitosis (live imaging of tagged JUN, mitotic ChIP-seq). Then check whether daughter cells re-activate target genes faster on the same stimulus. Retention through division is a strong criterion for stable cellular memory, and loss of bookmarking with preserved memory would argue against AP-1 being the carrier.

title: Stimulus washout and persistence time course
description: Give a brief AP-1-inducing stimulus (e.g., TPA or EGF pulse, or a doxycycline-inducible FOS/JUN pulse), then withdraw it and track AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and target transcription over days. Memory requires that AP-1 target enhancers stay open or primed after AP-1 itself has returned to baseline, so persistence beyond the signal is the key readout.

title: Re-stimulation of primed versus naive cells with AP-1 motif mutation
description: Compare the first and second responses to the same stimulus, measuring AP-1 target induction, Pol II loading, and enhancer accessibility. Memory predicts faster or stronger re-induction in previously stimulated cells. Also mutate AP-1 motifs at the primed enhancers with CRISPR to test whether the memory depends on those specific sites.

title: Inducible degradation of AP-1 during the memory window
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-based degron on endogenous FOS or JUN to remove AP-1 after priming but before re-stimulation. If AP-1 is the memory carrier, degradation should erase the re-induction advantage while leaving the first-response induction intact. Timing the degradation separately from the priming stimulus separates maintenance of memory from its initial establishment.

title: Coupled AP-1 and histone-mark profiling across time
description: Perform ChIP-seq or CUT&Tag for H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and H3K4me3 alongside AP-1 binding over the same time course. Memory-like behavior would show persistent activating marks at AP-1-bound enhancers after AP-1 has left them. Comparing these marks with a DNA-methylation or histone-mark-writer knockout shows whether the memory is chromatin-based or relies on AP-1 alone.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1 state heritability
description: Combine an AP-1 reporter or live-cell FOS/JUN readout with lineage barcoding to follow individual cells through several divisions after a pulse. Quantify how strongly AP-1 activity state in one generation predicts the state in descendants, and whether that correlation disappears when AP-1 is knocked down. Heritable, AP-1-dependent states would indicate cellular memory rather than simple reversible signaling.

title: Post-stimulus persistence of chromatin accessibility
description: Pulse cells with a defined AP-1 inducer (e.g., TPA or EGF), then wash out and track AP-1 occupancy (JUN/FOS CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and H3K27ac at AP-1 motifs over days. Memory requires that accessibility and enhancer marks remain after JUN/FOS binding has returned to baseline.

title: Acute JUN/FOS degradation after priming
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, then use an auxin-inducible degron to rapidly deplete JUN or FOS before re-stimulation. If primed responses and retained enhancer states survive depletion, the memory is carried by downstream chromatin rather than continued AP-1 presence. If they are lost, AP-1 itself is required to maintain the memory.

title: Binding-site dependence via dCas9 and motif mutants
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs at endogenous memory-associated enhancers. Separately, tether dCas9-p300 or dCas9-KRAB to these sites while leaving AP-1 motifs intact. Compare retention of the primed transcriptional response to determine whether specific AP-1 binding is necessary and whether writing a chromatin mark is sufficient.

title: Sister-cell lineage tracking of AP-1 activity states
description: Use a live AP-1 transcriptional reporter (destabilized fluorescent protein under an AP-1-responsive enhancer) with time-lapse microscopy to track cell lineages through several divisions. Measure whether prior high or low AP-1 history is heritable across sister cells and predicts later responses to a second stimulus, separating true memory from transient signaling noise.

title: Mitotic bookmarking and memory across cell division
description: Sort mitotic cells from primed and unprimed populations and perform ATAC-seq and AP-1 occupancy assays on mitotic chromatin to see whether AP-1 sites stay accessible during mitosis. Then test whether daughter cells retain the primed state, and whether blocking mitotic bookmarking factors removes the memory.

title: Persistence of chromatin state after AP-1 washout
description: Use an inducible AP-1 system (e.g., 4-OHT-activated FOS-ER or a dTAG-tagged JUN) to pulse AP-1 activity, then remove the inducer and track ATAC-seq, H3K27ac, and AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN) at target enhancers over days. If AP-1 is a memory mechanism, chromatin opening and reinduction capacity should persist after AP-1 protein returns to baseline.

title: Timed degron depletion to separate maintenance from encoding
description: Acutely degrade AP-1 (dTAG or auxin degron on JUN/FOS) at different times after priming: during induction, during a quiescent interval, and at late timepoints. If AP-1 is required only for encoding, degradation after the interval should not erase the memory; if AP-1 is continuously required for maintenance, the primed response will be lost. The readout is target-gene reinduction on re-stimulation.

title: Re-exposure kinetics with motif-mutant enhancers
description: Compare first- and second-exposure transcriptional kinetics (e.g., nascent RNA by TT-seq or smFISH) at endogenous loci, wild-type versus CRISPR-edited TGAGTCA (TRE) motifs in the enhancers. A memory role predicts faster or stronger second responses that disappear when the AP-1 site is mutated, while priming that is not memory would not depend on the motif.

title: Lineage-tracked AP-1 reporter for heritable memory
description: Express a destabilized live reporter of AP-1 activity (e.g., FOS promoter-driven d2EGFP) in cells, then track single-cell lineages by time-lapse imaging across several divisions after a transient stimulus. Test whether prior AP-1 activity history predicts the magnitude of future responses in daughter cells, and whether that correlation decays with generation number.

title: Scrambled-motif and matched-control statistical design
description: Perform JUN/FOS ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN and H3K27ac profiling at matched timepoints after stimulus, comparing AP-1-bound sites to a control set of shuffled or scrambled TRE-like motifs and GC/accessibility-matched random genomic regions. A memory mechanism should show sustained, AP-1-motif-dependent signal at lasting sites that exceeds what generic priming produces at the controls, so that any pattern found is specific rather than a sequence-composition artifact.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN after a transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with injury, TNF, or growth factor), then profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at multiple time points through washout and weeks later. Persistent AP-1 motif-containing open regions after signal withdrawal would indicate retained chromatin memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation or dominant-negative perturbation during priming vs. recall
description: Use degron-tagged JUN/FOS or A-FOS to remove AP-1 either only during the priming stimulus, or only during the later challenge. If memory needs AP-1 during priming (for establishment) and/or recall (for maintenance), enhancer accessibility and the faster or stronger secondary transcriptional response will be lost accordingly.

title: Prime-and-rechallenge transcriptional response assays
description: Measure RNA-seq or nascent transcription (PRO-seq) and single-cell responses to a second stimulus after varying rest intervals in primed versus naive cells. Link response magnitude to pre-existing AP-1 occupancy at each gene's enhancers, and map how long the memory lasts and how many cell divisions it survives.

title: Sufficiency test with optogenetic or chemically inducible AP-1
description: Briefly induce AP-1 using optogenetic or chemically inducible FOS/JUN, with no natural stimulus. Then test whether it creates stable accessible enhancers, histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) and an altered response to later signals, including after cell division. This tests whether AP-1 activity alone is sufficient to establish memory.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing in vivo
description: Use scATAC+RNA with lineage barcodes or AP-1 reporter/fate-mapping alleles in tissue such as skin wound repair, to follow descendants of previously AP-1-active cells. Compare their accessibility and function with those of AP-1-naive siblings, and test whether the memory is inherited through division and linked to AP-1 recruitment of BAF (SWI/SNF) and other chromatin remodelers.

title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or keratinocytes) to a defined, transient AP-1-activating stimulus (such as TPA, injury, or inflammatory cues), then perform ATAC-seq/CUT&Tag for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN) and H3K27ac at time points from hours to weeks after washout. Persistent AP-1-bound accessible sites after stimulus removal, relative to naive controls, would indicate memory.

title: Acute AP-1 perturbation during priming, maintenance, or re-stimulation
description: Use dTAG/AID degrons or dominant-negative A-FOS to deplete AP-1 only during the priming phase, only during the memory/maintenance phase, or only during the re-stimulation phase. If memory requires AP-1 for establishment but not maintenance (or vice versa), this distinguishes whether AP-1 is the initiator, the carrier, or only a reader of the memory.

title: Primed versus naive transcriptional response assays
description: Compare primed and naive cells upon second stimulation using RNA-seq, nascent transcription (PRO-seq/TT-seq), and live reporters, testing for faster or stronger induction of AP-1 target genes. Correlate the magnitude of the recall response with prior AP-1 occupancy at the corresponding enhancers to link AP-1 binding to functional memory.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Apply single-cell RNA+ATAC and clonal barcoding to primed populations across cell divisions to test whether AP-1 motif accessibility/activity is stably inherited by daughter cells and whether sister cells share memory states. Pair this with live-cell imaging of endogenously tagged FOS/JUN to see whether heritable differences in AP-1 level or dynamics predict later responses.

title: Locus-specific causal editing of AP-1 sites with chromatin-state readouts
description: Mutate or CRISPR-block individual AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers (or tether activators/repressors via dCas9) and measure whether priming-induced accessibility, histone marks, 3D contacts (Micro-C/HiChIP), and recall expression are lost. Also test whether pioneer-associated partners (e.g., BAF/SWI-SNF, p300) at these sites are required, to distinguish AP-1 as a causal memory element from a correlate.

title: Transient stimulus and washout with chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells to a defined AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or inflammatory cue), then wash out and perform time-resolved ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN, and RNA-seq over days to weeks. Persistence of AP-1-dependent open chromatin and primed gene expression after AP-1 activity returns to baseline would indicate memory.

title: Acute AP-1 removal during encoding versus maintenance
description: Use degron-tagged FOS/JUN or a dominant-negative (A-FOS) to remove AP-1 either during the initial stimulus (encoding) or after the stimulus has ended (maintenance). If blocking during encoding abolishes the enhanced secondary response but later removal does not, AP-1 is needed to establish but not sustain memory; the opposite pattern implies active maintenance.

title: Primed vs naive re-stimulation response assay
description: Compare transcriptional output (RNA-seq, nascent transcription by PRO-seq) and kinetics after a second stimulus in previously stimulated versus naive cells, with varying rest intervals. Quantify faster, stronger, or more sustained induction at AP-1 target genes and correlate it with AP-1 binding and H3K27ac at their enhancers to test functional memory.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Use scATAC/RNA multiome with lineage barcodes or sister-cell pairing to test whether AP-1-linked accessibility states and primed expression are inherited through cell divisions in clonal lineages. Heritability of states beyond what cell type or stochastic variation explains, together with bimodality of states, would support a memory mechanism.

title: Locus-specific AP-1 motif perturbation and artificial memory writing
description: Use CRISPR editing of AP-1 motifs, or dCas9-based recruitment or blocking of AP-1 or chromatin remodelers (e.g., SWI/SNF) at candidate enhancers, together with optogenetic or pulsed AP-1 activation. Determine whether motif loss erases memory and whether a synthetic pulse is sufficient to induce a persistent primed state, testing necessity and sufficiency.

title: Long-term chromatin accessibility tracking after a transient stimulus
description: Expose cells to a defined, transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, growth factor, injury signal), then perform time-resolved ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN and H3K27ac after washout (days to weeks, across cell divisions). Persistence of AP-1-motif-enriched accessible sites, and of AP-1 binding at them, after the stimulus is gone would indicate a memory state.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation or inhibition during versus after priming
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) FOS/JUN or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either only during the priming window or only during the later maintenance phase. If depletion during priming blocks memory but later depletion does not, AP-1 is needed for establishment; if late depletion erases it, AP-1 is needed for maintenance. Readouts are accessibility and the enhanced transcriptional response to re-stimulation.

title: Secondary-challenge transcriptional response in primed versus naive cells
description: Compare RNA-seq or nascent transcription (PRO-seq) after a second stimulus in primed versus naive cells, with and without AP-1 perturbation. Memory predicts faster or stronger induction of specific genes in primed cells, and these genes should be linked to AP-1-bound enhancers that remain open.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing of inheritance
description: Use single-cell RNA+ATAC (or live reporters of AP-1 activity) with barcoded lineage tracing to test whether sister cells share AP-1 target accessibility and expression states after division. Compare the persistence of AP-1 activity and chromatin state within clones against random cell pairs to separate heritable memory from continued upstream signaling.

title: Synthetic AP-1 recruitment to test sufficiency
description: Recruit AP-1 (or a FOS/JUN activation domain) to a reporter or endogenous locus with dCas9 or an inducible system for a pulse, then track whether the locus stays open and active after the recruiter is removed. Combine this with inhibition of pioneer factors or chromatin remodelers (e.g., BAF) and histone modification profiling to test whether AP-1 alone is sufficient to set a self-sustaining state and whether it acts through chromatin remodeling.

title: Long-term chromatin accessibility tracking after a transient stimulus
description: Expose cells to a defined brief AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), then perform ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for AP-1 (FOS/JUN) and H3K27ac at time points from hours to weeks after stimulus removal. Persistent AP-1-motif-enriched accessible regions after the signal has decayed would indicate a memory state, and their re-engagement could be compared with naive cells.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the memory phase
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative (A-FOS) AP-1 to remove function either during the priming stimulus or only after it, then measure maintenance of accessibility and transcriptional responses on re-stimulation. If depletion during priming but not after prevents memory, AP-1 is needed for establishment. If depletion after priming erases memory, it is needed for maintenance.

title: Secondary-challenge transcriptional response assay
description: Prime cells with a first stimulus, rest them, then re-stimulate. Use RNA-seq, nascent transcription (PRO-seq) or single-cell readouts to quantify faster or stronger induction of AP-1 target genes compared with unprimed controls. Test whether the enhanced response is gene-specific, tracks AP-1 binding sites, and persists through cell divisions.

title: Single-cell multiome and clonal tracing of memory inheritance
description: Combine single-cell RNA and ATAC-seq with clonal barcoding or live-cell imaging of AP-1 reporters (e.g., FOS–GFP) to test whether primed accessibility and AP-1 activity states are inherited by daughter cells. Comparing clonal sibling concordance with that of random cell pairs quantifies heritability and heterogeneity.

title: Site-specific perturbation of AP-1 motifs and pioneer activity
description: Use CRISPR base editing or dCas9-based tools to mutate or block AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or force AP-1 binding there with a synthetic recruiter in unprimed cells. Measure whether these changes alter retention of accessibility, histone marks and gene response, to distinguish AP-1 as the cause of memory from AP-1 as a marker. Pair this with BAF/chromatin remodeler inhibition to test the mechanism.

title: Stimulus–washout–restimulation time course with AP-1 perturbation
description: Expose cells to a defined stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), remove it, then restimulate after varying delays and measure the primed transcriptional response (RNA-seq, target gene induction). Compare acute AP-1 inhibition (dominant-negative FOS/A-FOS, degron-tagged JUN/FOS) during priming versus during recall to separate AP-1 requirement for establishing versus maintaining memory.

title: Longitudinal chromatin accessibility and AP-1 footprinting
description: Profile ATAC-seq, AP-1 subunit CUT&RUN/ChIP (FOS, JUN, FOSL), and H3K27ac at baseline, after stimulus, and weeks after stimulus clearance. Test whether AP-1 motif-containing enhancers stay accessible or bound after AP-1 levels return to baseline, and whether the retained sites predict faster or stronger re-induction.

title: Timed AP-1 degradation after memory establishment
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on JUN/FOS family members to deplete AP-1 only after the initial stimulus. Then measure whether enhancer accessibility, pioneer-like remodeling (SWI/SNF/BAF recruitment), and the recall response persist. If memory is maintained without AP-1, AP-1 acts as an initiator; if it is lost, AP-1 is a maintenance mechanism.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and reporter memory
description: Track AP-1 activity (FOS/JUN fluorescent knock-ins, AP-1 reporters) with target-gene reporters in single cells across repeated stimulations and through cell divisions. Quantify whether past activation history, such as pulse number, duration, and frequency, predicts later responses, and whether memory is heritable to daughter cells.

title: Sufficiency by synthetic AP-1 induction, with motif editing and in vivo validation
description: Optogenetically or chemically drive AP-1 transiently in naive cells and test whether this alone produces lasting accessibility and primed responses. Complement this with CRISPR deletion or mutation of specific AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers (or dCas9 epigenetic editing) to test necessity, and with in vivo validation in a model such as skin epithelial wound memory or trained immunity.

title: Longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN after a transient stimulus
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or epidermal stem cells) to a transient stimulus such as injury, TPA, or cytokines. Profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding from hours to weeks after the stimulus is withdrawn. Persistent AP-1-motif-associated accessibility or persistent AP-1 occupancy would indicate a memory-like state.

title: Phase-specific AP-1 degradation or dominant-negative block
description: Use degron-tagged FOS/JUN or inducible dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 activity during the priming phase, the rest (memory) phase, or the recall phase. Then measure secondary-challenge responses by RNA-seq. If AP-1 is required for maintaining memory rather than only establishing it, depletion during rest should abolish the enhanced recall.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage/history tracing
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC-seq on primed versus naive cells, with a fluorescent AP-1 reporter or barcoding to link each cell's past activation to its present state. Test whether cells with prior AP-1 activity keep distinct accessibility and faster transcriptional re-induction, and quantify whether the state is heritable across cell divisions.

title: Live-cell AP-1 reporter imaging and dynamics
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN, or an AP-1 transcriptional reporter, in single cells across repeated stimulation pulses and lineages. Measure whether response amplitude, kinetics, or baseline level depends on prior stimulus history, and whether that dependence persists through mitosis. This distinguishes a stable, self-sustaining state from transient signaling.

title: Targeted epigenome editing and sufficiency tests at AP-1 sites
description: Use dCas9 tools (e.g., dCas9-FOS or dCas9-KRAB) or motif mutation at specific AP-1-dependent enhancers. Test whether opening or closing them alters the response to a later challenge, and whether forcing AP-1 binding in naive cells can mimic memory. Combine this with histone mark profiling (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) and pioneer-factor partner tests (e.g., with BAF/SWI-SNF) to identify mechanism.

title: Long-term chromatin accessibility tracking after a transient stimulus
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, keratinocytes, or macrophages) to a defined, transient AP-1-activating stimulus such as TPA, injury, or inflammation. After the stimulus is removed, run time-resolved ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN family members, H3K27ac, and H3K4me1 over days to weeks and through cell divisions. Persistent open regions containing AP-1 motifs would indicate retained memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation or dominant-negative block during priming versus maintenance
description: Use degron tags (dTAG/AID) or inducible dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during priming or after memory has formed. Measure whether loss during priming prevents memory, and whether later loss erases it (accelerated transcriptional response and retained accessibility). This distinguishes AP-1 as an initiator from AP-1 as a maintainer.

title: Secondary challenge assays with single-cell multiome readout
description: Prime cells, rest them, and then re-challenge with the same or a different stimulus. Use paired scRNA/scATAC-seq to quantify faster, stronger, or more sensitized induction of AP-1 target genes in primed versus naive cells, and relate this to prior accessibility at specific enhancers. Single-cell resolution distinguishes a graded shift in all cells from an all-or-none switch in a subpopulation.

title: Live-cell reporters of AP-1 dynamics and lineage tracing
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or an AP-1 transcriptional reporter in single cells and follow them across divisions with lineage tracking. Test whether past activation history predicts later reporter activity or response in daughter cells, and compute autocorrelation and heritability of the activity state, to show whether the memory is cell-intrinsic and mitotically heritable rather than due to persistent external signals.

title: Epigenome editing and motif perturbation at memory loci
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs, or dCas9-based recruitment (e.g., dCas9-KRAB, dCas9-p300), at specific primed enhancers. Test whether motif disruption blocks retention of accessibility and enhanced re-induction at that locus, and whether forced opening can substitute for prior priming. Add in vivo checks, such as repeated skin wounding or tumor models, to test whether the effects are causal and functionally relevant.

title: Hysteresis curves of AP-1 activity under ramped stimulus
description: Expose cells to ramped-up then ramped-down stimulus (e.g., serum, TPA, or optogenetic ERK/c-Fos drive) and measure AP-1 activity (reporter, FOS/JUN levels, chromatin accessibility) at matched doses. A path-dependent loop, where the same dose gives different outputs on the up and down ramps, would indicate bistability or memory. Compare loop width after blocking AP-1 DNA binding with dominant-negative A-Fos.

title: FOS-driven tagging and reactivation of past-stimulated cells
description: Place a FOS-promoter-driven, inducible Cre/tdTomato tag in cells during a first stimulus, then restimulate days later. Test whether tagged cells respond faster or stronger than untagged neighbors, using live imaging or scRNA-seq. Add AP-1 knockdown between the two stimuli to test necessity for maintaining the memory.

title: Recall kinetics of primed enhancers
description: Profile ATAC-seq, JUN/FOS CUT&RUN, and H3K27ac after a primary stimulus and after a washout period of days to weeks. Identify AP-1-bound enhancers that stay open or marked after the signal ends, then test whether they drive faster transcription on rechallenge. Use CRISPRi or motif mutation at these enhancers to establish causality.

title: Autocorrelation and heritability modelling of AP-1 state in single-cell lineages
description: Track AP-1 reporter state in single cells over time with lineage tracing (time-lapse imaging or barcoding). Estimate the autocorrelation time and heritability of AP-1 state across divisions, and compare sister-cell concordance with random pairs. Fit hidden Markov or ODE models to separate a self-sustaining feedback state from slow decay.

title: Synthetic AP-1 positive-feedback circuit
description: Build a minimal AP-1 circuit with a doxycycline-pulsed JUN/FOS transgene and a positive-feedback AP-1 reporter, and test whether a transient pulse switches it into a stable ON state that persists after withdrawal. Break the feedback by mutating AP-1 sites in the promoter, or alter it by adding a destabilizing degron. The aim is to define the minimal conditions under which AP-1 stores information.

title: Hysteresis assay for AP-1 state
description: Ramp a stimulus (e.g., ERK/JNK activation or a titrated optogenetic c-Fos/c-Jun input) up and then down, and measure AP-1 target expression and chromatin accessibility at matched input doses on each leg. Different outputs at the same dose on the up and down legs (path dependence) would indicate memory, and the loop area would quantify it.

title: Prime–rest–rechallenge design with ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN and dominant-negative A-Fos
description: Give cells a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA or injury signal), allow a washout of days to weeks, then re-stimulate and compare transcriptional kinetics and amplitude with naive cells. Pair this with ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN to test whether sites that remain accessible after priming are those that drive faster, stronger secondary responses, and use dominant-negative A-Fos to test necessity.

title: Survival analysis of single-cell memory duration
description: Estimate the half-life of the memory state by live-cell imaging of AP-1 reporters (e.g., endogenously tagged FOS or an AP-1 GFP reporter) in lineage-tracked cells. Fit survival/hazard models to the time to loss of the state. Test whether the state is inherited across divisions and whether covariates such as cell cycle, histone-mark levels or AP-1 dose predict persistence.

title: Testing bistability of the AP-1 feedback loop
description: Build a mathematical model of the AP-1 loop (FOS/JUN autoregulation plus chromatin opening) and use it to predict bistability. Test this experimentally with single-cell flow cytometry or smFISH to look for bimodal distributions at intermediate input. Also remove AP-1 after induction by CRISPRi or degron (dTAG) to see whether the state sustains itself after the trigger is gone, as bistability predicts, or decays, as monostable dynamics predict.

title: Time-stamped recording of past AP-1 activity with lineage barcoding
description: Use a temporally inducible recorder (e.g., Cre-ER or a DNA-barcode tracer activated by AP-1 activity) to permanently mark cells that experienced AP-1 activation at defined times. Later, isolate marked and unmarked cells and profile them with single-cell multiome (RNA+ATAC) and motif-accessibility analysis to test whether past AP-1 exposure leaves durable, AP-1-motif-centered chromatin changes and altered functional responses.

title: Hysteresis loop mapping
description: Titrate a stimulus (e.g., EGF, TPA, or FOS/JUN induction) up and then down, and measure AP-1 activity (reporter, chromatin accessibility at AP-1 motifs) at each dose. Path-dependent, non-overlapping up and down curves at matched stimulus levels would show bistability-like memory, and the width of the loop would quantify its strength.

title: Priming assay with memory decay kinetics
description: Give a first stimulus, wash out for varied intervals (hours to weeks), then restimulate and compare transcriptional response magnitude and speed to naive cells by RNA-seq and nascent-transcript assays. Define the memory half-life and test whether memory is lost when AP-1 is acutely degraded (dTAG/auxin) only during priming versus only during recall.

title: Persistence of AP-1-dependent chromatin changes after AP-1 loss
description: Use ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN time courses after stimulus removal to test whether AP-1-dependent accessible sites and H3K27ac stay open once AP-1 binding itself disappears. Use footprinting and BAF/p300 occupancy to distinguish sites that retain the chromatin change independently of AP-1 from those needing continued AP-1 occupancy.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1 state inheritance
description: Use live-cell AP-1 reporters (e.g., FOS-GFP, AP-1 kinase translocation reporters) with time-lapse microscopy and lineage tracking through division. Calculate the autocorrelation of AP-1 state between mother and daughter cells and between sisters to determine whether states are heritable beyond what shared cytoplasm or signaling would explain.

title: Feedback-network perturbation and model fitting
description: Build an ODE model of AP-1 with positive autoregulation (the JUN promoter has AP-1 sites) and chromatin-state variables, fit it to dose and time-course data, and predict the effect of breaking the loop. Test the predictions by CRISPR mutation of AP-1 sites at the JUN/FOS loci and optogenetic pulsing of AP-1 factors, looking for loss of the persistent state when the feedback is cut.

title: Hysteresis loop mapping
description: Titrate a stimulus (e.g., TNF, serum, or optogenetic c-Fos/c-Jun induction) up and then down. Measure single-cell AP-1 activity and target-gene expression to test whether the response at identical input depends on prior history, and quantify loop area and decay time after stimulus removal.

title: Bistability testing with live AP-1 reporters and pulsed stimulation
description: Use live-cell AP-1 reporters (e.g., FOS-GFP or AP-1 TRE reporter) with microfluidic pulses of varied duration, frequency and amplitude. Fit single-cell state-transition models to test whether AP-1 supports two stable states and whether transient pulses can flip cells permanently.

title: Time-series profiling of chromatin that persists after AP-1 loss
description: Perform time-series ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors (FOS, JUN) and H3K27ac/H3K4me1, and Hi-C at intervals after stimulus withdrawal. Identify enhancers that remain accessible after AP-1 binding is lost, and test whether persistence correlates with AP-1 motif density and with faster re-induction on rechallenge.

title: Acute AP-1 depletion after the initial stimulus
description: Use a dTAG or AID degron, or dominant-negative A-FOS, to rapidly deplete AP-1 after the initial stimulus and at various later times. Test whether the primed state and the faster second response persist without AP-1 (chromatin-based memory) or are lost (AP-1 self-sustaining memory).

title: Mother-daughter and sister correlation analysis of AP-1 state
description: Perform time-lapse imaging of AP-1 reporter cells with lineage tracking, then compute mother-daughter and sister-cell correlations of AP-1 state across divisions, treating it as a heritable trait. Compare the decay of correlation to that of a non-heritable noise model, and perturb with cell-cycle arrest or CRISPRi of AP-1 positive-feedback loops (e.g., JUN autoregulation) to test mechanism.

title: Hysteresis measurement with up and down dose ramps
description: Ramp the dose of a stimulus (e.g., TPA or growth factor) up and then down in cells, and quantify AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy, chromatin accessibility and target transcription at matched doses. A path-dependent loop, where the same dose gives different outputs on the way up and down, would show that AP-1 retains a memory of past input.

title: Bistability test via single-cell state landscapes
description: Use live-cell reporters of AP-1 activity (e.g., FOS-GFP knock-in) with time-lapse imaging to build single-cell trajectories after transient stimulation. Fit a dynamical-systems (energy-landscape) model and test for bimodal, self-sustaining states that persist after the stimulus is removed.

title: Prime-rest-restimulate recall challenge with AP-1 inhibition during priming
description: Give cells a primary stimulus, rest them for varied intervals, then re-stimulate and measure faster or stronger induction of AP-1 target genes by RNA-seq and ATAC-seq. Compare with naive cells and with cells in which AP-1 is acutely degraded (dTAG) or blocked with a dominant-negative (A-FOS) during priming only, to test whether AP-1 is necessary for the recall response.

title: Information-theoretic analysis of retained enhancer accessibility
description: Use time-resolved CUT&RUN/ATAC at AP-1 motifs after stimulus washout and compute mutual information between past stimulus history and current chromatin state. Ask whether AP-1 motif-containing sites retain more information than other sites. Test causality by CRISPR base-editing of motifs at selected enhancers.

title: Lineage tracing across divisions with sibling-pair and mitotic-bookmarking assays
description: Label cells with a heritable barcode or Cre-based memory reporter at the time of AP-1 activation and follow their daughters for many divisions. Use sibling-pair and mitotic-bookmarking assays (live imaging plus mitotic-chromosome ChIP) to determine whether AP-1 binding or its downstream chromatin marks (H3K27ac, accessibility) are inherited and correlate with persistent expression.

title: Dose-history response curves
description: Expose cells to a ramped-up then ramped-down stimulus (e.g., optogenetic or chemical AP-1/FOS/JUN activation, or TPA/anisomycin) and measure target gene output and chromatin accessibility at matched doses on the up and down ramps. A non-overlapping loop (path-dependent output) indicates memory, and the loop area and the decay time after stimulus removal quantify its strength.

title: Prime–rest–rechallenge assay with kinetic comparison
description: Give a primary stimulus, impose a rest period of varying length, then rechallenge and compare AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN), transcription (nascent RNA-seq) and response speed or amplitude against naive cells. Faster or stronger secondary responses at AP-1 sites, with a defined decay half-life, would indicate memory. As a control, add dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS) only during priming to test whether AP-1 is required to establish the memory.

title: Bimodality and positive-feedback perturbation of a self-sustaining AP-1 state
description: Use single-cell live reporters (JUN/FOS promoter-driven fluorescence) and scRNA-seq to look for bimodal, self-sustaining states after a transient pulse. Then break candidate positive-feedback loops (e.g., JUN autoregulation, via CRISPRi of the AP-1 site in the JUN promoter) and test whether the persistent ON state collapses, which would show the memory is network-encoded.

title: Time-course profiling of chromatin after stimulus removal
description: Profile chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) and AP-1 occupancy at several time points after stimulus removal to find enhancers that stay open after AP-1 leaves. Compare sites where AP-1 persists with sites where only accessibility persists, and use motif and footprint analysis to tell whether AP-1 itself or downstream epigenetic marks retain the history.

title: AP-1 transmission through mitosis with cell-cycle-timed degron depletion
description: Use live imaging of tagged JUN/FOS through mitosis, mitotic-chromosome CUT&RUN, and lineage tracing of sister cells after a stimulus pulse, with acute degron (dTAG) depletion of AP-1 members at different cell-cycle phases. Transmission of memory to daughter cells only when AP-1 is present during mitosis would show a bookmarking-based memory mechanism.

title: Hysteresis analysis of response to rising and falling stimulus
description: Expose cells to a rising and then falling stimulus (e.g., serum/ERK or stress signals) and measure AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy, chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and target transcription at each step. If the up- and down-sweep curves fail to overlap at equal input, and the loop area depends on AP-1 dosage (via dominant-negative A-FOS), the state is history-dependent, as a memory mechanism requires.

title: Primed versus naive re-stimulation with phase-specific AP-1 degradation
description: Give a first stimulus, rest cells for days to weeks until FOS/JUN levels return to baseline, then re-stimulate and compare transcriptional kinetics and amplitude with naive cells (RNA-seq, nascent-RNA 4sU-seq). Test causality by acutely degrading AP-1 (dTAG/AID) only during the priming window versus only during the rest period, to determine when AP-1 is needed to establish versus maintain the memory.

title: Lineage tracing of persistently accessible AP-1-opened enhancers
description: After a transient stimulus, use single-cell multiome (scATAC plus RNA) or CUT&Tag to identify enhancers that stay accessible and marked (H3K27ac/H3K4me1) after AP-1 is no longer present. Pair with a lineage barcode to show that these marks are inherited by daughter cells and that their persistence predicts a stronger secondary response in a clone-specific way.

title: Bistability test with single-cell live imaging and ODE modelling
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and a target-gene reporter live in single cells across pulses of varying duration, then fit ODE models with positive feedback (AP-1 autoregulation at the FOS/JUN promoters). Memory is supported by a bimodal distribution, a critical threshold, and hysteresis. Perturbing the feedback loop (CRISPRi on the AP-1 site in the JUN promoter) should abolish bistability.

title: Mitotic bookmarking by AP-1
description: Test whether AP-1 stays bound to chromatin during mitosis or leaves a pioneer-like footprint, using live imaging of mitotic cells and CUT&Tag/ATAC on sorted mitotic cells. Then follow reactivation of the candidate genes in early G1 with or without AP-1 depletion at mitosis. Retained binding and faster post-mitotic reactivation of these loci versus non-bookmarked controls would show that AP-1 carries information across cell divisions.

title: Hysteresis curves with ramped-up and ramped-down stimulus doses
description: Expose cells to ramped-up then ramped-down stimulus doses (e.g., optogenetic or chemical activation of the AP-1 upstream kinases JNK/ERK) and measure AP-1 target gene output and chromatin accessibility at matched doses. A loop in which the same dose gives different outputs depending on history indicates bistable, memory-like behavior.

title: AP-1-driven lineage tracing of prior AP-1 activity
description: Use an AP-1 (Fos/Jun)-driven inducible Cre or recorder, as in Fos-TRAP labeling, to permanently mark cells that previously had AP-1 activity. Re-challenge the marked and unmarked populations after weeks and compare their transcriptional responses by scRNA-seq to see whether past AP-1 activity predicts a faster or stronger response.

title: Time-course profiling of enhancers that stay open after AP-1 leaves
description: Perform time-course ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors, BAF subunits, and H3K27ac before stimulation, after it, and after a long washout. Identify enhancers that stay open after AP-1 is gone, and test whether AP-1 motif content predicts which loci keep this latent state.

title: Feedback model and timed c-Jun perturbation to test bistability
description: Model AP-1 positive autoregulation (c-Jun promotes its own transcription) as a feedback circuit with ODEs, and predict the conditions for bistability. Then test it by transiently blocking c-Jun with a degron or dominant-negative A-Fos at different times and checking whether the high state persists, collapses, or can be reset, as the model predicts.

title: Recall assay for trained immunity with causal enhancer editing
description: Give cells a first stimulus, rest them, then give a second stimulus. Compare cytokine or target-gene response with and without AP-1 disruption (CRISPR of AP-1 motifs at specific enhancers, or acute degron depletion of Fos/Jun only during the priming window). If loss of AP-1 during priming alone abolishes enhanced recall, AP-1 is needed to establish the memory rather than only to read it out.

title: Primed versus naive hysteresis comparison
description: Pre-stimulate cells (e.g., with EGF, TPA, or a cytokine), withdraw the stimulus for varied rest periods, then restimulate and compare dose-response and induction-kinetics curves of AP-1 target genes against naive cells. Differences in amplitude, threshold, or speed of the second response, plotted across stimulus history, quantify memory.

title: Chromatin-state mapping after signal removal
description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN/ChIP for FOS/JUN, H3K27ac, and BAF remodeler marks, plus footprinting, in primed, rested, and naive cells to test whether AP-1-bound enhancers remain open after the signal is gone. Persistent accessibility at AP-1 motifs that correlates with enhanced re-induction would identify the chromatin carrier of memory.

title: Dose titration of memory erasure
description: Test how much perturbation is needed to erase memory by dose-titrating inhibitors of chromatin remodeling (BRG1/SWI-SNF), histone acetyltransferases, or DNA replication/cell division, and measure when the primed response reverts to the naive state. If memory decays only with disruption of AP-1-dependent chromatin and not with loss of AP-1 protein levels, chromatin structure rather than ongoing AP-1 activity carries the memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation in different time windows
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) JUN/FOS or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 during priming, during the rest period, or during restimulation, then read out the secondary response. Distinguishing a requirement for establishing memory from maintaining or reading it shows whether AP-1 carries the memory or only initiates it.

title: Single-cell, lineage-tracked mapping of AP-1 history to later response
description: Combine live reporters of AP-1 activity (FOS/JUN dynamics) with single-cell RNA/ATAC-seq and lineage tracing across divisions to relate each cell's past AP-1 dynamics to its later response. Heritability of response across sister cells and its decay over generations tests whether memory is cell-intrinsic and stable, as opposed to residual signaling.

title: Ramp-up/ramp-down hysteresis curves of AP-1 target state
description: Titrate a stimulus (e.g., optogenetically or chemically induced c-Fos/c-Jun, or ERK/TPA dose) up and then down in single cells, and measure AP-1 activity and target gene expression at steady state at each dose. Non-overlapping up and down dose-response curves (hysteresis width) would indicate state-dependent memory; compare the width with AP-1 perturbations (e.g., dominant-negative FOS, JUN phosphomutants).

title: Testing whether prior exposure predicts present state, using accessibility and binding
description: After a transient stimulus is withdrawn and current AP-1 and signaling levels are matched to naive controls, use ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag for AP-1 binding to measure enhancer accessibility and test whether prior exposure still predicts accessibility and transcriptional output. Regress the response on exposure history while controlling for present conditions, and determine whether AP-1 motif-containing sites account for the residual.

title: Autocorrelation and critical-slowing-down analysis of live AP-1 reporters
description: Image single-cell AP-1 reporter or endogenously tagged FOS/JUN dynamics over days, and compute autocorrelation time, variance, and relaxation rates after small perturbations at different stimulus doses. Rising autocorrelation and variance near a threshold, plus long relaxation times, indicate bistability or slow feedback, and the memory timescale is estimated directly.

title: Memory decay timescale via re-stimulation after variable rest
description: Give a priming pulse, wait for varied intervals (minutes to weeks, spanning cell divisions), then give a second test pulse and measure changes in response amplitude and kinetics. Fit the decay of the primed-versus-naive response difference to obtain the memory timescale, and compare it with AP-1 level, binding, and chromatin marks to test whether AP-1 is required for persistence.

title: Model-guided AP-1 depletion at different times after priming
description: Build a dynamical model with positive feedback (FOS/JUN autoinduction and chromatin) fit to ramp and relaxation data, and use it to predict thresholds. Test it by acutely degrading AP-1 (degron, CRISPRi) at different times after priming: if AP-1 carries the memory, loss after priming should erase the primed response; if chromatin carries it, the response should persist and could be restored when AP-1 is returned.

title: Washout time course of persistence after withdrawal
description: Give a transient stimulus (e.g., EGF, TPA, or injury signal), then remove it and track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN) and target gene expression over days of washout. Memory is indicated if accessibility and transcriptional priming persist well beyond AP-1 activity returning to baseline.

title: Exposure timing and dose design with re-stimulation and difference-in-differences
description: Compare cells exposed at different times or doses (early vs late, single vs repeated) against matched never-exposed controls, then challenge all with the same second stimulus. Use a difference-in-differences model on the response (gene induction, enhancer opening) to estimate the effect of exposure history, controlling for current AP-1 levels.

title: Lagged-term regression on single-cell multiome data
description: In single-cell RNA plus ATAC time series, regress the current state of target loci on both current AP-1 (FOS/JUN) activity and lagged AP-1 activity or past accessibility. A significant lagged coefficient after conditioning on present AP-1 supports memory, while dependence only on current levels supports regulation by ongoing signaling.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming versus before or during priming
description: Use degron-tagged JUN/FOS (dTAG or auxin-inducible) or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS. Degrade AP-1 only after the priming stimulus, then test whether accessibility and enhanced re-induction persist. Compare with degradation before or during priming to separate the role of AP-1 in establishing memory from its role in maintaining it.

title: Randomly assigned AP-1 pulse exposure by optogenetic or chemogenetic control
description: Use optogenetic or chemogenetic control of AP-1 pulses (such as light-inducible FOS/JUN) so that exposure history is assigned randomly across cells or wells, independent of cell state. Measure later chromatin and transcriptional outcomes as a function of pulse number, duration and timing, which gives causal dose-history relationships free of the selection confounds of endogenous exposure.

title: Stimulus pulse and washout retention assay of AP-1 chromatin state
description: Apply a transient stimulus (e.g., a defined pulse of TPA, a growth factor, or optogenetic c-Fos/c-Jun activation), then wash it out. Track AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), and target gene expression from hours to many cell divisions. Retention is shown if accessibility and output persist after AP-1 activity has decayed to baseline.

title: Dose-sweep hysteresis mapping of AP-1 targets
description: Ramp stimulus intensity up and then down in separate cell populations. Use single-cell readouts such as a reporter or scRNA-seq to measure AP-1 target output at each step. If the up and down response curves differ, with bimodal populations at intermediate doses, the system has hysteresis and bistability, which indicate memory rather than simple tracking of input.

title: Effect of the retained state on later responses
description: After a priming pulse and washout, challenge primed and naive cells with a second stimulus. Compare the speed, amplitude and gene set of the response, including whether it requires AP-1 or only chromatin accessibility. This tests whether the retained state causally changes output.

title: Timed degron or dominant-negative AP-1 perturbation to erase or rewrite memory
description: Add a degron or dominant-negative (e.g., A-Fos) at different times: during priming, only after washout, or at the time of the second challenge. If removing AP-1 after priming erases the memory, AP-1 is needed to maintain it. If removal only during priming blocks it, AP-1 is needed only to establish it, and the memory is held elsewhere (e.g., histone marks or other TFs). Test whether re-pulsing resets the state.

title: Durability testing under repeated stimulation, noise and division
description: Subject primed cells to repeated stimulation cycles, signaling noise (kinase inhibitor, fluctuating ligand), temperature or metabolic stress, and many cell divisions. Use live-cell AP-1 reporters in lineage-tracked single cells to measure how long the state lasts, how often it switches, and whether it is inherited by daughter cells. Fit a stochastic switching model to estimate memory half-life and robustness.

title: Chromatin profiling at multiple times after stimulus withdrawal
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with serum, TPA, or injury signals), then withdraw the stimulus and profile AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, ATAC-seq accessibility and H3K27ac at multiple times (days and cell divisions) after withdrawal. Persistence of AP-1-motif-linked accessible sites without the stimulus and without AP-1 re-expression indicates memory rather than ongoing signaling.

title: Comparison of AP-1 sites across cell states and lineages
description: Compare AP-1-bound enhancers across primed, naive, and descendant cells to classify sites as inherited (retained through divisions and differentiation) versus newly acquired (de novo from current signaling). Use motif grammar and conservation to distinguish stable memory sites from transient ones.

title: Barcoded lineage tracing with single-cell multiome to test heritability
description: Use barcoded lineage tracing with single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) to build clonal trees. Test whether AP-1 accessibility and target-gene expression states are shared among sister cells beyond what the current environment predicts. Phylogenetic-signal statistics (e.g., Pagel's lambda or heritability along the tree) separate heritable memory from convergent responses to shared signals.

title: Quantitative re-stimulation dose-response in primed versus naive cells
description: Measure the kinetics and amplitude of transcription (nascent RNA-seq, live reporters) in primed versus naive cells upon second stimulation. Faster or stronger induction of AP-1 targets in primed cells, quantified across priming doses and rest intervals, gives a memory signature with a measurable decay time.

title: Acute AP-1 removal after priming
description: Acutely degrade or knock out AP-1 (dTAG/AID degron, dominant-negative A-FOS) after priming. Then check whether accessibility and enhanced re-response persist, and whether re-expression is needed to re-open sites. This distinguishes AP-1 as initiator versus maintainer of memory, with other factors carrying it forward.

title: Time course of AP-1 binding and chromatin opening after stimulus
description: After a defined stimulus (e.g., serum, TPA, injury, or inflammatory cue), run time-resolved ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN family members, and H3K27ac at many time points during and long after signal withdrawal. Determine which AP-1-bound enhancers stay open or primed, and for how long, to establish whether a persistent record exists and how it decays.

title: Reading AP-1 imprints from sequential stimulation histories
description: Use single-cell multiome (scATAC plus RNA) with footprinting or motif-deviation analysis on sequential stimulation histories, such as stimulus A then B, to identify AP-1 imprints from each stimulus. Test whether sites opened by the first stimulus (AP-1-dependent) are distinguishable from sites opened by the second, and whether AP-1 subunit composition (FOS vs JUN vs ATF) encodes the identity of the earlier stimulus.

title: Naive versus pre-exposed cell response comparison
