description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus, wash out, rest them, then challenge with the same or a different stimulus. Compare transcription kinetics (nascent RNA, PRO-seq) and amplitude against naive cells, and test whether the faster or stronger response at primed loci depends on prior AP-1 occupancy.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at different times
description: Use degron (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative (A-FOS) tools to remove AP-1 during priming, during the rest period, or only at the challenge. Whether memory needs AP-1 only at priming, only during maintenance, or only at re-challenge separates establishment, maintenance and readout roles. Pair this with CRISPR mutation of specific AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers to test sufficiency and necessity at individual loci.

title: Numerical modeling of memory dynamics with lineage tracing
description: Fit a mathematical model (bistable or hysteretic feedback, including AP-1 positive autoregulation of JUN/FOS and chromatin-state inertia) to time-course and dose-response data, and predict memory duration and decay by cell division. Validate by live-cell imaging of AP-1 reporters or fluorescent FOS and by sister-cell or lineage tracking, testing whether the state is inherited through mitosis, with mitotic bookmarking assays (imaging and CUT&RUN on mitotic cells).

title: Threshold comparison across graded stimulus doses or durations
description: Expose cells to graded doses or durations of an AP-1-inducing stimulus (e.g., serum, TPA, injury, inflammatory cue) and use single-cell imaging or scRNA-seq to compare cells just above versus just below the activation threshold. Test whether a sharp jump in later enhancer accessibility and gene responsiveness appears at the threshold, which would indicate a switch-like memory rather than a smooth dose-response.

title: Time-course linking past AP-1 occupancy to later responses
description: Perform longitudinal ATAC-seq, FOS/JUN CUT&RUN, and H3K27ac profiling in the same cell lineage before, during, and long after transient stimulation, after AP-1 levels return to baseline. Regress secondary response strength on prior AP-1 binding at each enhancer to test whether previously occupied sites remain accessible and more responsive after the original input is gone.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation restricted to the initial stimulus or the restimulation
description: Use a dominant-negative AP-1 (A-FOS) or a degron-tagged JUN/FOS to remove AP-1 either only during the initial stimulus or only during the later restimulation. Determine whether memory requires AP-1 only at the encoding stage, or also at maintenance and recall; the two windows should dissociate if so. This separates AP-1 as a causal carrier of memory from correlated factors such as chromatin remodelers or other transcription factors.

title: Control loci and control stimuli for specificity
description: Compare AP-1 motif-containing loci that were never bound with those that were, and compare cells given an unrelated stimulus (e.g., a different signaling pathway) with AP-1-stimulated cells. Add motif-mutation or CRISPR-edited enhancer controls so that any retained accessibility or priming is shown to be specific to prior AP-1 binding and not to general stress or cell-state changes.

title: Lineage tracking of transmission across divisions
description: Track lineages with live reporters or barcoded clones to measure whether the primed state persists through cell divisions and decays at a defined rate. Perturb candidate carriers (BAF/SWI-SNF recruitment, pioneer cofactors, histone marks, mitotic bookmarking of AP-1) to identify which mechanism transmits the memory, and fit a quantitative model to heritability versus decay.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation or inhibition after the stimulus
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus (e.g., serum, TNF, or an injury signal). After the stimulus is removed, acutely deplete AP-1 at defined delays using degron-tagged FOS/JUN or a dominant-negative (A-FOS), and measure whether the enhanced response to a second stimulus is lost. If memory requires AP-1 during the retention window and not only during priming, this separates maintenance from encoding.

title: Site-specific disruption of AP-1 motifs at enhancers
description: Use dCas9-based tools or base-editing motif mutation to block or remove AP-1 motifs at specific enhancers that gained accessibility after priming. Then test whether transcription of the linked genes upon re-stimulation is selectively reduced, which tests whether specific AP-1-marked loci causally carry the memory for particular downstream genes.

title: Decoding past stimulus history from AP-1 state
description: Collect single-cell multiome data (ATAC with AP-1 motif accessibility/ChromVAR, FOS/JUN levels) from cells with different prior stimulus histories (type, dose, duration), and train classifiers to decode that history from AP-1 features alone after a washout. Compare decoding from AP-1 features with decoding from other TFs or random features to test whether AP-1 specifically stores the information.

title: Washout-delay and distractor experiments to define retention timescale
description: Vary the washout interval between prime and challenge (hours to weeks, across cell divisions) and insert an unrelated pathway activator in between, while measuring AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN/ChIP) and secondary response magnitude. The decay curves of AP-1 binding and response, and their robustness to the added stimulus, define the memory timescale and whether memory survives division.

title: Live-cell reporters with sufficiency test by driving AP-1 in naive cells
description: Image endogenous-tagged FOS/JUN dynamics and an AP-1 target reporter in single cells with lineage tracking, testing whether past AP-1 activity levels predict later responses in the same cell and in daughters. Then drive AP-1 optogenetically or chemically in naive cells, without the original stimulus, to test whether AP-1 activity alone is sufficient to install the primed, persistent response.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-and-chase
description: Use light-inducible FOS/JUN (or optogenetic dimerization) to deliver defined pulses of AP-1 activity without any upstream signal, then measure whether a transient pulse alone leaves a lasting transcriptional or accessibility state and how its duration depends on pulse dose and frequency. This separates AP-1 sufficiency from upstream signaling.

title: Acute degron removal at different phases to separate maintenance from establishment
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN family members with dTAG/auxin degrons and deplete them only during priming, only after priming (during the memory interval), or only at recall. If memory requires AP-1 to persist, post-priming depletion should erase it, whereas a requirement only for establishment indicates AP-1 acts as an initiator of another memory carrier.

title: Single-cell AP-1 reporter lineage tracking by live imaging
description: Track endogenous AP-1 activity (knock-in fluorescent FOS/JUN or a synthetic TRE reporter) in individual cells and their daughters through division using time-lapse microscopy. Correlate pre-stimulus or ancestral AP-1 history with later response magnitude. Mother-daughter correlation beyond that explained by shared noise would show heritable memory at the single-cell level.

title: Perturbation of the AP-1 positive-feedback loop with mathematical modeling
description: Rewire or break the FOS/JUN autoregulatory loop (e.g., mutate TRE sites in the JUN/FOSL1 promoters, or add a synthetic feedback) and fit dynamical models to dose-response and hysteresis measurements. Observing bistability or hysteresis that is lost when the loop is cut would test whether AP-1 network topology itself encodes memory.

title: Targeted motif editing and dCas9 tethering at specific memory enhancers
description: Use base editing to mutate individual AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and conversely tether AP-1 or pioneer-like activation domains with dCas9 at motif-null sites. Measure locus-specific persistence of accessibility, nucleosome remodeling (e.g., SWI/SNF/BAF recruitment), and faster re-induction to establish locus-level sufficiency and necessity.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-pattern test of memory
description: Use optogenetically controlled FOS/JUN dimerization or nuclear translocation to deliver defined pulse patterns (duration, frequency, amplitude), then measure whether past pulse history alters later transcriptional output and enhancer opening after a long rest. This separates memory encoded by AP-1 dynamics from memory encoded by upstream signaling.

title: Single-molecule tracking of AP-1 residence on nucleosomal sites over time
description: In live cells, use HaloTag-JUN/FOS single-molecule imaging to compare residence times, bound fraction, and nucleosome engagement at primed versus naive loci or cells, including after stimulus removal. Longer-lived binding or altered search kinetics in primed cells would show a persistent molecular state rather than just a lingering chromatin mark.

title: Barcoded sister-cell lineage tracing through cell division
description: Split sister cells after priming, then track them with lineage barcodes and paired scRNA-seq/scATAC-seq. Test whether AP-1 activity states and primed responses are inherited across divisions and decay at a rate predicted by AP-1 turnover. High sister-cell concordance would indicate heritable memory rather than ongoing signaling.

title: Targeted epigenome editing to separate AP-1 sites from memory
description: After priming, use dCas9 tools (dCas9-KRAB, a TET/DNMT module, or CRISPR mutation of single AP-1 motifs) at selected primed enhancers. Test whether the recall response requires the AP-1 motif, the local chromatin state, or both, and rescue with AP-1-independent synthetic pioneer factor recruitment to determine whether AP-1 carries the memory or only establishes it.

title: Mathematical modeling of bistability with perturbation-based fits
description: Build ODE and stochastic models of AP-1 feedback loops (such as FOS/JUN autoregulation and chromatin positive feedback), then test the predicted hysteresis, critical slowing, and bimodal switching by titrating the priming dose and measuring recall in single cells. Agreement between model predictions and observed dose-history dependence would show whether AP-1 network topology can sustain memory.

title: Degron-based separation of establishment and maintenance
description: Use an acute degron (dTAG/AID) on JUN/FOS family members and degrade them only after priming but before re-challenge. If memory persists without AP-1 protein, it is stored elsewhere. If it is lost, AP-1 is needed for maintenance, not just establishment.

title: Optogenetic or synthetic AP-1 pulses to encode memory
description: Drive AP-1 with a light-inducible FOS/JUN or a synthetic AP-1 transactivator using defined pulse durations and frequencies, without the upstream stimulus. Then measure target-gene response to a later challenge to test whether AP-1 activity alone is sufficient to write memory, and how its dose and dynamics set memory strength.

title: Lineage-tracked inheritance of memory through division
description: Combine live imaging of an AP-1 reporter and a target-gene reporter with lineage tracking across several divisions after a transient stimulus. Compute mother-daughter and sister-cell correlations and the decay half-life, to test whether the memory state is mitotically heritable and clonal rather than a transient signaling effect.

title: Targeted AP-1 motif editing and synthetic AP-1 site insertion
description: Use base editing to mutate specific AP-1 motifs at a memory-associated enhancer, and insert AP-1 sites at a non-memory locus. Measure whether the locus gains or loses primed accessibility and faster re-induction, to test cis-level necessity and sufficiency.

title: Single-molecule footprinting of AP-1 residence and nucleosome occupancy
description: Apply single-molecule footprinting (e.g., Fiber-seq or SMF) and live single-molecule tracking of JUN/FOS before and after stimulus washout. Read out whether individual enhancer molecules stay nucleosome-free or bound, and measure AP-1 residence times. This distinguishes a stable remodeled state from continuous AP-1 occupancy, and from a bistable or hysteretic switch.

title: Optogenetic or degron pulse-chase of AP-1 timing
description: Use an optogenetically controlled or auxin-degron c-Jun/Fos to deliver defined activity pulses and to remove AP-1 at set times after priming (not only during it). If memory persists after degradation, AP-1 only initiates it; if memory decays when AP-1 is removed, AP-1 maintains it.

title: Single-molecule live imaging of residence time and re-binding
description: Track endogenously HaloTagged Fos/Jun by single-molecule tracking at defined loci (e.g., with a CRISPR-based locus label) in primed and naive cells. Test whether priming changes residence time, search kinetics, or the fraction of bound molecules, and whether the changes persist after AP-1 levels return to baseline.

title: AP-1 site editing and dCas9 recruitment at a single enhancer
description: Mutate or insert AP-1 motifs at a single memory-associated enhancer, or tether dCas9–Fos/Jun or dCas9–repressor to it. Test whether this locus alone is necessary and sufficient to give primed accessibility and a faster re-response, which separates causal local memory from global effects.

title: Pioneer-factor cooperation and nucleosome positioning test
description: Compare MNase-seq nucleosome maps and BAF (SWI/SNF) occupancy at AP-1 sites after priming. Apply acute BRG1 inhibition or degradation after priming to test whether AP-1-dependent remodeling holds sites open, and whether other factors such as CEBP, ETS, or glucocorticoid receptor are needed to maintain memory.

title: Lineage tracing of memory through cell division with 3D genome readout
description: Prime cells, track their lineages for several divisions by barcoding or live-cell imaging, and test the response in descendants. Add Micro-C or HiChIP at AP-1 enhancer–promoter loops and mitotic bookmarking assays on mitotic chromosomes, to determine whether AP-1-linked states are inherited and whether they depend on retained AP-1 or on a copied chromatin state.

title: Acute degron depletion after priming and before recall
description: Use an auxin/dTAG degron on an AP-1 member (e.g., FOS/JUN) and deplete it only after the priming stimulus is gone but before recall. Then measure whether enhancer accessibility and the faster recall transcription persist. This distinguishes AP-1 as maintainer of memory from AP-1 as only the initiator.

title: AP-1 motif editing at endogenous enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing or prime editing to mutate or insert single AP-1 motifs at selected enhancers. Then test whether a motif is necessary and sufficient for stimulus-induced accessibility that persists, and for primed re-induction of the linked gene.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse encoding with memory decay kinetics
description: Drive AP-1 with light-controlled FOS/JUN, or with a light-gated activator, using defined pulse durations, amplitudes and frequencies. Measure how long the primed state lasts and how it scales with dose. Bistability, hysteresis, or a threshold would indicate a self-sustaining memory circuit; simple decay would not.

title: Lineage-tracked memory inheritance through division
description: Barcode or live-image single cells, let them divide after priming, and sort sister cells. Measure AP-1 activity (reporter) and accessibility/recall response in sisters and in later generations, and compare sister concordance with that of random pairs. High concordance lasting many divisions in cells with no ongoing stimulus would indicate heritable memory.

title: Profiling nucleosomes and cofactors for AP-1 retention or handoff through mitosis
description: Run CUT&Tag for AP-1, SWI/SNF (BRG1/ARID1A) and p300, plus MNase or single-molecule footprinting, in interphase and mitotically arrested primed cells. Test whether AP-1 stays on the DNA through mitosis (bookmarking) or is replaced by other factors that keep the sites open. Then perturb the candidate partner to determine which one carries the memory.

title: Optogenetic/chemogenetic test of AP-1 pulse sufficiency
description: Use a light- or drug-inducible FOS/JUN (or degron-controlled) to deliver a defined transient AP-1 pulse in the absence of any natural stimulus, then test whether the cells show durable enhancer opening and enhanced responses to a later, unrelated cue. This separates sufficiency of AP-1 for imprinting from correlative occupancy.

title: Time-resolved degron: priming-only vs maintenance-only vs recall-only depletion
description: Use an acute auxin/dTAG degron on endogenous AP-1 factors and deplete them only during the priming window, only during the maintenance interval, or only at recall. Memory that requires AP-1 for establishment but not maintenance, or for both, distinguishes a trigger mechanism from a self-sustaining memory mechanism.

title: Synthetic enhancer reporters to test AP-1 motif sufficiency in cis
description: Integrate matched reporter constructs with wild-type, mutated, or spacing-altered AP-1 motifs (plus neighboring motifs such as ETS/CEBP) at a fixed genomic safe-harbor locus, and measure whether they acquire and keep a primed state after transient stimulation. This tests whether AP-1 motifs are sufficient in cis to encode memory independent of native context.

title: Single-cell lineage-tracked inheritance across divisions
description: Label sister cells with barcodes or time-lapse lineage tracing, with an endogenous AP-1 reporter, and compare memory strength (recall response) among sisters and cousins over several divisions. Heritable correlation beyond what is explained by AP-1 levels would indicate mitotic transmission, and mitotic-chromatin imaging or CUT&Tag of mitotic cells would test mitotic bookmarking.

title: Single-molecule dynamics and SWI/SNF dependence
description: Perform live-cell single-molecule tracking of Fos/Jun residence times at primed versus naive enhancers, and combine this with inhibition or degradation of SWI/SNF (BAF) to test whether sustained accessibility requires continual AP-1–BAF recruitment. Long residence times or BAF dependence would indicate an active mechanistic basis for memory, as opposed to a passive epigenetic remnant.

title: Acute degron depletion during maintenance versus priming
description: Use an auxin/dTAG degron on endogenous JUN/FOS family members and deplete AP-1 only during the maintenance phase (after the priming stimulus is gone) versus only during priming. If memory needs AP-1 only for establishment and not maintenance, AP-1 is not a self-sustaining memory mechanism; persistent dependence would support it.

title: Motif-mutated enhancers with epigenetic readout
description: Use CRISPR base editing to mutate single AP-1 sites at memory-associated enhancers. Then test whether primed accessibility, nearby H3K27ac, and faster re-induction of the target gene are lost. This tests whether the sites themselves are needed at specific loci, in contrast to global AP-1 loss.

title: Single-molecule residence imaging of FOS/JUN
description: Use live-cell single-molecule tracking of Halo-tagged FOS/JUN, with FRAP, in naive versus primed nuclei. Test whether residence time or bound fraction stays elevated at primed loci for days after the stimulus. This distinguishes lasting engagement from reactivation of binding.

title: Heritability through mitosis with lineage tracing
description: Sort or live-image primed cells and follow daughter cells across several divisions using an AP-1 reporter and a target-gene reporter. Add mitotic-bookmarking assays such as CUT&Tag on mitotically arrested cells. Quantify how memory decays over divisions and whether AP-1 bookmarking predicts which lineages retain memory.

title: Optogenetic test of AP-1 pulse sufficiency
description: Drive AP-1 activity with an optogenetic or chemogenetic FOS/JUN system, with no upstream signal, using varied pulse patterns (single, repeated, sustained). Measure whether this alone leaves lasting accessibility and a primed transcriptional response, and map the dose–duration threshold for memory. This tests sufficiency and the dynamics required, rather than only necessity.

title: Optogenetic/chemogenetic AP-1 pulse timing with memory persistence readout
description: Use light- or ligand-inducible FOS/JUN (or degron-controlled) to deliver defined pulses of AP-1 activity in AP-1-null cells, then measure whether enhancer accessibility and a reporter response persist after AP-1 is removed. Varying pulse duration, frequency, and delay before re-challenge defines the sufficiency, dose-dependence, and decay kinetics of memory.

title: Acute degron depletion after priming to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Prime cells, then rapidly degrade endogenous AP-1 (dTAG/AID on FOS/JUN/FOSL family members) only during the rest period and not during recall. If the memory persists without AP-1, AP-1 is an initiator rather than a maintainer, whereas loss of memory indicates continuous AP-1 requirement. Pair this with nascent-transcript and accessibility readouts.

title: Single-molecule footprinting and tracking of AP-1 occupancy and nucleosome positioning
description: Use Fiber-seq or single-molecule footprinting on primed versus naive cells to determine, on individual DNA molecules, whether AP-1 sites remain nucleosome-free or bound after signal decay. Live-cell single-molecule tracking of HaloTag-FOS/JUN could also test whether residence time or bound fraction differs in primed cells.

title: Lineage-barcoded sibling-split memory test
description: Use barcoded cells to split sibling clones before and after priming, then track them across divisions to see whether daughters inherit the primed state and for how many divisions it persists. Compare clonal concordance of recall responses with that of non-sibling cells to quantify mitotic heritability, and perturb AP-1 in one sibling set to test its role.

title: Targeted epigenome editing of AP-1 sites for locus-specific causality
description: Use dCas9-based tools (e.g., KRAB, TET1, or DNMT3A) or base editing of AP-1 motifs at selected enhancers in primed cells, then test locus-specific recall of the response. Conversely, tether AP-1 domains with dCas9 at a naive locus to test whether local AP-1 recruitment alone is sufficient to install heritable accessibility and faster reactivation.

title: Washout time course with acute degron depletion
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus, then after washout acutely degrade JUN/FOS (dTAG/AID) at different delays, measuring retention of chromatin accessibility (ATAC) and transcriptional responsiveness. If accessibility persists without AP-1, AP-1 was needed only for establishment; if it collapses, AP-1 actively maintains the memory.

title: Priming and re-stimulation hysteresis assay
description: Vary the number, duration, and spacing of stimulus pulses and measure the magnitude and kinetics of the second response (nascent RNA, e.g., PRO-seq) in primed versus naive cells. Test whether the enhanced response depends on AP-1 using A-FOS expressed only during priming versus only during recall.

title: Lineage-traced single-cell multiome in related cells
description: Use barcoded clones or sister-cell pairing with joint scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq to test whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target expression states are shared among related cells more than expected by chance after stimulus removal. Compare concordance across divisions to quantify heritability and its decay.

title: Live imaging of endogenous AP-1 reporters across divisions
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN and a target-gene reporter, then track mother-daughter lineages by time-lapse imaging to test whether activity states persist through mitosis and across generations. Pair this with mitotic CUT&RUN to test whether AP-1 bookmarks chromatin.

title: Motif editing and dCas9 tethering at memory enhancers
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers to test necessity for persistent accessibility and faster recall. Conversely, tether AP-1 or its pioneer domain via dCas9 to naive loci to test sufficiency to establish a heritable open state. Read out with ATAC, H3K27ac and reporter expression over weeks.

title: Washout time course of AP-1 occupancy and accessibility
description: After a transient stimulus, profile FOS/JUN CUT&RUN and ATAC footprinting at multiple times after washout to determine whether AP-1 binding and open chromatin persist beyond signaling and TF protein levels. Persistent sites that predict faster secondary transcription define candidate memory loci.

title: Stage-specific acute degradation of AP-1
description: Use dTAG/AID-tagged JUN/FOS to deplete AP-1 only during priming, only during the memory (washout) interval, or only at rechallenge, then measure the secondary response. This separates AP-1 as the initiator of memory from AP-1 as the maintainer of memory.

title: Single-cell multiome with sister-cell tracking
description: Combine live imaging of endogenously tagged FOS/JUN with sister-cell tracking and post-hoc multiome profiling. Test whether AP-1 state and chromatin accessibility are inherited across divisions and predict each cell's re-response. Mitotic retention can be checked at the same time.

title: Hysteresis and optogenetic dose-duration mapping
description: Drive AP-1 with optogenetic or titratable inputs across ramp-up and ramp-down sweeps and varied pulse patterns, then measure output. Path-dependent output (hysteresis) or a persistent state would indicate feedback-based memory.

title: Locus-specific motif editing and dCas9 perturbation
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers, or recruit AP-1 or dominant-negative A-FOS with dCas9, and measure the primed re-response by RNA and accessibility. Loss or gain of memory at single loci tests necessity and sufficiency independent of global AP-1 changes.

title: Stage-specific degron depletion to separate priming and recall
description: Endogenously tag FOS/JUN with a degron (or use A-FOS), and deplete AP-1 only during priming, only after washout, or only at restimulation. Measure the recall transcriptional response to test whether AP-1 is needed to establish memory, to maintain it, or only to read it out.

title: Longitudinal AP-1 occupancy versus accessibility after washout
description: Run CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac at multiple time points after a transient stimulus to identify sites that stay open after AP-1 leaves. Persistence of accessibility without AP-1 would indicate that AP-1 acts as an initiator, with the memory held in chromatin state.

title: CRISPR motif mutation of memory enhancers
description: Use base editing or CRISPR to disrupt AP-1 motifs at a few enhancers that show primed accessibility and faster re-induction, then test for loss of the memory effect. This gives causal, locus-specific evidence that AP-1 binding encodes the memory.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 dose and frequency titration with challenge response
description: Use light-controlled AP-1 activation with defined pulse numbers, durations, and intervals, then give a standard second challenge. Memory strength as a function of pulse pattern and decay interval would show whether AP-1 integrates stimulus history and over what timescale.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage tracking across divisions
description: Perform single-cell RNA+ATAC on primed versus naive cells over several divisions, using barcodes or sister-cell pairing, to link AP-1 motif accessibility to recall strength. Matched sister-cell behavior would show whether the memory is heritable and AP-1-dependent.

title: Timed degron depletion to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus, then acutely degrade FOS/JUN (dTAG/AID) at different times after washout, before restimulation. If memory (faster or stronger transcription, retained accessibility) is lost upon late depletion, AP-1 is needed to maintain it, not only to establish it.

title: Pulse-pattern optogenetic AP-1 activation with memory readout
description: Use optogenetic or chemically gated AP-1 to deliver defined pulse numbers, durations and intervals, then test the response to a later challenge. Dependence on pulse history and a decay time constant would show that AP-1 activity itself encodes memory, independent of upstream signaling.

title: Single-cell lineage-resolved tracking across divisions
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN together with a target-enhancer reporter, and follow sister cells through division after priming. Heritable differences in response, together with AP-1 mitotic retention, would test whether memory is carried by AP-1 or by downstream chromatin.

title: Motif-level CRISPR editing plus synthetic AP-1 recruitment
description: Delete or mutate AP-1 motifs at specific memory enhancers and test whether priming is lost. Conversely, recruit AP-1 to a neutral locus with dCas9 and test whether this creates a persistent, restimulation-competent state. This tests necessity and sufficiency at the locus level.

title: Hysteresis and bistability of the FOS/JUN feedback circuit
description: Measure single-cell dose-response with increasing versus decreasing stimulus, and perturb the FOS/JUN autoregulatory loop while fitting a mathematical model. Bimodality and hysteresis dependent on the loop would support a self-sustaining circuit memory that does not need a chromatin mark.

title: Timed degron depletion of AP-1: establishment vs. maintenance
description: Use dTAG/AID-tagged FOS/JUN family members and deplete them either during the first stimulus only, or only after stimulus withdrawal but before rechallenge. Measuring recall transcription and accessibility distinguishes AP-1 as an initiator from AP-1 as a continuously required maintainer of memory.

title: Long-chase occupancy and accessibility time course
description: Perform CUT&RUN for AP-1 subunits and ATAC-seq at multiple times after a transient stimulus, extending through many cell divisions. Test whether AP-1-bound, newly opened sites persist after AP-1 levels return to baseline, and whether persistence predicts a stronger rechallenge response.

title: Sufficiency test by synthetic AP-1 recruitment
description: Use optogenetic or chemically induced AP-1 activation, or dCas9-targeted AP-1 domains, at specific loci in naive cells with a pulse followed by withdrawal. If the locus retains accessibility and shows primed re-induction without the native stimulus, AP-1 is sufficient for memory.

title: Motif-level necessity at memory enhancers
description: Use base editing or CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at selected memory-associated enhancers, then run a stimulus, rest, and rechallenge paradigm. Compare chromatin marks and gene induction with unedited controls and with edits to neighboring non-AP-1 motifs to establish necessity in cis.

title: Single-cell lineage-resolved memory and mitotic bookmarking
description: Combine live-cell FOS/JUN reporters or barcoded lineage tracing with single-cell multiome readouts, and image or profile AP-1 on mitotic chromatin. Test whether sister cells share memory states and AP-1 occupancy, and whether blocking division or bookmarking alters inheritance.

title: Post-stimulus degron depletion of FOS/JUN before re-challenge
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus, then acutely degrade FOS/JUN (dTAG/AID) after the stimulus ends and before re-challenge. If the faster or stronger secondary response is lost, AP-1 is needed to maintain memory and not only to establish it.

title: Chromatin state tracking after stimulus washout
description: Run CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN and ATAC-seq plus H3K27ac at several times after stimulus removal. Compare how long AP-1 occupancy, accessibility and histone marks persist, and whether accessibility outlasts AP-1 binding, which would indicate AP-1 acts as an initiator and not a maintainer.

title: Single-cell imaging of history-dependent AP-1 responses
description: Image an endogenous FOS or AP-1 reporter in single cells through repeated stimulus pulses with variable intervals. Look for history-dependent responses and heritable states across divisions, and link them to later transcription by lineage tracking.

title: Motif-specific enhancer editing
description: Use CRISPR base or prime editing to mutate AP-1 motifs at selected primed enhancers, then compare the secondary response with unedited controls. This tests whether AP-1 binding at those specific sites is required for memory at the associated genes.

title: Synthetic AP-1 recruitment sufficiency test
description: Use dCas9 to recruit AP-1 or a pioneer-like FOS/JUN domain to a neutral reporter locus with a transient pulse. Then test whether the locus keeps a more accessible state and responds faster after recruitment has ended, which would show AP-1 is sufficient for memory.

title: Degron depletion of FOS/JUN after priming
description: Prime cells with a transient stimulus, then acutely degrade FOS/JUN (dTAG/AID) before re-stimulation. If enhanced response and accessibility persist without AP-1, memory is held elsewhere. If they collapse, AP-1 is required for maintenance.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse and re-stimulation
description: Use light-controlled AP-1 activation with defined pulse number, amplitude, and interval, then re-stimulate after variable delays. Measure the response and its decay half-life to test sufficiency, dose-dependence, and hysteresis of memory without other signaling inputs.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage barcodes
description: Do paired RNA+ATAC on primed and naive cells with heritable barcodes to track clones across divisions. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility and target expression are clonally inherited and whether they predict individual cells' re-stimulation response.

title: Mitotic bookmarking and residence-time measurements
description: Combine live-cell single-molecule tracking with CUT&RUN on mitotic-arrested cells to measure whether FOS/JUN remain bound at primed enhancers through mitosis. Compare residence times in primed and naive cells to assess whether binding is stable and heritable.

title: Motif-specific enhancer editing and forced AP-1 recruitment
description: CRISPR-mutate AP-1 motifs at persistently accessible enhancers to test necessity, and use dCas9-FOS/JUN to recruit AP-1 to naive loci to test sufficiency. Read out re-stimulation kinetics, accessibility, and H3K27ac, to separate AP-1 from other chromatin-based memory.

title: Prime, washout, and restimulate with acute AP-1 removal
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, wash out, then acutely degrade (dTAG/AID) c-Jun/Fos or express A-Fos either before or after the rest period, and measure the faster or stronger secondary response. If memory persists after AP-1 removal, AP-1 is only the initiator. If memory requires AP-1 during the rest period or at recall, AP-1 is needed for maintenance.

title: Time-resolved chromatin accessibility and histone marks at AP-1 sites
description: Run ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag (H3K27ac, H3K4me1, AP-1 factors) at several time points after priming and withdrawal. Test whether AP-1 motif-containing enhancers stay open or marked, and whether their persistence predicts the magnitude of the recall response.

title: Single-cell lineage-resolved memory with live AP-1 reporters
description: Tag endogenous Fos/Jun and a target gene with fluorescent reporters, and track primed cells and their descendants by live imaging across divisions. Compare sister-cell correlations and decay kinetics with those of unprimed controls to quantify heritability and test whether memory is cell-autonomous and AP-1 dependent.

title: Hysteresis and bistability test with a feedback model
description: Expose cells to increasing and then decreasing stimulus doses and measure single-cell AP-1 activity and target output, looking for bimodal distributions and path-dependent thresholds. Fit a model of c-Jun autoregulation, and test its predictions by breaking the feedback loop, for example by mutating the AP-1 site in the JUN promoter.

title: Locus-specific motif editing and dCas9 perturbation
description: At a memory-associated enhancer, base-edit the AP-1 motif or use dCas9-KRAB to close it, either before priming or after priming and washout. Then test recall of the target gene to determine whether the local AP-1 site is necessary for establishing the memory, for maintaining it, or for both.

title: Dimer-resolved binding and perturbation map
description: Use CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq with antibodies or epitope tags for individual FOS, JUN, ATF and MAF members before, during and after stimulus. Combine this with paralog-specific degron depletion to determine which dimers mark and maintain remembered loci, so that results are not averaged across the whole family.

title: Acute degron removal after the stimulus ends, at varied delays
description: Prime cells, wash out the stimulus, then rapidly degrade AP-1 factors (dTAG or AID) at different delays before restimulation. If the enhanced response and accessibility persist without AP-1, the memory is downstream of it. If they collapse, AP-1 is needed for maintenance and not only for establishment.

title: Separating memory from ongoing signaling input
description: Block upstream kinases (JNK, ERK) after priming and measure AP-1 phosphorylation, protein abundance, and binding over days. Pair this with a nuclear-localization or synthetic-input reporter to distinguish self-sustaining AP-1 states (such as positive feedback via FOS/JUN promoters) from continued signaling.

title: Single-cell lineage-tracked memory readout
description: Combine live-cell AP-1 reporters or endogenous FOS/JUN tagging with time-lapse imaging and lineage tracking through divisions, then restimulate and record each cell's response. Compare sister cells to test whether memory is heritable, digital or graded, and how much heterogeneity the population average conceals.

title: Synthetic AP-1 recruitment to test sufficiency
description: Use dCas9 or a tethered AP-1 DNA-binding domain to impose transient AP-1 binding at a naive enhancer or reporter, and track chromatin accessibility, histone marks and later inducibility after release. This tests whether AP-1 occupancy alone can establish a heritable state. Repeat across cell types and stimulus histories, such as repeated versus single pulses, to test context-dependence.

title: Dimer-specific degron and CUT&RUN time course
description: Use endogenous degron tags on individual Fos, Jun and ATF family members, together with paralog-specific CUT&RUN, to determine which AP-1 dimers bind during stimulation and which remain bound after the signal ends. Dimers whose acute loss erases the response are classified as memory-bearing, which distinguishes them from family members that are only transiently active.

title: AP-1 depletion after stimulus washout to separate AP-1 from its chromatin effects
description: Stimulate cells, wash out the stimulus, then deplete AP-1 (dTAG or a dominant-negative such as A-Fos) after the transcriptional response has returned to baseline. Compare ATAC-seq, H3K27ac and re-stimulation responses with and without depletion, to test whether AP-1-opened chromatin keeps the memory after AP-1 has gone.

title: Necessity and sufficiency tests with timed optogenetic or chemogenetic AP-1 control
description: Drive c-Fos/c-Jun with a light- or drug-inducible system without the natural stimulus, then test whether a pulse is enough to leave a lasting state. Block AP-1 during the original stimulus and test whether later memory is lost. This uses causal manipulation rather than correlation.

title: Enhancer-level perturbation of AP-1 motifs and pioneer context
description: Run a massively parallel reporter assay in the native chromatin context, using CRISPR base editing of AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers. Pair it with measurements of nucleosome occupancy and binding of other pioneer factors, to determine which motifs are needed to set and maintain the primed state.

title: Live imaging and multiomic lineage tracing of memory
description: Image AP-1 reporters, such as endogenous Fos-tagged knock-ins, in single cells through stimulation, washout and re-stimulation. Combine this with single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC) and barcode lineage tracing to determine whether memory is bistable, inherited through division, and heterogeneous across clones. Also test priming by comparing re-stimulation response size against a first-exposure control.

title: Paralog-resolved CUT&RUN and degron panel
description: Profile individual Fos/Jun/ATF/Maf family members by CUT&RUN before, during and long after stimulus, and use paralog-specific degrons to determine which dimer composition marks and maintains memory sites. This tests whether AP-1 acts as a single uniform factor.

title: Chromatin-state persistence after AP-1 removal
description: After a priming stimulus, measure accessibility (ATAC-seq), H3K27ac and H3K4me1 at AP-1 sites in cells where AP-1 is depleted or washed out, and compare them to cells where AP-1 remains. Persistence of the marks without AP-1 would place memory in chromatin rather than in the factor.

title: Timed acute degradation to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Use dTAG/auxin degradation or a dominant-negative A-Fos to remove AP-1 function at defined windows (during priming, after priming, or during restimulation), then measure the restimulation response. This separates a transient establishment role from a continuous maintenance role.

title: Genome-wide re-induction kinetics and priming
description: Compare naive and previously stimulated cells after a rest period using nascent RNA assays (PRO-seq, TT-seq) at restimulation, quantifying faster or stronger induction genome-wide. This measures memory as primed responsiveness, not only persistent expression of canonical targets.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing through divisions
description: Run single-cell ATAC plus RNA with barcoded lineage tracing or live AP-1 reporters, and follow clonal sister cells across divisions and rest periods to see whether memory is a heritable all-or-none state. Compare AP-1 motif accessibility with response in sister cells to test heterogeneity and inheritance.

title: Dimer-specific degron and mutant panel
description: Use acute degradation (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative lines (A-Fos, specific bZIP mutants) for individual Fos, Jun and ATF family members, and test which are needed for priming versus recall. This tests whether memory depends on a particular AP-1 dimer rather than on AP-1 as a whole.

title: Priming followed by AP-1 depletion during rest
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, wash it out, then degrade AP-1 during the rest period. Re-stimulate and measure whether the enhanced transcriptional response (nascent RNA, PRO-seq) persists without AP-1. If it does, AP-1 initiates memory but chromatin maintains it; if it does not, AP-1 itself maintains memory.

title: Time-resolved occupancy and accessibility tracking
description: Run CUT&RUN or CUT&Tag for AP-1 members, together with ATAC-seq and H3K27ac, at several points: during the stimulus, at hours and days after washout, and after re-stimulation. This shows whether AP-1 stays bound at primed enhancers or whether accessibility persists after AP-1 has left.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and response
description: Image endogenously tagged Fos/Jun, or use an AP-1 reporter, in single cells through repeated stimulations, and link each cell's earlier AP-1 history to its later response. This tests whether memory is a heterogeneous, cell-autonomous state, and whether it is inherited through division by lineage tracing.

title: AP-1 site editing and synthetic recruitment
description: Use CRISPR to mutate or insert AP-1 motifs at candidate enhancers, or to recruit dCas9 AP-1 activators or repressors. Then test whether the primed response, accessibility and re-induction speed change at those loci. This gives causal evidence at specific sites and tests whether AP-1 sites are sufficient to create memory at naive loci. Also perturb partners such as pioneer factors or SWI/SNF to identify other requirements.

title: Paralog- and dimer-resolved memory mapping
description: Run CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for individual FOS, JUN, and ATF family members, and for their dimers (for example by re-ChIP or proximity-based methods), before, during, and after stimulus withdrawal. This shows which specific AP-1 complexes persist at sites that give a memory response and which do not.

title: Acute degron depletion after memory is established
description: Make a degron (dTAG or AID) knock-in of a key AP-1 subunit, or express a dominant-negative such as A-FOS. Remove AP-1 only after stimulation has ended and test whether the primed accessibility and the faster re-induction on second challenge are lost. If AP-1 is needed to maintain memory, depletion should erase it. If it is needed only to establish it, the memory should persist.

title: Test for transfer to other factors and chromatin marks
description: Follow AP-1, histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1), DNA methylation, and co-factors (for example BAF/SWI-SNF and lineage factors) at memory loci over time after stimulus withdrawal. Combine this with chromatin-modifier inhibitors or catalytic-dead editing at those loci, to determine whether AP-1 itself holds the memory or only sets a chromatin state that does.

title: Restimulation time course with a primed-state readout
description: Give a first stimulus, wait for varying gaps (hours to weeks), then give a second stimulus of the same or a different type. Measure the speed and size of AP-1-dependent gene induction by nascent RNA (PRO-seq or TT-seq) and AP-1 binding. This tests for latent memory that appears only on restimulation, and for its duration and specificity.

title: Single-cell multiome with clonal barcodes and live AP-1 reporters
description: Use single-cell multiome (ATAC plus RNA) with clonal barcodes, plus live-cell AP-1 activity reporters, to follow whether memory is inherited through cell division in sister cells. Link each cell's past AP-1 activity to its later response. This separates heritable memory from population averaging and shows whether memory is all-or-none or graded.

title: Dimer-specific degron and CUT&RUN panel
description: Endogenously tag individual Fos, Jun, ATF and Maf family members with degrons, and map each one's occupancy and role at primed enhancers after a stimulus/rest/restimulus protocol. This tests which specific AP-1 composition, if any, carries memory, rather than treating AP-1 as a single factor.

title: Acute AP-1 depletion after establishment
description: Prime cells with stimulus, wash out, then rapidly degrade AP-1 (e.g., dTAG/auxin or dominant-negative A-Fos) during the rest phase only, and compare restimulation response with depletion applied during priming only. If memory persists after AP-1 loss, AP-1 is an initiator and not the maintainer; if it is lost, AP-1 is required for maintenance.

title: Chromatin-versus-AP-1 uncoupling with epigenome editing
description: Use dCas9-based tools to erase or install H3K27ac/accessibility at AP-1 motif enhancers, or mutate AP-1 motifs by base editing, and test whether memory follows the AP-1 site or the chromatin state. This separates AP-1 as the memory carrier from downstream chromatin marks that could be self-sustaining.

title: Live-cell single-cell AP-1 reporters with lineage tracking
description: Image endogenously tagged Fos/Jun and a transcriptional reporter in single cells through priming, rest, and restimulation, tracking lineages through divisions. Quantify whether the memory is bimodal, how it correlates with AP-1 dynamics, and whether daughter cells inherit it, rather than relying on bulk averages.

title: Single-cell multiome across stimuli, contexts and delays
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC (with AP-1 motif deviation analysis) in several cell types, such as fibroblasts, macrophages and T cells, with different priming stimuli, rest durations, and passage numbers. Test whether memory is graded, locus-specific, stimulus-specific and durable through divisions, and whether AP-1 motif activity predicts the secondary response across contexts.

title: Dimer-specific degron and CRISPR screen
description: Use acute degron tagging of individual Fos/Jun/ATF family members at different phases (during priming, after washout, before restimulation) with CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq to define which dimers establish versus maintain the memory state. This addresses heterogeneity among family members and separates initiation from maintenance.

title: Acute AP-1 depletion after priming
description: After priming and washout, when AP-1 levels have returned to baseline, rapidly deplete AP-1 or block its DNA binding (dominant-negative A-Fos, degron) and then restimulate. If memory persists and the sites keep H3K27ac and accessibility, the chromatin state rather than ongoing AP-1 activity carries the memory; if memory is lost, AP-1 is continually required.

title: Targeted editing of AP-1 motifs and enhancers
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs or use dCas9 epigenetic modifiers at memory-associated enhancers and measure the effect on re-induction of nearby genes. This tests whether persistent accessibility is functionally required rather than merely correlated.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage tracing
description: Combine scATAC/scRNA multiome with barcoded lineage tracing or live reporters of memory genes to ask whether memory is inherited by sister cells in a heterogeneous, all-or-none, or graded manner. Compare AP-1 motif accessibility and expression noise between memory-positive and memory-negative clones.

title: Stimulus-history time course with in vivo validation
description: Vary dose, duration, number of pulses and rest interval to build a memory decay curve, tracking kinetics, amplitude and Micro-C enhancer-promoter contacts at AP-1 loci. Repeat in an in vivo model such as skin wound or inflammatory memory in stem cells, with AP-1 perturbation, to test graded, decaying memory and physiological relevance.

title: Paralog-resolved CUT&RUN time course
description: Profile individual FOS, FOSL, JUN, JUND and ATF family members by CUT&RUN before, during, and days after the stimulus to determine which dimers remain at memory loci. This tests whether memory is carried by specific AP-1 complexes.

title: Acute degron removal after the stimulus
description: Prime cells, then deplete AP-1 with a dTAG or auxin degron (e.g., c-JUN, or a dominant-negative A-FOS) only after the stimulus has cleared. Measure whether the faster secondary response and open chromatin persist. If memory survives AP-1 loss, it is held in chromatin rather than in AP-1, distinguishing AP-1 as memory carrier from AP-1 as initiator of the chromatin change.

title: Long-term washout with matched accessibility, histone mark and AP-1 occupancy measurements
description: Measure accessibility, H3K27ac/H3K4me1 and AP-1 binding at several time points over many days and cell divisions after the stimulus ends. Comparing their decay kinetics shows whether AP-1 stays bound or only leaves behind marks, and avoids single-time-point snapshots.

title: Site-specific causal perturbation of AP-1 motifs
description: Use CRISPR base editing or dCas9-based tethering to mutate or recruit AP-1 at individual enhancers, then test the primed response of the linked genes after a rest period. This tests causality at individual loci rather than motif enrichment, and tests whether AP-1 binding alone is sufficient to create memory.

title: Single-cell multiome with live AP-1 reporters and lineage tracking
description: Combine live-cell imaging of endogenously tagged FOS/JUN with single-cell RNA and ATAC, and track daughter cells after division, to test whether memory is digital, heritable and tied to AP-1 state in each cell. Memory should appear as a bimodal, clonally inherited state that bulk averages would miss.

title: Reanalysis of public accessibility and AP-1 binding time courses after transient stimuli
description: Reanalyze public time-course chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) ChIP/CUT&RUN datasets from injury, inflammation, or stress models (e.g., epidermal wound, macrophage training, neuronal activity) to find loci that stay open long after stimulus withdrawal. Test whether this persistent accessibility is enriched for AP-1 motifs (chromVAR/HOMER) and for occupancy by AP-1 or its pioneer-like partners such as BAF/ARID1A.

title: Cross-dataset analysis of memory enhancers and AP-1 binding versus faster secondary response
description: Use public datasets of trained immunity, epithelial inflammatory memory, and repeated stimulation (ATAC, H3K27ac, RNA-seq) to identify enhancers that gain accessibility or H3K27ac after the first stimulus and persist. Test whether these enhancers predict faster or stronger transcription at re-stimulation, and whether AP-1 motif strength or ChIP occupancy at them predicts this effect beyond other TF motifs (regression/model comparison).

title: Integrative modeling of AP-1 dynamics and chromatin persistence using public data
description: Use public scRNA/scATAC or multiome time courses to estimate, per cell, AP-1 activity (FOS/JUN expression and regulon scores) and chromatin state over time. Use trajectory/lag analysis to ask whether transient AP-1 activity precedes durable accessibility changes, and whether AP-1 expression itself decays (signaling-driven) or is self-sustained.

title: Meta-analysis of AP-1 loss-of-function datasets for establishment versus maintenance
description: Collect public datasets with AP-1 perturbation (JUN/FOS knockouts, dominant-negative A-FOS, degron, or inhibitor treatments such as T-5224) paired with chromatin profiling. Compare the loss of accessibility and expression at memory loci when AP-1 is removed before, during, or after the stimulus (where timing information exists), to separate establishment from maintenance.

title: Cross-species and cross-tissue comparison of AP-1-dependent memory loci using human genetic and epigenomic resources
description: Overlay memory loci with public resources (ENCODE/Roadmap, GTEx, caQTL/eQTL, and AP-1 motif-altering variants) to test whether variants that disrupt AP-1 motifs change chromatin accessibility or response. Check conservation of AP-1-linked memory loci across species and tissues, and test whether they are enriched in chronic-disease GWAS loci such as psoriasis, IBD, or cancer.

title: Primed-versus-naive restimulation time course with ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) transiently with TNF, EGF or PMA, rest them for days to weeks, then restimulate and compare with naive cells. Measure chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), FOS/JUN binding (CUT&RUN), H3K27ac, and nascent transcription (PRO-seq/4sU-seq) to determine whether AP-1-bound sites stay open and respond faster or stronger. Estimated cost is about $8–12k.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation during the rest phase
description: Use a dTAG/auxin degron or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either only during the initial stimulus or only during the rest period, then restimulate. If memory requires continuous AP-1 occupancy, depletion during rest will erase the primed response. If AP-1 is only needed to establish memory, depletion during rest will not erase it, separating initiation from maintenance. Estimated cost is about $10–15k with existing degron lines or CRISPR knock-in.

title: Site-specific AP-1 motif perturbation and reporter test
description: Use CRISPR to mutate or delete AP-1 motifs, or use dCas9-KRAB/dCas9 blocking, at a few primed enhancers. Test whether memory of accessibility and of gene induction is lost. In parallel, run a lentiviral MPRA or reporter library with wild-type and mutated AP-1 motifs, integrated and chromatinized, to test sufficiency and motif-grammar rules (about $6–10k).

title: Single-cell multiome and live-cell imaging of heritability
description: Run 10x multiome (RNA + ATAC) on stimulated, rested and restimulated cells to link AP-1 motif activity (chromVAR) to single-cell memory states. Add a live-cell AP-1 reporter (e.g., a FOS promoter or AP-1 response element driving destabilized fluorescent protein) and track lineages by time-lapse across divisions to measure how long the state lasts and whether sister cells inherit it, which would indicate bistable or self-sustaining memory (about $12–18k).

title: Reanalysis of public datasets for AP-1 memory signatures
description: Analyze existing ATAC, ChIP and RNA-seq data from trained immunity, wound-healing, neuronal activity, and epithelial inflammatory-memory studies. Test whether sites that stay open after stimulus withdrawal are enriched for AP-1 motifs and binding, and whether this predicts faster re-induction. Check for co-occurrence with pioneer factors (e.g., CEBP, ETS) and for histone mark persistence, providing low-cost (under $2k compute) evidence of generality across systems.

title: Endogenous AP-1 reporter tracking across stimulus, washout and restimulation
description: Knock in fluorescent tags (e.g., c-Fos/JunB-mNeonGreen) or a live AP-1 transcriptional reporter (TRE-driven destabilized fluorescent protein) and image single cells over days through a first stimulus (e.g., EGF, TPA, or TNF), washout, and a second stimulus. Test whether response amplitude, kinetics and fraction of responders in the second round depend on the first, and how long that history effect lasts (memory decay time).

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1 state inheritance through divisions
description: Perform time-lapse imaging of AP-1 reporter levels in lineages after transient stimulation, quantifying the correlation of reporter state between mother, daughter and sister cells over multiple generations. Compare with the correlation expected from shared noise or cell-cycle effects to determine whether the AP-1 state is heritable (mitotically stable) and how many divisions it persists.

title: Bistability and hysteresis from dose-ramp imaging
description: Expose cells to ascending and then descending stimulus dose ramps while tracking an AP-1 reporter in each cell, and plot single-cell dose-response curves for each direction. Bimodal distributions and a hysteresis loop (different thresholds on the up and down ramps) would indicate a self-sustaining, positive-feedback memory state rather than a simple graded response.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse encoding with live readout of persistence
description: Control AP-1 activity optogenetically (light-inducible c-Jun/c-Fos dimerization or upstream ERK/JNK activation via optoSOS) with varied pulse number, duration and frequency, while imaging a separate AP-1 target reporter and the AP-1 factor itself. Determine which input histories produce persistent output after light off, which input dynamics are needed to establish memory, and whether it requires AP-1 positive autoregulation (c-Jun/FOS promoter feedback).

title: Live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and target loci with acute degradation
description: Co-image fluorescently tagged AP-1 (e.g., Halo-JunD/c-Fos) with single-molecule tracking for residence time and with live MS2/PP7 nascent transcript reporters on AP-1 target genes, or a chromatin-state live sensor, during primary and secondary stimulation. Test whether prior stimulation lengthens AP-1 binding dwell times, increases burst frequency, or primes loci to respond faster, and whether acute AP-1 degradation (degron tag, imaged) after the first stimulus abolishes the primed response, establishing necessity for memory maintenance.

title: Priming and rechallenge time course with chromatin accessibility readout
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or keratinocytes) to a transient AP-1-activating stimulus such as TPA, EGF, or wounding cues, wash it out, and rechallenge after days to weeks. Compare transcription and ATAC-seq/CUT&Tag (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) in primed versus naive cells to determine whether response magnitude and kinetics persist after AP-1 activity has returned to baseline.

title: Longitudinal single-cell multiome of AP-1 motif accessibility and expression
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC-seq (or lineage-barcoded sampling) at multiple times before, during, and long after transient stimulation. Quantify whether FOS/JUN family motif-accessible regions (e.g., ChromVAR scores) stay open in cells that previously had high AP-1 activity. Linking prior AP-1 dose to later accessibility and responsiveness in single cells distinguishes heritable memory from population heterogeneity.

title: Live-cell imaging of AP-1 dynamics and inheritance across divisions
description: Use a non-integrating AP-1 transcriptional reporter, or live-cell dyes or antibody-fragment imaging, in endogenous cells, and track single-cell AP-1 activity through repeated stimulations and cell divisions with lineage reconstruction. Correlate mother and daughter responses, and past history with present response, to test whether memory is cell-autonomous and mitotically heritable and whether it depends on pulse frequency or duration.

title: Pharmacological dissection of maintenance mechanisms
description: After priming, apply small-molecule inhibitors at distinct windows, such as JNK/MAPK inhibitors, BAF/SWI-SNF ATPase inhibitors, HDAC/HAT (p300/CBP) inhibitors, or DNA/histone methylation inhibitors, either during priming or only during the memory interval, and then rechallenge. Whether memory is lost when each is applied during establishment versus maintenance reveals whether AP-1 binding, continuous signaling, or chromatin changes carry the memory.

title: Footprinting and chromatin profiling in natural in vivo injury/inflammation models
description: Profile cells from tissues after resolved natural perturbations (e.g., skin wounding, inflammation, or aged vs. young tissue) using ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for JUN/FOS, and Hi-C or HiChIP, and compare with matched naive tissue. Persistent AP-1 motif footprints, retained enhancer-promoter loops, and faster re-induction of target genes on a second injury, correlated with the motif-containing regions opened by the first event, would support AP-1-dependent memory under physiological conditions without genetic manipulation.

title: Drosophila wing disc regeneration: JNK/AP-1 chromatin memory
description: After transient ablation (e.g., eiger or rpr pulse) in Drosophila wing imaginal discs, profile Fos/Jun (Kayak/Jra) binding and chromatin accessibility (CUT&RUN, ATAC-seq) in regenerated versus never-damaged tissue at multiple time points after healing. Then re-injure and test whether the primed enhancers show faster or stronger transcriptional and regenerative responses, and whether acute Fos/Jun knockdown (TARGET/Gal80ts) during the initial injury alone abolishes this priming.

title: Yeast Gcn4/Yap1 transcriptional memory with single-cell lineage tracking
description: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, expose cells to a transient stress (oxidative stress for Yap1, amino-acid starvation for Gcn4), then track reinduction kinetics of fluorescent reporter genes in microfluidic mother-machine lineages over several generations. Compare wild type with AP-1 binding-site mutants, nuclear-retention mutants, and chromatin-modifier deletions (e.g., Set1, H2A.Z) to determine memory duration, heritability, and whether the AP-1 factor itself or a chromatin mark carries the memory.

title: Zebrafish fin/heart regeneration enhancer memory with AP-1 motif perturbation
description: Use ATAC-seq, CUT&Tag for H3K27ac and Fos/Jun, and single-cell multiome in zebrafish fin or heart across injury, regeneration and repeat injury. Test necessity of AP-1 motifs by CRISPR deletion of injury-responsive enhancers, or by transient expression of dominant-negative AP-1 (A-Fos), to see whether lasting accessibility and faster re-response depend on AP-1 at the first injury.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulses with epigenetic readout in Drosophila S2 or zebrafish cells
description: Use optogenetic control of Fos/Jun activity or nuclear translocation (e.g., light-inducible Jun) to deliver pulses of defined duration, frequency and amplitude, then wash out and measure persistence of accessibility (single-cell ATAC), enhancer-reporter activity and nascent transcription (live MS2 imaging). Varying the input dynamics reveals thresholds for memory formation and whether the memory encodes history (dose/frequency) or only prior activation.

title: C. elegans FOS-1/JUN-1 (AP-1) in stress-induced and transgenerational memory
description: Expose C. elegans to transient stress such as wounding, pathogen or heat, and test whether fos-1/jun-1 targets show faster or stronger induction upon rechallenge, using auxin-inducible degradation of AP-1 factors only during the first exposure. Combine with tissue-specific ChIP/ATAC-seq and fluorescent reporters over later life stages and subsequent generations, to distinguish somatic from heritable memory and to separate AP-1 requirements for establishment versus maintenance.

title: Transient stimulus then washout: AP-1 binding and accessibility persistence
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a defined stimulus such as TPA, serum, or LPS, then wash out and run CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN and ATAC-seq at multiple time points (1 h to 14 days). Sites where AP-1 occupancy and accessibility persist after the stimulus has ended and AP-1 protein levels have returned to baseline are candidate memory loci.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to test maintenance versus initiation
description: Use dTAG or auxin-inducible degron knock-ins for FOS, JUN or the pioneer-like subunit, and degrade the protein either during stimulation or after memory is established. Compare ATAC-seq, H3K27ac ChIP and RNA-seq to determine whether AP-1 is required only to establish the accessible state or also to maintain it.

title: Primed re-stimulation functional assay with AP-1 perturbation at priming
description: Prime cells with a first stimulus, rest them for days to weeks, then re-stimulate and measure the speed and magnitude of transcription (nascent RNA, PRO-seq or 4sU-seq) compared with naive cells. Repeat with an AP-1 degron or dominant-negative (A-FOS) perturbation applied at priming only, to test whether AP-1 is needed to encode the enhanced response.

title: Single-cell multiome with lineage tracing across divisions
description: Perform single-cell RNA and ATAC (multiome) on primed and naive cells, with barcode lineage tracing or sister-cell pairing after division, and infer AP-1 motif activity (e.g., chromVAR). Test whether sister cells share accessibility and AP-1 activity states more than random cells do, and whether memory is heritable through mitosis and bimodal versus graded.

title: Mitotic bookmarking and locus-specific editing of AP-1 sites
description: Use live-cell imaging or single-molecule tracking of tagged JUN and FOS, plus CUT&RUN on mitotically arrested cells, to test whether AP-1 stays on chromatin during mitosis. Then use dCas9 or CRISPR motif mutation at selected memory enhancers to test whether the AP-1 site is necessary for persistent accessibility and the primed response, and use dCas9-KRAB to test sufficiency.

title: Single-cell multiome of previously stimulated versus naive cells
description: Perform joint scRNA/scATAC-seq at one time point long after stimulus withdrawal on primed and naive populations. Test whether AP-1 (FOS/JUN) motif accessibility, footprints, and target-gene expression remain elevated in primed cells, and whether primed cells carry a distinct, stable AP-1-linked chromatin state.

title: AP-1 binding and chromatin state profiling (CUT&Tag/ChIP) at memory loci
description: At a single post-stimulus time point, profile JUN/FOS occupancy together with H3K27ac, H3K4me1 and accessibility in primed versus naive cells. Test whether AP-1 stays bound at, or leaves, latent/primed enhancers, and whether the retained sites correlate with enhanced re-induction of nearby genes.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming
description: Prime cells, let the stimulus decay, then rapidly deplete AP-1 (dTAG/AID degron of JUN/FOS, or dominant-negative A-FOS). Measure chromatin accessibility and transcription at one later time point versus controls. Loss of the primed state means AP-1 is needed to maintain memory; persistence means AP-1 only initiates it.

title: Re-stimulation response test with AP-1 perturbation at a single endpoint
description: Give primed and naive cells, with or without AP-1 perturbation during priming only, an identical second stimulus. Measure RNA-seq or a reporter at one fixed time point afterward and compare the magnitude and speed of the response. This separates AP-1's role in establishing memory from its role in executing the response.

title: Single-cell AP-1 snapshot with lineage-based heritability
description: Use imaging or flow cytometry of endogenous tagged FOS/JUN with an AP-1 reporter in one fixed snapshot of a clonal population, such as sister cells or barcoded clones. Test whether high and low AP-1 states are shared among related cells beyond chance, which indicates heritable memory. Correlate the states with the history of the stimulus (e.g. a prior pulse) and with downstream targets.

title: Paired longitudinal ATAC-seq/CUT&Tag of AP-1 occupancy before, during, and after stimulus
description: Using serial biopsies or blood-derived cells (e.g., inflamed vs. resolved psoriatic skin, or fibroblasts/keratinocytes from patients), map accessibility, AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and H3K27ac at baseline, during inflammation and after resolution. Persistence of AP-1-motif-containing open sites after the signal is gone, relative to healthy donor controls, would show an AP-1-dependent epigenetic memory.

title: Ex vivo re-challenge of patient primary cells with AP-1 inhibition
description: Isolate cells from patients with prior inflammatory exposure (e.g., synovial fibroblasts from rheumatoid arthritis patients or airway basal cells from asthma patients) and from matched healthy donors, rest them in culture, then re-stimulate. Test whether faster or stronger transcriptional recall depends on AP-1 using a small-molecule inhibitor (e.g., T-5224) or dominant-negative FOS (A-FOS), measured by RNA-seq and chromatin accessibility.

title: Single-cell multiome with AP-1 motif activity inference across patient states
description: Perform scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq on patient tissue or blood across disease stages, and compute chromVAR/SCENIC AP-1 activity and footprinting per cell. Test whether a stable AP-1-high subpopulation persists across time points or after treatment, and whether its accessible regions predict relapse or recall gene expression.

title: AP-1 bookmarking across cell divisions in patient-derived cells
description: In patient-derived primary cells or organoids, use CUT&RUN/ChIP-seq on mitotically enriched versus interphase cells, and live imaging of endogenously tagged FOS/JUN alleles, to determine whether AP-1 stays on chromatin through division. Combine this with lineage-tracing barcodes or clonal expansion to test whether daughter cells inherit the AP-1 state, a requirement for cellular memory.

title: Linking AP-1 chromatin memory to genetic variants and clinical outcomes
description: Use patient-derived cells from genotyped cohorts to map chromatin accessibility QTLs and allele-specific AP-1 binding at disease-risk variants located in AP-1 motifs. Test whether AP-1-dependent memory signatures at these loci (including after therapy withdrawal) correlate with disease relapse, treatment response or sustained gene expression, with CRISPR editing in patient iPSC-derived cells for validation.

title: Mitotic live-imaging and CUT&RUN of AP-1
description: Image endogenously HaloTag-labeled FOS/JUN with single-molecule tracking in mitotic versus interphase cells, and perform CUT&RUN on FACS-sorted mitotic cells. This tests whether AP-1 stays on chromatin through division, and whether its mitotic retention at specific enhancers predicts which sites reactivate fastest after mitosis.

title: Single-molecule footprinting of AP-1 occupancy and nucleosomes
description: Use single-molecule footprinting (SMF/Fiber-seq) in primed and naive cells to resolve, on individual DNA molecules, AP-1 motif occupancy together with nucleosome positions and co-bound transcription factors. This tests whether memory is stored as a stable AP-1–nucleosome-remodeler configuration or as heterogeneous cell-to-cell occupancy that is quickly lost.

title: Motif-mutant enhancer knock-in with recall reporter
description: Use base or prime editing to mutate AP-1 sites at a few endogenous memory-associated enhancers. Then measure whether priming-induced accessibility and the stronger second transcriptional response are lost specifically at those loci. This is a cis-acting, locus-level causal test that is independent of global AP-1 knockdown and separates the memory role of AP-1 from its role in normal gene activation.

title: Optogenetic pulse patterns to map AP-1 dose and dynamics to memory
description: Drive endogenous AP-1 or its upstream kinases (e.g. optogenetic ERK/JNK) with pulses of different duration, frequency and amplitude. Quantify how each pulse pattern maps to lasting chromatin accessibility and to the response to rechallenge, to test whether memory is a thresholded or integrating function of AP-1 history, which a simple on/off priming design cannot reveal.

title: AP-1 family member composition and handoff to pioneer or lineage factors
description: Perform paired, time-resolved CUT&Tag for different FOS/JUN paralogs (e.g. FOSL1, JUNB, ATF3) and for pioneer or lineage factors during priming and during memory. Combine this with paralog-specific degradation to ask whether memory is carried by a specific AP-1 composition, or is handed off to a lineage transcription factor that maintains the sites after AP-1 is gone, distinguishing AP-1 as an initiator from AP-1 as a maintainer.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse duration and frequency with matched total dose
description: Use optogenetically controlled FOS/JUN (or light-gated dimerization) to deliver the same total AP-1 dose with different pulse durations and frequencies, then measure persistent accessibility and recall after washout. This tests whether memory is encoded by AP-1 dynamics (transient vs sustained) rather than by AP-1 presence alone, and defines a threshold for memory formation.

title: Synthetic AP-1-only activation without the native stimulus
description: Express a drug-inducible, AP-1-only synthetic activator (e.g., a constitutively active JUN/FOS fusion, pulsed and then removed) in naive cells and test whether it alone reproduces the primed accessibility and recall response of the natural stimulus. This sufficiency test separates AP-1 as a memory writer from other signaling arms such as NF-κB, MAPK or STAT that normally are co-activated.

title: Single-molecule nucleosome footprinting at memory loci
description: Use Fiber-seq or SMF/NOMe-seq on primed versus naive cells to read nucleosome positions and TF occupancy on single DNA molecules at AP-1 sites after washout. This shows whether memory is a stable open state in a subpopulation of alleles (bimodal, heritable) or a graded shift, and whether AP-1 is still bound or has been replaced by a remodeled nucleosome pattern.

title: Allele-specific memory in hybrid cells with a single mutated AP-1 site
description: In F1 hybrid or heterozygous cells, mutate the AP-1 motif on one allele and track allele-specific accessibility, H3K27ac and nascent RNA through priming, washout, and restimulation. Because both alleles share the same trans factors in one nucleus, any difference in memory is cis-encoded at the AP-1 site rather than due to a global cell state.

title: Mitotic bookmarking and replication-coupled retention assay
description: Combine CUT&Tag or live imaging of FOS/JUN on mitotic chromosomes with synchronization, EdU-based replication-timing and cell-cycle arrest experiments to test whether AP-1 stays on chromatin through mitosis. Comparing memory persistence in cells forced through division with that in arrested non-dividing cells shows whether memory depends on propagation across divisions or on a persistent chromatin state.

title: Single-molecule footprinting of nucleosome arrays after AP-1 loss
description: Use single-molecule footprinting (e.g., Fiber-seq or SMF/NOMe-seq) before, after, and long after stimulus to resolve whether AP-1-dependent loci retain remodeled nucleosome arrays and co-occupancy on the same DNA molecules after AP-1 leaves. Molecule-level bimodality of retained remodeled fibers without AP-1 binding would distinguish a chromatin-encoded memory from continued AP-1 occupancy.

title: Cell fusion or nuclear transfer to test chromatin-based versus AP-1 level-based memory
description: Fuse primed cells with naive cells (heterokaryons, with species-polymorphic SNPs to assign alleles) or transfer primed nuclei into naive cytoplasm, then ask whether primed enhancers stay open in cis while naive-derived ones remain closed. Cis-restricted persistence argues for chromatin-based memory, while trans-spreading implicates diffusible factors such as AP-1 levels or feed-forward loops.

title: Allele-specific memory with a single-allele AP-1 motif mutation
description: In F1 hybrid cells or heterozygous knock-in lines with an AP-1 motif mutation on only one allele, track allele-specific ATAC, H3K27ac, and nascent RNA after stimulus and rest to test whether priming is cis-encoded. A retained primed state only on the intact allele within a shared nucleus would show that memory is locally written rather than set by global signaling state.

title: AP-1 dynamics decoding with live-cell reporters and optogenetic pulse trains
description: Use endogenously tagged FOS/JUN with a live-cell reporter and an optogenetic upstream kinase or AP-1 activator to deliver pulses of varied amplitude, duration, and frequency, then measure the later response of a memory reporter in the same cells. Identifying a threshold, frequency dependence, or hysteresis (path-dependent response to the same input) would test for bistable memory and distinguish it from persisting signaling.

title: Pooled CRISPR screen for maintenance factors and AP-1 paralog composition
description: Run a pooled CRISPR screen after the washout period, with a sorted fluorescent reporter driven by a primed enhancer as the memory readout, targeting AP-1 family members, chromatin remodelers, histone modifiers, and partner transcription factors. Identify genes whose loss specifically erases maintenance but not the initial response, and determine the paralog composition of AP-1 dimers at late time points by re-ChIP or Co-IP, to identify the mechanism that holds the memory.

title: Single-molecule footprinting of AP-1 occupancy versus accessibility
description: Use SMF/Fiber-seq (or NOMe-seq) on primed and naive cells after washout to determine whether memory sites retain nucleosome-depleted, TF-bound molecules, or are accessible but unoccupied.
