Combining this with motif-mutated alleles tests whether residual accessibility is maintained by AP-1 itself or by other factors that act later.

title: Mitotic retention of AP-1 in live and fixed cells
description: Quantify FOS/JUN retention on mitotic chromosomes using live-cell imaging with HaloTag knock-ins, residence-time single-molecule tracking, and CUT&RUN on mitotically arrested, sorted cells. Compare retention at memory versus non-memory sites to test whether AP-1 physically carries the state through division.

title: Disruption of endogenous AP-1 positive-feedback loops
description: Map the endogenous loops sustaining AP-1 (FOSL1/JUN autoregulation, AP-1 sites in FOS/JUN promoters, and autocrine ligands such as AREG/IL1A) by CRISPRi of the AP-1 sites in those promoters or by neutralizing secreted factors, with conditioned-medium transfer controls. Loss of memory when the loop is cut but not when the chromatin is left intact would indicate that memory is circuit-based (bistability) rather than chromatin-based.

title: Paralog composition switching by time-resolved CUT&RUN and proteomics
description: Track which AP-1 dimers occupy memory sites across early, intermediate and late time points using paralog-specific CUT&RUN and BioID/mass spectrometry. If the AP-1 paralog identity or partner transcription factors (e.g., ATF3, BATF, TEAD) shift while accessibility is maintained, memory reflects a handoff rather than persistent AP-1 binding, which discriminates between models.

title: Allele-specific memory with motif-variant genetics
description: Use cells from hybrid or heterozygous individuals and allele-specific ATAC and RNA after priming to compare alleles differing in AP-1 motif strength (natural variants or base-edited alleles). Dose-dependent, cis-restricted persistence of accessibility and enhanced re-induction would show that memory is encoded locally at AP-1 sites, not in trans through diffusible signals.

title: Single-molecule footprinting of AP-1 occupancy versus accessibility
description: Use Fiber-seq or SMF/long-read methylation footprinting on primed versus naive cells to determine whether primed enhancers stay nucleosome-free without bound AP-1 (accessibility memory) or retain residual AP-1/co-factor footprints on the same DNA molecules. This distinguishes continuous AP-1 occupancy from AP-1 acting as a past trigger, and reveals single-allele heterogeneity.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-pattern titration
description: Drive FOS/JUN activity with an optogenetic or chemically gated system, varying pulse duration, frequency and amplitude while keeping total dose fixed. Then measure persistent chromatin accessibility and response to re-challenge to determine which temporal patterns (e.g., sustained versus pulsatile, as in ERK-to-FOS decoding) establish memory, and whether there is a threshold or bistable switch.

title: Paralog and dimer-composition swap during priming
description: Separately knock out or replace specific FOS/JUN/ATF/MAF family members, or force specific dimers, during priming. Use ChIP/CUT&RUN and accessibility assays to test whether memory depends on AP-1 dimer identity, for example FOSL1/JUNB versus FOS/JUN, and whether memory sites are bound by a distinct, long-lived dimer.

title: Mitotic bookmarking assay of AP-1
description: Image Halo-tagged FOS/JUN in live mitotic cells and perform CUT&RUN on synchronized mitotic cells and early G1 cells. Test whether AP-1 stays on memory enhancers through mitosis and re-binds them first after mitosis, versus accessibility being retained without AP-1, and compare with non-memory AP-1 sites.

title: Decoupling chromatin state from AP-1 with targeted histone and DNA-methylation editing
description: After priming, use targeted dCas9-based erasers or editors (e.g., KDM, HDAC, or DNA-methylation writers) at specific memory enhancers while AP-1 remains present, and use inhibitors of the relevant writers, to test whether H3K4me1, H3K27ac or DNA demethylation, rather than AP-1 itself, carries the memory. Also test whether the re-challenge response requires new AP-1 binding in the absence of the mark.

title: Mitotic bookmarking assay for AP-1
description: Use live-cell imaging and mitotic-chromosome CUT&RUN/ChIP on synchronized, nocodazole-arrested cells to test whether FOS/JUN family members remain bound at primed enhancers through mitosis. Then use rapid degron depletion only during M phase to test whether loss of bookmarking specifically reduces the primed response in daughter cells.

title: Dimer-composition-specific memory via paralog swap
description: Replace JUN/FOS family members with paralog-specific mutants (e.g., FOSL1 vs FOS, JUNB vs JUND, or leucine-zipper mutants with altered dimer preferences) and test which AP-1 dimer identities are required for lasting accessibility and recall. Combine with proteomics of dimer composition before and after priming to test whether memory reflects a shift in the AP-1 repertoire rather than total AP-1 level.

title: Single-molecule footprinting and Fiber-seq of memory enhancers
description: Use Fiber-seq or single-molecule footprinting to resolve single-allele chromatin states (nucleosome positions, TF occupancy) at AP-1 sites after stimulus clearance. This tests whether memory is a stable all-or-none allelic state with cis-linked co-occupancy, as opposed to a population-average rise in accessibility, and whether alleles in the primed state are inherited by daughter cells.

title: BAF and histone-modifier dependence of persistent accessibility
description: After priming, acutely inhibit BAF ATPase activity (e.g., a BRG1/BRM PROTAC or allosteric inhibitor) or block histone-modifying enzymes. Track whether accessibility at AP-1 sites decays and whether it can be restored without AP-1. This tests whether AP-1 sets the memory state while a self-sustaining chromatin or remodeler feedback loop maintains it.

title: Natural genetic variation in AP-1 motifs
description: Use allele-specific analysis in F1 hybrid cells or human cohorts to find AP-1 motif-altering variants at enhancers. Test whether the variants change allele-specific retained accessibility and recall after stimulation (e.g., caQTL or response-QTL in primed monocytes or keratinocytes), providing a native, within-cell control for cis-acting, AP-1-dependent memory.

title: Single-molecule footprinting of memory enhancers
description: Use Fiber-seq or SMF (long-read methylation footprinting) on primed versus naive cells to read single-chromatin-fiber occupancy at AP-1 loci. Test whether memory is a bimodal, all-or-none fiber state (open, with AP-1-motif footprints lost or retained) in which the fraction of open fibers, rather than the average, carries memory, and whether it is inherited after replication.

title: Replication-coupled inheritance test with synchronized and arrested cells
description: Prime cells, then compare memory retention in cells that divide (tracked by EdU/cell cycle), cells arrested (CDK4/6 inhibitor, contact inhibition), and cells blocked in S-phase passage. If AP-1-linked accessibility persists in non-dividing cells but is diluted or re-established only with a specific mark in dividing cells, this distinguishes self-sustaining feedback from mitotic bookmarking, for example using mitotic-chromosome CUT&Tag of FOS/JUN.

title: Perturbation of AP-1 positive-feedback autoregulation
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 sites in the promoters or enhancers of FOSL1, JUN and JUNB, or clamp their levels with a synthetic constitutive promoter. Measure the stimulus dose-response curve for ascending versus descending doses by single-cell flow cytometry or smFISH, and test whether bistability or hysteresis disappears.

title: Mass spectrometry of AP-1 dimer composition and phosphorylation across the memory window
description: Perform quantitative proteomics (IP-MS or targeted PRM) of AP-1 family members and their partners (ATF, MAF, BAF subunits), plus chromatin phosphosites, at baseline, post-stimulus, and during rest. Test whether memory correlates with a shifted FOS/JUN paralog composition, e.g., a switch from FOS to FOSL2/JUNB, rather than with persistent total AP-1 occupancy.

title: Sequence-to-function modeling of AP-1 motif grammar across systems
description: Train a sequence-to-function neural network (e.g. ChromBPNet) on accessibility from primed and naive states across several cell types and in vivo injury models. Use in silico motif ablation and motif-spacing/cooperativity analysis to predict which AP-1 sites hold memory, then validate the top and bottom predictions with MPRA or genomic editing of memory versus non-memory sites.

title: Single-molecule footprinting at primed enhancers
description: Apply Fiber-seq or SMF (long-read methylation footprinting) to primed versus naive cells to determine, on single DNA molecules, whether AP-1 motifs are occupied, nucleosome-free, or remodeled but unoccupied after stimulus washout. This distinguishes persistent AP-1 occupancy from retained nucleosome depletion without AP-1 bound, and shows whether memory is stored per allele (in cis) rather than per cell.

title: Allele-specific memory in hybrid cells with one-allele motif mutation
description: Use F1 hybrid cells (e.g., B6xCast fibroblasts) and allele-specific ATAC/RNA-seq after priming, combined with a heterozygous AP-1 motif edit, to test whether memory is cis-encoded at the locus or carried by diffusible trans factors (e.g., elevated FOS/JUN levels). Retention only on the unedited allele within the same nucleus would indicate a locus-intrinsic mechanism.

title: Mitotic bookmarking assays for AP-1
description: Perform live-cell imaging and CUT&Tag on mitotically arrested, synchronized, or sorted mitotic cells to test whether FOS/JUN remain bound to chromosome at primed sites. Also test whether acute mitosis-specific degradation (degron with nocodazole release timing) impairs re-establishment of accessibility in G1. This tests the specific mechanism by which AP-1 could transmit state through division.

title: Co-factor handoff mapping and sequential perturbation
description: Run time-resolved CUT&RUN/ChIP-exo and motif-grammar analysis (e.g., deep-learning models such as ChromBPNet trained on naive versus primed ATAC) to identify which co-factors (CEBP, ETS, RUNX, TEAD, BAF/SWI-SNF) take over occupancy after AP-1 leaves. Then apply inducible BAF inhibition (e.g., BRM014 or degraders) after priming to test whether memory depends on a co-factor that takes over maintenance rather than on AP-1 itself.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse titration of memory formation
description: Use optogenetic control of FOS/JUN activity or upstream JNK/ERK with defined pulse durations, frequencies, and amplitudes, then measure retained accessibility and re-challenge response days later. Mapping which dynamic features (sustained vs pulsatile, FOS vs JUN dominance, dimer composition) establish memory determines the threshold and encoding logic, and tests sufficiency independent of any natural stimulus.

title: Acute AP-1 degron with long-term memory readout
description: Using endogenous dTAG/AID degrons on FOS, JUN and ATF family members, degrade AP-1 at defined times after a transient stimulus (e.g., TNF, wounding, or neuronal activity). Then track whether the induced chromatin and transcriptional state persists for weeks after AP-1 loss, which distinguishes a state that AP-1 initiates from one that AP-1 must keep maintaining.

title: Lineage-traced single-cell multiome of stimulus history
description: Barcode cells, expose them to a transient stimulus, split them into sister lineages, and profile them by joint scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq after many divisions. Compare sister-cell concordance in AP-1 motif accessibility and target expression with unstimulated controls to measure heritable memory directly and determine its stability.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-train dose-response
description: Deliver light-inducible FOS/JUN activation in pulses varying in duration, frequency, and number. Use live reporters and later chromatin profiling to determine which temporal patterns leave lasting accessibility and reactivation priming, testing whether AP-1 encodes stimulus history through its dynamics rather than its presence.

title: Targeted de novo AP-1 site editing and dCas9 tethering
description: Use base editing or CRISPR knock-in to create or destroy single AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers. Separately, recruit dCas9-tethered AP-1 or a pioneer-dead mutant to those loci. Test at single-locus resolution whether AP-1 binding is necessary and sufficient for an enhancer to remember a stimulus, including after the factor is removed.

title: Cross-tissue in vivo memory comparison with chromatin-regulator perturbation
description: In mouse skin, immune and neuronal models, map AP-1 occupancy, accessibility, histone marks and SWI/SNF (BAF) engagement after an inflammatory or injury challenge and again after recovery. Then perturb BAF or histone modifiers and test secondary-challenge responses, to determine whether AP-1 memory depends on partner chromatin remodelers and whether it generalizes across tissues.

title: Transient AP-1 pulse with long-term chromatin tracking
description: Use optogenetic or degron-controlled c-Fos/c-Jun to deliver a defined pulse, then remove it and follow the same cells and their descendants with single-cell multiome (ATAC plus RNA) and lineage barcodes for weeks to months. This tests whether AP-1-opened enhancers and the resulting transcription persist after AP-1 is gone, and for how many cell divisions.

title: Acute AP-1 depletion after priming to test maintenance versus initiation
description: Prime cells with a stimulus such as injury, inflammation or stress, then rapidly degrade all AP-1 (dTAG or dominant-negative A-Fos) at varying delays and measure whether the primed accessibility and faster re-induction persist. If memory persists without AP-1, AP-1 is only an initiator and other factors maintain it. If it is lost, AP-1 is required for maintenance.

title: Single-locus editing of AP-1 motifs in memory enhancers
description: Mutate or epigenome-edit individual AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers (e.g., base editing at the endogenous locus) and test whether secondary-stimulation response, H3K27ac and accessibility memory are selectively lost. This separates AP-1 binding itself from correlated cofactors such as pioneer factors, and the effect size per motif quantifies how much memory depends on it.

title: Single-molecule imaging of AP-1 residence across mitosis
description: Track endogenously tagged Fos/Jun with live single-molecule imaging, and perform CUT&Tag/ChIP on sorted mitotic and post-mitotic cells, to measure whether AP-1 stays bound to mitotic chromosomes (bookmarking) and re-engages the same sites after division. Pair this with a reporter at a primed gene to test whether bookmarking predicts which daughter cells retain memory.

title: In vivo AP-1 activity lineage recording in mice
description: Build a mouse with a Fos/AP-1-activity-driven recorder (Cre or base-editing barcode) to permanently label cells that experienced AP-1 activity during wound, infection or neuronal activity. Months later, compare labeled with unlabeled cells in the same tissue for chromatin state, response to rechallenge and function, and perturb AP-1 in a matched cohort to test causal necessity.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after the stimulus ends
description: Prime cells (e.g., macrophages, fibroblasts, or neurons) with a stimulus, then use degron tags (dTAG/AID) on FOS, JUN, and ATF family members at different times after priming. Compare whether the enhanced secondary response persists when AP-1 is removed during the rest period, which separates AP-1 as the memory carrier from AP-1 as only the initiator.

title: Single-cell lineage-tracked memory with live AP-1 reporters
description: Track endogenous knock-in tagged FOS/JUN and a reporter in single cells over days through cell divisions, using lineage barcoding or time-lapse imaging. Test whether AP-1 levels or binding history in a mother cell predict the secondary response of its daughters better than other variables such as cell state or NF-κB dynamics.

title: AP-1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility time course
description: Run CUT&RUN/ATAC-seq/footprinting at high time resolution during and after priming to measure whether AP-1 motifs at latent enhancers stay accessible, H3K27ac-marked, and AP-1-bound after the factor's own levels return to baseline. Pair this with testing dependence on BAF/SWI-SNF to show whether memory resides in the chromatin state left by AP-1 or in continued AP-1 binding.

title: Targeted epigenome editing and AP-1 site mutagenesis at memory enhancers
description: Use CRISPR base editing of AP-1 motifs, or dCas9-based recruitment or erasure of acetylation or methylation, at individual memory-associated enhancers. Test whether motif mutations block memory acquisition, whether erasing marks after priming ablates memory without changing AP-1 levels, and whether artificially forcing the marks produces memory without priming.

title: In vivo cross-context memory tests with predictive modeling
description: Prime animals, for example with injury, stress, or neuronal activity, and measure re-challenge responses in the same tissue months later. Combine this with AP-1 occupancy data from the same cells to fit models that predict which genes show memory, then test the predictions with AP-1 perturbations in vivo and in human-derived cells with prior exposure, to determine when AP-1 is necessary, sufficient, or only correlated across tissues.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after a priming stimulus
description: Prime cells (e.g., macrophages, fibroblasts, or neurons) with a stimulus, then use degron tags (dTAG/AID) on FOS, JUN, and ATF family members to remove AP-1 at defined times after priming. Measure whether the enhanced secondary response persists without AP-1 during maintenance, distinguishing AP-1 as an initiator from AP-1 as a maintainer of memory.

title: Single-molecule imaging of AP-1 residence and occupancy across cell divisions
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN with HaloTag and track them in single cells and their lineages through priming, rest, and restimulation. Combine with CUT&Tag on sorted descendants to test whether AP-1 remains bound at primed enhancers, or whether occupancy is lost and later re-established by other factors.

title: Enhancer editing: AP-1 motif mutation versus chromatin-state rewriting
description: Use base editing or prime editing to disrupt AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers, and use dCas9 epigenome editors to restore accessibility or histone marks without AP-1. Test whether the memory phenotype requires the motif sequence, the accessible chromatin state, or both, and whether restoring accessibility is enough to rescue memory.

title: Lineage-resolved single-cell multiome with barcoded stimulation history
description: Combine single-cell ATAC and RNA sequencing with heritable lineage barcodes and a recordable stimulation history (e.g., a CRISPR-based or immediate-early-gene-driven recorder). Model how AP-1 motif accessibility and target-gene responsiveness correlate between sister cells, to estimate how heritable AP-1-linked memory is and for how many generations.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse titration with dynamical modeling
description: Drive AP-1 with light-controlled FOS/JUN or upstream kinases using different pulse durations, frequencies, and amplitudes, and read out later response using live reporters and chromatin profiling. Fit dynamical models to test whether memory shows hysteresis or bistability, and whether it depends on the temporal pattern of AP-1 activity or only on total dose.

title: Acute AP-1 degron with memory-persistence readout
description: Using endogenous FOS/JUN family dTAG/AID degrons, transiently stimulate cells (e.g., with inflammation or injury), then degrade AP-1 at defined times after the stimulus is removed. Measure whether enhancer accessibility and faster re-induction persist for weeks without AP-1, which would separate AP-1's role in establishing memory from its role in maintaining it.

title: Single-cell multiome tracking of lineage-barcoded clones through stimulus, rest and restimulation
description: Profile barcoded cells with paired scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq before, after, and during restimulation, linking AP-1 motif accessibility and target response at the clone level. Test whether primed enhancers and response magnitude are inherited clonally independent of current AP-1 levels, and whether this maps to specific subsets of AP-1-bound loci.

title: Live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and single-locus reporters across cell divisions
description: Follow single cells and their descendants for days after a pulse, using knock-in fluorescent FOS/JUN together with MS2/nascent-transcript reporters at primed target genes. Compare AP-1 residence time, AP-1 bursting history, and the later response of each lineage to determine whether memory is carried by AP-1 itself, by chromatin state, or by neither.

title: Targeted epigenome editing to uncouple AP-1 binding from chromatin priming
description: Use dCas9 tools to force AP-1 site occupancy without a stimulus, and to block or mutate motifs at endogenous enhancers and erase associated marks (H3K27ac, accessibility, SWI/SNF recruitment). The finding was that priming required AP-1-dependent remodeler recruitment but not sustained AP-1, and that artificial chromatin opening alone reproduced memory only at some loci, defining a necessary and sufficient hierarchy.

title: In vivo cross-tissue and cross-stimulus comparison with AP-1 perturbation
description: Use mouse models with inducible, tissue-specific AP-1 dominant-negative (A-FOS) expression, expose them to repeated stimuli (skin injury, infection, neuronal activity), and compare the secondary response with naive animals in matched cells. This tests whether memory depends on AP-1 in some tissues (e.g., epithelial stem cells) but not others, and whether stimulus history is encoded by which AP-1 family members are present at which enhancers.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after a priming stimulus
description: Prime cells (e.g., fibroblasts, macrophages, or neurons) with a stimulus, then use degron tags (dTAG/AID) to rapidly deplete FOS/JUN family members after priming but before restimulation. If the enhanced secondary response and chromatin accessibility persist without AP-1, AP-1 is only an initiator. If they vanish, AP-1 actively maintains the memory.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Combine barcoded lineage tracing with paired scATAC/scRNA and live AP-1 reporters. Compare sister cells across several divisions after transient stimulation, and test whether AP-1 motif accessibility and response magnitude are inherited more strongly than expected from shared lineage or noise.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulses with decay-kinetics mapping
description: Deliver defined optogenetic or chemogenetic pulses of AP-1 activity varying in dose, duration, and spacing. Measure how long enhancer accessibility, H3K27ac, and transcriptional hyperresponsiveness last, producing a quantitative memory curve that shows whether AP-1 activity alone is sufficient to write memory and how its persistence compares with that of other transcription factors.

title: Locus-specific AP-1 site editing and dCas9 recruitment
description: Use CRISPR base editing to mutate individual AP-1 motifs at memory-associated enhancers. Separately, use dCas9-based recruitment of AP-1 or of chromatin remodelers (SWI/SNF, BAF) to naive loci. Together these test whether AP-1 binding at a specific site is necessary and sufficient for maintained accessibility and faster reactivation, independent of global AP-1 changes.

title: In vivo cross-tissue memory comparison with live-binding imaging
description: Run parallel experiments in mouse tissue (e.g., skin inflammatory memory, neuronal activity, or trained immunity) with AP-1 knockouts. Pair the knockouts with single-molecule tracking of AP-1 residence time and CUT&Tag over weeks. The goal is to determine whether AP-1 stays bound to enhancers, only leaves behind a pioneer-opened chromatin state, or is replaced by other factors, and whether this holds across tissues.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-and-removal memory test
description: Use an optogenetically controlled c-Jun/c-Fos (or degron-tagged) system to deliver a transient AP-1 pulse, then rapidly remove it and track chromatin accessibility and target gene expression for weeks across cell divisions. Memory is supported only if the accessible state and transcription persist after AP-1 is gone, and it is refuted if they decay with the half-life of AP-1 itself.

title: Single-cell lineage-traced multiome of stimulated clones
description: Barcode single cells before an inflammatory or injury stimulus, let sister clones expand, then run paired scATAC/scRNA on sibling cells with and without re-challenge. Greater within-clone than between-clone similarity of AP-1 motif accessibility and re-stimulation response would indicate heritable memory rather than stochastic or continuous signaling.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, then use dTAG/AID degradation of FOS, JUN, or the pioneer-like partner BAF at defined times after priming and measure the secondary response. If primed enhancers stay open and responsive without AP-1, AP-1 is only an initiator; if they close, AP-1 actively maintains the memory.

title: Live imaging of endogenous AP-1 binding dynamics at memory loci
description: Tag endogenous JUN/FOS with HaloTag and use single-molecule tracking, together with a locus-specific live reporter of a memory enhancer, in dividing cells. Measure residence time, mitotic bookmarking, and post-mitotic re-binding to test whether AP-1 stays on mitotic chromosomes and re-establishes the same sites, or is lost and the sites are re-specified by other factors.

title: Epigenome editing: AP-1 site versus downstream chromatin marks
description: In primed cells, use CRISPR base editing to mutate AP-1 motifs at memory enhancers, and use dCas9 tools to deposit or erase H3K27ac, H3K4me1, or DNA methylation at the same loci. Determine which manipulation abolishes the enhanced second response and its inheritance, showing whether the AP-1 motif and binding are necessary or whether downstream chromatin marks carry the memory.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation with long-term chromatin memory readout
description: Use dTAG/AID degrons on FOS/JUN family members to remove AP-1 at defined times after a transient stimulus (e.g., wound, TNF, or inflammatory priming). Then measure whether enhancer accessibility, H3K27ac and the secondary-response transcriptional boost persist over weeks of cell divisions. This distinguishes AP-1 as maintainer of memory from AP-1 being needed only to establish it.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of primed enhancers
description: Combine barcoded lineage tracing with paired scATAC/scRNA before stimulation, after rest, and after restimulation. Test whether sister cells retain AP-1 motif-accessible enhancers and an enhanced re-response more similarly than unrelated cells. Heritable, clone-correlated states that outlast AP-1 protein levels would show that memory is carried epigenetically.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse patterns and their chromatin and response effects
description: Drive endogenous FOS/JUN or a synthetic AP-1 with optogenetic or chemically induced pulses of varying duration, frequency, and amplitude. Then measure which patterns leave residual chromatin opening, pioneer-like nucleosome displacement, and altered future responses, to test whether AP-1 dynamics encode a stored history rather than just a transient signal.

title: Dissecting AP-1 sites by locus-specific editing and epigenome writing
description: At endogenous memory-associated enhancers, mutate AP-1 motifs, or use dCas9 to place or remove acetylation, methylation and SWI/SNF (BAF) recruitment, with and without AP-1 present. Testing which of these changes is necessary and sufficient for a primed re-response shows whether the memory lies in AP-1 binding itself or in downstream chromatin marks it leaves behind.

title: Cross-tissue and human comparison of AP-1-dependent memory
description: Compare AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN), accessibility and responses across tissues with documented memory, such as post-inflammation epithelial stem cells, trained-immunity monocytes and injured neurons, in mice with conditional AP-1 knockouts. Add human cells from people with prior exposure (e.g., BCG vaccination, past inflammatory episodes) to test whether AP-1-dependent memory is general and to define its duration and reversibility.

title: Persistence after transient stimulus
description: Give cells a brief pulse of a stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine) and track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) occupancy and target gene expression by time-course CUT&RUN and RNA-seq for days to weeks after withdrawal. Memory is supported if a subset of AP-1 sites and genes stay in an altered state long after the AP-1 proteins themselves return to baseline.

title: Priming and re-stimulation challenge
description: Compare naive cells with previously stimulated cells in a second challenge, measuring the speed and amplitude of transcription (nascent RNA, live reporters) at AP-1 targets. Hypersensitive responses specific to AP-1 sites that disappear when AP-1 is blocked only during priming would indicate AP-1-dependent memory.

title: Chromatin accessibility and pioneer function at memory loci
description: Run ATAC-seq, histone mark profiling (H3K27ac, H3K4me1), and Micro-C before, during, and after stimulation to find enhancers that AP-1 opens and that stay open after the signal is gone. Test whether CRISPR motif mutation or acute AP-1 loss (dTAG on JUN/FOS, or dominant-negative A-FOS) blocks both opening and later maintenance.

title: Timed AP-1 degradation to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Remove AP-1 acutely at different times (during induction, versus after the memory state is established) using degrons or inducible dominant negatives. If AP-1 is needed only to establish memory, the state persists after loss; if it is also needed to maintain it, the state decays. This separates initiation from maintenance and from epigenetic carriers such as histone marks.

title: Single-cell and lineage tracking of inheritance through division
description: Use live-cell AP-1 reporters, lineage barcoding, and paired single-cell multiome (RNA and ATAC) to follow whether the stimulated state passes to daughter cells and in what fraction. Mathematical models can then test whether persistence is bistable or self-reinforcing (e.g., a JUN/FOS positive feedback loop) or better explained by a slowly decaying signal.

title: AP-1 occupancy versus persistent chromatin after signal withdrawal
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., macrophages or fibroblasts) with a transient signal, then withdraw it and run time-course CUT&RUN/ATAC-seq for FOS/JUN occupancy and accessibility. Test whether accessible, H3K27ac/H3K4me1-marked enhancers persist after AP-1 itself has left, which would indicate AP-1 acts as a trigger that leaves a lasting chromatin change rather than needing continuous presence.

title: Acute degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use auxin/dTAG degron alleles of FOS/JUN family members (or a dominant-negative A-Fos) before, during, and long after the priming stimulus. If AP-1 is needed only at priming but not at recall, it is an initiator; if depletion during the memory phase erases enhanced re-induction, AP-1 is the maintenance mechanism.

title: Prime–rest–restimulate recall assay with motif-dependent enhancers
description: Measure faster or stronger re-induction by RNA-seq/PRO-seq after a second stimulus following a rest period, and link genes showing memory to AP-1 motif content. Validate with CRISPR deletion or base-editing of AP-1 motifs at specific memory enhancers, plus reporter assays, to show the motif is necessary for the primed response.

title: Single-cell lineage tracking of AP-1 history and heritability
description: Combine live-cell AP-1 reporters (or a FOS-GFP knock-in) with single-cell multiome (RNA+ATAC) and barcoded lineages to test whether sister cells share the primed state after division and after the stimulus is gone. Heritability beyond what shared environment explains would show the memory is cell-intrinsic, and loss of the state over generations would quantify its decay time.

title: Pioneer-like activity and cooperative chromatin remodeling in vitro
description: Test whether AP-1 can open nucleosomal DNA and recruit SWI/SNF (BAF) using reconstituted nucleosome binding assays, single-molecule footprinting, and BAF inhibitor/degrader experiments in cells. If BAF recruitment is required for retained accessibility after AP-1 leaves, it provides a mechanistic link between transient AP-1 binding and a durable epigenetic state.

title: Single-cell map of AP-1 occupancy after transient stimulus
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., macrophages or fibroblasts with TPA or LPS), wash out, and track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN), and H3K27ac at single-cell resolution over weeks. Memory would appear as a discrete, persistent pattern of retained accessible sites that outlast the stimulus and AP-1 levels.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after the stimulus (necessity test)
description: Use degron-tagged (dTAG/AID) FOS or JUN, or dominant-negative A-FOS, to remove AP-1 at defined times: during priming, after priming, and before re-challenge. Compare secondary transcriptional responses and accessibility to distinguish AP-1 as initiator of memory from AP-1 as ongoing maintainer.

title: Site-specific AP-1 motif editing or dCas9 tethering (sufficiency test)
description: Mutate AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers with CRISPR, or tether FOS/JUN with dCas9 to naive loci, and measure whether the locus becomes accessible and primed and shows faster or stronger induction on later stimulation. This tests whether AP-1 binding at specific sites is causal for retained state rather than only correlated.

title: Sister-cell comparison of memory heritability
description: Combine barcoded lineage tracing with live reporters of AP-1 activity or scRNA/scATAC, and compare sister cells after a pulse. If memory is heritable, sister cells should share response magnitude and AP-1 state more than random pairs through divisions, and the decay rate would give a persistence timescale.

title: Patterned signal pulses with optogenetics or microfluidics
description: Deliver patterned pulses (fast/slow, strong/weak, single/repeated) of signal and measure how pulse history sets AP-1 composition (FOS vs. FOSL, JUN dimer mix), chromatin state, and later response. Fit a mathematical model of feedback and hysteresis to test whether AP-1 creates bistable, history-dependent states and to predict which histories are remembered.

title: Transient AP-1 stimulus with delayed transcriptome and accessibility readout
description: Expose cells to a defined pulse of AP-1-activating signal (e.g., serum, TPA, or an optogenetic c-Fos/c-Jun driver), then wash it out and measure the transcriptome and chromatin accessibility (RNA-seq, ATAC-seq) days to weeks later and after cell divisions. Memory is supported if primed cells respond faster or more strongly to a second challenge than naive cells, long after AP-1 activity has returned to baseline.

title: Time-resolved AP-1 binding and chromatin accessibility profiling
description: Run CUT&RUN or ChIP-seq for FOS/JUN family members alongside ATAC-seq and H3K27ac profiling at time points during and after the stimulus. Test whether AP-1 opens enhancers that remain open or acetylated after AP-1 has left, which would show that memory is held in chromatin rather than in continued AP-1 occupancy.

title: Acute degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Fuse endogenous FOS or JUN to a degron such as dTAG or AID, or use a dominant-negative A-FOS. Degrade AP-1 before priming, right after priming, or just before the second stimulus, and measure the recall response. If memory persists when AP-1 is removed after priming, AP-1 acts as the writer; if it is lost, AP-1 is needed to maintain the memory.

title: Single-cell and lineage-tracked heritability of AP-1 states
description: Use live-cell reporters of AP-1 activity (e.g., a FOS promoter reporter or a JUN kinase translocation reporter) combined with lineage tracking or barcoding, plus single-cell multiome (scRNA and scATAC) data. Measure whether AP-1 state or enhancer accessibility is inherited by daughter cells more than expected by chance, and whether it is bimodal or hysteretic, as expected for a self-sustaining feedback loop.

title: Motif-editing and positive-feedback perturbation of memory loci
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs, or use dCas9 effectors to block or tether them, at candidate memory enhancers. Separately, perturb the c-Jun autoregulatory loop. Then test whether recall of the second response and persistence of accessibility depend on these sites and on the loop, giving causal evidence beyond correlation.

title: Transient-pulse persistence and decay kinetics
description: Give cells a brief, defined stimulus (e.g., EGF/TPA/anisomycin pulse) and track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) protein, chromatin occupancy, and target gene expression by live reporters and time-course CUT&RUN well after the stimulus ends. Fit decay curves to distinguish a transient early peak from a self-sustaining state that persists for many cell divisions, and test whether persistence outlasts the half-lives of AP-1 proteins and mRNAs.

title: Accessibility persistence with AP-1 degradation during or after priming
description: After a priming stimulus, use ATAC-seq and CUT&Tag for H3K27ac/H3K4me1 to identify loci that stay open once the stimulus is gone. Then acutely degrade FOS/JUN (dTAG/AID) either during priming only or after priming only, to test whether AP-1 is needed to establish or to maintain the accessible state, which separates a memory mechanism from a transient trigger.

title: Primed versus naive re-stimulation response across rest intervals
description: Compare transcriptional response magnitude and speed to a second stimulus in primed versus naive cells at varying rest intervals, using RNA-seq and single-cell readouts. Plot memory decay against rest time, and ask whether AP-1 motif-containing enhancers show faster or stronger induction and whether an AP-1 dominant-negative (e.g., A-FOS) expressed only during priming abolishes the enhanced second response.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1 states across divisions
description: Use live-cell AP-1 activity reporters (e.g., endogenously tagged FOS/JUN or a TRE-driven fluorescent reporter) with time-lapse imaging of mother-daughter pairs to measure whether AP-1 activity state is inherited and correlated between sister cells beyond what shared stimulus explains. Quantify autocorrelation across generations to distinguish heritable bistable states from re-induced noise.

title: AP-1 motif perturbation and mitotic bookmarking
description: Use CRISPR to mutate or dCas9-block specific AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, and perform mitotic-arrest CUT&RUN/imaging to test whether AP-1 stays on mitotic chromosomes as a bookmark. Test necessity and sufficiency by determining whether motif loss erases the retained accessibility and primed response, and whether tethering JUN/FOS to a naive locus can create a durable open state after release.

title: Transient stimulus with AP-1 chromatin tracking
description: Give cells a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), then measure after the stimulus is gone whether AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, accessibility (ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN), and primed target-gene responses persist for days to weeks. Compare naive and pre-exposed cells on re-stimulation to quantify faster or stronger transcription, the hallmark of memory.

title: Acute AP-1 removal at defined windows
description: Use dTAG/AID degron alleles or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 during the initial stimulus, during the resting interval, or during restimulation. This separates whether AP-1 is needed only to establish memory or also to maintain it, and shows whether AP-1 is necessary rather than merely correlated.

title: Lineage-tracked single-cell multiome heritability
description: Pair scATAC/scRNA multiome with lineage barcodes or sister-cell pair analysis to test whether AP-1-opened chromatin states and gene expression are inherited across divisions in a clonal pattern. Compare their persistence with that in cells with matched exposure but no AP-1 activation, and test whether the similarity between sister cells exceeds chance.

title: Live-cell reporters of AP-1 dynamics and feedback
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN and a target-gene reporter in single cells over repeated pulses, measuring whether history changes amplitude, timing, or the bistable on/off state. Fit mathematical models (positive feedback, hysteresis) to test whether memory arises from self-sustaining AP-1 circuit dynamics versus slow chromatin changes.

title: Sufficiency test by synthetic AP-1 activation and chromatin editing
description: Induce AP-1 artificially (optogenetic or chemogenetic JUN/FOS, or dCas9-tethered AP-1 at selected enhancers) in naive cells, then withdraw it and ask whether the enhancer stays open, retains H3K27ac, and responds more strongly later. Control with DNA-binding or transactivation mutants and test the contribution of cofactors such as the BAF complex, which tests sufficiency for memory-like states.

title: Chromatin profiling after transient stimulus and long washout
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a transient AP-1-activating stimulus such as TPA or a stress signal, then withdraw it for days to weeks. At matched time points, run ATAC-seq, CUT&Tag for AP-1 subunits (FOS, JUN), and H3K27ac. Accessibility or binding that persists at the same loci after AP-1 activity returns to baseline would indicate a memory-like imprint.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-chase with reporter memory
description: Put AP-1 activity under optogenetic or chemogenetic control, for example a light-inducible c-Jun/FOS dimerizer. Deliver pulses of varied number, duration and spacing, then measure single-cell reporter output and endogenous target transcription after a washout. Compare naive cells with pre-pulsed cells to measure hysteresis, priming and decay time, and test for slow, cumulative integration of repeated pulses.

title: Acute degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use a dTAG or auxin-inducible degron on JUN/FOS, or a dominant-negative A-FOS, and deplete AP-1 before, during, or after the stimulus. If the memory state persists after AP-1 removal, AP-1 is needed only for establishment; if the state collapses, AP-1 is needed for maintenance. Read out the effect with nascent RNA-seq (PRO-seq) and accessibility.

title: Multiome lineage tracing of inheritance
description: Combine single-cell multiome (RNA + ATAC) with a barcoded lineage tracer on stimulated cells and follow them through several divisions after the stimulus ends. Test whether sister cells share AP-1 motif accessibility and target-gene expression more than unrelated cells do, which would indicate mitotic inheritance. Add live-cell imaging of an AP-1 reporter to track the state across divisions.

title: Pioneer-like activity and feedback-loop perturbation
description: Test whether AP-1 stabilizes memory through nucleosome remodeling (BAF recruitment) or positive feedback (FOS/JUN autoregulation). Use CRISPRi or mutation of AP-1 motifs at memory loci, BAF ATPase inhibitors, and a reporter of motif-dependent accessibility. In parallel, fit a mathematical bistability model to dose–response and washout data. Loss of memory after motif or feedback disruption would support a direct mechanistic role for AP-1, and would show that the primed state persists because of its structure rather than continuing input.

title: AP-1 occupancy and accessibility after stimulus withdrawal
description: Test whether AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and chromatin accessibility persist at enhancers days to weeks after a transient stimulus (e.g., serum, TPA, or injury) is removed. Use time-course CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq on primed versus naive cells, and compare the sites with persistent H3K27ac and accessibility that mark memory.

title: Acute degradation to separate maintenance from initiation
description: Prime cells, then use a degron (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during priming or after it. Re-challenge the cells and measure the transcriptional recall response by RNA-seq. If memory needs AP-1 only at initiation, the primed state should persist after later removal. If AP-1 is needed to maintain it, the state should collapse.

title: Single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics and recall
description: Image endogenously tagged JUN/FOS, or AP-1 reporters, in single cells through repeated stimulations. Test whether a cell's past AP-1 activity predicts the amplitude or speed of its later response, and whether lineage or sister-cell correlations persist across divisions.

title: Enhancer priming with sequential stimulation and motif mutagenesis
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs, or dCas9 to block them, at selected enhancers, then test whether first-versus-second-stimulus responses, such as faster or stronger induction of nearby genes, depend on those motifs. Pair this with nucleosome-remodeling readouts (BAF/SWI-SNF recruitment, MNase) to test whether AP-1 itself opens and maintains the sites.

title: Synthetic AP-1 memory switch and sufficiency test
description: Transiently express or optogenetically activate AP-1 in naive cells. Test whether this alone creates a self-sustaining, heritable accessible state, and whether it persists through cell divisions with mitotic bookmarking (live-cell and mitotic-chromosome ChIP). Model the results with feedback-loop equations, such as JUN autoregulation, to predict bistability and hysteresis, and test the predictions by titrating the stimulus dose up and then down.

title: Stimulus-withdrawal ATAC/CUT&Tag time course
description: Stimulate cells (e.g., with TPA, injury, or inflammatory signal), then remove the stimulus and track AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding, chromatin accessibility, and H3K27ac at AP-1 motif sites over days to weeks. Persistent accessibility after AP-1 levels return to baseline would mark sites with memory. The question is whether the sites stay accessible and marked after the driving signal stops.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming (degron/dominant-negative)
description: Prime cells, then use an inducible degron (dTAG/AID) or dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during priming or only during the later memory phase. Compare the secondary response (transcription, accessibility) to determine whether AP-1 is needed to establish memory, maintain it, or both; loss of memory after later AP-1 removal would indicate maintenance.

title: Primed versus naive re-stimulation with single-cell multiome
description: Run single-cell RNA and ATAC on naive cells, primed cells after rest, and re-stimulated primed cells. Test whether the memory state is a stable subpopulation and whether faster, stronger induction of target genes correlates with prior AP-1 motif accessibility. Quantify heterogeneity and the fraction of cells that remember.

title: Motif- and site-specific causal perturbation
description: Use CRISPR base editing or deletion of AP-1 motifs at candidate memory enhancers, or dCas9-based tethering of AP-1 or chromatin remodelers, and measure the effect on retained accessibility and on the recall response. Compare with control enhancers that are accessible but lack AP-1 motifs, to test whether AP-1 binding at a specific site is necessary and sufficient for memory, not just correlated with it.

title: Lineage tracing and cell-division persistence
description: Mark primed cells (e.g., with a FOS-driven Cre or reporter) and follow their progeny through divisions in vivo or in organoids. Measure whether accessibility, AP-1 occupancy, and enhanced responses are inherited over generations and whether they are lost on a predicted schedule. Pair with live-cell imaging of AP-1 reporters to distinguish a self-sustaining feedback loop (e.g., FOS/JUN autoregulation) from a chromatin-based memory.

title: Stimulus–washout–restimulus ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN time course
description: Stimulate cells (e.g. with serum, TPA or an inflammatory signal), wash out the stimulus, and rest them for days. Profile chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding and H3K27ac by CUT&RUN. Restimulate and compare the transcriptional response with that of naive cells. Persistent open sites that carry AP-1 motifs and give faster or stronger induction would support memory.

title: Acute degron depletion of AP-1 after the priming window
description: Use dTAG or auxin degrons on FOS, JUN, or a dominant-negative A-FOS at defined times, degrading AP-1 only after priming has finished, then measure whether the accessible sites and enhanced response persist. If AP-1 is needed only to establish memory, the state should survive its removal; if it is needed to maintain memory, the state should decay.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Run paired scRNA/scATAC with barcoded lineages, or sister-cell pairs after division. Test whether AP-1 motif accessibility (chromVAR scores) and target gene expression are more concordant between sisters than between random cells, and combine this with prior-stimulus history. Mitotic inheritance of the primed state would indicate a memory mechanism rather than transient signaling.

title: Live-cell AP-1 imaging across repeated pulses and mitosis
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS or JUN, or an AP-1 transcriptional reporter, in single cells over repeated pulses and across cell divisions. Quantify the dependence of response amplitude on pulse history, the decay time, and mother-daughter heritability. Add live imaging and ChIP/CUT&RUN on mitotic cells to see whether AP-1 stays on chromatin through mitosis. A history-dependent response (hysteresis) would be quantitative evidence for memory.

title: Site-specific perturbation of AP-1 motifs and imposed AP-1 occupancy
description: Use CRISPR base editing to mutate individual AP-1 motifs at primed enhancers. Use dCas9 fused to a pioneer-like factor or acetyltransferase to impose AP-1 occupancy artificially. Then measure whether memory of the earlier stimulus (accessibility, histone marks, enhanced induction of the nearby gene) is lost or gained locally. Testing necessity and sufficiency at specific loci assesses causality separately from global AP-1 effects.

title: Transient stimulus then washout: ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN persistence
description: Expose cells to a transient AP-1-activating stimulus (e.g., TPA, injury, or cytokine), then wash out and profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at days to weeks. Open sites that persist after AP-1 itself returns to baseline would indicate memory.

title: Acute degron depletion to separate maintenance from initiation
description: Use an auxin-inducible degron or dTAG on JUN/FOS at defined times (before, during, or after the priming stimulus) and measure whether accessibility and re-stimulation response are lost. If depleting AP-1 after priming does not erase the memory, it is needed only to establish it. If depletion erases it, AP-1 is also needed to maintain it.

title: Re-stimulation kinetics of primed versus naive cells
description: Prime cells with a first stimulus, rest them, then give a second challenge. Use time-resolved RNA-seq or nascent transcription (PRO-seq) to compare induction speed and magnitude with naive cells, and test whether this depends on AP-1 motif-bearing enhancers. Use enhancer-motif mutants or dCas9 blocking of selected sites to test causality.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracing of memory inheritance
description: Combine single-cell RNA and ATAC with live reporters of AP-1 activity, and track cells across divisions by barcodes or time-lapse imaging. Test whether primed accessibility and responsiveness pass from mother to daughter cells and whether they decay in a heritable, cell-autonomous way rather than reflecting continuing signaling.

title: Synthetic AP-1 activation and epigenetic mark readout
description: Use optogenetic or chemogenetic control of FOS/JUN, or a dCas9-AP-1 tether, to impose AP-1 activity at a chosen locus, then remove it. Measure H3K27ac, H3K4me1 and DNA methylation, and whether the locus stays open without AP-1 through a feed-forward loop; sufficiency is the strongest test of memory.

title: Long-term chromatin accessibility time course after a transient stimulus
description: Expose cells to a brief stimulus (e.g., TPA, growth factor, or injury), then profile ATAC-seq and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) CUT&RUN at intervals from hours to weeks after the stimulus is removed. Persistence of AP-1-dependent open sites after AP-1 binding has decayed would indicate memory. Compare these sites with those of naive cells.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use a degron (dTAG/AID) on FOS or JUN, or a dominant-negative such as A-FOS, and remove AP-1 at different times after the stimulus: before, during, and long after. If accessibility and the faster re-induction of target genes persist after AP-1 is gone, AP-1 is needed only to establish the memory. If they collapse, AP-1 is needed to maintain it.

title: Re-stimulation challenge: primed vs. naive transcriptional response
description: Give two pulses of stimulus separated by variable rest intervals and measure nascent RNA (PRO-seq or scRNA-seq) of AP-1 target genes after the second pulse. Memory predicts faster or stronger induction in primed cells, with a decay time that can be fitted to a model. Test whether this priming requires AP-1 by degrading it only during the first pulse.

title: Single-cell multiome and lineage tracing of inheritance through division
description: Run paired scATAC/scRNA-seq on sister cells after live imaging of an AP-1 reporter or barcoded lineage tracing. This tests whether AP-1-opened chromatin states are inherited by daughter cells in a clonal pattern and persist across several divisions without ongoing AP-1 activity. Compare within-clone and between-clone similarity of chromatin state and response.

title: Synthetic AP-1 recruitment with histone-mark profiling
description: Transiently recruit AP-1 (optogenetic or dCas9-tethered FOS/JUN) to a specific locus or reporter. Test whether accessibility, H3K27ac and the response to a later stimulus persist after recruitment ends. Profile cooperating factors and chromatin remodelers (BAF, p300) at the site to see which are needed for persistence. This tests whether AP-1 is sufficient to create a heritable state, not just correlated with one.

title: Transient-stimulus ATAC/CUT&RUN time course with washout
description: Expose cells (e.g., fibroblasts or macrophages) to a brief stimulus that induces FOS/JUN, then wash out and profile AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN) and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) over days to weeks. Persistent AP-1-dependent accessible regions after FOS/JUN levels return to baseline would indicate memory. Compare to naive cells.

title: Acute degron depletion during induction versus maintenance
description: Use dTAG/AID degrons on FOS, JUN or other AP-1 members and remove AP-1 either during stimulation or only after the stimulus has ended. This distinguishes whether AP-1 is required only for establishing accessibility or continuously for maintaining it. Read out chromatin state and faster transcription on secondary challenge.

title: Two-pulse priming assay with AP-1 motif perturbation
description: Give two stimulus pulses separated by a rest interval and measure the transcriptional response (RNA-seq, nascent PRO-seq) in primed versus naive cells. Use CRISPR mutation or dCas9-KRAB repression of specific AP-1 motifs at candidate enhancers to test whether those sites are necessary for the enhanced second response.

title: Single-cell multiome lineage tracking of AP-1 history
description: Combine single-cell RNA and ATAC with a fluorescent AP-1 reporter or barcoded lineage tracing to link past AP-1 activity to current chromatin state across cell divisions. Test whether daughter cells inherit the accessibility and responsiveness of mother cells and whether inheritance depends on AP-1 dosage, quantifying heritability versus noise.

title: Live-cell imaging and mathematical modeling of AP-1 dynamics
description: Track AP-1 activity with live reporters and single-molecule imaging of FOS/JUN residence times in stimulation-washout experiments, then fit models to test for bistability or hysteresis (self-sustaining state) versus passive decay. Test predictions such as dose-dependent persistence thresholds by titrating the stimulus and by perturbing feedback loops (e.g., JUN autoregulation).

title: Chromatin accessibility time course after transient stimulus
description: Give cells a brief pulse of a stimulus that induces AP-1 (FOS/JUN), such as serum, TPA or injury. Track ATAC-seq, CUT&Tag for AP-1 and H3K27ac, and RNA-seq for days to weeks after AP-1 returns to baseline. A memory mechanism would leave persistent open AP-1 motif sites that outlast the signal; compare with naive cells to test whether the marks persist and alter a second response.

title: Primed versus naive re-stimulation with acute AP-1 degradation
description: Stimulate cells twice with a rest interval between, and measure whether the second transcriptional response is faster or larger than the first. Then use degron-tagged (dTAG/auxin) FOS or JUN to remove AP-1 either during priming or only during the rest period, to separate AP-1 as the writer of the memory from AP-1 as its reader or maintainer.

title: Dose-and-duration single-cell live imaging of AP-1 dynamics
description: Use live reporters (FOS-GFP, AP-1 transcriptional reporters, JUN-N-terminal-kinase sensors) in single cells. Give pulsed or escalating inputs. Test whether the history of AP-1 activity, such as its dynamics, cumulative integral and frequency, predicts later gene expression and cell fate better than current AP-1 levels do. Analyze with information-theoretic and hysteresis measures, and look for inheritance of states in daughter cells after division.

title: Allele-resolved single-cell multiome and Hi-C/Micro-C of AP-1 targets
description: In stimulated and rested cells, use single-cell ATAC plus RNA with Micro-C or HiChIP to test whether AP-1 binding leaves lasting enhancer-promoter contacts and nucleosome remodeling (BAF recruitment). Then use dCas9 or motif mutation to disrupt the AP-1 site at individual enhancers. If the site is required for persistent accessibility and for the faster second response, that indicates locus-specific memory; allele-specific edits provide within-cell controls.

title: Mechanistic model fitting with perturbation and held-out validation
description: Fit a mechanistic model (e.g., bistable feedback or chromatin-state model) to time-resolved AP-1 occupancy, accessibility, and expression data. Use it to predict which loci retain memory, how long it lasts, and the effect of removing or overexpressing AP-1 or its cofactors. Test predictions with held-out tissue data such as wounded epidermis, neurons after activity, or T cells. Compare AP-1-dependent memory with alternatives (histone marks, DNA methylation, other pioneer factors) by ablating each.

title: Stimulus-primed re-challenge with ATAC/CUT&RUN time course
description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus (e.g., TPA, wounding cytokines), withdraw it for days to weeks, then re-stimulate and compare transcription to naive cells. Profile chromatin accessibility and AP-1 (FOS/JUN) binding at each stage to see whether AP-1-bound sites stay open and give faster or stronger gene induction, that is, whether the sites retain a lasting change after the signal is gone.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation after priming to separate initiation from maintenance
description: Use degron or dominant-negative (A-FOS) tools to remove AP-1 either during priming or only after the stimulus ends but before re-challenge. If AP-1 is needed only to establish memory, the primed state will persist after depletion; if it is also needed to maintain it, the primed response will be lost. Readouts are RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, and histone marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me1).

title: Single-cell multiome and live reporter tracking of heritability
description: Combine scRNA/ATAC multiome with live imaging of an AP-1 activity reporter (a TRE-driven fluorescent protein) or endogenously tagged FOS/JUN. Follow lineages through division after a pulse to test whether the primed state passes to daughter cells and how long it lasts, and compare cell-to-cell variability and decay kinetics with non-primed controls.

title: Site-specific perturbation of AP-1 motifs and neighboring chromatin state
description: In primed cells, use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs at selected enhancers, or use dCas9 to recruit or block AP-1 there. Test whether the enhancers' memory-linked accessibility and faster re-induction depend on the motif. Also use dCas9-based editing of neighboring chromatin marks to test whether AP-1 acts through those marks or independently of them.

title: In vivo lineage tracing in tissue-repair models
description: In a mouse model such as skin wounding or inflammation, label cells that experienced AP-1 activity (e.g., with Fos-driven CreER), then give a second challenge weeks later. Compare chromatin accessibility and response magnitude between labeled and unlabeled cells. Add AP-1 loss-of-function to show that the memory requires AP-1 and does not merely correlate with it.

title: Transient stimulus with long-term chromatin accessibility tracking
description: Expose cells to a brief pulse of a stimulus (e.g., serum, TNF, or injury) that activates AP-1 (FOS/JUN), wash it out, and profile accessibility and AP-1 binding by ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN at days to weeks. Persistence of open regions containing AP-1 motifs after the stimulus is gone would show a lasting memory footprint. Naive and pulsed cells provide the baseline comparison.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation at defined times (degron, dominant-negative A-FOS)
description: Use a degron-tagged JUN/FOS or inducible A-FOS to remove AP-1 either during the stimulus or after it has ended. If accessibility and faster re-induction persist after post-stimulus AP-1 loss, the memory is self-sustained by chromatin; if they decay, AP-1 is continuously required for maintenance. Comparing the two timings separates initiation from maintenance.

title: Priming and re-stimulation transcriptional response assay
description: Give two stimulus pulses separated by rest intervals of varying length, and measure nascent transcription (PRO-seq or EU-seq) and target-gene RNA after the second pulse. Faster or stronger induction in primed than naive cells, at AP-1 target genes only, would indicate memory. The decay time of the enhanced response quantifies memory duration, and AP-1 knockdown before priming tests necessity.

title: Single-cell multiome and live reporter lineage tracing
description: Combine single-cell RNA and ATAC sequencing with live-cell imaging of an AP-1 activity reporter (or endogenous tagged FOS) across cell divisions. Track whether daughter cells inherit the primed state, which would show mitotic heritability. Use the data to ask whether memory is a bistable, all-or-none state or a graded one, and to assess cell-to-cell variability in it.

title: Sufficiency test by targeted AP-1 recruitment with histone and DNA-methylation readouts
description: Recruit JUN or FOS to a synthetic reporter or a chosen enhancer with dCas9 or a Gal4 system for a limited time, then release it and watch the reporter over many cell divisions. Pair this with ChIP or CUT&Tag for H3K27ac and H3K4me1 and with methylation profiling, and test cooperation with the SWI/SNF (BAF) complex using a BRG1 inhibitor. Persistent activity and marks after release would show that AP-1 alone is sufficient to set a memory state. A lack of persistence would show that it is not.

title: Heritability of AP-1 state across clonal lineages
description: Use live-cell reporters of AP-1 activity (e.g., TRE-driven fluorescent protein) with long-term imaging and cell tracking to quantify mother-daughter and sister-sister correlations in reporter level. Fit the decay of correlation with generation number to estimate a memory half-life. Pair this with single-cell RNA/ATAC profiling of sorted high- and low-reporter cells to confirm that the imaging readout reflects a broader transcriptional state.

title: Transient stimulation plus timed AP-1 removal
description: Deliver a brief AP-1-activating stimulus (cytokine, drug pulse, matrix stiffening, or scratch wound), then use degron-tagged FOS/JUN family proteins to eliminate AP-1 either during the stimulus or only after it has subsided, and determine which window is required for the persistent downstream phenotype. If AP-1 is needed only transiently to establish a state that persists without it, that favors an initiator role; if continued presence is required, it acts as a self-sustaining maintenance circuit.

title: Chromatin footprint persistence after signal withdrawal
description: Run time-course ATAC-seq, CUT&RUN for AP-1 factors, and histone modification profiling (H3K27ac, H3K4me1) across stimulation and a long washout. Test whether AP-1-motif-containing enhancers opened during stimulation remain accessible and primed long after AP-1 occupancy and target transcription return to baseline. Still-open enhancers that reactivate faster upon restimulation would be direct evidence of a stored chromatin trace.

title: Restimulation kinetics as a memory assay
description: Compare naive cells with cells that experienced a prior stimulus days or weeks earlier, measuring the speed, amplitude, and dose threshold of AP-1 target induction on a second exposure using nascent transcription readouts. Faster or stronger secondary responses that scale with the chromatin changes would define memory as an altered input-output relationship rather than a static expression difference.

title: Synthetic perturbation of the AP-1 feedback loop
description: Use CRISPRa/CRISPRi or inducible expression to force AP-1 activity on or off for a defined window in otherwise unstimulated cells, then follow whether the induced state persists after the perturbation ends. Test whether mutating AP-1 binding sites at self-reinforcing loci, including FOS/JUN autoregulatory enhancers, abolishes persistence, thereby testing sufficiency and identifying the cis-elements that maintain the state.

title: Stimulus washout time course of AP-1 occupancy versus chromatin state
description: Deliver a defined transient stimulus (growth factor, cytokine, or drug pulse), then profile AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN family members), chromatin accessibility, and target gene expression at densely sampled time points after washout. Memory is supported if enhancer accessibility and transcriptional output outlast both the stimulus and the AP-1 protein burst.

title: Heritability of AP-1 state measured by clonal lineage tracing
description: Use expressed DNA barcodes combined with single-cell RNA and ATAC profiling to ask whether cells sharing a recent ancestor also share high or low AP-1 target activity. Quantify how well barcode identity predicts AP-1 state as a function of generations elapsed, giving a direct estimate of the memory half-life in cell divisions rather than hours.

title: Acute degron removal of AP-1 subunits after the state is established
description: Knock degron tags into the endogenous FOS, FOSL1, and JUN loci so the proteins can be eliminated within minutes at chosen times. Compare degradation during stimulation with degradation long after it, to determine whether AP-1 is required only to establish the state or must be continuously present to maintain it, which distinguishes a true memory element from a persistent signaling readout.

title: Second-stimulus challenge to test priming and faster reactivation
description: Expose cells to one stimulus pulse, allow a long recovery, then re-stimulate and measure response speed, amplitude, and fraction of responding cells relative to naive controls. A faster or larger response in previously exposed cells, measured together with AP-1 motif accessibility at the responsive enhancers, serves as the functional assay for memory.

title: Live single-cell reporters linking AP-1 dynamics to downstream fate
description: Build knock-in fluorescent reporters for an AP-1 subunit and for a downstream target gene, then image individual cells continuously through and beyond a stimulus while tracking lineage relationships. This tests whether transient differences in AP-1 activity at the time of stimulation predict divergent long-term states in daughter cells, and whether that prediction decays over time.

title: Clonal heritability of AP-1 activity
description: Expand single-cell-derived clones carrying an AP-1 transcriptional reporter and heritable barcodes, then compare between-clone versus within-clone variance in reporter level and AP-1 motif accessibility. Fit the decay of clonal correlation versus division number to estimate a memory half-life and test it against protein-dilution expectations.

title: Pulse-chase perturbation with washout
description: Transiently induce AP-1 with a degron-tagged or optogenetic FOS/JUN construct (or suppress it with A-FOS), then withdraw the perturbation and track accessibility, expression, and phenotype for weeks. A state that outlives the pulse suggests AP-1 writes memory; collapse on washout suggests it only maintains an ongoing state.

title: Acute AP-1 removal in already primed cells
description: Apply rapid degradation of AP-1 subunits in cells already in a primed state, such as drug-tolerant persisters or previously stimulated cells. Measure whether memory-associated enhancer accessibility, H3K27ac, and the enhanced recall response are lost, to separate continuous AP-1 occupancy from a self-sustaining chromatin mark.

title: Re-stimulation kinetics as the functional readout
description: Prime cells, allow the primary response to resolve, then re-stimulate and measure response latency, amplitude, and responding-cell fraction by live imaging or time-resolved sequencing. Memory predicts faster or larger secondary induction specifically at AP-1-bound loci, which should vanish when AP-1 sites are mutated.

title: Motif-resolution causal mapping at candidate memory enhancers
description: Use base or prime editing to disrupt individual AP-1 motifs at enhancers that remain open after the signal ends, with scrambled and neighboring-motif controls. If these motifs store the memory, editing should abolish retained accessibility and the primed response while leaving the acute primary response intact.

title: Barcoded lineage tracing across a state transition
description: Use clonal DNA barcodes to split sister cells, measuring AP-1 motif accessibility or FOS/JUN levels in one half and challenging the other half with a stimulus such as a drug or differentiation cue. Test whether the pre-measured AP-1 state predicts the clone's eventual fate, which is the core test of a heritable, predictive memory.

title: Degron-based timed removal to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Tag c-JUN/c-FOS with an auxin or dTAG degron (or express dominant-negative A-FOS) and deplete AP-1 either during a priming stimulus or only after it ends. If post-stimulus depletion erases the primed response even though the initiating signal is gone, AP-1 is required for maintaining the memory.

title: Persistence and heritability timescales of an endogenous AP-1 reporter
description: Track an endogenous AP-1 reporter, such as a knock-in FOS-HaloTag or an AP-1 motif-driven fluorophore, by live imaging across many divisions. Extract state autocorrelation times, mother-daughter correlations, and switching rates to distinguish true multigenerational memory from slow protein turnover.

title: Decoupling AP-1 binding from chromatin accessibility
description: Perform paired ATAC-seq and CUT&RUN for JUN/FOS before, during, and long after stimulation. Test whether stimulus-opened enhancers remain accessible after AP-1 unbinds. This asks whether AP-1 acts as a pioneer factor that establishes a latent chromatin memory that is read out on restimulation.

title: Targeted activation and removal of specific AP-1 enhancers
description: Use dCas9-VPR or targeted recruitment of JUN to a defined set of AP-1-bound enhancers, plus CRISPRi or deletion to remove them. Test whether transiently imposing the AP-1 state suffices to install a long-lived primed phenotype and whether removing those elements abolishes memory of prior exposure.

title: Acute degron depletion staged across a pulse-chase
description: Tag FOS/JUN family members with an auxin or dTAG degron and deplete AP-1 either during a transient stimulus or only after it has been withdrawn, then assay whether the stimulus-induced state persists. This separates a role for AP-1 in establishing a state from a requirement for continuous AP-1 activity to maintain it, which is the core claim of a memory mechanism.

title: Heritability of AP-1 activity across divisions by live imaging
description: Use a fluorescent AP-1 (TRE) transcriptional reporter and an endogenously tagged JUN/FOS protein, and track individual cells through several divisions. Compute mother-daughter and sister-sister correlations and the autocorrelation half-life of AP-1 activity. Memory predicts correlations that persist well beyond protein and mRNA turnover timescales and are transmitted through mitosis.

title: Chromatin priming and re-stimulation kinetics at AP-1 motifs
description: Perform time-resolved ATAC-seq, AP-1 CUT&RUN, and footprinting after stimulus withdrawal to identify regions that stay accessible without ongoing signaling, then re-challenge cells and ask whether those retained, AP-1-motif-containing enhancers are the ones that reactivate faster or more strongly. Causality can be tested by CRISPRi or base-editing the AP-1 motifs in the retained peaks.

title: Lineage barcoding to link prior AP-1 state to later cell fate
description: Barcode cells, sort or record high- versus low-AP-1 cells with a reporter at an early timepoint, and assay the fate of their barcode-matched descendants (e.g., drug survival, differentiation, invasion) days to weeks later. A memory mechanism predicts that early AP-1 state predicts clonally concordant later outcomes, and that perturbing AP-1 in the interim removes that predictive power.

title: Hysteresis and feedback test with a tunable synthetic AP-1 circuit
description: Drive AP-1 activity with a dose-tunable inducible FOS/JUN construct and measure the output while ramping the input up and then back down, looking for bistability and hysteresis rather than a single dose-response curve. Also map AP-1 binding at its own and its partners' loci to test whether an autoregulatory positive-feedback loop, a simple molecular basis for such memory, is present in the cell type of interest.

title: Pulse-chase test of whether the state outlives the trigger
description: Deliver a transient AP-1 stimulus (drug or cytokine pulse, or optogenetic/degron-controlled FOS/JUN induction), withdraw it, and track AP-1 target accessibility (ATAC-seq) and transcription (RNA FISH, scRNA-seq) over days to weeks. A memory mechanism should show target-state persistence long after AP-1 protein returns to baseline, and the difference between chromatin and transcript decay indicates which layer stores the information.

title: Lineage barcoding to measure heritability across divisions
description: Barcode cells, let clones expand, then split sister cells and profile them with paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq (or MemorySeq-style enrichment for slowly fluctuating genes). Quantifying how much more similar AP-1 motif accessibility and AP-1 target expression are within clones than between clones gives a direct estimate of how many generations the state is inherited.

title: Acute AP-1 removal at defined times after state establishment
description: Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on c-Jun/c-Fos (or a dominant-negative A-Fos) to remove AP-1 either during state establishment or only after the state is already set, and compare outcomes. If AP-1 is required to establish but not to maintain the memory, late degradation should leave the accessible/primed state and its phenotype largely intact.

title: Re-stimulation kinetics as a functional memory assay
description: Give cells a first stimulus, allow full recovery, then re-stimulate after varying intervals. Measure the speed and amplitude of AP-1 target induction and of the downstream phenotype (e.g., drug tolerance, migration, differentiation competence). Faster or stronger secondary responses that decay with rest interval and are abolished by AP-1 loss during the first exposure indicate a trained/primed memory.

title: Identifying the chromatin layer that maintains the mark at AP-1 sites
description: At AP-1-bound enhancers that stay open after the stimulus, profile in parallel histone modifications (H3K4me1/H3K27ac CUT&RUN), nucleosome positioning, DNA methylation, pioneer-factor and BRD4/cohesin occupancy, and enhancer-promoter contacts (Micro-C). Then test causality by targeting erasers or writers (dCas9-LSD1, dCas9-p300) to those sites to see which perturbation removes or installs the memory.

title: Pulse-chase of AP-1 activity with clonal lineage tracing
description: Transiently induce AP-1 (e.g., optogenetic or degron-controlled FOS/JUN, or a brief TPA pulse), then follow barcoded clones by single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq across many divisions. This measures how long an AP-1-opened chromatin and expression state persists after the inducing signal is gone, and whether persistence is heritable within clones.

title: Priming assay with repeated AP-1 stimulation
description: Give cells a first AP-1-activating stimulus, wash out and rest for days to weeks, then rechallenge and compare response magnitude, speed, and gene set to naive cells. A memory mechanism predicts faster or stronger reactivation at previously bound loci, which can be mapped by comparing ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN peaks before, between, and after the two stimuli.

title: AP-1 depletion during encoding versus during the memory window
description: Use an auxin or dTAG degron to deplete FOS/JUN either only during the initial stimulus (encoding) or only during the rest period (maintenance), then test whether the primed state survives. This separates a role for AP-1 as an initiator of the state from a role as a continuously required maintainer.

title: Mitotic transmission: AP-1 bookmarking and post-division state recovery
