description: Combine live imaging of tagged JUN/FOS through mitosis with mitotic chromatin profiling (e.g., CUT&RUN on sorted mitotic cells) and sister-cell comparisons of expression after division. Concordance between sister cells beyond what noise predicts, plus retention of AP-1 at mitotic chromatin, would support heritable rather than merely slow-decaying memory.

title: Perturbation of AP-1 motif content at specific enhancers
description: Use base editing or prime editing to delete or add TRE/CRE motifs at candidate memory enhancers, then measure whether the primed/persistent transcriptional state is lost or gained at those loci. Pair this with a synthetic reporter carrying a tunable number of AP-1 sites to determine how motif density relates to the duration of state retention.

title: Pulse-chase stimulation with time-resolved AP-1 and chromatin readouts
description: Deliver a transient stimulus (e.g., a brief cytokine, growth-factor, or drug pulse), wash it out, and track AP-1 protein levels, AP-1 motif accessibility (ATAC-seq), and target-gene expression over many days. Memory is supported if accessibility at AP-1-bound enhancers and the primed transcriptional response persist long after the AP-1 proteins and the original signal have decayed.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of AP-1 state heritability
description: Use expressed DNA barcodes for clone tracking combined with single-cell RNA-seq or a live AP-1 reporter to test whether sister cells and clonal descendants share AP-1 activity levels. Measuring how the correlation of AP-1 state between relatives decays over generations gives the memory timescale and shows whether the state is heritable or transient.

title: Degron-based acute removal to separate maintenance from establishment
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN family members with an auxin or dTAG degron so AP-1 can be eliminated acutely before, during, or long after a priming stimulus. If removal after priming erases the retained accessibility and the faster/stronger secondary response, AP-1 actively maintains the memory rather than only establishing it.

title: Restimulation challenge assays quantifying the memory benefit
description: Compare naive versus previously primed cells in a second challenge (same stimulus, a different stimulus, or a drug-resistance assay) and measure response latency, amplitude, fraction of responding cells, and cell-fate outcome. A genuine memory mechanism should produce a quantitatively faster or larger response that scales with prior AP-1 activation and is abolished by AP-1 perturbation.

title: Targeted AP-1 installation and removal at specific enhancers
description: Use dCas9-fused AP-1 activation domains, dominant-negative A-FOS, or engineered motif deletions at candidate enhancers to install or remove AP-1 occupancy in the absence of any stimulus. Sufficiency (synthetic AP-1 recruitment alone creates a long-lived primed state) and necessity (motif deletion blocks memory at that locus but not globally) together form a causal test, and pairing it with CUT&RUN for cofactors and histone marks identifies the molecular carrier of the memory.

title: Hysteresis measurement under ramped stimulus
description: Slowly ramp a stimulus such as TGF-β, a drug, or serum up to a peak and back down. At each step, measure AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN for FOS/JUN), AP-1 motif accessibility (ATAC) and target expression in single cells. If AP-1 holds a memory, the up and down paths will differ, and AP-1 knockdown should shrink the area between them (loop area) more than it changes the response at steady state.

title: Degradation of AP-1 during the post-stimulus interval with restoration before re-challenge
description: Prime cells, then acutely degrade AP-1 subunits with degron-tagged FOS/JUN/FOSL (dTAG or AID) during the post-stimulus interval and restore them before re-challenge. If the memory survives removal, AP-1 is needed only to read it out. If it is lost, AP-1 is needed to maintain the memory.

title: Lineage-based decay of correlation in AP-1 target accessibility
description: Use lineage barcoding (e.g., Rewind or clonal scRNA/ATAC) to measure how strongly sister, cousin and second-cousin cells agree on AP-1 target accessibility after a transient stimulus. Fit the drop in correlation per generation to estimate a memory half-life in cell divisions. Compare this with lines in which AP-1 motifs are mutated or AP-1 is inhibited.

title: Mutual information between stimulus history and cell state, partitioned by AP-1 accessibility
description: Expose cells to random combinations of past stimulus histories, then use single-cell multiome to estimate the mutual information between each cell's history and its current state. Divide that information into the part carried by AP-1 motif accessibility and the part that is not, and test how much is lost with AP-1 perturbation.

title: Erasure treatments and single-site base editing of AP-1 sites
description: After priming, apply defined erasure treatments (passage time, forced divisions, HDAC or BAF inhibitors) to identify what removes faster re-induction on a second challenge. Then use base editing on single AP-1 sites at the enhancers showing memory to test whether destroying one site removes the memory only at that locus.

title: Hysteresis mapping with stimulus ramp up and down
description: Ramp a stimulus (serum, TGF-beta, or a MAPK inhibitor) up in fine dose steps and then back down, measuring AP-1 factor levels, AP-1 motif accessibility, and target gene output at each step by single-cell ATAC/RNA. A reproducible open loop between the ascending and descending branches, which collapses when AP-1 is acutely degraded with dTAG-FOS/JUN at a matched point on each branch, would indicate AP-1-maintained bistable memory rather than slow relaxation.

title: Heritability analysis across lineage trees
description: Combine live imaging of an AP-1 activity reporter with expressed lineage barcodes so that each cell's state can be placed on a family tree, then compute intraclass correlation of AP-1 activity and of AP-1-dependent target expression between sisters, cousins, and increasingly distant relatives. Fitting the decay of correlation with generation number gives a memory half-life in cell divisions, and the analysis can be repeated under AP-1 degradation to ask whether AP-1 carries the inherited state or merely correlates with it.

title: Mutual information between stimulus history and present state
description: Expose cells to randomized sequences of stimulus pulses, then at a later readout time estimate the mutual information, in bits, between the past pulse sequence and current single-cell AP-1 occupancy, chromatin accessibility, and transcriptome. Memory is quantified as information about the past that persists after the stimulus is gone. The causal test is whether this information drops sharply when AP-1 is degraded during the stimulus-free interval but not when an unrelated abundant factor is degraded.

title: Frequency-response and step-response profiling with optogenetic AP-1
description: Use a light-controlled AP-1 (optogenetic FOS/JUN dimer or LOV-caged degron) to deliver pulse trains across a wide range of frequencies and duty cycles while holding total AP-1 dose constant, and record downstream enhancer accessibility and gene output. Construct a frequency-response plot and look for low-pass filtering plus persistence of output long after input ceases, which would distinguish a system that integrates and retains input from one that simply tracks its input; the measured time constants are then used to predict responses to novel input waveforms.

title: DNA recorder under an AP-1-responsive promoter
description: Place a CRISPR base-editing or recombinase-based recorder under an AP-1-responsive promoter so that each episode of AP-1 activity leaves a cumulative edit in the genome, then read the recorded history and the current chromatin and expression state from the same single cell. This tests whether cells with a larger record of past AP-1 activity retain a distinguishable present-day state, using a within-cell comparison of past and present.

title: Memory-kernel system identification with patterned optogenetic input
description: Drive the pathway with optogenetically delivered, patterned input sequences (varying pulse amplitude, duration, interval, and frequency, including pseudo-random m-sequences) while live-imaging a FOS/JUN translocation reporter and an AP-1-driven transcriptional reporter, then fit a Volterra or linear-nonlinear model to extract the memory kernel. A memory element would show a long-tailed kernel and history-dependent gain that disappears when AP-1 dimerization is blocked, whereas a simple signal relay would show a short, stimulus-locked kernel.

title: Mutual information between stimulus history and AP-1 state after washout
description: Expose cells to a defined library of past stimulus histories, then after a long washout quantify, cell by cell, the mutual information between which history a cell experienced and its current AP-1 occupancy, AP-1 motif accessibility, and target transcript counts. This yields the number of bits of past experience retained, a decay-rate curve for that information over time and divisions, and a direct test of how much of the retained information is lost when AP-1 components are degraded during the washout.

title: Decay of AP-1 state similarity across sister, cousin, and second-cousin cells
description: Use live lineage-tracking microscopy plus endpoint single-cell multiome on microdissected sibling pairs to measure how similarity in AP-1 state between sisters, cousins, and second cousins decays with generational distance after a transient stimulus. Compare the measured decay constant against a null model of random molecular partitioning at mitosis, to distinguish actively maintained, heritable AP-1 states from passive dilution of leftover protein.

title: DNA-writer recording of past AP-1 activity
description: Place a base-editing or recombinase-based DNA writer under an AP-1-responsive promoter so that each episode of AP-1 activity is permanently recorded in a genomic barcode, with recording windows gated by an inducible component. Sequence the barcode together with the cell's current phenotype to test whether a cell's recorded AP-1 history, rather than its present AP-1 level, predicts later behavior such as drug tolerance or differentiation bias.

title: Separate write, read, erase and overwrite tests of AP-1 memory
description: Test each operation separately: write by pulsing exogenous FOS/JUN alone without an upstream stimulus; read by assaying target output after the pulse has fully decayed; erase by targeted degron-mediated removal or dCas9-based site-specific displacement of AP-1 at defined enhancers; and overwrite by introducing a competing dimer such as a different bZIP partner. Memory is supported only if the pulse alone is sufficient without the original stimulus and locus-specific erasure selectively eliminates the corresponding response.

title: Hysteresis loop mapping with graded stimulus
description: Raise a stimulus such as TGF-beta, serum, or a drug in graded steps and then lower it, measuring AP-1 target accessibility and reporter output in single cells at each step. A difference between the ascending and descending branches indicates history dependence. Test AP-1 dependence by attempting to eliminate the difference with A-Fos or a FOS/JUN degron.

title: Lineage-barcoded pedigree tracking and heritability estimation
description: Use clonal barcoding plus single-cell ATAC and RNA to compute the heritability of AP-1 site accessibility across cell divisions and sister-cell pairs, partitioning variance into clone-of-origin versus noise. Heritability and decay half-life across generations are used to estimate a persistence timescale.

title: Optogenetic FOS/JUN pulses to measure retention, write threshold and recall
description: Deliver pulsed optogenetic FOS/JUN dimerization of defined amplitude and duration, then assay retention time, minimum stimulus duration needed to establish memory, and enhanced response to a second stimulus. Plotting retention versus stimulus parameters distinguishes a bistable self-sustaining state from a slowly decaying state or a pure signal relay.

title: Faster re-induction after return to baseline with phase-specific AP-1 degradation
description: Prime cells, wait until the transcriptional response fully returns to baseline, then re-stimulate and measure response latency and amplitude. Degrading AP-1 selectively during the interval between stimuli versus during re-stimulation separates a role for AP-1 in storing the memory from a role in executing the response.

title: Survival analysis of serially passaged clones
description: Follow single-cell-derived clones with differing initial AP-1 activity over serial passaging, using Cox proportional-hazards models in which the event is loss of the primed phenotype, such as drug tolerance or accessibility state. Covariates such as AP-1 motif occupancy, partner TF identity, and CpG methylation indicate which features predict durable versus transient memory.

title: Mutual information between stimulus history and cell state, with and without AP-1
description: Expose cells to several defined stimulus histories, then use single-cell multiome to estimate the mutual information between each history and the cell's present state, with and without conditioning on AP-1 footprint and activity. If AP-1 is the memory, it should account for nearly all of the history information, so conditioning on it should leave almost none.

title: Compare memory half-life with AP-1 half-lives
description: Using pulse-chase designs, measure how fast the primed response fades after a single stimulus. Compare that rate with the half-lives of FOS/JUN proteins (e.g., HaloTag pulse-chase) and of AP-1 chromatin occupancy (CUT&Tag time courses). If the memory lasts much longer than both, AP-1 is more likely to initiate the memory than to store it.

title: AP-1 sufficiency test by transient tethering
description: Use a dCas9 fusion or a chemically induced AP-1 recruitment system to tether AP-1 at chosen enhancers for a short time without any stimulus, then release it. Afterwards, check whether those loci stay accessible and respond more strongly to a later challenge, testing sufficiency of AP-1 for memory.

title: Test whether memory transfers between nuclei or stays on the chromatin
description: Fuse primed cells with naive cells to form heterokaryons, or move nuclei into enucleated cytoplasts, and use species- or allele-specific readouts. If the memory transfers to the naive nucleus, it is carried by a diffusible factor such as AP-1 protein; if it stays with the primed chromatin, it is stored in the chromatin itself (in cis).

title: Stimulus order dependence
description: Give cells stimulus A then B, or B then A, with matched total exposure, and measure end states and later response to a drug. Then test whether the effect of order disappears when AP-1 is inhibited, or can be predicted from AP-1 footprints left by the first stimulus.

title: Stimulus-ramp hysteresis measurement
description: Slowly ramp a stimulus (e.g., TPA, EGF, or drug dose) up and then back down. At each step, measure single-cell AP-1 activity with a live reporter and AP-1 motif accessibility with scATAC. If the downward path does not retrace the upward path (an open hysteresis loop whose width persists over time), the system has memory; if AP-1 motifs are knocked out, that memory should disappear.

title: Timed AP-1 removal after a transient stimulus to test maintenance versus initiation
description: Use an inducible degron (dTAG-FOS/JUN) or a dominant-negative A-FOS to remove AP-1 at different times after a transient stimulus. Measure whether chromatin accessibility and the faster re-response persist. This shows whether AP-1 only establishes the memory (it survives AP-1 removal) or must continuously maintain it (it decays with a measurable time constant).

title: Heritability estimation with lineage barcodes
description: Use lineage barcoding (e.g., Rewind or ClonMapper) to track sister and cousin cells across several divisions after a stimulus, and calculate how strongly AP-1 target accessibility and expression correlate within each lineage. If within-clone correlation decays slowly across generations, and more slowly than for non-AP-1 programs, this is evidence that AP-1 carries a heritable state.

title: Pulse-train response and transfer-function fitting of AP-1 dynamics
description: Use optogenetic ERK/RAS control or microfluidics to deliver pulse trains that vary in frequency, duration, and spacing. Then fit linear and nonlinear transfer-function models to AP-1 reporter dynamics and downstream enhancer opening. If the fitted decay time constant is much longer than the turnover of AP-1 protein and mRNA, the memory sits downstream of AP-1 (e.g., in chromatin), not in AP-1 levels themselves.

title: Prime-and-challenge recall test with edited AP-1 motifs
description: Prime cells, let them rest until AP-1 levels return to baseline, then challenge them again and measure how fast and how strongly AP-1 target genes respond, including in contexts such as drug-resistance priming. Repeat this in lines where base editing has destroyed the AP-1 motifs at specific memory enhancers. Loss of the faster, stronger second response without a change in the first response would show that the memory is carried at those AP-1 sites.

title: Relatedness-based heritability of AP-1 activity via lineage barcoding
description: Use barcode lineage tracing to identify sister and cousin cells, then measure how similar related cells are in AP-1 activity (FOS/JUN RNA FISH and AP-1 motif accessibility) and in their later response to a stimulus, across several generations. If AP-1 carries memory, its similarity between relatives should decay at the same rate as the similarity in response, and this shared similarity should disappear when AP-1 is knocked down.

title: Mutual information between past stimulus history and current single-cell state
description: Expose cells to defined stimulus histories, remove the stimulus, and wait varying times. Then calculate the mutual information between the past history and the present single-cell state (scATAC/scRNA) at AP-1 targets versus non-AP-1 loci. Test whether AP-1 inhibition lowers the number of bits retained or makes the information fade faster.

title: Predicting time since stimulation from AP-1 chromatin features
description: Collect a time series after the stimulus is removed and train a model that predicts the time since stimulation from AP-1-bound enhancer accessibility and histone marks. If AP-1 chromatin features predict elapsed time much better than transcripts do, AP-1 is a persistent record of the past.

title: Stimulus-order dependence (A-then-B versus B-then-A)
description: Treat cells with two signals in the order A-then-B and B-then-A, using equal doses and equal total exposure. Measure the final transcriptional and phenotypic state. A memory mechanism predicts that order will matter, so test whether the order effect corresponds to AP-1 dimer composition and disappears when the AP-1 family is blocked.

title: Accumulation of subthreshold repeated stimuli
description: Give cells repeated stimulus pulses that are each too weak to trigger a response, at different spacings. Test whether AP-1 occupancy and accessibility build up stepwise until the cells reach a persistent state, and whether the summed AP-1 signal predicts when the switch occurs. This would show AP-1 integrating and storing past exposure.

title: Retention-interval and spaced-versus-massed stimulation test
description: Give cells one stimulus pulse, wait a variable retention interval, then give an identical test pulse and quantify enhanced response (faster or larger AP-1 target induction by scRNA-seq or live reporters) as a function of interval length and of massed versus spaced stimulation pulses. A genuine memory system should show a quantifiable retention decay constant and a greater effect of spaced than massed stimulation, and knocking down specific Fos/Jun family members should selectively flatten that curve.

title: Write-maintain-erase assay with dCas9-Fos/Jun at a single enhancer
description: Use dCas9-Fos/Jun fusions to transiently establish the active state at a naive AP-1-bound enhancer, remove the dCas9 fusion, then assay persistence of accessibility and transcription over many days. Finally, erase the state with targeted motif disruption or a repressive domain and re-establish it. Independent, locus-specific establish/erase/re-establish cycles would separate true memory from continuous instructive signaling.

title: Mutual information between stimulus history and AP-1 state
description: Expose cells to many randomized stimulus histories (sequences of cytokine, growth factor or drug pulses). Compute the mutual information between the past input sequence and the present single-cell AP-1 chromatin or expression state to estimate how many bits of history are retained and for how long. Compare channel capacity in wild-type versus AP-1 motif-mutant or Fos-degron cells to quantify AP-1's specific contribution to memory capacity rather than to instantaneous response.

title: Lineage-distance autocorrelation of AP-1 state
description: Combine an evolving CRISPR lineage recorder with single-cell multiome readout so each cell's AP-1 accessibility state can be placed on a reconstructed division tree, then measure how the correlation in AP-1 state decays with lineage distance and number of intervening mitoses. Heritable memory predicts correlation that persists over several generations and decays with division number rather than elapsed time.

title: Pulse-chase dating of the memory carrier
description: Use heavy amino acid labeling of Fos/Jun proteins together with labeled-histone nucleosome turnover measurements at the same loci, chasing both after stimulus withdrawal, to determine which molecular layer carries the persisting signal. If target-gene memory outlives the labeled AP-1 protein pool but tracks the age of nucleosomes or DNA methylation at AP-1 sites, memory is stored in chromatin that AP-1 deposited, a distinction that sustained-expression experiments alone cannot make.

title: Pulse, washout, and subthreshold-challenge retention assay
description: Deliver a calibrated stimulus pulse of defined amplitude and duration (e.g., TPA, TNF, or growth factor for 15-120 min), wash it out completely, then at intervals from hours to weeks challenge cells with a subthreshold dose too weak to re-write the state, scoring AP-1 target induction, AP-1 motif accessibility, and FOS/JUN occupancy. Memory is indicated by a larger response in pulsed than naive cells long after FOS/JUN protein has returned to baseline.

title: Accelerated decay experiments with extrapolated retention half-life
description: Because the memory may outlast a practical experiment, accelerate its loss by raising proliferation rate, forcing and counting divisions by dye dilution, or shifting temperature, and fit the decay rates to extrapolate a retention half-life under normal conditions. This yields a quantitative result, such as the number of divisions over which the AP-1-encoded state persists, rather than a binary answer.

title: Rate-dependent hysteresis of stimulus versus AP-1 output
description: Sweep stimulus dose slowly up and then back down at several sweep rates, measuring AP-1 activity and target output in single cells. Test whether the dose-response forms a hysteresis loop whose area grows with sweep speed and collapses at very slow sweeps; identical doses giving different outputs on the ascending and descending arms would show that state depends on history, not just current input.

title: Imaging the chromatin feature that forms and disappears with the stored state
description: Pair functional readouts with in-situ structural measurements of the proposed storage medium: live-cell imaging of tagged FOS/JUN, single-cell ATAC or CUT&Tag time courses, and DNA or nascent RNA FISH at specific AP-1-bound enhancers. The aim is to show that a defined chromatin feature (nucleosome eviction, enhancer-promoter contact) appears when memory is established and disappears when it is lost. Memory is supported only if the feature's lifetime matches functional retention in the same cells.

title: Erase, rewrite, and repeated cycling with targeted perturbations
description: Erase the stored state with AP-1-directed interventions (auxin degron on FOS/JUN, dominant-negative A-FOS, or dCas9-KRAB/HDAC recruitment to specific AP-1 enhancers), re-apply the stimulus to test rewriting, and repeat write/erase cycles to detect degradation or drift. Clean erasure by an AP-1-specific perturbation with intact rewriting would indicate AP-1 is the causal storage element rather than a correlate of another persistent change.

title: Decoding stimulus history from AP-1 state across a decay time course
description: Expose cells to a panel of distinct transient stimuli, wash out, and at log-spaced delays profile AP-1 family occupancy and AP-1 motif accessibility (CUT&RUN plus ATAC-seq). Train a classifier to predict which stimulus a cell or sample previously received from AP-1-associated features alone, plot accuracy versus delay, and compare with classifiers built on non-AP-1 features, so memory is quantified as a decodability half-life.

title: AP-1 degradation timed after the stimulus has ended
description: Degrade AP-1 subunits (dTAG or auxin degron on FOS/JUN family members) only during the post-stimulus interval, after the acute response has resolved. Test whether the history-dependent behavior disappears while the acute response remains intact, which would show that AP-1 is needed for the history effect but not for the original input response.

title: Installing a foreign AP-1 state in naive cells
description: In naive cells, synthetically establish an AP-1 state by inducible expression of a defined FOS/JUN dimer combination, or by dCas9-based recruitment of AP-1 to the enhancer set marked by stimulus A. Then challenge the cells with a common second stimulus. If AP-1 carries the memory, these cells should produce the stimulus-A-specific downstream response even though they never saw stimulus A.

title: Clonal barcoding with single-cell ATAC/RNA to measure memory timescale
description: Combine heritable clonal barcoding with paired single-cell ATAC/RNA at multiple timepoints after a transient stimulus to test whether AP-1 site accessibility and AP-1 target expression are concordant within clones and discordant between clones. The decay of clone-level autocorrelation gives a direct memory timescale and distinguishes heritable epigenetic storage from slowly decaying protein-level carryover.

title: Dose and sequence experiments distinguishing an integrator from a correlated readout
description: Vary stimulus amplitude, duration, number of pulses, and inter-pulse interval, then test whether AP-1 occupancy predicts the later response better than the stimulus parameters do, i.e., whether AP-1 is a sufficient statistic that accounts for the input history. Pair this with mediation analysis and with partial AP-1 ablation at graded degrader doses to test whether response magnitude scales with the amount of AP-1 remaining.

title: Graded re-stimulation after a known priming peak
description: Prime cells with a calibrated stimulus amplitude (e.g., serum, TGF-β, or stiffness), let signaling fully relax, then re-challenge parallel wells across a dose ladder spanning below and above the priming dose. Read out de novo AP-1 target transcription with live-cell FOS/JUN-family reporters and nascent RNA (SLAM-seq) to time response onset precisely. Memory is indicated if the transcriptional response stays suppressed until the dose exceeds the prior peak and then rises sharply, with the breakpoint tracking the priming amplitude.

title: Memory decay kinetics versus delay, division number, and chromatin-perturbing conditions
description: Repeat a prime/probe protocol while varying the inter-stimulus interval, the number of cell divisions (tracked by dye dilution or FUCCI sorting), and perturbations such as HDAC or BRD4 inhibition, replication stress, and osmotic chromatin decompaction. Fit the shift in re-activation threshold to an exponential or stretched-exponential decay to obtain a memory half-life and to identify which perturbations erase, accelerate, or protect the AP-1 record, distinguishing true storage from slow signal clearance.

title: Latent AP-1 enhancers as the memory-associated feature
description: At each time point of a memory assay, perform ATAC-seq, AP-1 CUT&RUN, and H3K4me1/H3K27ac profiling to identify sites that open during the first exposure and remain open (or newly nucleosome-depleted) after signaling returns to baseline. Correlate the number and residual accessibility of these retained sites, site by site, with the measured re-activation threshold across priming doses.

title: Causal closing and opening of retained AP-1 sites
description: Use dCas9-KRAB/DNMT3A to selectively close the retained AP-1 enhancers identified previously, and dCas9-p300 or synthetic AP-1 tethering to open them in naive cells, then repeat the graded re-stimulation assay. If these elements carry the memory, closing them should abolish the threshold shift and opening them should produce a primed response in cells never exposed to the stimulus.

title: Single-cell inference of maximum past dose and cumulative-dose dependence
description: Perform single-cell multiome (ATAC+RNA) on cells with hidden exposure histories, and fit the breakpoint in AP-1 target output versus log(stimulus dose) to infer a per-cell maximum-past-dose amplitude. Validate against the known true peak dose and test cell-to-cell spread. Contrast one large exposure with many sub-threshold cycles delivering equal cumulative dose, to determine whether AP-1 records only the historical maximum or accumulates with cumulative exposure.

title: Persistence modeling of chromatin time series after a stimulus pulse
description: Give cells a brief AP-1-inducing stimulus (e.g., a TPA or cytokine pulse, then washout). Profile accessibility (ATAC-seq) and AP-1 binding (CUT&RUN) at many time points over days to weeks, and fit a decay model to each locus. AP-1-bound sites that stay open after AP-1 protein returns to baseline, while matched non-AP-1 sites return to normal, would be candidate memory loci.

title: Time-resolved responses to an AP-1-only pulse
description: Use an inducible or degron-tagged Fos/Jun construct to deliver a pulse that activates only AP-1. Estimate local-projection-style responses at each later time point for chromatin state and for gene induction after a standard rechallenge. This tests whether AP-1 alone is sufficient to leave a lasting mark, separate from the other pathways a natural stimulus activates.

title: AP-1 removal at different phases and inhibition of candidate carriers
description: Use acute degradation (dTAG/auxin) of AP-1 subunits at three points: during the priming pulse, during the quiet interval, or only at rechallenge. In parallel, inhibit candidate carriers such as SWI/SNF recruitment, H3K4me1 writers, or cooperating lineage transcription factors. If memory survives removal of AP-1 during the interval but depends on a co-factor, AP-1 initiates the memory but does not maintain it.

title: Barcoded lineage difference-in-differences across divisions
description: Barcode clones, split sister lineages into primed and unprimed arms, and compare their rechallenge responses at increasing numbers of divisions after priming (a difference-in-differences design). Pair this with mitotic-chromosome CUT&RUN to show whether AP-1-dependent memory is passed through mitosis (bookmarking) or fades with dilution.

title: Allele-specific comparison using natural variation in AP-1 motifs
description: In F1 hybrid cells or donor panels, identify enhancers where a SNP disrupts the AP-1 motif on one allele. Compare allele-specific accessibility and expression memory after priming. If AP-1 drives the memory, it should persist only on the allele with an intact motif, within the same nucleus.

title: Dose hysteresis loops for AP-1 activity
description: Step a stimulus (TPA, TNF, growth factor, or a targeted inhibitor) slowly up through a dose series and then back down through the same doses, reading AP-1 activity at each step with live FOS/JUN reporters and smFISH for AP-1 target genes. A down-ramp trajectory displaced from the up-ramp trajectory forms a hysteresis loop and defines the dose window in which AP-1 state depends on history rather than current input.

title: Bistable-range mapping with history-matched cells
description: Prepare two populations under identical current conditions but opposite histories (previously high AP-1 versus naive), then place both at a series of intermediate stimulus levels for many divisions. The range of inputs over which the two populations stably maintain different AP-1 activity and target-gene output is the empirical bistable range.

title: Critical-slowing-down statistics in single-cell AP-1 reporter traces
description: Apply critical-slowing-down diagnostics (lag-1 autocorrelation, variance, and recovery time) to long-term live imaging of an AP-1 transcriptional reporter after brief optogenetic or drug pulses, as cells approach a transition point in stimulus dose. Rising autocorrelation, variance, and recovery time near the inferred threshold would support bistability rather than a graded dose response.

title: Chromatin profiling of past stimulation in cells with naive-like transcription
description: After stimulus removal, profile ATAC-seq, AP-1 CUT&RUN, and H3K4me1/H3K27ac at AP-1 motifs in AP-1-bound enhancers of cells that are transcriptionally indistinguishable from naive cells, to see whether the chromatin still reflects prior exposure. Pairing this with lineage barcoding tests whether the chromatin state predicts which cells reactivate fastest on re-stimulation, i.e. whether it reflects functional memory rather than an inert residual change.

title: Transient AP-1 pulse to test state switching and reversibility
description: Deliver a short, defined pulse of AP-1 activity alone (optogenetic JUN/FOS dimer or auxin-degron release) without the upstream stimulus, then remove it and follow cells for weeks. If supra-threshold pulses drive a self-sustaining high state while sub-threshold pulses relax back, AP-1 is sufficient to set the memory. In reverse, acute AP-1 degradation in memory-bearing cells tests whether the state can be switched back below the threshold.

title: Stimulus cycling with a transient AP-1 loss
description: Prime cells with stimulus A, then transiently remove AP-1 function for a defined window (degron-tagged cJun/FOSL1 or inducible A-FOS), then restore AP-1 and re-challenge with A. If the primed response returns intact, memory is independent of AP-1; if the transient loss erases the faster/larger secondary response, AP-1 itself is the storage element. Varying the duration and depth of AP-1 loss gives a dose-response for erasure.

title: Priming-duration scaling of memory decay
description: Vary priming duration (t_w) over a wide range, then at many rest times (t) after withdrawal measure AP-1 motif accessibility (ATAC/CUT&Tag) and the magnitude of the secondary response. Test whether decay curves from different t_w collapse onto a single function of t/t_w. Such scaling would indicate that AP-1 enhancer states integrate exposure history rather than acting as a simple on/off switch.

title: Remaining chromatin state after stimulus removal
description: Remove the stimulus and map AP-1 occupancy, enhancer accessibility, H3K4me1/H3K27ac, and cohesin-dependent contacts at AP-1 sites, at matched transcriptional baselines. Loci that retain AP-1 footprints after the transcriptional response has fully decayed are candidate carriers of the memory, and their overlap with the sites reactivated fastest on re-challenge quantifies how much of the memory they explain.

title: Single-cell overlap between primed and recall states
description: Use lineage barcoding plus paired scATAC/scRNA to compute a configuration overlap between each clone's primed state and its state after rest and re-challenge. A broad, bimodal overlap distribution restricted to AP-1-bound regions would indicate that a subset of cells and a specific set of AP-1 loci carry the memory, rather than a uniform population-level shift.

title: Frequency-resolved response to oscillating stimulation
description: Deliver the stimulus as square-wave pulse trains across several decades of period (minutes to days) using microfluidics or optogenetic control of the AP-1 pathway. Measure response amplitude and phase lag of AP-1 target output. Slow components whose characteristic relaxation time grows with prior priming duration would demonstrate history-dependent AP-1 dynamics that change with the age of the priming, and comparing with and without AP-1 degradation localizes those slow modes.

title: Priming learning curve with a decay term
description: Stimulate cells a controlled number of times with systematically varied rest intervals and fit the re-challenge response to a Wright-type learning curve in which cumulative exposures are discounted by a decay factor, yielding a per-gene and per-enhancer AP-1 memory half-life. Adding an unrelated second stimulus measures transfer of the primed response, separating stimulus-specific memory from a general increase in responsiveness.

title: Timed degron depletion at encoding, storage, and recall
description: Use dTAG/auxin degron alleles of FOS, JUN, JUNB, and ATF3 to deplete AP-1 only during the first stimulus, only during the quiescent storage interval, or only just before re-challenge, with washout and re-expression controls. If AP-1 is the memory store rather than the writer or reader, only storage-window depletion should erase the primed response.

title: Partitioning memory among AP-1 protein, chromatin, and network feedback
description: In the same primed cells, measure AP-1 protein residence time (pulse-chase SILAC, FRAP), the chromatin state (ATAC-seq, FOS/JUN CUT&RUN, H3K4me1/H3K27ac, DNA methylation at AP-1 motifs), and AP-1 autoregulatory feedback dynamics. Then test whether primed accessibility outlasts AP-1 protein by many half-lives. Persistence after the protein is gone localizes the memory to AP-1-established chromatin; decay that tracks protein turnover localizes it to AP-1 itself.

title: Sister-cell split with clonal barcodes and transplantation
description: Barcode cells and let clones divide, then challenge one sister branch and use its response to predict the response of the untouched sister after the same priming history, as a function of intervening divisions. This gives a mitotic retention rate that separates heritable memory from noise. Transplanting primed cells into a naive microenvironment tests whether memory travels with the cell or with its context.

title: Heterokaryon fusion and nuclear/cytoplasmic swap
description: Fuse primed to naive cells (and primed nuclei to naive cytoplasts via enucleation or nuclear transfer) with allele-distinguishable reporters, then score allele-specific AP-1 target induction in the hybrid. Dominance of the primed state and whether it is nucleus- or cytoplasm-borne identifies the physical substrate, and recruitment of the naive genome would indicate a diffusible trans-acting AP-1 memory rather than a cis-chromatin one.

title: Persistence regression with lineage tracing and mediation analysis
description: Expose cells to a transient stimulus, withdraw it, and track barcoded clones over many divisions with longitudinal scATAC/scRNA, regressing later response amplitude on past exposure dose. Then run mediation analysis to ask how much of the persistence coefficient is carried by retained AP-1 motif accessibility/FOS-JUN occupancy versus alternative carriers such as DNA methylation, H3K4me1, BAF retention, or residual protein.

title: Degron removal of AP-1 during the memory window
description: Apply an auxin or dTAG degron to FOS/JUN family members only after stimulus withdrawal and before restimulation. If AP-1 maintains memory, degradation confined to this latent period should erase enhanced recall despite an intact exposure history.

title: Matched never-occupied AP-1 motif control loci
description: Use CRISPR to mutate AP-1 motifs that gained stable accessibility after the transient stimulus, alongside sequence- and expression-matched AP-1 motifs that were never occupied. Memory should be lost only for the first set, which would exclude generic AP-1 dependence or motif-adjacent genomic context.

title: Allele-specific analysis in F1 hybrid cells
description: In F1 hybrid cells, use heterozygous SNPs that disrupt AP-1 motifs. Both alleles share the same trans environment and exposure history, so allele-specific differences in retained priming and recall isolate the cis function of the AP-1 motif. Heterozygous SNPs that do not affect motifs serve as controls.

title: Dose-threshold comparison with optogenetic AP-1 induction
description: Finely titrate the stimulus to locate the sharp threshold at which AP-1 enhancer priming switches on, then compare cells just below versus just above the threshold (sorted on a live AP-1 reporter) for long-term recall. In addition, induce FOS/JUN optogenetically without the original stimulus, to alter AP-1 activity by a route that bypasses other stimulus-induced changes.

title: Hysteresis measurement by up and down dose titration
description: Titrate an AP-1-driving input (serum, TGF-beta, substrate stiffness, or inducible MEK) up a dose series and then back down the same series, reading an AP-1 target reporter in single cells at each step. A memory mechanism should give a hysteresis loop whose width quantifies stored information, whereas slow signal decay should not; single-cell readout distinguishes true per-cell bistability from graded responses with heterogeneous thresholds.

title: Time-dependent versus division-dependent decay of the primed state
description: After a transient AP-1 pulse, split cells into cycling versus arrested conditions (CDK4/6 inhibition, contact inhibition, thymidine block) matched for elapsed time, and measure decay of the primed state per hour versus per cell division. Replication-coupled dilution of a chromatin mark predicts division-dependent decay, whereas protein- or feedback-based persistence predicts time-dependent decay.

title: Pan-AP-1 family degron with clearance and restoration
description: Tag all expressed bZIP partners (FOS/FOSB/FOSL1/JUN/JUNB/JUND) with degrons so the entire family can be cleared for defined windows after priming and then restored. Recovery of the primed state would show that AP-1 reads or writes memory stored elsewhere, while permanent loss would show that AP-1 occupancy itself stores the memory. Single-factor knockdowns cannot make this distinction because of redundancy.

title: Synthetic AP-1 motif-array library for minimal sufficient memory encoding
description: Integrate at one fixed safe-harbor site a library of synthetic loci varying AP-1 motif number, affinity, spacing, flanking nucleosome-positioning sequence, and core promoter, then deliver a standardized AP-1 pulse and assay which configurations remain active days later. This tests whether AP-1 sites alone suffice to build a memory element and identifies the sequence features that convert transient binding into a persistent state.

title: Allele-specific cis test with heterozygous AP-1 motif disruption
description: Disrupt the AP-1 motif on only one allele of candidate memory enhancers (or use F1 hybrid or heterozygous lines with natural motif-disrupting variants) and measure allele-resolved accessibility and nascent transcription before, during, and long after a stimulus pulse. Because both alleles share the same nucleus, trans environment, and stimulus history, persistent loss of priming only in cis would indicate that AP-1 binding at that element carries the memory.

title: Division-coupled dilution test: protein versus chromatin storage of memory
description: Pulse-chase label AP-1 subunits (SNAP/HaloTag or photoconvertible Dendra-FOS/JUN/JUNB) and measure each subunit's protein half-life and nuclear residence time alongside the decay of functional memory, in parallel in cycling versus pharmacologically arrested (or contact-inhibited) cells. If memory half-life scales with division-driven dilution of a long-lived AP-1 pool rather than with elapsed time in arrested cells, the memory is a protein reservoir rather than a chromatin state; the two regimes make opposite quantitative predictions.

title: Synthetic minimal AP-1 memory circuit with tunable hysteresis
description: In a cell type with little endogenous AP-1 activity, build an orthogonal bZIP (AP-1 leucine zipper fused to a non-native DNA-binding domain) driving a synthetic enhancer array in which motif number, spacing, and feedback strength are systematically varied, and drive it transiently with a small-molecule or light input. Measure the hysteresis width and bistability boundary of the resulting input-output curves to determine whether AP-1's autoregulatory architecture is by itself sufficient to store a stable state, and which design parameters set memory duration.

title: Mutual information across combinatorial stimulus histories
description: Expose cells to all sequences of a small set of distinct stimuli (e.g., 3 inputs in 2-3 step orders, including order permutations and repeats), then after a long washout read out single-cell chromatin and transcription plus AP-1 dimer composition (multiplexed proximity ligation or dimer-specific CUT&Tag). Compute the mutual information between past history and present state to quantify how many bits are stored and whether the stored code is order-dependent (non-commutative), which would distinguish a combinatorial AP-1 memory from a single scalar variable reflecting how recently cells were stimulated.

title: Allele-specific cis test of AP-1 motifs in F1 hybrid cells
description: Use F1 hybrid cells (e.g., mouse F1 fibroblasts/ESCs or human trio-derived lines) whose haplotypes differ at thousands of AP-1 motifs, and measure allele-specific accessibility and transcription at primed enhancers long after a transient stimulus. Both alleles share the same nucleus, trans-environment, and AP-1 protein pool, so persistent allelic imbalance that tracks AP-1 motif strength would indicate that the motif itself, not correlated chromatin features, carries the memory. This can be extended by prime-editing single motif variants in the weaker haplotype.

title: Optogenetic AP-1 dose, duration and pulse-number series to test sufficiency for memory
description: Use a light-controlled AP-1 (optogenetic FOS/JUN dimerization or LOV-caged bZIP) to deliver pulses of AP-1 activity that vary in amplitude, duration, and pulse number at fixed integrated dose, in the absence of the upstream stimulus, then assay memory weeks later. This tests whether memory depends on integrated dose, peak amplitude, or pulse number. Memory installed without the physiological signal, or erased by a counter-pulse of a repressive bZIP, would establish sufficiency with a quantitative dose-response relationship rather than a binary knockout result.

title: Division-coupled versus time-coupled decay of the primed state
description: Measure decay of the primed state as a function of cell division number rather than elapsed time, comparing cycling cells, slowly cycling cells (CDK4/6 inhibition or contact inhibition), and reversibly arrested cells, with divisions tracked by dye dilution or live imaging. Replication-coupled chromatin memory should lose a fixed fraction per S phase, whereas protein-level or autoregulatory-feedback memory should decay on a clock-time scale independent of division number.

title: Allele-resolved test of whether memory acts in cis
description: In F1 hybrid or SNP-rich cells, or in clones with the AP-1 motif deleted from only one allele of a target enhancer, prime the cells and then measure allele-specific accessibility, nascent transcription (allele-resolved PRO-seq or intronic smFISH with SNP probes), and reactivation kinetics on rechallenge. If memory is carried by chromatin at the site, the two alleles should remember independently and discordantly; if it is carried by a diffusible AP-1 pool or feedback loop, both alleles should behave identically.

title: Transient recruitment of FOS/JUN to a naive synthetic locus
description: Integrate a motif-free synthetic reporter locus at a defined genomic position and recruit FOS/JUN bZIP domains to it for a controlled pulse using dox-inducible dCas9 or zinc-finger fusions. Then withdraw the recruiter and measure whether accessibility and expression persist for days and through cell divisions. Repeat with dimerization-dead, DNA-binding-dead, and transactivation-dead variants, and with recruited partners removed, to identify which AP-1 activity is sufficient to install a heritable state at a locus with no prior history.

title: Dimer composition and cross-stimulus interference
description: Test whether the identity of a remembered stimulus is stored in which FOS/JUN family dimer occupies a site. Measure dimer composition over time with pairwise proximity ligation, split-fluorophore dimer reporters, or crosslinking mass spectrometry. Combine this with an interference design: prime with stimulus A, challenge with an unrelated AP-1-activating stimulus B, then test for A. Overwriting, saturation, or retroactive interference between stimuli would show the memory has limited capacity and is written in dimer composition, not only in general enhancer opening.

title: Pulse-chase of AP-1 protein molecules
description: Knock HaloTag into FOS and JUN, pulse-label the existing protein pool with a bright dye, chase with a blocking ligand, and use single-molecule tracking plus chromatin fractionation. Determine whether the same old molecules remain bound at primed sites, are re-deposited after mitosis, or are replaced by newly synthesized protein while memory persists. Residence times and the fraction of old protein retained set an upper bound on how much memory the protein itself can carry versus what must be passed to chromatin.

title: Heterokaryon fusion to separate cis-chromatin memory from trans-acting AP-1 protein
description: Fuse a primed cell (prior transient stimulus) with a genetically distinguishable naive cell and use allele-specific ATAC-seq/RNA-seq to determine whether the primed chromatin state is maintained only on the experienced genome or is imposed in trans on the naive genome by the shared AP-1 protein pool. Cis-restricted persistence would indicate chromatin-encoded memory, whereas dominant trans conversion would indicate that AP-1 is a long-lived diffusible signal rather than a memory element.

title: Comparing AP-1 protein lifetime with memory lifetime
description: Use HaloTag pulse-chase labeling (plus SILAC turnover measurement) of endogenously tagged FOS/JUN to measure degradation and mitotic dilution rates of the AP-1 protein molecules present at the time of stimulation, and compare these decay kinetics quantitatively with the decay of the primed phenotype in the same cells. Memory that substantially outlives the original protein pool, with no sustained new synthesis, cannot be explained by slow transcription-factor decay and requires a self-propagating mechanism.

title: Decoupling the AP-1 autoregulatory circuit from AP-1 protein level
description: Place JUN/FOS expression under exogenous doxycycline control at the endogenous locus while deleting the endogenous AP-1-bound autoregulatory enhancers, so that AP-1 protein levels can be clamped independently of feedback. If transient stimulation no longer produces a persistent state despite identical AP-1 protein levels, memory is a property of the self-reinforcing circuit rather than of AP-1 occupancy per se.

title: Synthetic minimal AP-1 memory element
description: Integrate synthetic arrays of TRE/AP-1 motifs (varying motif number, spacing, flanking nucleosome-positioning sequences, and partner motifs such as TEAD or ETS) upstream of an inert reporter at a defined safe-harbor locus, then deliver a transient AP-1 pulse and measure how long accessibility and reporter expression persist. This tests whether AP-1 binding sites alone are sufficient to convert a transient input into a stable state, and defines the minimal sequence requirements.

title: Decoding stimulus history from single-cell AP-1 profiles
description: Expose cells to ordered combinations of distinct AP-1-activating inputs (e.g., growth factor, mechanical stretch, cytokine) in different sequences and intervals. Train a classifier on single-cell AP-1 binding/accessibility profiles to decode each cell's stimulus history, and quantify mutual information between past input and present state as a function of elapsed time and number of divisions. A memory mechanism should preserve stimulus identity and order rather than collapsing all histories onto a single magnitude axis.

title: Separating time-decay from division-dilution of the memory
description: Measure decay of the AP-1-associated state as a function of completed divisions rather than elapsed time, comparing cycling cells (dye dilution or FUCCI-sorted generations) against cells arrested for the same duration (contact inhibition, CDK4/6 inhibition). Then use repli-ATAC or nascent-chromatin capture to time how fast accessibility is re-established behind the replication fork at AP-1 sites. A heritable memory should decay per generation with active post-replicative re-establishment, whereas a long-lived protein or RNA pool should decay per unit time and be diluted.

title: Synthetic TRE array to measure memory capacity
description: Integrate a library of synthetic reporter loci at a fixed safe-harbor site that systematically vary TRE/CRE motif number, affinity, spacing, and co-occurring partner motifs, then deliver a single calibrated stimulus pulse and measure how long each configuration holds its expression state. This gives a quantitative dose-response between binding-site configuration and memory half-life, and identifies whether storage requires cooperative multi-site occupancy or a partner factor.

title: Mutual information between stimulus history and AP-1 state
description: Deliver defined stimulus sequences differing in order, dose, and spacing (A-then-B versus B-then-A, pulsed versus sustained). Compute the mutual information between stimulus history and single-cell AP-1 occupancy/accessibility, and compare it with the same measure for the rest of the transcriptome. This determines how much information about past stimulation AP-1 carries and whether it encodes order and magnitude or only prior exposure versus none.

title: Old-versus-new protein pulse-chase to identify the memory substrate
description: Use HaloTag pulse-chase labeling of endogenous FOS, JUN, JUND, and FRA1 combined with single-molecule tracking and FRAP to measure dimer composition, residence time, and turnover of the protein molecules present during the memory window. If memory resides in a slowly exchanging long-lived dimer pool (e.g., JUND/FRA1) rather than in chromatin, old labeled protein should remain locus-bound across the memory period; if chromatin is the substrate, newly synthesized protein should be recruited to the same sites.

title: Two-phase CRISPR screen for maintenance factors after stimulus withdrawal
description: Run a genome-wide CRISPRi/ORF screen in which perturbations are induced only after the stimulus is withdrawn, scoring loss of a stable AP-1-driven reporter or loss of primed restimulation. This separates maintenance factors from factors required for the acute response. Hits dispensable for induction but required for persistence would define the machinery that maintains the AP-1 state and allow memory to be erased selectively without blocking signaling.

title: Heterokaryon test of cis versus trans memory
description: Fuse a stimulus-primed cell with a naive cell (nuclei distinguished by labeled histones or species-specific SNPs) and use per-nucleus nascent intron FISH plus single-nucleus ATAC to ask whether the naive nucleus acquires the primed program. If memory is carried by diffusible trans factors, both nuclei should converge; if it is stored in cis at chromatin, the two nuclei should retain distinct AP-1 target states in the shared cytoplasm.

title: Decay per cell division versus per unit time
description: Measure memory decay (reporter output, target-gene expression, AP-1-site accessibility) in parallel populations held non-dividing (CDK4/6 inhibition, contact inhibition, serum starvation) versus freely cycling, and fit decay as a function of elapsed time versus number of completed divisions. Decay per division implicates replication-coupled dilution of a chromatin-templated state, whereas decay per unit time implicates protein turnover or a self-sustaining feedback loop.

title: Synthetic enhancer library defining the architecture that converts a pulse into a persistent state
description: Integrate at a single safe-harbor landing pad a barcoded library of synthetic enhancers that systematically vary AP-1 motif number, affinity, spacing, flanking partner motifs (TEAD, RUNX, NF-kB), and nucleosome-positioning sequences, then measure reporter output and barcode-level accessibility days after a single stimulus pulse. This maps the design rules by which AP-1 binding sites are sufficient to store a past input, separating sequence-encoded memory capacity from endogenous locus context.

title: Decoding stimulus history from single cells with mutual information
description: Expose cells to a panel of distinct transient inputs (different cytokines, doses, durations, pulse orders), then at a long delay perform joint scRNA-seq/scATAC-seq and train a classifier to recover which input each cell experienced, quantifying the mutual information (in bits) between past stimulus and present state. Repeat under AP-1 perturbation to test whether AP-1 carries the stored information by measuring how much recoverable information about the past is lost, rather than only whether some genes change.

title: In vitro replication of AP-1-bound chromatin
description: Assemble nucleosomal arrays containing AP-1 sites, load purified Fos/Jun dimers (and candidate cofactors), and replicate the templates in Xenopus egg extract or a reconstituted replisome system. Assay occupancy and accessibility on the two daughter templates with and without free AP-1 in solution, to test whether AP-1 can survive or be re-templated through replication fork passage, versus requiring rebuilding from the soluble pool each cycle.

title: Synthetic enhancer library at a landing pad
description: Integrate a barcoded library of synthetic enhancers at a single neutral genomic landing pad, systematically varying AP-1 motif number, affinity, spacing, and co-occurring partner motifs, then deliver one defined stimulus pulse and track reporter expression and accessibility for days. This gives a quantitative sufficiency map of which cis-regulatory architectures convert a transient input into a persistent output, independent of endogenous locus history.

title: Comparing memory duration with AP-1 protein lifetime
description: Use HaloTag pulse-chase or SILAC on endogenously tagged FOS/JUN to measure protein half-lives and dilution-by-division rates in the same cells in which memory duration is assayed. If the phenotypic memory substantially outlasts the integrated lifetime of all AP-1 protein present at the end of the stimulus, the information cannot reside in AP-1 protein levels and must be passed to a chromatin- or feedback-based store.

title: Mitotic bookmarking and single-molecule residence time as the heritability mechanism
description: Combine single-molecule tracking of Halo-FOS/JUN through mitosis with mitotic-chromosome CUT&RUN in synchronized cells to ask whether AP-1 remains bound to memory enhancers during mitosis. Then test separation-of-function mutants (e.g., bZIP phospho-site or DNA-binding-surface variants) that selectively abolish mitotic retention without altering interphase binding, and ask whether memory survives cell division.

title: Dimer identity versus total AP-1 amount as the stored variable
description: Quantify the full bZIP dimer repertoire (FOS/FOSB/FRA1/FRA2 with JUN/JUNB/JUND, plus ATF partners) in single cells over the memory window, using dimer-specific proximity ligation or split-reporter/BiFC panels, together with per-cell response magnitude on restimulation. Test whether the memory-predictive variable is which dimer species persists rather than total AP-1 activity, which would indicate a combinatorial code.

title: Mutual information between stimulus history and AP-1 state
description: Deliver programmed pulse trains that vary amplitude, duration, number, and inter-pulse interval (using microfluidics or optogenetic input), and compute the mutual information between past input sequence and present AP-1 state or chromatin readout at single-cell resolution. This quantifies in bits how much stimulus history AP-1 stores and distinguishes multi-state memory from a single slowly relaxing variable, since true memory should preserve information about pulse order and spacing, not just cumulative dose.

title: Time-based versus division-based decay and mitotic bookmarking
description: Measure decay of the primed state (accessibility and re-response amplitude) in matched populations that are cycling or reversibly arrested (CDK4/6 inhibitor or G0, with FUCCI staging), to determine whether memory half-life is set in hours or in cell divisions. Also use Halo-tagged Fos/Jun live imaging and mitotic-chromosome CUT&RUN to test whether AP-1 is retained on condensed chromatin, which a division-counting memory would require.

title: Single-molecule tracking of AP-1 binding kinetics in naive versus primed cells
description: Use HaloTag single-molecule tracking, FRAP, and AP-1 hub imaging to compare residence time, bound fraction, and target-search time of JunB/Fos in naive versus primed cells held at matched AP-1 protein levels by a titratable degron. This tests whether memory is stored as faster or more stable rebinding kinetics at primed sites rather than as higher steady-state occupancy, and predicts how fast memory should recover after transient AP-1 removal.

title: Memory interference between two AP-1-dependent programs
description: Prime cells with stimulus A, then deliver an unrelated AP-1-inducing stimulus B, and ask whether B erases, overwrites, or leaves intact the A-specific primed response (and vice versa), including a titration of B's strength. A shared, limiting trans-acting AP-1 pool predicts dose-dependent retroactive interference, whereas locus-local chromatin storage predicts independence. Adding an excisable AP-1 decoy-site array provides an orthogonal test of a limiting pool.

title: Information-theoretic sufficiency test with stimulus-history microfluidics
description: Deliver defined sequences of stimulus histories in a microfluidic device to cells carrying a live AP-1 activity reporter and a downstream response reporter. Compute the mutual information I(history; AP-1 state) and the conditional information I(history; response | AP-1 state). If AP-1 is the memory substrate, the conditional term should fall to near zero, which would show AP-1 is on the causal path rather than merely correlated with history.

title: Allele-specific memory in F1 hybrid or heterozygous-donor cells
description: In F1 hybrid mouse cells or human donor cells heterozygous at thousands of AP-1 motifs, perform allele-resolved ATAC and nascent RNA before and long after a transient stimulus. Test whether the persistent (memory) state tracks the motif-disrupting allele in cis. The many natural motif variants provide a genome-scale, internally controlled causal test, and motifs showing memory loss without loss of acute induction identify those needed specifically for maintenance.

title: Pulse-chase separating AP-1 establishment from maintenance
description: Use an optogenetic or chemically inducible AP-1 construct, plus a degron on endogenous Jun/Fos family members, to deliver a defined transient pulse, then chase for many days while tracking target-gene expression and chromatin accessibility. Depleting AP-1 at staggered times after the pulse distinguishes whether AP-1 is needed only to establish the state or is continuously required to maintain it, which discriminates a memory mechanism from a simple persistent signal.

title: Lineage-barcoded sister-cell concordance of AP-1 target states
description: Barcode single cells and profile single-cell RNA and ATAC after several divisions. Quantify how much more similar AP-1 target expression and AP-1 motif accessibility are between clonal relatives than between unrelated cells, as a function of generations since the common ancestor. The decay of this concordance gives a quantitative memory half-life in cell divisions rather than in hours.

title: Hysteresis mapping of AP-1 dose-response
description: Expose cells to graded stimulus levels on both an ascending and a descending ramp and read out AP-1 activity with a live reporter at single-cell resolution. A reproducible gap between the up and down curves is a signature of a bistable, self-reinforcing circuit, and its absence would argue that AP-1 relays rather than stores information.

title: Sort-and-regrow stability assay with an endogenous AP-1 reporter
description: Knock a fluorescent reporter into an endogenous AP-1 target locus, sort the top and bottom expression deciles, regrow each population, and measure how quickly the full expression distribution is regenerated. Compare the relaxation timescale with cell-cycle time and mRNA/protein half-lives to determine whether the state is heritably stable or slow-fluctuating noise.

title: Prime-and-challenge transcriptional priming with enhancer deletion
description: Prime cells with a stimulus, wait until AP-1 protein and target transcripts return to baseline, then rechallenge and measure the speed and amplitude of the nascent transcriptional response. Delete individual AP-1-bound enhancers by CRISPR and apply a heterologous second stimulus to test whether the memory is localized to specific elements and whether it is stimulus-specific or general.

title: Epoch-resolved degron mapping of when AP-1 is needed
description: Tag FOS and JUN with auxin- or dTAG-inducible degrons and deplete them in narrow windows: during the priming stimulus, during the washout interval, or only at restimulation. Then score the primed response, to distinguish AP-1's role in establishing, maintaining, and reading out the memory, which a simple knockout cannot do.

title: Heritability half-life from sister- and cousin-cell correlations
description: Combine heritable clonal barcoding with single-cell multiome (or live imaging of an AP-1 reporter) to measure how the correlation in AP-1 target expression and AP-1-site accessibility decays with the number of divisions separating two related cells. The decay constant gives a memory half-life in generations, which is compared with the AP-1 protein half-life to test whether the memory outlasts AP-1 protein.

title: Optogenetic pulse histories with a cross-stimulus prime/challenge matrix
description: Use optogenetic control of ERK or JNK to deliver precisely defined pulse histories (amplitude, duration, number, spacing), then measure the response to a later challenge. Extend this to a prime-A/challenge-B matrix across different stimuli to test whether AP-1 stores a stimulus-specific or a generic trace, since specificity distinguishes memory from general hypersensitivity.

title: Synthetic TRE arrays as a minimal sufficient memory element
description: Build a library of integrated reporters that vary the number, affinity, and spacing of AP-1 motifs plus the presence of nearby cofactor motifs, stimulate once, and measure how long each architecture sustains a primed state. This tests sufficiency rather than correlation at endogenous loci and yields a design rule for how much memory a given enhancer architecture can hold.

title: Mitotic retention and single-molecule residence time in primed cells
description: Image Halo-tagged JUN/FOS retention on mitotic chromosomes (with mitotic CUT&RUN as the genomic counterpart) and use single-molecule tracking of bound fraction and residence time in naive versus primed cells. Longer residence or mitotic retention in primed cells would indicate a mechanism for heritability, whereas unchanged kinetics would point to chromatin or cofactors instead.

title: Pulse-washout-rechallenge with varying gap length
description: Deliver a defined pulse of AP-1 activation (optogenetic FOS/JUN or a short growth-factor or stress pulse), wash out, then rechallenge cohorts after systematically increasing gaps to measure how long the primed response amplitude persists. The resulting decay curve gives a memory half-life that can be compared with AP-1 protein and mRNA turnover rates, distinguishing true memory from slow relaxation.

title: Hysteresis test for bistable AP-1 feedback
description: Titrate an AP-1-activating input up from zero and down from saturation, measuring steady-state AP-1 reporter output at matched doses along each arm. Non-overlapping up and down curves at the same dose would demonstrate hysteresis, indicating a self-sustaining feedback memory rather than a passive stimulus-tracking response.

title: Sister-cell and lineage-tree partitioning of AP-1 state heritability
description: Combine live imaging of an AP-1 activity reporter with tracked lineage trees (or expressed lineage barcodes with single-cell multiome) to compute how correlated AP-1 state is between sisters, cousins, and unrelated cells. This partitions AP-1 variation into heritable and transient components and directly estimates how many generations the state survives.

title: Degron separation of AP-1 protein from its chromatin footprint
description: After priming, acutely degrade FOS/JUN family members with dTAG or auxin-inducible degrons during the memory window, then restore them and rechallenge. If the primed response survives transient AP-1 loss, memory is stored in chromatin or another substrate rather than in persisting AP-1 protein.

title: Chromatin-perturbation screen during the memory window
description: Apply inhibitors or targeted knockdowns of candidate chromatin machinery (SWI/SNF, EP300, BRD4, HDACs, specific histone modifiers) only in the interval between priming and rechallenge, with no perturbation during either stimulus. Hits that selectively erase the primed response identify the physical substrate maintaining AP-1-associated memory and distinguish it from effects on AP-1 signaling itself.

title: Separating establishment from maintenance with acute AP-1 degradation
description: Establish a primed state with a defined stimulus, then use dTAG or auxin degrons to acutely deplete JUN/FOS family proteins only after the stimulus is withdrawn, and ask whether the accessible enhancers, enhancer-promoter contacts, and faster re-induction persist. If memory persists without AP-1 protein, AP-1 establishes a chromatin mark rather than being the memory itself; if memory collapses, AP-1 is continuously required.

title: Memory half-life in cell divisions from lineage-resolved live imaging
description: Image a destabilized AP-1 activity reporter in a tracked lineage tree after a stimulus pulse, and compute mother-daughter, sister, and cousin correlations to extract a memory half-life in cell divisions rather than hours. Repeating this in cycling versus arrested cells separates replication-coupled dilution of the state from time-dependent decay, distinguishing chromatin-based inheritance from slow protein turnover.

title: Hysteresis scan for bistability in the AP-1 feedback loop
description: Titrate a tunable AP-1 input (optogenetic FOS/JUN or a graded growth factor dose) upward in one population and downward in a pre-activated population, then measure AP-1 target expression per cell at matched doses. A reproducible gap between the ascending and descending branches would be direct evidence that AP-1 autoregulation supports two stable states, a mechanistic signature expected of a memory module.

title: Synthetic AP-1 motif reporter series testing sufficiency
description: Integrate at a single safe-harbor locus a library of reporters that systematically vary AP-1 motif number, affinity, spacing, and neighboring pioneer-factor motifs, then measure both acute induction and persistence after the stimulus ends. This tests whether AP-1 sites alone are sufficient to encode memory or only do so in specific sequence contexts, separating AP-1's inducer role from its memory role.

title: Allele-specific maintenance in hybrid cells
description: In F1 hybrid or heterozygously motif-edited cells, perform allele-resolved ATAC and nascent transcription after stimulus withdrawal to test whether the primed state is maintained in cis at individual alleles. Persistent allelic asymmetry would show the memory is encoded in the chromatin of the locus, while symmetric behavior would indicate memory resides in trans in the cellular AP-1 pool.

title: Lineage-resolved heritability of AP-1 activity
description: Barcode single cells (LARRY/Watermelon-style) and profile sister and cousin cells by scRNA-seq or live AP-1 reporter imaging to compute how AP-1 activity autocorrelates across divisions. Compare the decay constant for AP-1 target output with that of other signaling-responsive programs to test whether the AP-1 state is heritable rather than merely stimulus-driven.

title: Degron separation of establishment from maintenance
description: Tag FOS/JUN with a degron and deplete AP-1 either before stimulation or hours after the state has formed, then read out accessibility (ATAC) and restimulation response. Memory predicts that the primed state persists after AP-1 protein is removed, whereas a sustained-signal model predicts collapse.

title: Prime-rest-rechallenge transcriptional priming assay
description: Deliver a defined transient stimulus, wash out, and rest cells for varying intervals and division numbers, then rechallenge and measure the amplitude and latency of AP-1 target induction by nascent RNA (TT-seq or single-molecule FISH). Faster or larger secondary responses that decay with time and divisions quantify the strength and lifetime of the memory.

title: Synthetic AP-1 site array for sufficiency
description: Integrate arrays of AP-1 motifs (and motif-scrambled controls) at a neutral genomic locus adjacent to a reporter, then drive AP-1 binding transiently with an optogenetic or chemically inducible Fos/Jun module. Persistent reporter expression and accessibility after induction ends would show that AP-1 binding is sufficient to write a heritable state, independent of pre-existing locus context.

title: Persistence of AP-1-primed state through replication and mitosis
description: Compare persistence of AP-1-primed accessibility in cycling cells versus cells arrested pharmacologically or in post-mitotic states, and perform mitotic-chromosome CUT&RUN to test for AP-1 bookmarking. This distinguishes a slowly decaying protein or chromatin state from a replication-heritable epigenetic mechanism and identifies the step where memory is copied or lost.

title: Sister-clone splitting to quantify heritability of AP-1 state
description: Barcode a clonal population, split it into sister subclones after a defined number of divisions, and compare AP-1 reporter activity and AP-1 target-gene expression between sisters versus random pairs. The intraclass correlation as a function of elapsed divisions yields the half-life of the AP-1 state and separates true heredity from transient, stimulus-driven fluctuation.

title: Washout-and-rechallenge priming assay
description: Transiently induce AP-1 (growth factor, optogenetic FOS/JUN dimerization, or an inducible construct), wash out, wait for AP-1 protein and transcript levels to return to baseline, then re-stimulate and measure response amplitude and kinetics. A faster or larger secondary response in previously stimulated cells with indistinguishable current AP-1 levels would indicate stored memory rather than persistent signaling.

title: Acute degron depletion to separate stored chromatin state from ongoing AP-1 activity
description: Use a dTAG or auxin degron on FOS and JUN family members to acutely remove AP-1 protein for hours to days, then restore it. Measure enhancer accessibility (ATAC) and target expression before, during, and after depletion. If the pre-depletion enhancer landscape is re-established in the same cells, memory is carried by something other than AP-1 occupancy itself; if it resets to a naive state, AP-1 occupancy is the memory.

title: Sorting AP-1-high and AP-1-low cells with retrospective lineage tracing
description: Sort AP-1-reporter-high and -low cells from a barcoded population and let each grow out for several weeks. Measure both the reporter distribution and a functional fate (e.g., drug survival or invasion) in the progeny. With barcode recovery, test whether a clone's AP-1 state at time zero predicts its fate at a later time, which is the operational definition of a memory mechanism.

title: Hysteresis and bistability mapping of the AP-1 dose response
description: Expose cells to a graded series of stimulus doses approached from below and from above (stepping up from zero versus stepping down from saturating stimulus) and measure single-cell AP-1 activity at matched steady-state doses. Overlapping curves indicate passive relay of the signal; a hysteresis loop with a bistable regime would show AP-1 is wired as a self-sustaining memory switch, and mutating AP-1 motifs in FOS/JUN's own regulatory elements should abolish the loop.

title: Lineage-barcoded sister-cell split assay to measure memory half-life
description: Barcode cells, deliver a brief AP-1-activating stimulus, then let clones divide and split related cells so that one is profiled (scRNA-seq or reporter level) while its relative is challenged later. The concordance between relatives as a function of elapsed generations gives a quantitative memory half-life in divisions, and distinguishes heritable memory from slowly decaying protein that is diluted equally in all cells.

title: Degron time-window dissection of establishment, maintenance, and recall
description: Use dTAG or auxin degrons on endogenously tagged FOS and JUN to remove AP-1 protein only during the stimulus, only during the quiescent interval, or only at the time of the second challenge. If memory survives depletion during the interval but not during the stimulus, the information is stored in something AP-1 deposits rather than in AP-1 itself.

title: Post-replication single-molecule footprinting of AP-1 enhancers
description: Combine nascent-strand labeling with single-molecule methyltransferase footprinting (Fiber-seq/SAMOSA) to ask whether AP-1 motifs on newly replicated daughter chromatin are re-opened and co-occupied in cis, and how fast. This tests whether the state is re-established on both daughter molecules after each round of replication, a requirement for epigenetic memory.

title: Two-pulse potentiation kinetics and information content
