title: Dose-and-interval mapping of memory decay in single cells
description: Systematically vary stimulus strength, duration, and the gap before re-stimulation, reading out per-cell response amplitude and AP-1 site accessibility. Fitting the resulting surface tests whether the system behaves like a bistable switch, a slowly decaying analog trace, or simple residual protein.

title: Timing of AP-1 degradation after state establishment
description: Tag FOS/JUN with auxin degrons and establish an AP-1-dependent cell state (e.g., drug-tolerant melanoma, activated fibroblasts). Then degrade AP-1 after establishment while tracking accessibility, nascent transcription, and state markers hourly, with washout and re-induction. A state that survives acute AP-1 loss but cannot be re-established would show that AP-1 establishes the memory without storing it.

title: Hysteresis curves with a tunable synthetic AP-1 input
description: Drive AP-1 with a dose- and duration-tunable synthetic input (inducible FOS-JUN dimer or optogenetic dimerizer) and map the full up-and-down dose-response of enhancer accessibility and target gene output. Memory is then quantified as the area of the hysteresis loop and the width of the bistable range, and compared across cell types.

title: Memory half-life measured per cell division
description: Combine a live AP-1 activity reporter with lineage barcoding and continuous imaging to follow the stimulus-induced state through known numbers of mitoses in single lineages. Fit the decay of mother-daughter and cousin-cousin correlations to separate decay by division from time-dependent decay, distinguishing heritable chromatin memory from a slowly decaying protein.

title: Temporal ordering of AP-1 binding and accessibility after replication fork passage
description: Use EdU-capture-coupled ATAC and CUT&RUN to determine, at minute-scale resolution after fork passage, whether AP-1 reoccupies its sites before accessibility returns or the reverse. Also image AP-1 retention on mitotic chromosomes. The temporal ordering identifies the physical carrier of the memory rather than just its correlates.

title: AP-1 motif mutations that disrupt recall but not the initial response
description: Use CRISPR to mutate individual AP-1 motifs in candidate memory enhancers, in cells and in a mouse epithelium with wound or inflammatory memory, then assay the response to the second stimulus as well as the first. A mutation that leaves the naive response intact but abolishes the faster or stronger recall response would show that those sites are the memory element itself.

title: Sister-cell concordance of AP-1 state after division
description: Use expressed lineage barcodes plus single-cell multiome (ATAC + RNA) to compare AP-1 motif accessibility and target-gene output between sister and cousin cells across increasing numbers of divisions. Heritability is indicated by concordance that decays with lineage distance. Live imaging of tagged FOS/JUN through mitosis tests whether the factor itself is retained on chromatin as the physical carrier.

title: Acute degron removal of AP-1 after the stimulus is withdrawn
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN family members with an auxin or dTAG degron, let cells establish a primed state, then deplete AP-1 only after the inducing stimulus has been washed out. If accessibility and re-inducibility collapse during depletion and fail to return after the protein is restored, AP-1 is actively maintaining the state rather than having merely initiated it.

title: Decay curves and second-challenge test
description: Deliver a transient stimulus, then measure AP-1 enhancer accessibility, binding, and transcriptional output at a dense timecourse out to weeks, re-challenging a subpopulation at each timepoint. Memory predicts a measurable half-life of the stored state plus a faster, larger, or lower-threshold second response in the cells that retained the AP-1 state.

title: Writing a state with synthetic AP-1 recruitment
description: Use chemically controlled dCas9 or LID-tag recruitment of FOS/JUN activation domains to specific endogenous enhancers, hold it briefly, then release. Persistence of accessibility and expression after release, in cells that never received the original stimulus, would establish that AP-1 occupancy alone is sufficient to install the memory.

title: Saturation mutagenesis of endogenous AP-1 (TRE) sites
description: Base-edit or prime-edit individual AP-1 motifs across a panel of primed enhancers, varying motif affinity, number, and spacing. Score initial induction and long-term retention separately. Sites required for retention but not for induction would separate the memory function from the response function at single-basepair resolution.

title: FOS/JUN residence time versus persistence of accessible sites
description: Measure single-molecule chromatin residence times of FOS/JUN/JUNB by live-cell single-particle tracking and compare them with the persistence of the accessible sites those factors create (ATAC-seq time-chase over multiple divisions). Cellular memory requires the site to outlive the factor by orders of magnitude; matched timescales would instead indicate continuous driving rather than a stored mark.

title: Accessibility and AP-1 binding decoupled from transcription
description: Run matched ATAC-seq, AP-1 CUT&RUN, and nascent transcription (PRO-seq/TT-seq) time courses long after stimulus withdrawal. Identify loci that stay open and AP-1-bound without ongoing nascent transcription. A long silent but primed window that leads to faster, larger induction on restimulation would indicate a latent memory element.

title: Second-hit amplification as the functional readout
description: Prime cells, wait, then re-challenge and quantify gains in response rate, amplitude, and the fraction of responding cells at candidate AP-1 memory loci. Show specificity by deleting the TRE motif or CRISPRi-silencing the individual primed enhancer, so that amplification is lost locus-specifically rather than only upon global AP-1 depletion.

title: Erasure threshold titration
description: Titrate candidate memory erasers in a dose-by-duration design: cell-cycle arrest versus forced divisions, replication inhibition, p300/HDAC inhibition, BAF/SMARCA4 degron, H3.3 and histone-chaperone knockdown, and AP-1 subunit degrons. Map which conditions collapse primed accessibility. The identity and magnitude of the insult required distinguishes replication-coupled, remodeler-dependent, and histone-variant-based memory mechanisms.

title: Maintenance of the primed state without ongoing AP-1, with clonal heritability
description: Use auxin/dTAG degrons to remove AP-1 protein completely after priming and test whether the primed, open state is maintained and still re-inducible without AP-1. Combine with lineage-barcoded single-cell multiome (scATAC + scRNA) to test clonal heritability of the primed state across divisions, distinguishing a self-sustaining state from one requiring continuous AP-1.

title: Decoupling AP-1 occupancy from its chromatin trace
description: After a transient stimulus, run parallel time courses of AP-1 protein levels (FOS/JUN immunofluorescence, degron-tagged reporters) and of chromatin state at AP-1 motifs (ATAC-seq, FOS/JUN CUT&RUN, H3K27ac). Memory is supported only if accessibility and enhancer marks persist long after AP-1 occupancy has decayed.

title: Restimulation latency as a readout of a stored trace
description: Stimulate, let the response fully subside, then restimulate at a range of intervals while imaging an AP-1 target reporter in single living cells to quantify response latency, amplitude, and responder fraction. Faster or larger second responses that decay as a function of the inter-stimulus interval give a quantitative memory half-life.

title: Acute AP-1 degradation separating establishment from maintenance
description: Use dTAG or auxin-inducible degradation of FOS/JUN applied either during the initial stimulus or only afterward, during the putative memory window. Persistence of the memory trace despite post-stimulus depletion would localize memory to chromatin, whereas its collapse would show memory depends on sustained AP-1 presence.

title: Genomic recorder of past AP-1 activity
description: Engineer an AP-1-responsive enhancer driving a recombinase or base editor that writes a permanent DNA barcode when AP-1 is active, then read the written mark jointly with scRNA-seq or ATAC days later. This tests, cell by cell, whether a past AP-1 episode predicts present transcriptional and chromatin state independently of current AP-1 levels.

title: Dilution versus turnover of the memory state in proliferating and arrested cells
description: Compare memory persistence in proliferating versus cell-cycle-arrested cells and assay AP-1 retention on mitotic chromosomes by CUT&RUN, distinguishing stepwise loss per division from continuous chromatin turnover. Analyze which sites retain versus lose the state (motif strength, cooperating factors, CpG content, enhancer-promoter contacts) to identify determinants of durable memory.

title: Clonal barcoding of first and second responses
description: Use heritable lineage barcodes (e.g., Watermelon/FateMap-style) to stimulate cells, let them divide through a rest period, then re-stimulate, and ask whether high- and low-responding cells fall into the same clones both times. AP-1 memory predicts clonally heritable second-response amplitude that correlates with first-response AP-1 target output, whereas a non-memory model predicts clone-independent, resampled variability.

title: Identifying which Fos/Jun dimer maintains the mark
description: Because AP-1 is a family of heterodimers, apply subunit-specific degron tags (FOS, FOSL1, JUN, JUNB, ATF3) and deplete each only during the quiescent interval between stimulations, leaving induction intact. Pair this with CUT&RUN time courses of each subunit at memory enhancers to distinguish a continuously occupied maintenance dimer from an initiating dimer that acts transiently while the mark is kept by something else.

title: Decay-rate comparison of occupancy, accessibility, and output
description: After a pulsed stimulus, measure in the same time course the decay kinetics of AP-1 protein, AP-1 ChIP/CUT&RUN occupancy, ATAC accessibility, H3K4me1/H3K27ac, and nascent transcription at the same loci. Memory is indicated by a quantitatively longer accessibility half-life than occupancy half-life at a specific enhancer subset, while loci where all layers decay together serve as internal negative controls.

title: Synthetic enhancer grammar for persistence
description: Build an MPRA/synthetic-locus library, integrated at a fixed landing pad, that varies TRE/AP-1 motif number, spacing, affinity, partner-motif identity, and flanking nucleosome-positioning sequence. Score which designs convert a transient stimulus into weeks-long accessibility and faster re-induction. Validate the top rules by prime-editing the corresponding motifs at endogenous memory enhancers to show the predicted design features are causally required.

title: Memory through DNA replication and cofactor requirement during rest
description: Compare memory retention in cycling cells versus pharmacologically or contact-arrested cells. Use nascent-chromatin capture (NCC or repli-ATAC) to determine whether AP-1 binding and accessibility are re-established on daughter strands within one cell cycle. In addition, apply acute MLL3/4, BRD4, or BAF (SMARCA4) inhibition only during the rest interval to identify which cofactor maintains the mark once AP-1 levels have returned to baseline.

title: Stimulus pulse-chase with acute AP-1 degradation
description: Deliver a transient stimulus (serum, TGF-beta, or a targeted inhibitor), wash out, and track AP-1 factor levels, chromatin accessibility at AP-1 motifs (ATAC-seq), and H3K27ac/H3K4me1 over days to weeks. Memory requires the open, primed state to persist after AP-1 protein has decayed; acute degradation (dTAG/auxin) of FOS/JUN at defined times after the pulse distinguishes whether AP-1 is the stored memory or only the factor that establishes the primed state.

title: Lineage barcoding plus AP-1 reporter across cell divisions
description: Combine heritable lineage barcodes (e.g., Watermelon/CellTag-style) with a live AP-1 transcriptional reporter and single-cell RNA/ATAC readout, so that an individual cell's AP-1 state before a perturbation can be linked to the behavior of its descendants many divisions later. Memory predicts intra-clone concordance of AP-1 activity and downstream fate that exceeds what is expected from shared transient signaling, and that concordance should decay with a measurable half-life in generations.

title: Dose-response to repeated stimulation
description: Stimulate cells, allow full return to baseline, then restimulate at varying intervals and doses, measuring transcriptional output amplitude, latency, and fraction of responding cells. A memory mechanism predicts potentiated or faster secondary responses (or a leftward-shifted dose-response) specifically at AP-1-dependent loci. This priming should be abolished by degrading AP-1 during the rest interval if AP-1 maintains it, or preserved if AP-1 only established it.

title: 3D genome anchoring of AP-1-primed enhancers
description: Use Micro-C or region-capture Hi-C together with AP-1 CUT&RUN before, during, and long after a transient stimulus to ask whether AP-1 establishes persistent enhancer-promoter contacts that outlast the signal. Stable loops anchored at AP-1 sites that remain after factor loss would be a structural substrate for memory, testable by degron removal of AP-1 or by CRISPRi silencing of individual anchors.

title: Single-cell transient AP-1 perturbation in otherwise identical cells
description: In a clonal, unstimulated population, use dCas9-based activation or optogenetic FOS/JUN dimerization to transiently drive AP-1 only in sparse, trackable cells. Follow those cells and their progeny by live imaging and matched single-cell multiome. If a brief, cell-autonomous AP-1 pulse alone shifts long-term state and drug response relative to neighbors in the same dish, AP-1 is causally sufficient for memory rather than a correlate of upstream signaling.

title: Comparing FOS/JUN protein decay with persistence of accessibility
description: Pulse-stimulate cells, wash out, and run matched time courses of FOS/JUN protein levels (quantitative immunoblot, Halo-tag pulse-chase) alongside chromatin accessibility and nucleosome positioning at AP-1 motifs (ATAC-seq plus AP-1 CUT&RUN). Memory is supported only if the accessible state at AP-1-bound enhancers outlasts the protein by many half-lives; co-decay would instead indicate ongoing signaling.

title: Time-resolved AP-1 dimer composition at sites
description: Perform time-resolved CUT&RUN for FOS, FOSB, FRA1/FRA2, JUN, JUNB, and JUND together with co-IP of dimer composition at matched timepoints. Ask whether short-lived FOS-containing dimers at a given site are replaced by longer-lived FRA1/JUND dimers or by resident lineage factors. A site-preserving change in dimer composition would be a concrete mechanistic form of AP-1 memory.

title: Mitotic dilution as the decay clock
description: Pair a stimulus pulse with FUCCI/live imaging and with cell-cycle arrest (CDK4/6 inhibition or contact arrest). Measure how many divisions the primed state survives using re-stimulation reporters and ATAC-seq on cells sorted by division number via dye dilution. Decay scaling with divisions implies a replication-coupled chromatin carrier, whereas decay on clock time regardless of division implicates slow protein or RNA turnover.

title: Degron separation of establishment versus maintenance
description: Tag endogenous FOS and JUN with dTAG or AID degrons and deplete them either before stimulation, during the first hour of response, or only after the state is established. A memory function requires that post-establishment depletion preserves primed accessibility and accelerated secondary responses, while early depletion abolishes both.

title: Clone-resolved second-hit restimulation
description: Lineage-barcode cells, stimulate, allow a long rest period, then restimulate and use single-cell RNA-seq/ATAC-seq to ask whether enhanced re-induction is heritable within clones rather than only a population average. Shared priming among sister cells of the same clone distinguishes an inherited chromatin state from averaging over transient responders.

title: Sister-cell concordance as a memory clock
description: Live-image an endogenous FOS/JUN reporter through cell division, then measure the correlation in restimulation response between sister cells versus randomly paired cells. The decay of this concordance as a function of time since division yields a direct half-life for the heritable AP-1 state, with cousin and second-cousin comparisons separating true heritable memory from shared microenvironment.

title: AP-1 degron washout after priming
description: Tag FOS/JUNB with dTAG or auxin-inducible degrons and acutely degrade the protein during defined windows after a priming stimulus, then restimulate. If the primed response survives AP-1 protein loss, AP-1 writes a memory stored elsewhere (chromatin); if memory collapses with the protein, AP-1 itself is the storage medium.

title: Latent enhancers across a prime-rest-restimulate time course
description: Collect matched ATAC-seq, AP-1 CUT&RUN, and nascent transcription (PRO-seq or intronic scRNA-seq) across a prime, long rest, and restimulation time course. Identify sites that retain accessibility during rest even after AP-1 occupancy decays. Test whether these retained, AP-1-motif-enriched sites are the loci that respond faster or higher to the second stimulus.

title: Lineage barcoding to trace AP-1-high ancestry
description: Combine heritable lineage barcoding (CRISPR recorders or static barcodes such as Watermelon/FateMap) with single-cell ATAC and RNA to ask whether drug-tolerant or hyper-responsive cells descend preferentially from AP-1-high ancestors. This quantifies how many generations the AP-1 state persists and how much of final-state variance it explains.

title: Memory decay constant from spaced stimuli, plus ectopic motif arrays
description: Deliver two identical stimulus pulses separated by systematically varied intervals (minutes to many days, spanning several divisions) and fit response amplitude versus inter-pulse interval to extract a memory decay constant. Test whether it matches the decay of AP-1-site accessibility rather than AP-1 protein. As a sufficiency test, insert synthetic AP-1 motif arrays at ectopic naive loci and ask whether they acquire the same memory behavior.

title: Washout–recall assay with AP-1 tracking
description: Stimulate cells (serum, TGF-beta, MAPK activation, or drug), wash out, wait a defined interval, then re-challenge, while separately tracking endogenously tagged AP-1 proteins (FOS/FOSL1/JUN), AP-1-motif chromatin accessibility, and transcriptional output. The memory signature is a faster or larger second response at a time when AP-1 protein has already decayed to baseline, which distinguishes a persistent AP-1 occupancy model from a latent primed-chromatin model.

title: Clonal heritability of AP-1 state by lineage barcoding
description: Barcode cells (e.g., CellTag-style) and sort on a live AP-1 activity reporter. Then use scRNA-seq and time-lapse lineage tracing to measure how strongly AP-1 state and the primed response correlate between sister, cousin, and more distant relatives as a function of generations since division. This separates heritable memory from cell-intrinsic noise and gives a quantitative memory half-life in cell divisions.

title: Timed degron and optogenetic control of AP-1 in encoding, storage, and recall windows
description: Use dTAG or auxin-inducible degrons on AP-1 subunits, or optogenetic AP-1 constructs, to remove or supply AP-1 activity selectively during the encoding phase, the storage interval, or the recall challenge. Comparing these three windows separates whether AP-1 establishes the memory, is required to maintain it, or is only needed to read it out.

title: Single-molecule footprinting of primed enhancers during the memory interval
description: Apply long-read single-molecule footprinting (nanopore methyltransferase footprinting, or CUT&RUN with long-read sequencing) at primed enhancers during the memory interval to test whether AP-1 is still bound or whether the state has passed to nucleosome positioning, DNA methylation, cohesin, or mitotic bookmarking. Including mitotic time points tests whether AP-1 bookmarks its target enhancers through chromosome condensation.

title: Frequency encoding of input history
description: Deliver the upstream stimulus as pulse trains of systematically varied frequency, amplitude, and duration using microfluidics or optogenetics, then compute the mutual information between past input history and the current AP-1-dependent chromatin and transcriptional state. This tests whether AP-1 acts as a leaky integrator that stores a running record of stimulation history rather than an instantaneous reporter of present signaling.

title: Prime–rest–rechallenge with windowed AP-1 degradation
description: Stimulate cells (serum, TGF-β, wounding, or drug), allow full return to baseline transcriptome, then restimulate days later and quantify whether the secondary response is faster, larger, or qualitatively different. Use an auxin- or dTAG-inducible degron on FOS/JUN to remove AP-1 selectively during the priming window, the rest (storage) window, or the recall window, to distinguish whether AP-1 acts as the writer, maintainer, or reader of the memory.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing of the primed state through quiescence
description: Combine a live AP-1 transcriptional reporter with expressed lineage barcodes (e.g., Watermelon/CellTag-style) so that individual primed cells and their descendants can be re-identified at rechallenge and profiled by scRNA-seq. This distinguishes per-cell memory from a population-level artifact in which a pre-existing responsive subpopulation is selected or expanded, and measures what fraction of cells retain the state.

title: Division-coupled decay and mitotic bookmarking assay
description: Prime cells, then use CFSE dilution or a FUCCI/division-counting reporter to sort descendants by number of divisions completed, and measure memory half-life in cell divisions rather than hours. In parallel, perform mitotic-chromosome CUT&RUN and live imaging of tagged FOS/JUN in mitosis to test whether AP-1 remains bound to memory enhancers during mitosis, which would allow the state to be copied to daughter cells.

title: Dimer composition at memory enhancers
description: Apply sequential/dual CUT&RUN (or CUT&Tag with antibodies against FOS, FOSB, FRA1, FRA2, JUN, JUNB, JUND) plus quantitative IP–mass spectrometry across the priming, resting, and recall phases to determine whether the persistent feature is a specific long-lived dimer, such as a FOSB/ΔFOSB-containing complex, rather than total AP-1 occupancy. Then swap dimer identity by targeted knock-in or degron and test whether memory duration tracks the dimer's protein half-life.

title: Single-molecule binding kinetics and optogenetic pulse decoding
description: Use HaloTag single-molecule tracking and FRAP on endogenous JUN/FOS to measure residence time, bound fraction, and search kinetics at primed versus naive enhancers, testing whether memory is stored in binding dynamics even when ChIP-level occupancy appears unchanged. Pair this with optogenetic or chemically dimerizable AP-1 to deliver defined pulse amplitudes, durations, and frequencies, identifying the minimal dynamic input that produces a lasting accessibility change measured by time-resolved ATAC-seq.

title: Timed degron depletion to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Tag FOS and JUN with dTAG or auxin degrons, deliver a defined stimulus pulse, then acutely deplete AP-1 at staggered delays while tracking accessibility (ATAC) and occupancy (CUT&RUN). Memory predicts that early depletion collapses the primed state while late depletion leaves a stable plateau. Run with and without cell-cycle arrest to distinguish replication-coupled dilution from active erasure, and repeat with FOS/FOSB/JUNB swaps to test which family member carries the memory.

title: Heritable barcoding to measure how long memory survives mitosis
description: Heritably barcode single cells (Watermelon/CellTag plus single-cell multiome), stimulate, allow several divisions, then restimulate and ask whether primed accessibility and faster re-induction propagate down clonal trees. The key measurement is the decay constant of sister- and cousin-cell correlation in AP-1 site accessibility as a function of generation number, distinguishing true inheritance from stochastic resampling.

title: Causal test that retained AP-1 sites drive the second response
description: An open chromatin site is not necessarily a functional memory element. Challenge primed cells with a second stimulus and measure nascent transcription (TT-seq, Pol II CUT&RUN, or live MS2 imaging of burst frequency and latency). Then silence (CRISPRi) or delete the retained AP-1 elements to test whether the potentiated response disappears.

title: Test whether AP-1 memory depends on insulated 3D chromatin neighborhoods
description: Map Micro-C and CTCF alongside ATAC-seq before, during, and after stimulation, then degrade cohesin/RAD21 and insert synthetic CTCF boundaries next to a memory locus. If primed accessibility spreads in cis and is stopped by an engineered boundary, AP-1 memory is a property of an insulated neighborhood rather than an independent per-site mark.

title: Hysteresis and bistability in synthetic AP-1 site arrays
description: Build synthetic reporter arrays that vary AP-1 site number, spacing, and affinity, then measure the full ascending and descending dose-response to a tunable stimulus. A genuine memory mechanism should show hysteresis, with non-overlapping ascending and descending curves and a sharp switch-like threshold in site number, whereas a passively relaxing system retraces the same curve in both directions.

title: Separating AP-1 role in establishing versus reading memory with acute degron depletion
description: Tag FOS/JUN family members with auxin or dTAG degrons and deplete them either during a transient stimulus or only after washout, then assay ATAC-seq/CUT&RUN accessibility at AP-1 enhancers and the amplitude and latency of a second response. If memory requires AP-1 only during encoding but survives its post-stimulus removal, AP-1 establishes the mark. If the potentiated second response collapses whenever AP-1 is absent, AP-1 is continuously required for readout rather than storing the memory.

title: AP-1 mitotic bookmarking and inheritance of potentiated re-induction
description: Image endogenously tagged FOS/JUN/ATF in live mitotic cells (plus mitotic CUT&RUN and H3S10ph-matched controls) to quantify retention on condensed chromatin at specific enhancers. Also stimulate mother cells, track single daughter cells by lineage imaging, and test whether potentiated re-induction is inherited and whether it is lost when bookmarking is disrupted by an AP-1 DNA-binding-deficient or mitosis-evicted mutant.

title: MPRA of AP-1 motif syntax under stimulus–washout–restimulus
description: Build a synthetic reporter library systematically varying TRE/CRE motif number, spacing, affinity, and flanking partner motifs (TEAD, RUNX, CEBP, nucleosome-positioning sequences). Measure each variant's output after a single stimulus versus a stimulus–washout–restimulus protocol, to identify which cis-regulatory arrangements confer memory (faster, larger, or lower-threshold second responses) rather than mere responsiveness.

title: Single-cell dose-response-to-memory transfer functions
description: Use live-cell endogenous FOS/JUN translational reporters with a dynamic transcriptional readout to measure, in the same cell, integrated AP-1 activity during a first graded stimulus and the magnitude of a later response (hours to weeks later). Fitting the resulting transfer function distinguishes graded (analog, dose-proportional) memory from digital latching, and shows whether cell-to-cell variability in memory is predicted by AP-1 level or by a downstream bistable element.

title: Targeted erasure and decay-rate measurement at individual AP-1 enhancers
description: After the stimulus is gone, use dCas9-LSD1/HDAC/DNMT3A tethering, enhancer deletion, or CRISPRi tiling at specific stimulus-induced AP-1-bound enhancers, and test whether the potentiated second response is selectively erased while the naive response is preserved. In parallel, measure memory half-life across a washout time course with and without proliferation arrest to determine whether decay is set by chromatin turnover, dilution by cell division, or active removal.

title: Allele-resolved AP-1 reporters
description: Use SNP-resolved allele-specific RNA FISH or dual-color knock-in reporters at the two alleles of an AP-1 target (e.g., AXL, SERPINE1) to test whether the same allele remains the high-expressing one across days and through cell division. Allele-autonomous, cis-restricted persistence implies chromatin-encoded memory rather than a diffusible trans-factor set point.

title: Pulse-release kinetics of FOS/JUN
description: Place FOS/JUN under optogenetic or dTAG/auxin degron control, deliver a defined pulse, then fully remove the factor and measure the decay half-life of the downstream state (ATAC accessibility, target RNA, drug-resistant colony formation) relative to division time. Persistence across many divisions after the input is gone is the operational signature of memory; rapid relaxation marks it as a maintained steady state.

title: Lineage barcoding with AP-1 reporter sorting and timed perturbation
description: Combine barcode lineage tracing (retrospective clone recovery, as in Rewind/FateMap) with sorting on an AP-1 activity reporter to test whether AP-1-high cells are the same clones that later survive drug selection. Pair this with timed gain- and loss-of-function of AP-1 to distinguish AP-1 as an instructive inducer of the state, a permissive reader, or merely the terminator of an already-established transition.

title: Time course of chromatin marks at primed enhancers after factor withdrawal
description: Run a CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag time course for AP-1 occupancy, H3K27ac, H3K4me1, and nucleosome positioning at primed enhancers after factor withdrawal. Add DNA-FISH/Hi-C for enhancer repositioning and mitotic-chromosome staining for AP-1 bookmarking in synchronized cells. This separates heritable chromatin marks that outlive the factor from re-recruitment of AP-1 each cycle.

title: Transcriptional burst kinetics and inheritance with MS2 imaging
description: Use MS2 live-cell imaging of an AP-1 target gene to quantify whether the remembered state is encoded in burst frequency versus amplitude, and measure sister-cell correlation of burst frequency after mitosis. Compare a second stimulus pulse with a naive first pulse: faster and larger reinduction plus inherited burst frequency is a quantitative memory signature distinguishable from residual mRNA or protein carryover.

title: Decay kinetics of AP-1-associated chromatin after varied stimulus dose and duration
description: Stimulate cells with varying doses and durations, withdraw the stimulus, and profile FOS/JUN CUT&RUN, ATAC-seq, and H3K4me1/H3K27ac over hours to weeks at the same loci. Memory is supported if accessibility and H3K4me1 outlast AP-1 occupancy and accumulate with the number of prior exposures rather than returning to baseline.

title: Bimodal single-cell re-response test
description: Use single-cell RNA/ATAC plus a live AP-1 target reporter to compare naive versus previously stimulated populations upon restimulation, testing statistically for bimodality (a discrete latent state) rather than a uniform graded shift. Confirm that the high mode corresponds to cells retaining accessibility at AP-1 sites.

title: Clonal barcode lineage tracing of the primed state
description: Because memory must survive mitosis, barcode cells, stimulate, sort responders, expand, and restimulate to ask whether responsiveness is again concentrated in the same barcodes. Sister-cell split experiments then quantify how many divisions the correlation persists, giving a heritability half-life for the AP-1 primed state.

title: Degron depletion to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Tag endogenous FOS, JUN, and JUNB with dTAG/AID degrons and acutely deplete them either during the initial stimulus or only during the post-stimulus memory window. Persistence of memory after later depletion implies AP-1 writes a chromatin mark it no longer needs to hold, whereas loss of memory implies continuous AP-1 occupancy is itself the memory.

title: MPRA of AP-1 enhancer motif syntax
description: Build an integrated massively parallel reporter library varying AP-1 motif number, spacing, affinity, and flanking partner motifs (TEAD, RUNX, lineage factors). Measure which configurations sustain elevated output after stimulus withdrawal, to determine whether memory resides in AP-1 sites alone or in their sequence context.

title: Quantitative memory transfer function from dose, duration, and rest interval
description: Stimulate cells across a matrix of AP-1-inducing doses and durations, wash out, wait defined intervals, then apply a deliberately sub-threshold second pulse and read out target induction by scRNA-seq or a live transcriptional reporter. Fitting response amplitude and latency against first-pulse strength and rest interval yields a memory gain curve and decay half-life, the minimal quantitative signature a memory mechanism must show.

title: Motif insertion/deletion library for motif syntax
description: Build an MPRA plus CRISPR knock-in library that inserts TRE/CRE motifs at varied copy number, spacing, and flanking context into naive and endogenous loci, and deletes them from memory-competent enhancers. Measure which configurations retain accessibility and poised transcription after stimulus withdrawal, to separate motif presence from motif syntax as the carrier of memory.

title: Nucleosome occupancy and accessibility after stimulus washout
description: Run a washout time course combining ATAC-seq, Fos/Jun CUT&RUN, and high-resolution MNase footprinting to test whether enhancers remain nucleosome-depleted and H3K4me1/H3K27ac-marked after AP-1 occupancy falls below detection. Decoupling of accessibility from occupancy indicates a stored chromatin state, whereas synchronous loss indicates AP-1 merely reports ongoing signaling.

title: Degron timing to separate establishment from maintenance
description: Tag endogenous Fos/Jun family members with auxin- or dTAG-inducible degrons and deplete them before stimulus, immediately after enhancer opening, and days into the rested state. Memory that survives late acute depletion but is lost when depletion occurs in a defined early consolidation window implies AP-1 acts on a stable substrate, whereas loss at any time implies AP-1 itself is the store.

title: Clonal heritability and mitotic bookmarking
description: Use expressed lineage barcodes with a split-clone design to test whether re-challenge responsiveness after several divisions is clone-correlated rather than randomly distributed across the population. Pair this with live imaging and single-molecule residence-time measurements of Halo-tagged Fos/Jun during mitosis to test whether AP-1 physically bookmarks target enhancers through cell division.

title: Comparing AP-1 occupancy decay with accessibility decay after washout
description: Pulse cells with a stimulus and run parallel washout time courses of AP-1 protein abundance (Halo-tag live imaging, quantitative immunoblot), AP-1 occupancy (CUT&RUN), and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq). Memory is supported if a class of sites retains accessibility and H3K4me1/H3K27ac for many AP-1 protein half-lives after occupancy is undetectable, with a bimodal decay-time distribution rather than one that tracks occupancy.

title: Timed degron removal to map the window of AP-1 dependence
description: Tag endogenous FOS/JUN/JUNB with dTAG or AID degrons and degrade AP-1 at a graded series of delays after a priming pulse, then assay survival of the primed enhancer landscape and the potentiated secondary response. The delay at which degradation no longer erases memory defines the handoff from AP-1 to a maintenance mechanism such as nucleosome positioning, a partner transcription factor, or DNA methylation loss.

title: Clonal inheritance of the primed state through division
description: Combine expressed lentiviral barcodes with a split-clone design: prime a population, allow 1-8 divisions without stimulus, then assay one half of each clone by scATAC/scRNA-seq and challenge the other half. Quantify heritability as within- versus between-clone concordance of AP-1-site accessibility and secondary-response magnitude, and distinguish dilution from faithful copying by the slope across division number.

title: Dual-pulse live imaging of transcriptional bursting at single-allele resolution
description: Knock MS2/PP7 cassettes into AP-1 target genes and live-image transcriptional bursting across a priming pulse, a rest interval, and a second pulse. Test whether memory appears as shortened latency, higher burst frequency, or reduced cell-to-cell variance, and whether the same alleles that fired first fire again, establishing allele-level rather than only cell-level memory.

title: Synthetic AP-1 enhancer series to relate site number to memory
description: Integrate at a single safe-harbor locus a panel of reporters with 1, 2, 4, or 8 canonical TRE sites plus half-site and spacing variants, and measure both initial induction and retained memory after washout. Supralinear scaling of memory depth with site number alongside linear scaling of initial induction would implicate cooperative, self-reinforcing occupancy as the storage mechanism rather than proportional signal readout.

title: Per-site decay constants of AP-1 sites after transient stimulus
description: Run a dense time course (hours to weeks) after a transient stimulus measuring FOS/JUN occupancy (CUT&RUN), chromatin accessibility (ATAC), and AP-1 protein levels, fitting a per-site decay constant to classify elements as transient versus long-lived. Memory predicts a reproducible subpopulation whose accessibility half-life far exceeds that of AP-1 occupancy. Single-molecule tracking of Halo-JUN would test whether persistence reflects longer residence time rather than more protein.

title: Acute degron depletion after memory is established
description: Tag FOS/JUNB and paralogs with dTAG/AID degrons and deplete them only after priming. Survival of primed accessibility and enhanced secondary response would imply storage downstream of AP-1 (nucleosome state, histone marks, DNA methylation), whereas collapse would imply AP-1 occupancy itself is the memory substrate. Re-adding AP-1 tests reversibility.

title: Clonal barcoding plus multiome for heritability through division
description: Combine heritable lentiviral barcodes (Rewind/FateMap-style) with scATAC+scRNA multiome to test whether primed AP-1 states are concordant within clones and transmitted across mitoses. Quantify within- versus between-clone variance in AP-1 motif accessibility over 5-20 divisions, in cycling versus arrested cells, to separate heritable epigenetic memory from slow protein-level hysteresis.

title: Synthetic AP-1 element libraries to define cis-regulatory rules for persistence
description: Genomically integrate a library of thousands of synthetic elements varying TRE/CRE motif identity, affinity, copy number, spacing and helical phasing, nucleosome-positioning sequence, and partner motifs (TEAD, RUNX, ETS, NF-kB), reading out both acute and weeks-later retained activity. This identifies the minimal cis-regulatory sequence features that convert a transient input into a stored one.

title: Combinatorial stimulus-sequencing experiments
description: Deliver two or three distinct AP-1-activating inputs (growth factor, cytokine, mechanical stretch) in all permutations and intervals. Test whether the final AP-1 chromatin landscape and response amplitude depend on order and spacing or only on the set of stimuli. Order dependence would indicate a sequence-sensitive trace, set dependence would indicate a record of past exposures without order, and interval titration gives the memory capacity and timescale.

title: Sister-cell/clonal recurrence test of AP-1 memory heritability
description: Barcode a population (e.g., Watermelon/ClonMapper-style lineage barcodes), stimulate transiently, let clones expand, and re-stimulate. If AP-1 is a memory mechanism, the secondary AP-1 response magnitude should be much more correlated among cells sharing a barcode than among unrelated cells, and this intraclonal correlation should decay over a measurable number of divisions. Combine with split-clone designs (one half naive, one half primed) and single-cell multiome to show that the heritable unit is AP-1 motif accessibility rather than a generic proliferative state.

title: Mitotic bookmarking by FOS/JUN at memory enhancers
description: Test whether AP-1 remains chromatin-bound through mitosis by performing CUT&RUN/CUT&Tag for FOS/JUN and ATAC-seq on mitotically arrested and sorted primed vs. naive cells, paired with live-cell Halo-JUN imaging and FRAP on condensed chromosomes to measure residence time. Then test necessity with a cell-cycle-restricted auxin/dTAG degron that removes AP-1 only during the M-phase window, asking whether daughter cells lose the primed response while cells degraded in G1 retain it.

title: Degron-based separation of AP-1 roles in establishment, maintenance, and re-stimulation
description: Using dTAG- or auxin-tagged endogenous FOS/JUN (and a FOS-family-wide degron to address redundancy), degrade AP-1 in three nonoverlapping windows: during the priming stimulus, during the quiescent memory interval, and only at re-stimulation. Score secondary response amplitude, latency, and enhancer accessibility. This distinguishes AP-1 as the factor that establishes accessibility at latent enhancers, as a continuously required maintenance factor, or merely as a reader of a trace stored by other means (e.g., H3K4me1, CTCF loops, DNA methylation).

title: Pulse-number and dose layering to test cumulative memory
description: Deliver controlled trains of stimulus pulses (varying number, amplitude, and spacing, ideally with optogenetic or small-molecule-gated AP-1 input) and ask whether primed AP-1 enhancer accessibility and secondary output accumulate in discrete, stimulus-countable increments rather than tracking only the most recent or the integrated dose. Fitting the resulting response surface discriminates a cumulative recorder from a slow-relaxation filter, and identifies the subset of AP-1 sites that show stepwise accumulation for follow-up.

title: Single-molecule footprinting of residual state at memory enhancers
description: Apply single-molecule methyltransferase footprinting (SMF/Fiber-seq) at AP-1 memory enhancers days after the stimulus has decayed, to distinguish on individual DNA fibers between persistent low-level AP-1 occupancy, nucleosome-depleted chromatin without bound factor, and fully reclosed chromatin. Quantify the fraction of molecules in each state and test, with paired scSMF/transcriptome readout, how that fraction predicts single-cell secondary response, to determine whether the retained state is a structural chromatin remnant rather than ongoing signaling.

title: Barcoded lineage tracing across drug exposure
description: Introduce heritable random barcodes (e.g., CellTag or lentiviral barcode libraries) into a clonal population before treatment, then sequence barcodes in survivors and in pre-treatment cells. Matching barcodes between the two timepoints shows whether survivors come from a pre-existing subclone or arise de novo from drug-induced reprogramming.

title: Pre-treatment single-cell multiomics predicting survival
description: Perform paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq (or CITE-seq) on untreated cells, then compare the profiles of cells that later survive versus die using a lineage-linked readout such as barcodes or live-cell photoconversion. Identifying transcriptional or chromatin-accessibility signatures that predict survival would reveal whether tolerance is present before the drug is given.

title: Live-cell reporter tracking of individual fates
description: Use fluorescent reporters (e.g., FUCCI for cell-cycle phase, ERK-KTR for pathway activity, and a drug-efflux or stress reporter) in time-lapse microscopy during drug exposure. Link each cell's reporter state before and during treatment to its eventual death or survival to identify which dynamic signaling or cell-cycle states confer tolerance.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screens under a strong-dose survival bottleneck
description: Run pooled CRISPR knockout or CRISPRi/a screens at high library coverage under a strong drug dose that kills most cells, then compare guide representation in survivors against untreated controls. Hits enriched in survivors identify genes whose loss or gain is needed for tolerance, and comparing them with resistance screens from chronic exposure separates transient from stable mechanisms.

title: Chromatin and metabolic profiling of sorted survivors with reversibility tests
description: Sort or harvest surviving cells after a short drug pulse and profile their chromatin (CUT&Tag for H3K27ac/H3K4me3, ATAC-seq), metabolism (mitochondrial respiration, lipid and iron/ferroptosis markers), and proteome against bulk controls. Then test whether the survivor state is reversible by drug holidays and by inhibiting the implicated epigenetic or metabolic pathways, which distinguishes an adaptive epigenetic state from a fixed genetic one.

title: Lineage tracing with barcoded clones
description: Introduce heritable random DNA barcodes (e.g., CRISPR-based or lentiviral) into a clonal population, treat with the targeted drug, and follow barcode frequencies over time and in persister-enriched fractions. This shows whether survival is pre-determined in a subset of clones (pre-existing tolerance) or arises stochastically or by induction during treatment, and how many independent lineages contribute to the surviving population.

title: Pre-treatment single-cell profiling linked to fate
description: Perform single-cell RNA-seq and/or ATAC-seq on untreated cells, then use live-cell reporters or sorting to isolate cells that will survive versus die after drug exposure, and compare their baseline transcriptional and chromatin states. Identifying a predictive signature (e.g., stemness, drug-efflux, or cell-cycle markers) would show whether survival is encoded before treatment.

title: Time-resolved live-cell imaging of drug response
description: Use fluorescent reporters for the drug target pathway (such as ERK activity or cell-cycle sensors) together with longitudinal microscopy to track individual cells from drug addition through death or survival. This captures the kinetics of signaling changes, whether survivors show delayed or incomplete pathway suppression, and whether they divide during treatment.

title: Pooled CRISPR screens for persistence modifiers
description: Run genome-wide CRISPR knockout or CRISPRa/i screens under sustained drug exposure and compare guide representation in surviving cells versus controls at multiple timepoints. Hits enriched in survivors identify genes whose loss or gain enables tolerance, and can be validated for causal roles in persistence.

title: Epigenetic and chromatin perturbation to test memory of survival
description: Measure chromatin accessibility, histone marks, and DNA methylation in persister cells sorted after drug withdrawal versus drug-naive cells, then perturb candidate epigenetic regulators (e.g., KDM5 family, DNMTs, or BET proteins) to see if persistence is reversed. Comparing drug-naive, persister, and drug-removed-regrown populations separates transient adaptive states from stable, heritable changes.

title: Barcoded lineage tracing with drug exposure, washout and re-challenge
description: Label each founder cell with a unique heritable DNA barcode, expose the population to the targeted drug, and sequence barcodes in survivors versus the pre-treatment pool. Shared barcodes across survivors indicate whether persisters are pre-existing, clonally selected, or arise from a non-genetic switch in many cells. Adding washout and re-challenge arms tests whether the surviving state is reversible.

title: Single-cell multi-omics time course during treatment
description: Profile scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq (or multiome) on cells at baseline, early after drug exposure, and at several later timepoints, then compare the trajectories of cells that die with those that persist. Pre-treatment states that predict survival, such as chromatin accessibility at lineage or stress genes, can be identified and tested for causality.

title: Live-cell reporter imaging linked to cell fate
description: Use fluorescent reporters for cell cycle (e.g., FUCCI), stress signaling (e.g., NF-κB or p53 activity), or a drug-target pathway readout, and track individual cells with time-lapse microscopy through treatment. Retrospectively correlating each cell's reporter dynamics before and during drug exposure with its eventual death or survival reveals the dynamic signatures that distinguish persisters.

title: Pooled CRISPR screen comparing survivors with controls
description: Run genome-wide or epigenome-focused CRISPR knockout or CRISPRi screens under drug treatment and sequence guides in survivors versus untreated controls. Genes whose loss either eliminates or enriches persisters point to regulators of tolerance, and follow-up with arrayed validation can separate primary survival mechanisms from bystander effects.

title: Metabolic and epigenetic profiling of sorted persisters
description: Sort drug-tolerant cells using a reporter or viability-based gate and profile them for mitochondrial function, metabolite levels, histone modifications, and chromatin accessibility, compared with sensitive cells. Then test whether pharmacologically perturbing the identified pathway (e.g., OXPHOS inhibition or a histone demethylase inhibitor) changes the survival fraction, to establish whether the state is functionally necessary.

title: Barcoded lineage tracing across drug pulses
description: Introduce heritable cellular barcodes (e.g., CellTag or lentiviral barcode libraries) into a clonal population, apply the targeted drug, and track which barcoded lineages survive. Compare barcode frequencies before and after treatment, and across washout and re-challenge, to determine whether survivors were pre-existing rare clones or arose through drug-induced reprogramming.

title: Pre-treatment sorting and profiling of future survivors
description: Use live-cell reporters or surface markers to sort cells before drug exposure. Profile the sorted subpopulations and the survivor fraction with single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq. This tests whether a transcriptional or chromatin state that predicts survival already exists in the untreated population.

title: Live-cell signaling and cell-cycle reporters linked to fate
description: Express biosensors such as ERK or AKT kinase translocation reporters and FUCCI cell-cycle markers, then image individual cells continuously through drug addition and record their fate. Correlate signaling amplitude, dynamics, and cell-cycle phase at the time of treatment with eventual survival to identify dynamic states that predict persistence.

title: Genome-wide and single-cell CRISPR screens under drug pressure
description: Run pooled CRISPR knockout or CRISPRi screens with the drug, comparing guide representation in surviving versus dying cells, and follow up hits with Perturb-seq to see how each perturbation shifts the persister state. Hits in chromatin, signaling, and stress-response genes indicate mechanisms enabling survival, and validation of top candidates tests whether they are necessary and sufficient.

title: Metabolic and epigenetic profiling with drug washout and re-challenge
description: Measure metabolic state (for example NAD(P)H fluorescence lifetime imaging, mitochondrial respiration, and metabolomics) and key histone marks or chromatin accessibility in pre-treatment, early-treatment, and surviving cells. Then remove the drug and re-challenge: if survivors retain their metabolic or epigenetic signature across several passages, this indicates heritable adaptive memory, whereas loss of the signature indicates a reversible tolerance state.

title: Single-cell lineage barcoding with drug-response tracking
description: Label a clonal cancer population with heritable DNA barcodes (e.g., CRISPR-based lineage tracers), treat with the targeted drug, and track which lineages persist and how their transcriptomes and chromatin states differ before treatment. This separates pre-existing drug-tolerant clones from cells that switch state after exposure.

title: Pre-treatment single-cell multi-omics to find predictive baseline states
description: Profile untreated cells with paired scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq (or CITE-seq) and use machine learning to identify baseline features, such as expression of stress, quiescence, or drug-efflux genes, that predict which cells will survive. Validate by sorting the predicted tolerant subpopulation and testing its drug response.

title: Live-cell imaging with reporter-based fate tracking
description: Use fluorescent reporters for cell cycle (e.g., FUCCI), signaling activity (e.g., ERK or AKT biosensors), and drug-target engagement, and follow individual cells over days of treatment. This reveals whether survivors were in a slow-cycling or signaling-low state before drug exposure, or whether they adapt over time.

title: Time-resolved persister-state transitions with pulse-chase drug exposure
description: Expose cells to the drug for short pulses, then wash out and sort survivors at multiple timepoints for bulk or single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq. This distinguishes stable genetic or epigenetic persistence from transient, reversible drug-tolerant states that re-enter the cell cycle after drug withdrawal.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screens for survival and resistance mechanisms
description: Run pooled CRISPR knockout or CRISPRi/a screens under sublethal drug doses. Compare sequencing of survivors with the starting population to identify genes that enable survival without acquired mutations. Follow up hits with combination-drug tests to determine whether the survival machinery is a druggable vulnerability.

title: Single-cell lineage barcoding with drug-response tracking
description: Introduce heritable DNA barcodes (e.g., CRISPR-based scar or lentiviral barcode libraries) into a clonal population, treat with the targeted drug, and track barcode frequencies and transcriptomes over time. This reveals whether survivors are pre-existing clones or arise from non-genetic state transitions, and whether they share a common precursor identity.

title: Pre-treatment single-cell profiling to identify predictive states
description: Perform scRNA-seq and/or ATAC-seq on untreated cells, then sort or computationally back-trace the cells that later survive (e.g., via live-cell reporters or FACS-based pulse-labeling of persisters). Comparing survivors to non-survivors before drug exposure identifies baseline chromatin, metabolic, or cell-cycle features that predispose cells to persistence.

title: Live-cell reporter tracking of persister emergence
description: Use fluorescent reporters for drug-target pathway activity, cell-cycle phase (e.g., FUCCI), or stress signaling (e.g., NRF2, p53) combined with time-lapse microscopy under drug. Following individual cells from drug addition to survival or death reveals whether persistence is tied to a transient signaling or cell-cycle state at the time of treatment.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screens for survival versus drug sensitivity
description: Run pooled CRISPR knockout or CRISPRi/a screens under sublethal and lethal drug doses, sequencing guides in surviving cells at multiple time points. Hits enriched among survivors identify genes whose loss or gain shifts the fraction of persisters, pointing to the pathways that confer tolerance rather than resistance.

title: Epigenetic and metabolic perturbation of persister fraction
description: Measure persister frequency after perturbing chromatin regulators (e.g., HDAC or KDM inhibitors), histone marks, or metabolic pathways (e.g., oxidative phosphorylation, lipid or iron metabolism) before and during drug exposure, and assess whether the survival fraction changes. Dose-response and reversibility experiments distinguish heritable epigenetic memory from reversible metabolic or stress-induced tolerance.

title: Single-cell lineage barcoding with drug-response tracking
description: Introduce heritable random DNA barcodes (e.g., CellTag or CRISPR-based lineage recorders) into a clonal population, treat with the targeted drug, and track which barcoded lineages persist. This separates pre-existing drug-tolerant clones from cells that switch state after treatment, and shows whether survival is inherited or stochastic.

title: Time-resolved single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq of persister emergence
description: Profile cells at high temporal resolution from before treatment through early drug exposure and into the persister state, measuring transcriptome and chromatin accessibility. Identifying the cells that diverge early and the regulatory programs they activate can reveal pre-existing transcriptional or epigenetic states that predispose to survival.

title: Live-cell reporter imaging linked to fate
description: Use fluorescent reporters for candidate survival pathways (e.g., drug target activity, stress signaling, cell-cycle phase) and time-lapse microscopy under drug to link each cell's pre-treatment reporter state to its eventual fate. This tests whether a measurable pre-treatment state predicts survival.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screens comparing survivors and non-survivors
description: Run pooled CRISPR knockout or CRISPRi/a screens under the targeted drug and compare guide enrichment in surviving cells versus a drug-naive control, with time-course sampling. Hits that alter survival frequency, especially those that act without changing baseline growth, point to the genes and pathways that mediate tolerance.

title: Measuring non-genetic cell-to-cell variability and testing extremes
description: Measure drug-target expression, drug efflux, and metabolic state across single cells in the pre-treatment population, then sort or enrich cells at the extremes and re-test their survival. These experiments, which isolate high- and low-variability subpopulations, show whether non-genetic variation drives the survival fraction and how quickly it reverts.

title: Single-cell lineage tracing with barcoded clones
description: Introduce heritable random DNA barcodes into a clonal population, treat with the targeted drug, and use barcode sequencing plus scRNA-seq to determine whether survivors arise from a pre-existing transcriptionally distinct subpopulation or from clones already present before treatment. Comparing pre-treatment and post-treatment barcode frequencies distinguishes pre-existing resistance from drug-induced reprogramming.

title: Time-resolved single-cell RNA and ATAC profiling during drug exposure
description: Profile chromatin accessibility and gene expression at many early time points after drug addition to track which cells change state and when. Identify the earliest divergent cells and the regulatory programs (e.g., chromatin opening at specific transcription factor motifs) that precede survival, to reveal the mechanism of the persister state.

title: Genome-wide CRISPR screens comparing survivors to the bulk population
description: Run pooled CRISPR knockout or CRISPRi/CRISPRa screens under drug treatment and compare guide enrichment in surviving cells against untreated controls, including sorted fast-cycling versus slow-cycling subsets. Genes whose guides are enriched or depleted in survivors indicate the genes and pathways required for persistence and suggest candidate vulnerabilities to target.

title: Live-cell reporters and single-cell tracking of drug response
description: Use fluorescent reporters for cell-cycle phase, drug-target pathway activity, or stress signaling, combined with time-lapse microscopy, to follow individual cells from drug addition through survival or death. Correlating each cell's reporter state before drug exposure with its fate tests whether survival is predictable from a measurable pre-treatment state or is stochastic.

title: Drug washout and re-challenge of sorted persister cells
description: Sort surviving cells, remove the drug, and measure regrowth, drug sensitivity, and epigenetic memory over multiple generations, comparing them with naive cells. Whether the persister phenotype is reversible (non-genetic, plastic) or stably inherited (genetic or epigenetic) reveals the underlying mechanism and informs whether intermittent dosing or combination therapy could prevent survival.

title: Lineage-barcode analysis of pre-existing versus induced survivor states
description: Label individual clones with lentiviral barcodes, apply the drug, and use scRNA-seq to ask whether survivors come from a pre-existing, diverse set of transcriptional states or from a single clone. Compare survivor clone composition against the pre-treatment population to separate selection from induced switching.

title: Hazard analysis of single-cell death times
description: Track thousands of individual cells with a live death or proliferation reporter (e.g., FUCCI plus a caspase sensor) under constant drug, and model death times with Weibull or exponential hazard functions. A constant hazard suggests stochastic survival, while age-dependent or heritable hazards point to a memory-driven, pre-existing tolerant state.

title: Pulse-chase dye or histone-tag dilution to estimate persister state timescale
description: Pulse-label cells with a dilutable dye or histone tag, then apply the drug and measure how long labeled survivors persist and how their label dilutes. This estimates the timescale of the tolerant state, whether it is stable and heritable or transient and reversible, and the rate at which non-persisters convert into it.

title: Spatial mapping of persister niches
description: Use multiplexed spatial imaging (e.g., MERFISH or CODEX) on treated tumor sections or organoids to map where persister cells are located. Correlate their positions with local microenvironment features such as hypoxia, ECM stiffness, vasculature, and cell-cell contact. This tests whether survival is niche-dependent rather than cell-intrinsic.

title: System identification of the drug-response feedback network
description: Apply short drug pulses and collect time-resolved phosphoproteomics and transcriptomics at dense intervals. Fitting a network model to this response can reveal feedback loops or bistable switches that let a subset of cells remain in a low-signaling, drug-tolerant stable state, and can predict which perturbations would push survivors back out of it.

title: Lineage-barcoded scRNA-seq to test for pre-existing survivor transcriptional states
description: Label the parental line with a high-complexity lentiviral barcode library, then use scRNA-seq to profile barcoded cells before and early during drug exposure. Test whether survivor barcodes are enriched for pre-existing transcriptional states rather than being randomly distributed or induced by the drug.

title: Survival modeling of live single-cell reporters
description: Track individual cells under continuous drug with a live reporter combining cell-cycle (FUCCI) and stress-pathway biosensors, recording time to death. Fit Cox or frailty survival models against pre-treatment reporter levels and lineage history; a heavy-tailed hazard distribution would indicate a subpopulation with intrinsically lower hazard.

title: Early-warning signals of a drug-induced state transition
description: Collect time-series single-cell expression data during low-dose drug exposure and track rising variance and lag-1 autocorrelation of key transcripts (critical slowing down) as a predictor of a bistable switch into the persister state. Validate causally by perturbing noise (for example, pulsed drug or heat shock) and checking whether the persister fraction shifts accordingly.

title: Re-challenge assay for tolerance memory
description: Sort surviving cells, expand them drug-free for multiple passages, and then re-challenge with drug. Track whether tolerance decays (indicating reversible, epigenetically or transcriptionally maintained memory) or persists (suggesting a stable heritable state), and profile chromatin accessibility by ATAC-seq at each stage to map the regulatory basis of the memory.

title: Spatial mapping of persister niches in 3D tumor models
description: Combine multiplexed spatial imaging (MERFISH or CODEX) with a drug-penetration readout such as a fluorescent drug analog or mass-spectrometry imaging in spheroids or tumor sections. Test whether persisters cluster in low-drug, hypoxic, or cell-contact-protected regions, and whether their transcriptional state tracks the local microenvironment rather than an intrinsic property.

title: Label retention to test whether persisters are slow-cycling
description: Label cells with a dilution dye or histone-H2B reporter, then sort the slow-cycling, label-retaining fraction and challenge it with the drug. Compare survival and regrowth kinetics of label-retaining versus label-diluted cells to test whether persisters are quiescent and whether dormancy alone explains survival.

title: Pre-treatment state variability and survival prediction
description: Measure the spread of pre-treatment states (live-cell ERK/AKT kinase translocation reporters, cell-cycle reporters, and drug-efflux levels) across thousands of cells in each clone. If survivors come from the tail of a pre-existing distribution, baseline states should predict survival before drug exposure, which can be tested by sorting cells on those states prior to treatment.

title: Barcode-overlap (mark-recapture) estimation of founder lineage number in persisters
description: Transduce cells with a high-complexity lineage barcode library (e.g., LARRY-type), split into replicate arms, and compare barcode overlap among surviving persisters. Overlap statistics (Lincoln-Petersen estimator) estimate how many distinct founder lineages make up the persister pool and whether survival is stochastic and independent across replicates or concentrated in a few predetermined clones.

title: Drug-pulse, washout and re-challenge cycles with chromatin profiling
description: Apply drug pulses of varying length, withdraw the drug, and re-challenge over multiple cycles. Pair this with ATAC-seq and H3K27ac/H3K4me3 profiling at each step to test whether a surviving state carries epigenetic memory that persists after drug removal, and whether the memory is reset or retained across generations.

title: Pulse-chase label dilution and single-cell WGS of persister lineages
description: Pulse-label cells with a nucleotide analog such as EdU or BrdU at drug exposure. Track label dilution alongside clonal mutation accumulation using single-cell whole-genome sequencing. This shows when each surviving lineage diverged, whether survival came from a pre-existing subclone or a drug-induced transition, and how many divisions persisters undergo before regrowth.

title: Heritable lineage barcoding before and after treatment
description: Tag each founder cell with a heritable lineage barcode (e.g., CRISPR scar or lentiviral barcode) before treatment, then sequence barcodes in survivors. Comparing barcode frequencies before and after drug exposure shows whether persisters come from pre-existing clones or arise de novo, and how much of the survival is clone-specific.

title: Early-warning signals of entry into the persister state
description: During drug exposure, record live-cell ERK, AKT, and NF-κB translocation reporters together with cell-cycle reporters in single cells. Test whether rising variance and rising lag-1 autocorrelation (critical slowing down) in single-cell trajectories before the state shift predict which cells enter the persister state.

title: Decay and reset of drug tolerance after drug-free passaging
description: Sort survivors and culture them through repeated drug-free passages, re-challenging at each step with dose-response curves. The rate at which tolerance decays, and whether it is reset by a drug holiday, distinguishes a stable epigenetic memory from a transient, reversible stress state and from genetic resistance.

title: Pooled CRISPR screen under pulsed dosing with pooled-testing deconvolution
description: Run a genome-wide CRISPR knockout or activation screen under pulsed drug dosing and deconvolve guide enrichment in survivors using pooled-testing statistics. Genes whose perturbation reliably changes survival in the pooled design point to regulators of the persister state and can be validated individually.

title: Spatial mapping of survivor niches
description: Use multiplexed spatial transcriptomics or imaging to map where surviving cells sit relative to hypoxic zones, stromal or immune neighbors, and vasculature. Enrichment of survivors in particular niches, followed by niche-disruption experiments, would show whether the microenvironment, rather than intrinsic cell state, protects them.

title: Lineage barcoding with pre-treatment transcriptome profiling
description: Label each cell with a heritable lentiviral barcode, profile transcriptomes before drug exposure, and then sequence the survivors. If survivors were already enriched for particular pre-treatment states, the population contains stochastic state diversity that pre-exists drug; if not, the state is induced by the drug.

title: Per-cell time-to-death survival analysis
description: Run long-term live-cell imaging with FUCCI and caspase or ERK activity reporters, then fit Kaplan-Meier curves and frailty or mixture models to each cell's time-to-death. A survivor fraction with a near-zero, constant hazard indicates a distinct tolerant state, whereas a uniformly slowed hazard indicates a shared, graded response.

title: Persistence of drug-tolerant state after drug withdrawal
description: Apply a defined drug pulse, withdraw the drug, and track whether survivors retain their tolerant state across generations. Pair this with ATAC-seq and histone-mark pulse-chase reporters to measure how quickly the state relaxes and whether it depends on an epigenetic memory that persists after the stimulus is gone.

title: Spatial mapping of survivors in residual tumors
description: Use multiplexed spatial imaging (MERFISH or CODEX) on residual tumors from treated animals to map where survivors sit relative to vasculature, hypoxia, stromal interfaces, and immune niches. Spatial clustering of survivors in specific microenvironments would indicate that the microenvironment, not intrinsic cell identity, determines which cells survive.

title: Mutual-information biomarker screen with CRISPR validation
description: Measure single-cell pre-treatment features such as target-pathway activity, drug-efflux levels, and cell-cycle phase, and compute the mutual information between each feature and later survival. Then knock out the top-ranked genes in a pooled CRISPR screen under drug to test which features causally drive survival rather than merely correlating with it.

title: Hazard analysis of single-cell death times
description: Track individual cells by live imaging under constant drug and fit Weibull or other hazard models to their time-to-death. A shape parameter near 1 suggests random, state-independent survival, while a shape far from 1 points to survival governed by cell age, cycle phase, or an accumulating state.

title: Spatial point-pattern analysis of surviving colonies
description: Map the position of every surviving cell or colony on the culture and apply point-pattern and spatial autocorrelation statistics (e.g., Ripley's K, Moran's I). Clustering would implicate local microenvironment such as density, oxygen, or drug gradients, whereas a random scatter would support intrinsic stochastic survival.

title: Lineage-barcode and single-cell transcriptome reconstruction of persister ancestry
description: Combine CRISPR lineage barcodes with single-cell transcriptomes to reconstruct the lineage tree of surviving cells. Few early founder clades with pre-existing transcriptional states would suggest pre-selection, while many independent lineages converging on a shared state after treatment would suggest adaptive induction.

title: Mutual information between pre-treatment states and survival
description: Sort live cells by pre-treatment reporter or transcriptional state and quantify the mutual information between that state and eventual survival after drug exposure. Near-zero information would indicate survival is essentially random, while significant information would identify which features are predictive and how much of the outcome they explain.

title: Pulsed-dosing system identification of feedback in survivor cells
description: Apply pulsed or step drug inputs of varying amplitude and duration while recording live signaling reporters. Then estimate an input-output transfer function for each cell using control-engineering methods. Oscillatory responses, delayed responses, or bistable switching in the fitted model would indicate feedback loops or memory elements that let a subpopulation stay in a tolerant state.

title: Lineage barcode analysis of mean and variance of clone survival
description: Barcode thousands of genetically identical cells, then track each clone's survival across repeated drug pulses and drug holidays. Compare each clone's mean and variance in survival to separate stochastic bet-hedging (random variation in survival odds) from heritable, clone-specific tolerance.

title: Hazard-model analysis of time to death from live-cell reporters
description: Use live-cell imaging with fluorescent viability and cell-cycle reporters (e.g., FUCCI) to record each cell's time to death under drug. Fit hazard models (Weibull, mixture models) to test whether survivors are a memoryless stochastic subpopulation or a distinct, age-independent class with a lower hazard rate.

title: System identification of signaling dynamics
description: Use ERK or AKT translocation reporters to record pulsatile signaling in single cells, then fit transfer functions or feedback gain and damping parameters to each cell's response to a drug step input. Test whether survivors show systematically different feedback gains or response bandwidths before treatment, which would point to a dynamical rather than genetic basis for survival.

title: Time-resolved single-cell RNA and ATAC profiling of tolerance emergence
description: Sample cultures at many time points during the first days of drug exposure for single-cell RNA and ATAC profiling. Order the cells along a reconstructed trajectory to show when and how a tolerant state emerges, and whether it arises from a pre-existing population or develops progressively under treatment.

title: Phylogeny reconstruction with CRISPR lineage recorders
description: Use inheritable CRISPR-Cas9 lineage recorders to reconstruct the phylogeny of the cell population. Then test whether survivors cluster in particular clades (heritable, high-survival lineages) or are scattered across the tree (independent stochastic escapes), and sequence those clades for shared expression or copy-number features.

title: Clone-level variance analysis of pre-existing drug response
description: Treat each clone's drug response as having a mean and variance in growth rate. Combine DNA barcode lineage tracking with single-cell growth measurements before treatment. Then test whether survivors come from clones with high pre-treatment variance, or from random rare early-arising events, as in a Luria-Delbrück fluctuation process.

title: Classifier-based decoding of pre-treatment cell states
description: Record time-lapse fluorescent reporters (e.g., ERK activity, FUCCI cell cycle, NRF2) in untreated cells and train a classifier on the pre-drug state of each cell. Then index-sort cells by predicted survival, expose them to the drug, and sequence or profile the survivors to validate which pre-treatment features predicted tolerance.

title: Dye-dilution pulse-chase to infer survivor cell histories
description: Label cells with a division-tracking dye such as CFSE, then treat and measure the dye content of survivors by flow cytometry. Dim cells (dye diluted) indicate recent division, whereas bright cells (dye retained) indicate quiescence or slow cycling before treatment. This reveals whether tolerance is linked to a slow-cycling state.

title: Drug-withdrawal cycles to test epigenetic memory
description: Expose cells to the drug, withdraw it for several cycles, and track chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) and the repressive mark H3K27me3 (CUT&Tag) at each step. If tolerant cells keep an epigenetic state that persists after withdrawal and only slowly reverts, that memory would explain survival and could be targeted with epigenetic inhibitors.

title: Spatial mapping of survivors in tumor spheroids
description: Grow tumor spheroids or biopsy slices and use multiplexed spatial transcriptomics or imaging to map where survivors sit relative to oxygen, nutrient, and drug-penetration gradients. Survivors clustered in a particular location would point to environmental protection rather than an intrinsic cell property.

title: Weibull-type fitting of single-cell drug response
description: Expose many replicate wells of clonal cells to a range of drug doses and record each cell's time-to-death or death threshold by live imaging. Fit a Weibull or extreme-value distribution to these single-cell thresholds: a low shape parameter with a long tail would indicate that survival is set by a rare high-tolerance tail rather than by the population mean.

title: Retrospective tracing of survivors to pre-treatment state
description: Use fluorescent reporters or lineage barcodes to record each cell's state before treatment, then sort survivors and matched non-survivors and profile them by scRNA-seq or ATAC-seq. Comparing survivors back to their pre-treatment signatures identifies the pre-existing feature (for example, an efflux, stress, or chromatin state) that predicted survival.

title: 3D spatial mapping of survivor locations in spheroids or organoids
description: Grow tumor spheroids or organoids, treat them, and use multiplexed spatial imaging (e.g., MERFISH or imaging mass cytometry) to map where surviving cells sit relative to hypoxia, drug gradients, vasculature, or neighboring cell types. This tests whether survival clusters at specific microenvironmental locations rather than being randomly distributed.

title: Pre-treatment marker threshold calibration
